AI.conclusion: Offline policy-guided expert coordination enables robust deployment of biomedical AI under distribution shifts without retraining, by intelligently routing, calibrating, and adapting across heterogeneous experts; the approach is validated across multiple datasets and tasks and is publicly released.

title: Calibrated Partial Resets: Preventing Policy Collapse in Continual Reinforcement Learning
summary:
Neural networks are hindered by accumulating dormant neurons and loss of expressivity throughout training, particularly in non-stationary data settings, such as continual supervised and reinforcement learning. Recently, neuron resets have been used to maintain gradient flow and restore plasticity. However, full unit reinitialization often sacrifices peak performance and can destabilize training, leading to policy collapse.
  To preserve plasticity without destabilizing training, we propose Calibrated Partial Resets (CPR), an optimizer that periodically pulls low-utility neurons toward their initialization, with pull strength scaled by each neuron's utility. Unlike binary reset methods, partial resets avoid brittleness; unlike uniform decay, calibrated utility-scaling concentrates adjustment on the units that need it most.
  Among compared methods, only CPR avoids policy collapse over 400M training steps in SlipperyAnt, and it outperforms prior decay and reset-based methods on Continual MetaWorld and Continual MinAtar benchmarks. Ablations reveal a tunable trade-off between plasticity and peak performance, highlighting utility-scaled reinitialization as a promising direction for continual learning.

AI.tldr: Calibrated Partial Resets (CPR) optimize continual learning by selectively perturbing low-utility neurons toward initialization, scaled by per-neuron utility, to preserve plasticity and avoid destabilization; empirically improves continual RL benchmarks and mitigates policy collapse.
AI.motivation: Neurons may become dormant or lose expressivity during training, especially in non-stationary data (continual supervised and reinforcement learning). Full unit reinitialization can boost plasticity but harms peak performance and stability. CPR aims to maintain gradient flow while avoiding disruptive resets.
AI.method: Identify neuron utility, periodically apply partial resets to low-utility neurons, pulling them toward their initialization with strength scaled by utility. This contrasts with binary resets (discrete) and uniform decay (unscaled).
AI.result: CPR avoids policy collapse over 400M steps in SlipperyAnt and outperforms prior decay/reset methods on Continual MetaWorld and Continual MinAtar. Ablations show a tunable trade-off between plasticity and peak performance.
AI.conclusion: Utility-scaled partial reinitialization is a promising direction for continual learning, providing a controllable balance between plasticity and stability without sacrificing peak performance.

title: SGTP: Sampling-based Game-Theoretic Planning for Real-Time Multi-Vehicle Autonomous Racing
summary: Autonomous multi-vehicle racing requires real-time planning of diverse competitive behaviors in intense interactions. Existing planners often struggle to balance strategic diversity and computational efficiency. To address this challenge, we propose Sampling-based Game-Theoretic Planning (SGTP), a real-time framework that combines game-theoretic reasoning with GPU-accelerated sampling of control sequences and dynamics rollouts. Sampled trajectories are ranked using a game-aware cost to capture competitive interactions and generate diverse racing behaviors. Our planner then performs feasibility selection by explicitly enforcing track-boundary and dynamic collision-avoidance constraints, ensuring safe and reliable transitions between racing strategies. Extensive simulations on challenging tracks show that SGTP achieves a 95.24% win rate and a 99.35% task-completion ratio in highly interactive races, with a mean computational time of 0.095 s over multiple iterative solving steps. We also demonstrate the successful application of SGTP in large-scale scenarios with up to 10 agents. We release our code and provide an open-source benchmark of multi-agent autonomous racing algorithms to facilitate future research. Project page: https://sgtp-racing.github.io/.

AI.tldr: Introduces SGTP, a real-time sampling-based game-theoretic planner for autonomous racing that uses GPU-accelerated sampling, game-aware costs, and explicit feasibility checks to deliver diverse, safe racing strategies with high performance and scalability.
AI.motivation: Address the trade-off between strategic diversity and computational efficiency in competitive, multi-vehicle racing; enable safe real-time planning under intense interaction.
AI.method: Combine game-theoretic reasoning with GPU-accelerated sampling of control sequences and dynamic rollouts; rank trajectories using game-aware costs; enforce track boundary and dynamic collision-avoidance constraints for feasible policy transitions; scalable to up to 10 agents; provide open-source benchmark.
AI.result: Extensive simulations on challenging tracks show SGTP achieves 95.24% win rate and 99.35% task-completion, with mean planning time ~0.095 s per iteration; succeeds in large-scale scenarios with up to 10 agents; code release and benchmark.
AI.conclusion: SGTP delivers real-time, diverse, and safe multi-agent racing strategies with competitive performance and scalability; contributes a reusable framework and open benchmark to advance research.

title: Atmospheric Diffusion-Guided Spatio-Temporal Transformer for Nuclear Radiation Forecasting
summary: Nuclear radiation, the energy released during atomic decay, poses persistent risks to public health and the environment, and concerns have only grown since the Fukushima accident and the recent commencement of treated-water discharge. Modern monitoring networks now record radiation levels and accompanying weather conditions at thousands of stations, opening the door to nationwide forecasting that can inform emergency response, agricultural advisories, and routine public-safety decisions. However, turning this abundance of monitoring data into reliable forecasts is difficult for three reasons. First, the time series at each station are highly non-stationary, shaped by radioactive decay, weather variability, and irregular human interventions. Second, monitoring stations are severely unevenly distributed in space. Roughly 78% of Japan's stations sit in less than 6% of the country, clustered near Fukushima, which breaks the assumptions of standard graph-based models. Third, radiation co-evolves with heterogeneous context such as wind, temperature, and humidity through atmospheric transport processes that purely data-driven models struggle to capture from observations alone. In this study, we introduce NRFormer+, a spatio-temporal Transformer for nationwide nuclear radiation forecasting. NRFormer+ couples non-stationary temporal attention and density-adaptive spatial attention with a new atmospheric diffusion module that estimates how meteorology drives radiation dispersion and injects this physical signal into the network as an architectural prior. NRFormer+ delivers state-of-the-art accuracy on both datasets across all 13 baselines, reducing sudden-change MAE by up to 19.1% over the strongest baseline at comparable inference latency. Our code and datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/tfeilyu/NRFormer_Plus.

AI.tldr: NRFormer+ is a spatio-temporal Transformer for nationwide nuclear radiation forecasting that handles non-stationary time series, uneven station distribution, and atmospheric transport by integrating non-stationary temporal attention, density-adaptive spatial attention, and a physics-informed atmospheric diffusion module; it achieves state-of-the-art accuracy with up to 19.1% MAE improvement and shares code/datasets publicly.
AI.motivation: Forecasting nuclear radiation across a nationwide, unevenly distributed monitoring network is critical for emergency response, agriculture, and public safety. Challenges include non-stationary time series due to decay and weather, sparse/clustered stations, and radiation co-evolution with meteorology through atmospheric transport.
AI.method: Proposes NRFormer+, a spatio-temporal Transformer that combines: (1) non-stationary temporal attention to model evolving temporal dynamics; (2) density-adaptive spatial attention to handle uneven sensor distribution; (3) an atmospheric diffusion module that estimates dispersion driven by meteorology and injects this physical signal as an architectural prior to guide learning.
AI.result: The model achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on two datasets, across 13 baselines, with up to 19.1% reduction in sudden-change MAE at comparable inference latency; code and datasets are publicly available.
AI.conclusion: NRFormer+ effectively integrates data-driven temporal/spatial modeling with a physics-informed dispersion module to address non-stationarity, sparse/inhomogeneous sensor layouts, and atmospheric coupling, advancing nationwide radiation forecasting and enabling reproducibility through open resources.

title: LENS: Adaptive Spatio-Temporal Zooming for Keyframe Sampling in Long-Form Videos
comment: Accepted at ECCV 2026. Project page: https://zhangce01.github.io/LENS/
summary: Despite rapid progress in Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs), understanding long-form videos is still bottlenecked by limited context windows. While recent keyframe sampling methods attempt to mitigate this by distilling video inputs into a compact set of query-relevant frames, navigating the vast spatio-temporal search space remains challenging, as spatial detail and temporal coverage often conflict. To address this, we introduce LENS, a training-free keyframe sampling framework that dynamically decides when to zoom in for fine-grained details and when to zoom out for broader context based on the text query. Concretely, LENS adaptively allocates a limited frame budget between spatial zoom-ins, which highlight query-relevant regions within individual frames, and temporal zoom-outs, which expand the temporal scope through multi-frame aggregation, enabling the model to reason across multiple granularities while capturing both high-fidelity details and long-range context. Across diverse long-form video benchmarks, LENS consistently outperforms prior state-of-the-art keyframe sampling methods and delivers substantial gains over uniform sampling, improving Video-MME accuracy from 53.3% to 60.7% with Qwen2.5-VL.Code is available at https://github.com/zhangce01/LENS.

AI.tldr: Training-free keyframe sampling (LENS) that adaptively balances spatial zoom-in and temporal zoom-out to enhance long-form video understanding in MLLMs, achieving notable accuracy gains.
AI.motivation: Long-form video tasks are constrained by limited context windows; existing keyframe sampling reduces video to few frames but struggles to preserve both spatial details and temporal context; need a lightweight, query-driven approach that dynamically allocates a frame budget.
AI.method: LENS dynamically allocates a fixed frame budget between spatial zoom-ins (region-focused frames) and temporal zoom-outs (multi-frame aggregation) guided by the text query; training-free, no additional model training required; operates across frames to capture multi-granularity information.
AI.result: Outperforms prior state-of-the-art keyframe sampling across diverse long-form video benchmarks; gains over uniform sampling; Video-MME accuracy with Qwen2.5-VL improves from 53.3% to 60.7%; code released.
AI.conclusion: A practical, training-free sampling framework that improves long-form video reasoning by adapting spatial and temporal resolution to the query, enabling better multi-granularity reasoning with minimal overhead.

title: Conformal Cascade: Distribution-Free Accuracy Guarantees for Multi-Tier LLM Inference
summary: Large language model (LLM) cascades reduce inference cost by routing easy queries to a small model and deferring hard queries to a larger one. Production cascades govern this deferral through a confidence threshold, but LLM confidence scores are miscalibrated, the threshold must be tuned per model pair and per domain, and no setting yields a formal bound on cascade accuracy. We introduce \textbf{Conformal Cascade} (CC), a multi-tier inference framework that uses conformal prediction set size as the deferral rule: accept when the calibrated set collapses to a single answer, defer otherwise. The procedure delivers a distribution-free, finite-sample accuracy guarantee. By a per-tier union bound, the prediction set at the accepting tier covers the correct answer with probability at least $1 - Kα$ for any user-specified $α$; under a selection-preservation condition (consistent with, but not strictly implied by, our marginal coverage results), the bound tightens to $1 - α$. We further characterise expected cascade cost as an explicit function of $α$ and the calibration-set acceptance rate. Across 18 multiple-choice benchmarks spanning science, medicine, commonsense, and standardized exams, evaluated on two-tier cascades drawn from four open-weight model families, CC strictly improves over the strongest calibration-tuned heuristic cascade on the majority of family--benchmark pairs, with the largest gains on reasoning-heavy benchmarks where majority vote is unreliable; on easier benchmarks the cascade commits the vast majority of queries to the small model at no accuracy cost. Extension to open-ended generation requires an answer-clustering step that we leave for future work. The method requires no model training and only black-box API access.

AI.tldr: Conformal Cascade (CC) uses conformal prediction to govern when to defer from a small model to a large model in LLM cascades, providing distribution-free, finite-sample accuracy guarantees and improving over calibration-based baselines across 18 benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Alleviate inference cost in LLM cascades by robustly deciding deferral points without relying on poorly calibrated confidence scores; aim for formal guarantees on cascade accuracy.
AI.method: Treat each tier as a predictor with conformal prediction calibration; use the size of the calibrated prediction set to decide acceptance (single answer) vs deferral; derive a finite-sample bound via a per-tier union bound and a selection-preservation condition; analyze expected cascade cost as a function of α and acceptance rate; conduct two-tier cascades with four open-weight model families across 18 diverse benchmarks.
AI.result: CC achieves distribution-free accuracy guarantees; under per-tier union bound, correct answer covered with probability at least 1−Kα, tightening to 1−α under selection-preservation; outperforms the best calibration-tuned heuristic cascades on the majority of model-family pairs, especially on reasoning-heavy tasks; on easier tasks, it routes most queries to the small model without sacrificing accuracy; no training required and only black-box access.
AI.conclusion: Conformal Cascade provides a practical, theory-backed deferral mechanism for LLM cascades with finite-sample guarantees, improving over calibration-based methods; extension to open-ended generation is possible via answer clustering; relies on calibration data and assumes selection-preservation for tighter guarantees.

title: Decompose and Reorganize: Planning with Primitives and Visuomotor Policies Learned from Demonstrations
summary: Successfully automating dexterous, long-horizon robotic manipulation requires frameworks capable of both high-level reasoning and fine-grained execution. Traditional task and motion planning (TAMP), while excellent at symbolic planning, is often brittle in contact-rich operations. Simultaneously, imitation learning (IL), while effective in manipulation tasks with visual feedback, is limited by its low capability in spatial generalization and multi-stage operation. To reconcile their complementary strengths and limitations, we propose DR-LfD (Decomposed and Reorganized Skills Learned from Demonstrations), a framework that seamlessly integrates visuomotor policies into a TAMP-gated decision-making system. Based on contact relationships, DR-LfD decomposes human demonstrations into atomic skills, which are reproduced as visuomotor policies or object-centric primitives. The initiation, termination, and constraints of the visuomotor policies are carefully modeled and implemented in a TAMP-compatible form, enabling reorganization of skills learned from different sources. DR-LfD transforms the learning problem from one requiring exponential demonstration data over possible skill sequences to one whose demonstration burden scales with the number of distinct skill types, with limited data for each skill. Through comprehensive real-world and simulation benchmarking across diverse scenarios, we demonstrate the strong performance of DR-LfD on tasks involving multiple steps, unseen setups, and physical constraints. Project website: https://dr-lfd.github.io/DR-LfD-website.

AI.tldr: A DR-LfD framework decomposes demonstrations into atomic skills and integrates visuomotor policies with a TAMP-based planner, reducing data needs and enabling robust long-horizon manipulation.
AI.motivation: To combine the strengths of task and motion planning (planning robustness in contact-rich tasks) with imitation learning (data efficiency and perceptual feedback) for dexterous manipulation.
AI.method: Decompose demonstrations based on contact relationships into atomic skills; implement as visuomotor policies or object-centric primitives; model initiation, termination, and constraints in a TAMP-compatible form; allow reorganization of skills learned from different sources; scale demonstration burden with the number of skill types.
AI.result: Real-world and simulation benchmarks show strong performance on multi-step tasks, unseen setups, and physically constrained scenarios, with improved generalization and reduced data requirements.
AI.conclusion: DR-LfD provides a scalable framework that unifies visuomotor policies with TAMP, enabling robust, long-horizon manipulation across diverse environments.

title: Steering topology distributions for unified generative design of architected metamaterials
summary: Architected metamaterials derive their functions from structure, creating vast opportunities to program physical responses through topology design. However, existing design methods are often tailored to individual design problems, making limited use of topology knowledge for effective and broadly applicable design as objectives, constraints, and physical functions change. Here we introduce Generative Topology Optimization (GenTO), a unified framework that turns a learned topology prior into a reusable design engine. GenTO trains a diffusion model on a large full-order topology dataset and then iteratively steers the resulting topology distribution toward task-specific high-performing regions using user-defined physical objectives and constraints. This shifts the object of optimization from a single structure to a task-adapted topology distribution. Across topology design problems spanning thermal extremization, multi-objective morphology control, property-targeted auxetic design, and vibration transmission design, GenTO reuses pretrained topology priors for heterogeneous tasks, preserves structural diversity, and reaches high-performing solutions supported by numerical benchmarks and experimental validation. These results establish reusable topology knowledge as a unified principle for effective and scalable architected metamaterial design.

AI.tldr: GenTO introduces a diffusion-model–based framework that learns a topology prior from a large dataset and reuses it across diverse metamaterial design tasks, enabling task-adapted distributions that yield diverse, high-performance solutions.
AI.motivation: Current topology optimization methods are problem-specific and do not exploit transferable topology knowledge across tasks; a reusable prior could improve performance, diversity, and scalability across design objectives and constraints.
AI.method: Train a diffusion model on a large full-order topology dataset to learn a prior; for a given task, steer the topology distribution toward regions of high performance under user-defined objectives/constraints, effectively shifting optimization to a task-adapted distribution.
AI.result: Applied to thermal extremization, multi-objective morphology control, property-targeted auxetic design, and vibration transmission design; demonstrates reuse of pretrained priors, preserved diversity, and high-performing solutions validated numerically and experimentally.
AI.conclusion: Reusable topology knowledge via a learned prior provides a unified, scalable design principle for architected metamaterials, enabling broad applicability across design problems.

title: FIDAC: An Easy-to-use Pipeline to Extract and Interpret Interpersonal Distance From Video
summary: The distance between persons reveals significant information about their perception of each other. However, such information is not easily extractable and interpretable from video input. We developed an open-sourced library, Facial Interpersonal Distance Analysis and Coding (FIDAC) that transforms facial detection results into actionable data about location and interpersonal distance. This tool merges data from multiple open-source facial detection models, strategically compensating for gaps in any individual model. In addition, we include methods for more accurate tracking, such as a pipeline for human coding of the selection of faces and a benchmarking tool to reduce depth distortion. For next steps, we plan on building upon FIDAC by evaluating its effectiveness at measuring interpersonal distance at various depths and orientations while further integrating features of proxemic analysis such as synchrony into its software.

AI.tldr: FIDAC is an open-source library that converts facial detection outputs into actionable proximity data by fusing multiple detectors, with tracking and depth-bias reduction tools, aiming to enable measurement and analysis of interpersonal distance and proxemic synchrony.
AI.motivation: Understanding interpersonal distance yields social information but is difficult to extract from video; a transparent, reproducible tool is needed to quantify location and distance between people for proxemic analysis.
AI.method: Developed FIDAC to merge data from several open-source facial detectors, compensating for gaps by ensemble fusion; adds a pipeline for manual face selection coding and a benchmarking tool to mitigate depth distortion; designed for improved tracking and data quality.
AI.result: Description of a modular, open-source tool with detector fusion, tracking enhancements, and depth-distortion benchmarking; no empirical results reported in the abstract; emphasizes planned evaluations of depth/orientation and proxemic features.
AI.conclusion: Future work includes evaluating interpersonal distance measurement across different depths and orientations and integrating proxemic features such as synchrony into FIDAC.

title: Lantern: Conflict-Aware Gradient Blending for Physics-Guided Diffusion Models in Calorimeter Simulation
summary: Monte Carlo simulation of calorimeter showers is a principal bottleneck for the High-Luminosity LHC, and diffusion models have emerged as fast, high-fidelity surrogates. Their denoising objective is purely statistical, however: a model can minimize it while placing the physics wrong. Existing physics-informed generative methods cannot close this gap, because they assume a closed-form law, a governing PDE residual or a hard per-sample constraint, that a shower does not supply: no per-sample PDE governs a stochastic cascade, and energy conservation fixes only one scalar per shower. Standard metrics ignore the correlation structure across calorimeter layers and voxels, comparing showers only in a physics feature space. We address both gaps. We introduce the Correlation Frobenius Distance (CFD), a single normalized score for correlation fidelity at layer-wise and voxel-wise scales. We then encode the soft per-sample structure available in a shower as two physics-aware auxiliary losses: a variance-stabilized voxel residual loss grounded in counting statistics, and a graph Laplacian loss over the detector geometry. We combine both with denoising through GradBlend, which anchors the step magnitude to the denoising gradient while letting the auxiliary steer its direction, yielding Lantern, a physics-guided diffusion surrogate. On CaloChallenge Dataset 2, injecting the physics losses through task-symmetric rules such as PCGrad, GradNorm, IMTL-G, and ConFIG inflates FPD by 2-100x relative to denoising alone, whereas GradBlend admits the same signal without regression and, with the Laplacian loss, Lantern improves both FPD and CFD. Our ablation on the auxiliary loss scheduler shows that the voxel residual loss, whose gradient conflicts with denoising, requires a terminal denoising-only phase to preserve shower fidelity, whereas the non-conflicting Laplacian loss is insensitive to the schedule.

AI.tldr: Introduces Lantern, a physics-guided diffusion surrogate for calorimeter shower simulation, centered on a Correlation Frobenius Distance (CFD) metric to capture layer- and voxel-scale correlations. It adds two physics-aware auxiliary losses (variance-stabilized voxel residual loss and graph Laplacian loss) and uses GradBlend to anchor denoising steps while steering direction with physics cues. On CaloChallenge Dataset 2, naive physics-injection strategies inflate FPD, whereas Lantern improves both FPD and CFD; voxel loss requires a terminal denoising phase and Laplacian loss is schedule-insensitive.
AI.motivation: To overcome the mismatch between purely statistical denoising objectives and the stochastic, correlated nature of calorimeter showers, and to provide a correlation-aware evaluation metric (CFD) to guide physically faithful surrogate models beyond per-sample PDEs or hard constraints.
AI.method: Introduce CFD as a single normalized measure of correlation fidelity across layers and voxels. Propose two physics-aware auxiliary losses: (1) a variance-stabilized voxel residual loss grounded in counting statistics, (2) a graph Laplacian loss over the detector geometry. Integrate these via GradBlend into a diffusion surrogate named Lantern, which anchors step sizes to the denoising gradient while letting auxiliary losses steer direction. Compare with task-symmetric rules (PCGrad, GradNorm, IMTL-G, ConFIG) on CaloChallenge Dataset 2.
AI.result: For physics-informed losses, standard rule-based scheduling inflates FPD by 2–100x relative to denoising alone, while GradBlend preserves the signal. Lantern with Laplacian loss improves both FPD and CFD; voxel residual loss requires a terminal denoising phase due to gradient conflicts. Laplacian loss is schedule-insensitive.
AI.conclusion: CFD provides a robust, correlation-focused evaluation for calorimeter showers. Lantern demonstrates that physics-guided diffusion with carefully designed auxiliary losses can achieve better correlation fidelity without regressing the denoising objective, though some auxiliary losses require careful scheduling; non-conflicting Laplacian guidance proves robust across schedules.

title: Room-Mediated Co-occurrence for Zero-Shot Object-Centric Semantic Navigation via Frontier Scoring
summary: Zero-shot ObjectNav methods increasingly use vision-language priors, but direct object-object similarity in the latent space is often a weak proxy for spatial co-occurrence. We present an analytical, training-free semantic navigation pipeline that mediates object relationships through a compact room lexicon. Each object label is mapped to a CLIP-derived Room Probability Vector (RPV), and object-target co-occurrence is computed from RPV distribution overlap. These scores are projected onto a value map using geodesic flood-fill propagation (Fast Marching Method), with adaptive signal decay, and are used to rank frontiers by semantic score for navigation. Together, these components form an integrated, training-free, object-centric pipeline for open-vocabulary zero-shot navigation. Results show that our object-centric approach improves Success Rate (SR) and Success by weighted inverse Path Length (SPL) by a relative 3% and 1.3%, respectively, compared to image-holistic baselines on the HM3D dataset validation split, while preserving interpretability and open-vocabulary flexibility. Code is available at: uts-ri.github.io/RPV-SemNav.

AI.tldr: A training-free, open-vocabulary semantic navigation approach that uses CLIP-derived Room Probability Vectors (RPVs) to map object labels into room-level priors, computes object-target co-occurrence via RPV overlap, and propagates a value map with geodesic Fast Marching to rank frontiers for navigation.
AI.motivation: Mend the mismatch between latent object-object similarity and spatial co-occurrence in zero-shot navigation by leveraging interpretable room-level priors rather than learned joint embeddings.
AI.method: Map each object label to an RPV derived from CLIP. Compute object-target co-occurrence from distribution overlap of RPVs. Project these scores onto a value map via geodesic flood-fill propagation (Fast Marching Method) with adaptive signal decay. Rank frontiers by semantic score for navigation. Training-free, integrates object-centric priors for open-vocabulary navigation.
AI.result: Relative improvements of SR by 3% and SPL by 1.3% over image-holistic baselines on HM3D validation, while preserving interpretability and open-vocabulary flexibility. Code provided at the authors' site.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates that a compact, training-free semantic prior based on room-level semantics can enhance zero-shot ObjectNav, offering interpretable and scalable performance improvements and complementing vision-language models.

title: HOBA: Hierarchical On-Policy Bidding Agents for Adaptive Online Advertising
summary: Online advertising bidding systems typically deploy multiple offline-trained expert models (e.g., PID controllers, model predictive control, offline RL policies) but face two critical limitations: lack of online adaptability to non-stationary auction markets, and reliance on costly manual tuning of hyperparameters such as bid bounds and budget pacing constraints. We propose HOBA (Hierarchical On-policy Bidding Agents), a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework that decouples strategic reasoning, model selection, and bid execution across three time scales. At the high level, a large language model infers hyperparameters from contextual signals through a Think-Act-Observe-Reflect loop with historical experience retrieval. At the mid level, a SARSA agent dynamically selects among expert models, incorporating causal adjustment to eliminate selection bias. At the low level, a dynamic expert pool (PID, MPC, IQL, Decision Transformer) executes bids under high-level constraints. This design confines online learning to discrete expert selection rather than continuous bid optimization, significantly reducing exploration risk while maintaining adaptability. Experiments on the AuctionNet benchmark and a large-scale A/B test demonstrate consistent improvements over state-of-the-art baselines. In a large-scale online deployment, HOBA delivered substantial business value, achieving a +3.6\% increase in target cost, proving the effectiveness of our hierarchical multi-agent bidding paradigm.

AI.tldr: HOBA is a hierarchical RL framework for online bidding that decouples strategy, model selection, and bid execution across three time scales. It uses a large language model to infer hyperparameters at the top level via a Think-Act-Observe-Reflect loop with experience retrieval, a mid-level SARSA agent to select among expert bidding models with causal adjustment to remove selection bias, and a dynamic pool of bid-execution experts (PID, MPC, IQL, Decision Transformer) under high-level constraints. This design confines online learning to discrete model selection, reducing exploration risk while preserving adaptability. Demonstrations on AuctionNet and large-scale A/B testing show improvements over baselines, including a +3.6% increase in target cost in deployment.
AI.motivation: Address non-stationary auction markets and the high cost of manually tuning hyperparameters (e.g., bid bounds, budget pacing) in offline-trained expert bidding policies by introducing online adaptability and automated hyperparameter inference within a hierarchical framework.
AI.method: Three-tier architecture: (1) high level uses a large language model to infer hyperparameters from context through a Think-Act-Observe-Reflect loop with historical experience retrieval; (2) mid level uses a SARSA agent that dynamically selects among an ensemble of expert bidding models, applying causal adjustment to mitigate selection bias; (3) low level maintains a dynamic pool of bidding experts (PID, MPC, IQL, Decision Transformer) that execute bids under the high-level constraints. Online learning is restricted to discrete expert selection to reduce exploration risk.
AI.result: Empirical validation on the AuctionNet benchmark and a large-scale online A/B test show consistent improvements over state-of-the-art baselines. In a large deployment, HOBA achieved a +3.6% increase in target cost, indicating practical business value.
AI.conclusion: A hierarchical multi-agent bidding paradigm that confines online learning to expert selection can achieve robust online adaptability with reduced exploration risk, delivering measurable gains in both benchmark and real-world deployments.

title: OpenPVMapper: A Multi-source, Nationwide Database of Rooftop Photovoltaic Systems in France
summary: Rooftop photovoltaic (PV) systems account for the vast majority of PV grid connections, yet no open, comprehensive, installation-level dataset of these systems exists: public registries aggregate data only above a capacity threshold, and remote sensing-based detection efforts, while extensive, are typically confined to a single method, a limited geographic scope, or a single point in time. We introduce OpenPVMapper, a nationwide, multi-source database of rooftop PV installations in mainland France, built by aggregating and reconciling complementary sources: a deep learning-based detection pipeline deployed on nationwide aerial imagery, OpenStreetMap and a probabilistic building-level detection dataset. The resulting database contains 1,135,850 installations, totaling approximately 15.01~GWp of installed capacity, each documented with its provenance, detection method, and, where available, a manual validation flag. Manual review of a stratified sample of 1,862 installations places the database's overall precision at approximately 74--75\%, with corroboration across independent sources bringing a substantial, quantified precision gain. By aggregating independent sources rather than relying on any single detection method, OpenPVMapper reaches a level of confidence beyond what any one source could provide on its own, while remaining extensible to further sources as they become available. It is released under an open (CC-BY) license alongside the full source code used to build it.

AI.tldr: OpenPVMapper is a nationwide, multi-source open dataset of rooftop PV installations in France, combining DL-based imagery detection, OpenStreetMap, and probabilistic building-level data to produce 1.14M installations (~15 GWp).
AI.motivation: There is no open, installation-level rooftop PV dataset that aggregates multiple sources; existing registries have thresholds and remote-sensing methods are often limited in scope, time, or method.
AI.method: Integrates a deep-learning rooftop PV detection pipeline on nationwide aerial imagery with OpenStreetMap data and a probabilistic, building-level detection dataset; reconciles detections across sources; includes manual validation flags and a stratified precision evaluation on 1,862 samples.
AI.result: 1,135,850 installations totaling ~15.01 GWp; provenance and detection method documented; manual validation flag; precision ~74–75% with corroboration across sources; dataset released under CC-BY with open source code.
AI.conclusion: Multi-source aggregation yields higher confidence than any single method; dataset is extensible to additional sources and scalable for broader deployment studies; provides open, reproducible resource for PV deployment and capacity studies.

title: Score-Based Stabilization for Time-Dependent Problems
summary: We propose a score-based stabilization framework for numerical simulation of partial differential equations, in which a learned score model defines a stabilization operator applied to provisional numerical updates. This operator augments standard time-stepping schemes by enforcing structure and physical consistency through a correction that drives iterates toward the manifold of admissible states. We show that the stabilization operator acts as a contraction toward this manifold, yielding a correction mechanism with basin-conditional stability. Numerical experiments on Advection, Korteweg-de Vries (KdV), Nonlinear Schrodinger (NLS), and Burgers' equations demonstrate improved robustness, suppression of nonphysical instabilities, and preservation of qualitative dynamics.

AI.tldr: A score-based stabilization operator contracts updates toward the admissible-state manifold, enhancing robustness and preserving dynamics across several PDEs.
AI.motivation: Standard discretizations can exhibit nonphysical instabilities and drift from physical constraints; a data-driven mechanism is needed to enforce structure during time stepping.
AI.method: Introduce a learned score model that defines a stabilization operator applied to provisional updates. This operator is contractive toward the manifold of admissible states, providing basin-conditional stability and augmenting conventional time-stepping schemes.
AI.result: Numerical experiments on Advection, Korteweg–de Vries (KdV), Nonlinear Schrödinger (NLS), and Burgers equations show improved robustness, suppression of nonphysical instabilities, and preservation of qualitative dynamics.
AI.conclusion: A general, data-driven stabilization framework that enforces physical consistency during PDE time integration, with strong stability and qualitative-dynamics benefits across multiple nonlinear PDEs.

title: A Causality-aware Infer-diagnose-refine Framework for Test-time Modality Adaptation in VLA Models
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models predict sequential actions to execute tasks specified by language instructions, conditioned on visual observations and proprioceptive states. However, how to fuse modalities in VLA models remains an open problem, since robot manipulation involves dynamic phases, such as long-distance movements and close-range interactions, in which the importance of visual observations may vary over time. In this paper, we propose an infer-diagnose-refine (IDR) framework, a model-agnostic framework that can be integrated with diverse VLA architectures for refining action predictions at test time. IDR first infers actions under factual and counterfactual scenarios of visual observations, and then diagnoses the causal effects of visual observations as the estimated dynamic importance, which is finally used to refine the action predictions in a training-free manner. We further design a causality-aware action refiner to realize the IDR framework, including zero-padding interventions for inferring counterfactual actions, norm-based quantification for diagnosing causal effects, and gated residual fusion for refining actions. Extensive experiments on both simulation benchmarks and real-world tasks show improvements in overall performance across multiple VLA backbones, demonstrating the efficacy of dynamically adjusting visual importance at test time.

AI.tldr: IDR: a model-agnostic, test-time refinement framework for VLA models that infers and diagnoses the causal impact of visual observations to dynamically adjust action predictions.
AI.motivation: Fusion of modalities in vision-language-action (VLA) models is challenging due to dynamic phase-based visual importance; current models treat visual input statically, potentially misguiding actions during long-distance vs. close-range manipulation.
AI.method: Infer-Diagnose-Refine (IDR): at test time, infer actions under factual and counterfactual visual observations; diagnose the causal effect of visuals as dynamic importance; refine actions without retraining using a causality-aware refiner that employs zero-padding interventions, norm-based causal diagnostics, and gated residual fusion.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on simulation benchmarks and real-world tasks shows performance gains for multiple VLA backbones, indicating improved robustness by adjusting visual emphasis over time.
AI.conclusion: IDR demonstrates that test-time, model-agnostic refinement driven by causal analysis of visual inputs can enhance VLA performance, supporting dynamic attention to visuals across task phases.

title: LivingArena: Do LLMs Know What Other LLMs Don't? Peer-Probing as Scalable Evaluation
summary: Evaluating frontier LLMs is challenging: static benchmarks suffer from contamination and saturation -- leaving users unable to distinguish top models and developers blind to specific failure modes -- while human preference is subjective. In this paper, our question is: \emph{Do LLMs know what other LLMs don't? And can we leverage this dynamic for evaluation?} We present \textbf{LivingArena}, an automated, contamination-resistant evaluation framework. In this framework, models take turns proposing questions, aiming to pose items that opponents cannot answer correctly. Questioners are encouraged to actively identify and exploit opponents' knowledge boundaries, receiving rewards when the answerer fails, while the answerer is rewarded otherwise. To ensure questions contain objectively verifiable answers, a judge panel of strong models validates them, penalizing questioners if validation fails. Evaluating ten frontier LLMs, LivingArena yields a stable Elo leaderboard. Our behavioral analyses show that models identify and exploit their peers' cognitive boundaries: self-play and tournament logs indicate that they localize and double down on opponents' weak dimensions. Beyond static knowledge recall, peer probing measures factual rigor and the higher-order ability to probe an opponent's weaknesses, correlating only weakly with human preference and offering a scalable, low-cost approach to continuous evaluation.

AI.tldr: A dynamic, contamination-resistant evaluation framework (LivingArena) where LLMs propose questions to probe peers, judged by strong models, yielding an Elo leaderboard; reveals that models exploit peers' weaknesses and provides scalable, low-cost evaluation that correlates weakly with human preferences.
AI.motivation: Address core shortcomings of static benchmarks (contamination, saturation) and the subjectivity of human preferences by leveraging peer awareness among frontier LLMs to surface specific, verifiable weaknesses.
AI.method: Iterative self-play where a questioner proposes items aimed at exposing opponents’ gaps; rewards for successful exploitation and for accurate challenge; a judge panel of strong models validates questions and penalties for invalidations; evaluated on ten frontier LLMs; outputs an Elo-style ranking and activity logs.
AI.result: LivingArena produces a stable Elo leaderboard; models effectively identify and exploit peers’ cognitive boundaries; peer probing measures align weakly with human preferences but offer scalable, low-cost evaluation for continuous monitoring.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic, peer-aware evaluation complements static benchmarks and human judgments by capturing higher-order weaknesses and factual rigor, enabling scalable, contamination-resistant assessment of frontier LLMs.

title: OrganLens: Organ-Specific Representation Learning for CT Foundation Models
summary: A CT examination captures multiple organs, but many biomedical questions concern abnormalities, prognosis, or longitudinal change in a specific organ. These questions require a separate representation for each organ within the same CT volume. Existing CT foundation models commonly produce a single volume-level representation, while recent anatomy-aware methods either encode pre-separated organ volumes or explicitly disentangle images into organ token groups. The former may remove clinically relevant surrounding context, while the latter does not condition a shared encoder on a selected organ before its features are formed. We introduce OrganLens for organ-specific representation learning through self-supervision. An organ identity conditions a shared CT encoder, while organ-specific distillation and anatomy-mask supervision shape features for anatomy-weighted pooling into organ-specific representations. At inference, the shared model produces 11 organ-specific representations without external segmentation masks. We evaluate OrganLens on CT-RATE, RAD-ChestCT, INSPECT, and NLST across diverse acquisitions and downstream evaluations. Relative to CT-pretrained DINOv2, heart representations raise CT-RATE cardiomegaly AUROC from 0.910 to 0.953, while lung representations improve the Harrell C-index for NLST lung-cancer mortality by 14.2\%. The global representation reaches INSPECT Recall@10 of 33.09\% and 32.04\% for text-to-image and image-to-text retrieval, respectively. Across organ-related tasks, anatomically matched representations provide stronger task-relevant signal, while the global representation retains broad utility. OrganLens offers a scalable approach to organ-specific CT representation learning with a shared encoder. More broadly, it provides the medical research community with a reusable framework for studying organ-specific disease across cohorts and clinical endpoints.

AI.tldr: OrganLens learns 11 organ-specific representations from a single CT encoder by conditioning the encoder on organ identity with organ-specific distillation and anatomy-mask supervision, enabling organ-focused downstream tasks without external segmentation; achieves stronger organ-specific signals and retains a useful global representation across cohorts and endpoints.
AI.motivation: CT questions often target abnormalities, prognosis, or longitudinal change in a specific organ, requiring organ-specific representations. Existing methods either require pre-separated organ volumes (risking loss of contextual information) or disentangle tokens without conditioning a shared encoder on the target organ, limiting performance and scalability.
AI.method: A shared CT encoder is conditioned by organ identity. Organ-specific distillation and anatomy-mask supervision shape features to produce anatomy-weighted pooling into organ-specific representations. At inference, 11 organ representations are produced without external segmentation masks. Trained and evaluated on multiple CT datasets (CT-RATE, RAD-ChestCT, INSPECT, NLST).
AI.result: Compared with CT-pretrained DINOv2, heart representation boosts CT-RATE cardiomegaly AUROC from 0.910 to 0.953; lung representation improves NLST lung-cancer mortality Harrell C-index by 14.2%. The global representation achieves INSPECT Recall@10 of 33.09% (text-to-image) and 32.04% (image-to-text). Across organ tasks, anatomically matched representations provide stronger task-relevant signals, while the global representation maintains broad utility.
AI.conclusion: OrganLens provides a scalable framework for organ-specific CT representation learning with a shared encoder, enabling organ-specific disease study across cohorts and endpoints while maintaining a generalizable global representation.

title: Semantic Space Search Trajectory Networks
comment: 18 pages, 12 figures, submitted to EA 2026: 17th Biennal International Conference on Artificial Evolution
summary: Search Trajectory Networks (STNs) are a graph-based tool for visualizing and characterizing the behavior of optimization algorithms. STNs' reliance on discretization of the search space has largely confined them to low-dimensional or combinatorial settings. We introduce a methodology for constructing STNs in semantic spaces, defined as the space of a model's predictions on a fixed sample set. Our approach discretizes semantic vectors and aggregates them into network nodes via agglomerative clustering with complete linkage under a normalized Hamming distance. Since any predictor can be summarized by its semantic vector, this method enables comparison of learning dynamics across otherwise incomparable algorithm families. We apply semantic space STNs to classification and regression tasks solved using different machine learning algorithms, recovering known qualitative differences between them. Additionally, we use semantic space STNs to study neural network generalization by contrasting standard training with the label randomization regime of Zhang et al. (2017). The resulting STNs exhibit consistent structural differences, training on real labels produces denser, more efficient and more centralized graphs than training on shuffled labels. Together, our results show that semantic space STNs capture functional training dynamics arising from the interaction between learning algorithms and data, providing a tool for analyzing and comparing learning dynamics across machine learning models and training regimes.

AI.tldr: Semantic-space STNs enable cross-model comparison of learning dynamics by clustering semantic predictions; applied to classification/regression and label-randomization; reveal systematic differences in training dynamics and generalization.
AI.motivation: Overcome discretization limitations of traditional STNs by operating in semantic space defined by model predictions on a fixed sample, enabling comparison across diverse algorithms.
AI.method: Construct STNs by discretizing semantic vectors and aggregating into nodes via agglomerative clustering (complete linkage) using normalized Hamming distance; compare learning dynamics across algorithm families on classification and regression tasks; analyze neural network generalization under label randomization (Zhang et al. 2017).
AI.result: Semantic-space STNs recover known qualitative differences between learning algorithms; under real vs randomized labels, STNs differ in density, efficiency, and centrality; demonstrate consistent structural differences across tasks.
AI.conclusion: Semantic-space STNs capture training dynamics arising from the interaction between learning algorithms and data and provide a practical tool for comparing learning dynamics across models and training regimes.

title: P3: Probabilistic Policy Propagation for Stable VAE-Based Robot Learning
summary: Variational Autoencoders are widely used to encode high-dimensional and noisy observations in robotics. However, their stochastic latent creates a mismatch with Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO): an effective policy marginalizes over the latent distribution, whereas former implementations estimate its probability ratio and KL divergence using only one latent sample. We identify a fundamental but overlooked theoretical cause: naive single-sample approximations in stochastic latent space induce significant variance and bias in the surrogate loss. To address this, we introduce P^3 (Probabilistic Policy Propagation), a distribution-aware optimization framework for VAE-based policies. $P^3$ couples moment-based probabilistic method for stable and efficient learning with sampling-based calibration for robust policy behavior under latent uncertainty. In our experiments, P^3 boosts data efficiency from 64.6% to >96%, reduces convergence steps by >20%. Furthermore, P^3 is evaluated on challenging humanoid parkour tasks and shows an effective foundation for VAE-based PPO. Code is available at https://github.com/ylyem9x/P3_Open.

AI.tldr: P^3 (Probabilistic Policy Propagation) introduces a distribution-aware optimization framework for VAE-based policies within PPO. It addresses high variance and bias from single-sample latent estimates by combining a moment-based probabilistic method with sampling-based calibration, improving data efficiency and convergence on complex tasks.
AI.motivation: Naive single-sample approximations in stochastic latent spaces of VAE-based policies create large variance and bias in PPO surrogate losses, hindering data efficiency and robust policy learning under latent uncertainty.
AI.method: Integrates a moment-based probabilistic approach with sampling-based calibration to propagate latent uncertainty through the PPO objective, yielding a distribution-aware optimization for VAE-based policies (P^3).
AI.result: Significant improvements in data efficiency (from 64.6% to >96%), faster convergence (reducing steps by >20%), and effective performance on challenging humanoid parkour tasks; code released.
AI.conclusion: P^3 provides a solid foundation for VAE-based PPO by mitigating latent-space inference issues, offering robust, data-efficient learning under stochastic latent representations.

title: Personalization, Personas, and Forecasting in Value Alignment
summary: LLM behavior may be conditioned by human identity in several ways: they may be asked to adapt to users, role-play populations, or forecast how people would answer value-laden questions. We test whether these framings are interchangeable using the World Values Survey (WVS). We evaluate GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 2.5 Flash, and Qwen3-235B on 101 WVS-derived questions across 13 language-country slices, comparing a language-only baseline with user-country, persona-country, and third-person prompts. Across 21,008 model-response rows, prompt framing is a first-order determinant of cultural alignment: country cues often shift answers substantially, but not all shifts move toward matched human response distributions. Third-person forecasting yields the strongest directional alignment for three of the four hosted models, while personalization and role-play are weaker or less stable. Alignment gains concentrate on salient value dimensions such as religiosity, gender roles, and work-oriented material values, whereas institutional trust and democracy-related questions remain difficult. These results show that prompt framing is not a cosmetic choice in cultural value elicitation; it changes both model behavior and measured alignment.

AI.tldr: Prompt framing substantially alters LLMs' alignment with cultural value distributions; third-person forecasting often yields strongest directional alignment across models, while personalization and role-play are less stable. Effects concentrate on salient values (religiosity, gender roles, work values); trust and democracy topics remain challenging.
AI.motivation: Investigate whether different identity-based framings (user-country, persona-country, third-person) are interchangeable for eliciting cultural values from LLMs and how they compare to a language-only baseline, using World Values Survey data as a benchmark.
AI.method: Evaluate four LLMs (GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Qwen3-235B) on 101 WVS-derived questions across 13 language-country slices; compare language-only baseline against prompts: user-country, persona-country, and third-person; analyze 21,008 model-response rows for alignment and shifts.
AI.result: Country cues cause substantial shifts in answers; not all shifts align with human distributions. Third-person forecasting yields the strongest directional alignment for three of the four models; personalization and role-play show weaker or unstable effects. Alignment gains concentrate on religiosity, gender roles, and work-valued dimensions; institutional trust and democracy questions remain difficult to align.
AI.conclusion: Prompt framing significantly shapes model behavior and measured cultural alignment, not just cosmetic variation; careful framing is essential in studies of AI–cultural value elicitation, with model- and domain-specific differences in how alignment manifests.

title: LGFNet: A CTC-Guided Local-Global Fusion Framework for Single-Channel Sleep Staging
summary: Sleep staging remains challenging due to long-range temporal dependencies, ambiguous stage transitions-particularly in N1-and substantial distribution shifts across subjects, sampling rates, and EEG montages. These difficulties are further amplified in single-channel, low-latency scenarios required by wearable and real-world applications. To address these issues, we propose LGFNet, a CTC-guided sequence-to-sequence framework for robust sleep staging. LGFNet introduces a Local-Global Fusion encoder that jointly models fine-grained temporal dynamics and long-range sleep structure, overcoming the limitations of conventional serial hybrid architectures. A CTC-Attention joint training paradigm is adopted to unify temporal alignment with context-dependent modeling, enabling more accurate recognition of stage boundaries and transitions. Furthermore, a three-stage decoding strategy is devised, leveraging CTC-guided decoding and Viterbi-based smoothing to reduce error accumulation and enforce physiological consistency. Extensive cross-dataset evaluations on five public benchmarks demonstrate that LGFNet consistently outperforms state-of-the-art single-channel methods. In particular, on Sleep-EDF-78, LGFNet surpasses DMIN by +1.27% accuracy, +1.74% macro-F1, and +1.93% kappa, with pronounced gains on N1 and transition segments, highlighting its robustness and strong generalization across diverse sampling rates, montages, and recording environments.

AI.tldr: Proposes LGFNet, a CTC-guided seq-to-seq framework with Local-Global Fusion encoding and three-stage decoding for robust single-channel sleep staging; achieves state-of-the-art results across five benchmarks, notably on N1 and transitions.
AI.motivation: Sleep staging suffers from long-range dependencies, ambiguous stage transitions (especially N1), and cross-subject/distribution shifts across sampling rates and montages. Single-channel, low-latency requirements in wearables demand robust, generalizable models.
AI.method: Local-Global Fusion encoder jointly models fine-grained temporal dynamics and long-range sleep structure; CTC-Attention joint training to align sequence and context; three-stage decoding with CTC-guided decoding and Viterbi-based smoothing to reduce error accumulation and enforce physiological consistency; cross-dataset evaluation on five public benchmarks.
AI.result: LGFNet consistently outperforms state-of-the-art single-channel methods across five public datasets. On Sleep-EDF-78, it surpasses DMIN by +1.27% accuracy, +1.74% macro-F1, and +1.93% kappa, with pronounced gains on N1 and transition segments, indicating strong generalization across sampling rates, montages, and recording environments.
AI.conclusion: LGFNet delivers robust, generalizable single-channel sleep staging with improved boundary/transition recognition, enabling effective wearable and real-world applications.

title: Endpoint Replay: Compressing the Recency Buffer in Deep Reinforcement Learning
comment: Accepted at the Reinforcement Learning Conference (RLC) 2026, to appear in the Reinforcement Learning Journal (RLJ)
summary: Experience replay remains one of the most practical and useful algorithmic tools in the deep reinforcement learning (DRL) toolbox. Aside from the limited success of prioritized replay and specialized approaches for large asynchronous systems, most DRL algorithms make use of a large, uniformly sampled recency buffer---even the size, one million, remains unchanged. Could we store less data, reduce redundancy, or more effectively chain experience together to speed up value propagation and still retain the performance of large buffers? In this paper, we investigate a simple compression approach that stores representative transitions derived from the end-points of a chain of connected $n$-step sequences. By curating these end-points in a smaller recency buffer, our method maintains an effective memory horizon comparable to a standard large buffer while requiring an order of magnitude less storage. Through empirical evaluation, we demonstrate that this approach prevents the systematic bias inherent in naive compression strategies and matches the performance of traditional large buffers in the Pinball environment and the Atari 2600 benchmark.

AI.tldr: Compress experience replay by storing endpoints of n-step sequences in a small buffer, preserving memory horizon while reducing storage by an order of magnitude.
AI.motivation: Reduce storage and redundancy in experience replay without sacrificing performance, addressing the inefficiency of large uniform buffers in DRL.
AI.method: Represent transitions as endpoints of chains of n-step sequences and store these end-points in a smaller recency buffer to maintain effective memory horizon comparable to large buffers, avoiding naive compression biases.
AI.result: Empirically, this endpoint-based compression prevents the systematic bias of naive compression and matches the performance of big replay buffers on Pinball and Atari 2600 tasks.
AI.conclusion: Endpoint-based, end-point compression offers a storage-efficient replay strategy that preserves performance, providing a practical alternative to large uniform buffers in DRL.

title: When Does Legacy Data Start to Help? Emergent Transfer in Cross-Configuration Robot Learning
summary: Robotic hardware evolves over time, but demonstration data is often tied to a specific sensor and actuator configuration. This raises a practical and underexplored question: when does legacy data begin to benefit an upgraded robot? We study this question on a wheeled humanoid platform across two hardware generations, where both the camera and gripper are changed while the overall morphology remains fixed. Contrary to the common assumption that more cross-configuration data is always helpful, we observe a grokking-like transition: legacy data remains ineffective until the upgraded configuration acquires a minimum level of task competence, after which co-training gains rise sharply before diminishing near saturation. We hypothesize that this task-dependent transition is governed by a transfer threshold and characterize the resulting three-phase pattern. Across real-robot manipulation tasks, we observe all three phases: no measurable benefit at low competence ($10.0\% \rightarrow 10.0\%$), a sharp gain after crossing the threshold ($23.3\% \rightarrow 86.7\%$ on flower insertion), and diminishing returns at high competence ($85.0\% \rightarrow 93.3\%$ on pen insertion). We provide a theoretical account based on gradient alignment and residual policy uncertainty, and derive a phase-aware rule for deciding when to collect more new-hardware data and when to reuse legacy demonstrations. We further validate this three-phase pattern on a mobile dual-arm watering task, with results consistent with our predictions.

AI.tldr: Legacy demonstration data only helps upgraded robots after crossing a transfer threshold; a three-phase transfer pattern emerges across hardware changes, explained by gradient alignment and residual policy uncertainty, yielding a phase-aware guide for data collection.
AI.motivation: Address the practical question of when legacy demonstrations from an older hardware configuration are beneficial for a robot with upgraded sensors/actuators, given fixed morphology.
AI.method: Empirical study on a wheeled humanoid platform across two hardware generations with changes to camera and gripper while morphology remains fixed; real-robot manipulation tasks (flower insertion, pen insertion) used to observe transfer phases; co-training of legacy and new data; theoretical analysis based on gradient alignment and residual policy uncertainty; derivation of a phase-aware data collection rule; additional validation on a mobile dual-arm watering task.
AI.result: Three-phase pattern observed: no measurable benefit at low competence (e.g., 10.0% to 10.0%), a sharp gain after crossing the transfer threshold (23.3% to 86.7% on flower insertion), and diminishing returns at high competence (85.0% to 93.3% on pen insertion); results replicated across tasks including mobile dual-arm watering; theoretical account and rule validated.
AI.conclusion: There exists a transfer threshold that governs when legacy data is beneficial for an upgraded robot; a phase-aware strategy can decide when to collect new hardware data versus reuse legacy demonstrations, improving data efficiency in cross-configuration transfer.

title: Unified Semantic Modeling Framework for Large-Scale Job Understanding at LinkedIn
summary: Job understanding is critical to LinkedIn's mission of connecting talent with opportunity. This task involves transforming unstructured and noisy job postings into standardized or derived job attributes that power numerous LinkedIn products. However, building a scalable, cost-efficient, and high-performing job understanding system remains challenging. In this paper, we present a unified semantic modeling framework powered by a small language model (SLM) to address the challenges. We begin by fine-tuning an open-source SLM using a suite of carefully curated synthetic tasks augmented with reasoning traces. These tasks jointly target taxonomy-guided classification and taxonomy-agnostic entity extraction. This allows the resulting model to acquire robust zero-shot generalization for job understanding in structured and unstructured contexts. Building upon this foundation, we introduce a multi-adapter architecture with attribute grouping to facilitate efficient task-specific adaptation while streamlining model management across diverse downstream attributes. Offline evaluations and online A/B tests demonstrate significant performance improvement while reducing operational complexity. Our work provides practical insights into building industry-scale text understanding systems.

AI.tldr: A unified semantic modeling framework that fine-tunes a small language model on synthetic tasks for robust zero-shot job understanding, paired with a multi-adapter architecture for efficient task adaptation; shows improved performance and reduced complexity in industry-scale settings.
AI.motivation: Transform noisy, unstructured job postings into standardized attributes to power LinkedIn products, addressing scalability, cost, and performance challenges.
AI.method: Fine-tune an open-source SLM on curated synthetic tasks with reasoning traces targeting taxonomy-guided classification and taxonomy-agnostic entity extraction; introduce a multi-adapter architecture with attribute grouping for efficient task-specific adaptation and streamlined model management; evaluate offline and via online A/B tests.
AI.result: Offline evaluations and online A/B tests show significant performance gains and reduced operational complexity.
AI.conclusion: Provides practical insights for building scalable, high-performing, industry-scale text understanding systems.

title: ObliCity: A Benchmark and Baseline for Roof-to-Ground Projection Displacement Correction
summary: Oblique-view urban remote sensing imagery inevitably exhibits geometric projection displacements between building roofs and footprints, leading to significant distortions in spatial structure. Existing approaches either ignore these deformations or handle them implicitly within segmentation-based frameworks, where progress is dominated by general segmentation advances rather than improvements in geometric correction. In this work, we explicitly define roof-to-footprint offset vector (RFOV) extraction as an independent learning task that decouples geometric alignment from semantic segmentation. To support this task, we introduce the Oblique City dataset (ObliCity), the first large-scale benchmark that integrates high-resolution UAV imagery and globally distributed satellite data, covering diverse city morphologies and camera perspectives. Methodologically, we reformulate DragOSM into DragRoof, an ODE-based framework inspired by human annotation behavior. By simulating the continuous process of dragging roofs toward their footprints, DragRoof learns deterministic, geometry-consistent offset fields and adaptively determines convergence through an end token. Extensive experiments on ObliCity demonstrate that DragRoof achieves state-of-the-art RFOV extraction performance, requiring fewer inference steps while delivering superior directional and length accuracy. Our dataset and model establish a principled foundation for studying projection displacement correction in oblique remote sensing imagery. The source code and dataset will be avaliable at https://github.com/likaiucas/DragRoof.

AI.tldr: Defines roof-to-footprint offset vector (RFOV) extraction as an independent task for oblique-view imagery, introduces the ObliCity dataset, and presents DragRoof (an ODE-based method) that achieves accurate, efficient RFOV estimation with fewer inference steps.
AI.motivation: Oblique remote sensing images exhibit projection displacements between roofs and footprints that distort spatial structure. Existing methods either ignore these deformations or embed them within segmentation, hindering geometric correction progress. An explicit RFOV task is needed to decouple geometry from semantics.
AI.method: Propose RFOV extraction as a standalone task; construct ObliCity, a large-scale dataset combining high-res UAV and global satellite imagery. Reformulate DragOSM into DragRoof, an ODE-based framework that simulates the continuous process of dragging roofs toward their footprints, learning deterministic, geometry-consistent offset fields and using an end token to adaptively determine convergence.
AI.result: On ObliCity, DragRoof achieves state-of-the-art RFOV extraction accuracy, requires fewer inference steps, and delivers superior directional and length accuracy compared to baselines.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a principled foundation for projection displacement correction in oblique remote sensing imagery via an explicit RFOV task and a dedicated dataset/model; code and data will be released to facilitate further research.

title: Interpretable GOHR Agents via Sparse Autoencoders
summary: A central challenge in interpreting learned decision-making systems is to determine whether their internal representations contain concepts that help explain their behavior. We report interpretability experiments for a tokenized autoregressive Transformer agent in the Game of Hidden Rules (GOHR). We focus on a compact two-rule task in which both hidden rules map object shapes to target buckets, but with different permutations. The policy is trained on episodes sampled from these two hidden rules and then evaluated with fixed weights. It is never given a rule label and does not use an explicit rule classifier; any rule information must be inferred implicitly from interaction history. In this setting, the correct rule is not identifiable before the agent tries an informative move and observes accept/reject feedback. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) trained on the agent's decision-token embeddings recover this structure. When held-out decisions are labeled by simple concepts such as the chosen shape or bucket, SAE dimensions that are highly selective for a concept cover most decisions where that concept is present. Individual SAE dimensions also correspond to interpretable strategies such as probing one rule hypothesis and switching after negative feedback.

AI.tldr: Sparse autoencoders reveal interpretable latent structure in a tokenized Transformer agent trained on a two-rule GOHR task; SAE dimensions align with concepts and strategies about hidden rules, enabling decoding of decision behavior without explicit rule labels.
AI.motivation: To understand whether learned representations encode concept-level explanations for behavior in decision systems, by examining internal token embeddings in a rule-learning environment where the rule is hidden and inferred only through feedback.
AI.method: Train a Transformer agent on GOHR with two hidden rules mapping shapes to target buckets (different permutations), no rule labels. After training, fix weights and analyze decision-token embeddings with sparse autoencoders (SAEs). Label some decisions by simple concepts (shape, bucket) to test selectivity; examine learned dimensions for concept selectivity and interpretability as strategies like testing a rule hypothesis and switching on negative feedback.
AI.result: SAEs recover the latent structure corresponding to the hidden rules; SAE dimensions that are highly selective for a concept cover most decisions involving that concept; some dimensions correspond to interpretable strategies (probe one rule, switch after negative feedback).
AI.conclusion: Internal representations in the Transformer encode concept-level information aligned with the hidden rules, and SAEs can extract interpretable factors corresponding to these concepts and decision strategies, suggesting that interpretability of learned policies can be achieved by posthoc latent-factor analysis.

title: Shared Voxel-Map-Based Cooperative Indoor UAV Guidance with a Multi-Agent Soft Actor-Critic Controller
summary: This paper presents a cooperative indoor UAV guidance framework that combines a shared voxel-map world model with a multi-agent Soft Actor-Critic (MASAC) controller. Multiple drones fuse 360 LiDAR observations into a common world-frame occupancy map, which is converted into a compact bird's-eye-view (BEV) representation and provided to each agent as an ego-aligned local crop. This integrate-in-world, act-in- ego design enables consistent multi-UAV spatial fusion whilst retaining decentralised continuous control. The policy combines BEV map features, near-field obstacle observations, and compact goal and peer-state information within a centralised-training, decentralised-execution framework. In simulation, the learned controller achieves a 90.3% success rate in corridor navigation, outperforming Astar planning, an artificial potential field controller, and a prior guidance method. To address residual sim-to-real mismatch, the simulation-trained policy is further adapted using offline imitation fine-tuning from real-world data. Real-world experiments in GNSS-denied indoor environments demonstrate stable two-UAV cooperative operation across increasingly chal- lenging obstacle layouts. The results show that shared voxel-map representations provide an effective and scalable spatial substrate for learned cooperative indoor UAV guidance.

AI.tldr: A cooperative indoor UAV framework fuses 360 LiDAR into a shared voxel map, converts to BEV crops, and uses MASAC under a centralized-training/decentralized-execution regime for scalable multi-UAV coordination; achieves high simulated success (90.3%) and robust real-world GNSS-denied operation after offline imitation fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Enable robust, scalable, cooperative indoor UAV navigation in GNSS-denied environments by fusing perception into a shared world-model and employing a centralised-training, decentralised-execution policy that coordinates multiple agents.
AI.method: Fuse 360 LiDAR into a common voxel occupancy map; convert to BEV, provide ego-aligned local crops to each agent; apply a multi-agent Soft Actor-Critic (MASAC) within a CTDE framework, utilizing BEV features, near-field obstacles, goal and peer-state; train in simulation and perform offline imitation fine-tuning with real data to mitigate sim-to-real gap; validate with real indoor experiments in GNSS-denied settings.
AI.result: Simulation achieves 90.3% success in corridor navigation, outperforming A* planning, artificial potential field controllers, and a prior method; real-world experiments show stable two-UAV cooperation across challenging obstacle layouts.
AI.conclusion: Shared voxel-map representations are an effective and scalable substrate for learned cooperative indoor UAV guidance, enabling consistent multi-UAV spatial fusion and decentralized control.

title: On the Use of LLMs for Specialised Terminology: A Good Alternative to Corpora?
summary: Specialised translation relies on the use of documentary and terminological resources, including corpora. These resources are particularly useful for terminology. However, their compilation and exploitation have several limitations: they require time, technical skills and access to data that can be difficult to collect. This study examines the extent to which LLMs can assist specialised translators in finding equivalents from English to French. We evaluate four proprietary models, GPT-4o, GPT-5.2, Claude Sonnet 4.5 and DeepSeek, in two specialised domains, Earth, Environmental and Planetary Sciences (EEPS) and Natural Language Processing (NLP). The experiment is based on 80 terms per domain and compares two prompting strategies: a terminology and a translation mode. The results highlight clear differences between models, prompting strategies and, to a lesser extent, domains. Claude Sonnet 4.5 achieves the best results in the most favourable configuration, while DeepSeek stands out for its greater stability. Analysis of confidence estimates also shows that they are only a partial indicator of terminological accuracy. Overall, the findings suggest that LLMs can be useful tools for specialised translators, but cannot, at this stage, replace specialised corpora. This research therefore paves the way for future work on the real practical usefulness of LLMs for specialised translators in work and educational contexts.

AI.tldr: LLMs can assist domain-specific translation by suggesting English→French equivalents, but cannot fully replace specialised corpora; results depend on model, prompting strategy, and domain; Claude Sonnet 4.5 often performs best; DeepSeek offers greater stability; confidence estimates are only partial indicators of accuracy.
AI.motivation: Evaluate the practical utility of large language models in supporting specialised translators with terminology extraction/translation tasks and to understand limitations of current LLM capabilities.
AI.method: Comparative evaluation of four proprietary LLMs (GPT-4o, GPT-5.2, Claude Sonnet 4.5, DeepSeek) across two specialised domains (Earth, Environmental and Planetary Sciences; Natural Language Processing). 80 terms per domain were used. Two prompting strategies were tested: a terminology-focused mode and a translation-oriented mode.
AI.result: Models show clear performance differences across models, prompting strategies, and domains. Claude Sonnet 4.5 achieved the best results in the most favorable configuration; DeepSeek demonstrated greater stability. Confidence estimates provided by the models were only a partial indicator of terminological accuracy.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can be useful tools for specialised translators but cannot replace specialised corpora at this stage. The work points to potential practical utility in work and educational settings and invites further research on real-world usefulness and how to best integrate LLMs with traditional terminological resources.

title: WHTMix: Efficient Stereo Depth Estimation via Walsh-Hadamard Token Mixing
