AI.motivation: Real-world tasks require models to leverage multimodal contextual cues, not just pre-trained knowledge. Existing benchmarks largely focus on textual contexts, leaving a gap for evaluating context learning from figures, tables, maps, and other modalities.
AI.method: Assemble a benchmark (CLBench-V) by combining converted public multimodal benchmarks with newly constructed datasets, spanning domains like science, finance, long-document understanding, spatial reasoning, and web-based VQA. Tasks are organized along three dimensions: context grounding, new information application, and new knowledge learning. Automated construction and filtering procedures are used to create the new datasets. Evaluation spans 3,443 instances across six recent multimodal models, with analyses of judge reliability, context length, image count, and failure cases.
AI.result: The best overall score across models is 0.2847, indicating room for improvement and that multimodal context learning is far from saturated. InternVL3.5-30B-A3B excels at context grounding and new knowledge learning, while Qwen3.5-Plus leads in new information application. Additional analyses shed light on reliability and failure modes.
AI.conclusion: CLBench-V provides a comprehensive, scalable benchmark and baselines for multimodal context learning, highlighting current limitations and model-specific strengths. The work facilitates future research by offering automated dataset construction, diverse domains, and open-source code.

title: Neurai-VN Benchmark: Standardized Machine Learning Models for Multimodal Digital Phenotyping in Mental Health Classification
summary: Digital phenotyping (DP) using smartphones and wearable devices has shown considerable potential for mental health monitoring. However, progress remains difficult to evaluate due to heterogeneous datasets, inconsistent preprocessing pipelines. In this study, we present a reproducible benchmark built upon the Neurai-VN dataset, a high-resolution, multimodal dataset comprising passive sensing and active assessment from wearable and smartphone devices, collected from 100 Vietnamese adults over two weeks. The benchmark defines four clinically relevant binary classification tasks evaluated using standardized subject-wise cross-validation. Representative linear, tree-based, and neural baseline models are evaluated across predefined feature configurations. Mean subject-level F1 scores across five cross-validation folds reached 0.71 for Healthy Control vs. Depression and Healthy Control vs. Clinical, while Healthy Control vs. Anxiety and Depression vs. Anxiety achieved 0.69 and 0.56, respectively. These benchmark results provide reproducible baselines for future research on multimodal DP for mental health classification tasks.

AI.tldr: A reproducible benchmark for multimodal digital phenotyping in mental health using Neurai-VN: four binary classification tasks evaluated with subject-wise cross-validation across linear, tree-based, and neural baselines; results show F1 around 0.71 for HC vs Depression/Clinical, 0.69 for HC vs Anxiety, and 0.56 for Depression vs Anxiety.
AI.motivation: To address fragmentation in DP for mental health due to heterogeneous datasets and preprocessing, and to establish a reproducible benchmark using a high-resolution multimodal dataset.
AI.method: Construct a benchmark on Neurai-VN (100 Vietnamese adults, 2 weeks) with passive sensing and active assessments. Define four binary classification tasks. Use standardized subject-wise cross-validation. Evaluate representative linear, tree-based, and neural baselines across predefined feature configurations.
AI.result: Mean subject-level F1 scores across five folds: HC vs Depression = 0.71; HC vs Clinical = 0.71; HC vs Anxiety = 0.69; Depression vs Anxiety = 0.56.
AI.conclusion: Provides reproducible baselines for multimodal DP-based mental health classification and a framework for evaluating future models on Neurai-VN.

title: HiFi-UMI: Learning Deployable Manipulation Policies from High-Fidelity UMI Data Alone
comment: 33 pages, 15 figures, 4 tables. Project page: https://cloud.simpleai.tech/simple-world-lab/hifi-umi/ Dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/simple-world-lab/HiFi-UMI-2K
summary: Learning deployable manipulation policies is bottlenecked by the scarcity of data that is both high-fidelity and scalable. Real-robot teleoperation is accurate but costly to scale; robot-free UMI capture scales readily, and current practice uses the resulting data mainly for pre-training, adding a small real-robot "anchor" at post-training. We ask whether raising the fidelity of robot-free UMI data, rather than shrinking the real-robot fraction, can remove that anchor. We present HiFi-UMI, a portable UMI data-production system co-designed for trajectory accuracy, inter-gripper relative pose, synchronization, and field of view: head-mounted offline stereo-inertial SLAM, native rather than reconstructed relative pose, a shared microsecond GPIO trigger, and two wide-angle cameras per hand covering ~200 degrees. It reaches 3 mm workspace-local end-effector accuracy without external tracking infrastructure. Using this corpus, we demonstrate zero-robot post-training: a policy post-trained solely on HiFi-UMI demonstrations deploys directly on a real robot and matches in-domain teleoperation across three backbones spanning the vision-language-action and world-action-model families, with success-rate differences of -2.5, +3.1, and -0.6 percentage points on StarVLA-QwenPI, OpenPI-pi_0.5, and LingBot-VA; the strongest policy reaches 85% on a precision insertion task, even though the teleoperation baseline is collected in the evaluation scene and no HiFi-UMI trajectory is. Pre-training on 4,000 hours from the same corpus lowers action error on ten unseen tasks by 41% and, on StarVLA-QwenPI, raises real-robot success by a further 18.1 percentage points. We open-source HiFi-UMI-2K, 2,000 hours of microsecond-synchronized, ultra-wide-FoV demonstrations, each automatically reconstructed and validated through simulation replay, as a large-scale, high-fidelity resource for the robot-learning community.

AI.tldr: HiFi-UMI demonstrates high-fidelity, scalable robot-free data for deployable manipulation. A zero-robot post-training claim is supported by a 2K-hour, tightly synchronized, wide FoV demonstration corpus; open-source resource enables zero-robot deployment with competitive performance across multiple backbones.
AI.motivation: Reduce reliance on costly real-robot data (anchor) by increasing fidelity of robot-free data to enable post-training transfer to real robots.
AI.method: HiFi-UMI system with head-mounted offline stereo-inertial SLAM, native relative pose, microsecond GPIO trigger, and two wide-angle cameras per hand; achieves ~3 mm end-effector accuracy; data pipeline includes automatic reconstruction and simulation replay; large-scale dataset (HiFi-UMI-2K, 2,000 hours) with synchronized demonstrations.
AI.result: Zero-robot post-training: policies trained solely on HiFi-UMI demonstrations perform comparably to teleoperation baselines across three backbones; success-rate deltas: -2.5, +3.1, -0.6 pp on StarVLA-QwenPI, OpenPI-pi_0.5, LingBot-VA; best policy reaches 85% on a precision insertion task. Pre-training on 4,000 hours reduces action error by 41% and increases real-robot success by 18.1 pp on StarVLA-QwenPI.
AI.conclusion: High-fidelity, scalable robot-free data can support zero-robot post-training, reducing or removing the need for an anchor; HiFi-UMI-2K provides a large, open resource for the robotics-learning community.

title: Aletheia: An Offline-First Clinical Decision Support System for Differential Diagnosis in Low-Resource Healthcare Settings
summary: Access to specialist clinical expertise remains severely limited across sub-Saharan Africa, where physician-to-patient ratios can fall below 1:25,000 in rural settings. Existing AI-assisted diagnostic tools predominantly require reliable internet connectivity and high-specification hardware, rendering them impractical for frontline healthcare workers in district hospitals and health centres. This paper presents Aletheia, an offline-first clinical decision support system designed for low-resource healthcare contexts across sub-Saharan Africa. Aletheia is built upon Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, fine-tuned using Quantised Low- Rank Adaptation (QLoRA) on a curated dataset of 27,000 clinical reasoning samples spanning 50 disease conditions with elevated prevalence in East Africa. Evaluation demonstrates a Top-1 diagnostic accuracy of 80.0%, Top-3 accuracy of 100.0%, BERTScore-F1 of 0.909, and METEOR of 0.467 across ten representative clinical case categories. The system achieves an Expected Calibration Error (ECE) of 0.275 and passes the Africa Deep Tech Challenge 2026 (ADTC 2026) memory budget constraint of 7 168 MB, achieving a peak inference RAM of approximately 3 630 MB on the standardised benchmark laptop. These results demonstrate the feasibility of deploying large language model-based clinical reasoning at the primary care level in resource-constrained settings without cloud infrastructure.

AI.tldr: Aletheia is an offline-first LLM-based clinical decision support system for sub-Saharan Africa, built on Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct and fine-tuned with QLoRA on 27k clinical reasoning samples across 50 East African diseases. It achieves strong diagnostic performance (Top-1 80%, Top-3 100%), high lexical similarity (BERTScore-F1 0.909, METEOR 0.467), and reasonable calibration (ECE 0.275) within a constrained memory budget (7,168 MB) and ~3.63 GB peak RAM, enabling cloudless deployment at primary care level.
AI.motivation: To overcome the shortage of specialist clinicians in sub-Saharan Africa by delivering accessible, offline AI-assisted clinical decision support that does not require internet connectivity or high-end hardware.
AI.method: Developed as an offline-first CDS using Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, fine-tuned via Quantised Low Rank Adaptation (QLoRA) on a curated dataset of 27,000 clinical reasoning samples spanning 50 diseases common in East Africa. Evaluation across ten representative clinical case categories measured with Top-1/Top-3 accuracy, BERTScore-F1, METEOR, and Expected Calibration Error (ECE); also assessed memory footprint against the Africa Deep Tech Challenge 2026 (ADTC 2026) constraint (7,168 MB) with peak RAM ~3.63 GB on a standard benchmark laptop.
AI.result: Demonstrated feasibility of deploying large language model-based clinical reasoning offline at the primary-care level in resource-constrained SSA settings: Top-1 accuracy 80.0%, Top-3 accuracy 100.0%, BERTScore-F1 0.909, METEOR 0.467, ECE 0.275; memory-budget-compliant with 7,168 MB and peak RAM around 3.63 GB.
AI.conclusion: The work shows that offline LLM-based clinical reasoning is feasible in low-resource SSA contexts without cloud infrastructure. It highlights potential for real-world deployment, while underscoring needs for external validation, safety assessment, workflow integration, and scalability across diverse SSA regions and pathogens.

title: MEDit-Bench: A Dataset for Evaluating Message-Driven Narrative Video Editing
summary: Video editing is fundamentally message-driven: even from the same source footage, the selected shots change depending on the narrative the editor wishes to convey. Benchmarks for a closely related task, video summarization, reduce editorial intent to a single, message-agnostic notion of saliency and thus do not account for this diversity. For evaluating message-driven video editing, we present \textbf{MEDit-Bench}, a dataset and benchmark, which pairs long-form videos with multiple editing messages and multiple professionally produced edits per message, demonstrating that different messages yield substantially different edits from the same source. We define an automatic evaluation protocol based on temporal alignment metrics, and find that an LLM-as-a-judge preference, a natural proxy for narrative quality, is unreliable for this task due to severe position bias. We additionally annotate each message with ambiguity and contextfulness scores, and show that both dimensions negatively correlate with model performance, establishing message difficulty as a meaningful stratification factor. Experiments with state-of-the-art MLLMs and reinforcement fine-tuned baselines show that while strong models approach human temporal alignment at lenient thresholds, all models fall behind humans at stricter criteria. A human perceptual study further confirms a large quality gap, with professional human edits remaining consistently preferred over model outputs.

AI.tldr: MEDit-Bench provides a dataset and benchmark for evaluating message-driven video editing, revealing substantial edits variation across messages, introducing temporal-alignment evaluation, showing reliability issues with LLM-based judges due to position bias, and revealing a persistent gap between modeled and human edits, especially under strict criteria.
AI.motivation: Video editing is inherently narrative-driven. Existing video-summarization benchmarks reduce editorial intent to a single, message-agnostic saliency objective and fail to capture diverse, message-specific edits. There is a need for a benchmark and evaluation protocol that account for multiple editing messages and professional edits per message.
AI.method: Construct MEDit-Bench by pairing long-form videos with multiple editing messages and multiple professionally produced edits per message. Define an automatic evaluation protocol based on temporal alignment metrics. Annotate each message with ambiguity and contextfulness scores. Evaluate state-of-the-art Multimodal LLMs and reinforcement-fine-tuned baselines; conduct a human perceptual study to compare outputs.
AI.result: Different messages yield substantially different edits from the same source. LLM-as-a-judge preferences are unreliable due to severe position bias. Ambiguity and contextfulness scores negatively correlate with model performance, indicating message difficulty as a stratification factor. Strong models approach human temporal alignment at lenient thresholds but fall behind at stricter criteria. Professional human edits are preferred in perceptual studies, confirming a quality gap between models and humans.
AI.conclusion: Message difficulty is a meaningful factor for evaluating and improving message-driven video editing. Current models approach but do not reach human-level performance, especially under stringent criteria; future work should enhance narrative-quality evaluation and reduce position biases in model judgments.

title: Beyond Single-Episode Optimization: Sliding-Window Aware Generative Auto-Bidding for Long-Term Advertising Effectiveness
summary: Auto-bidding systems optimize bids to maximize value under efficiency constraints such as Cost-Per-Action (CPA). Existing methods treat each day as an independent episode. However, many advertisers produce value so sparsely that per-day efficiency ratios become statistically unreliable, undermining advertiser retention. Platforms therefore evaluate window-level efficiency over sliding windows of $W{=}7$ days, ensuring fair evaluation and long-term advertising effectiveness. This creates cross-episode coupling: each day's bidding decisions affect up to $W$ overlapping windows, so setting daily targets requires anticipating future market conditions. We propose SWAG-Bid (Sliding-Window Aware Generative Auto-Bidding), a hierarchical framework decomposing this challenge into episode-level planning and step-level execution. The planner uses a Masked Trajectory Model to forecast markets and generate candidate plans, scored across all overlapping windows by Multi-Window Model Predictive Control Sampling (MWMS) with exponential confidence decay. The controller adjusts reliance on this guidance through a state-adaptive gate, Per-Step Gated Adaptive Layer Normalization (PSG-AdaLN), complemented by Return-to-Go and Cost-to-Go channels carrying budget and constraint information. Experiments on AuctionNet-Sparse and online A/B tests on AliExpress show that SWAG-Bid achieves competitive constraint satisfaction and value acquisition under sliding-window evaluation.

AI.tldr: SWAG-Bid: a hierarchical auto-bidding framework to handle sliding-window (W=7) evaluation; integrates a Masked Trajectory Model planner with Multi-Window Model Predictive Control Sampling, and a Per-Step Gated Adaptive LayerNorm controller with Return-to-Go and Cost-to-Go channels to manage budget/constraints, achieving competitive performance under sliding-window evaluation on AuctionNet-Sparse and AliExpress A/B tests.
AI.motivation: Per-day independence assumption in auto-bidding fails when advertiser value is sparse, causing unreliable daily efficiency; window-level evaluation over 7-day windows creates cross-episode coupling requiring planning across overlapping windows.
AI.method: Plan at episode-level with Masked Trajectory Model to forecast market and generate candidate plans; score candidates across all overlapping windows via MWMS with exponential confidence decay; control step-level execution with PSG-AdaLN gating; incorporate Return-to-Go and Cost-to-Go channels conveying budget/constraint information.
AI.result: SWAG-Bid achieves competitive constraint satisfaction and value acquisition under sliding-window evaluation; validated on AuctionNet-Sparse and in online AliExpress A/B tests.
AI.conclusion: Hierarchical planning-execution architecture effectively addresses cross-episode coupling in sliding-window auto-bidding, balancing long-horizon constraints with responsive per-step decisions.

title: SAM3D-Guided Object-Centric Representation Alignment for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown strong potential for general robot manipulation, but most existing models rely on 2D visual-language backbones and lack fine-grained 3D understanding of target objects, especially under occlusion, pose variation, scale changes, and precise spatial interaction. We propose an object-centric 3D representation alignment framework built upon $π_0$, using SAM3D as a frozen 3D teacher to provide target-object 3D priors during training. Specifically, we localize task-relevant objects with object recognition models, generate corresponding object masks, and use SAM3D to extract dense object-level 3D representations, which are aligned with intermediate visual features of $π_0$. This enables the policy to internalize target-object 3D information while preserving the original RGB-language-to-action inference pipeline without requiring depth, point clouds, masks, SAM3D, or additional 3D modules at test time. Simulation experiments show consistent improvements, achieving 99.1\% on LIBERO and an average length of 4.11 on CALVIN. Real-world experiments further demonstrate that our method is particularly effective in long-horizon manipulation scenarios where the robot must focus on different target objects across multiple subtasks.

AI.tldr: An object-centric 3D representation alignment framework for Vision-Language-Action robots that uses SAM3D as a frozen 3D teacher to inject target-object priors during training, aligning dense 3D representations with π0's visual features for robust task execution without test-time 3D modules.
AI.motivation: 2D visual-language backbones struggle with fine-grained 3D understanding of target objects under occlusion, pose variation, and scale changes; precise spatial interaction is essential for robust manipulation, necessitating 3D priors during training.
AI.method: Localize task-relevant objects, generate masks, use SAM3D to extract dense object-level 3D representations (priors), and align them with intermediate features of π0. The 3D priors are learned during training via a frozen 3D teacher, preserving the RGB-language-to-action pipeline at test time and avoiding extra 3D modules.
AI.result: In simulation, achieved 99.1% on LIBERO and an average length of 4.11 on CALVIN. Real-world experiments show strong performance in long-horizon manipulation across multiple subtasks and target objects.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework enhances target-object 3D understanding and spatial interaction in VLA models by injecting 3D priors during training while maintaining a simple test-time pipeline, with clear gains in both simulated and real-world long-horizon tasks.

title: AdaKP: Online Adaptive Knowledge-Point Selection for Reasoning-Oriented Reinforcement Learning
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards is a powerful paradigm for eliciting reasoning in large language models, yet it suffers from severe reward sparsity on competition-level mathematics. A common remedy injects atomic knowledge points (KPs) - short natural-language hints distilled from gold solutions - into the prompt. Existing methods, however, either fix this selection once offline or merely scale the monolithic quantity of injected text, leaving untouched the most informative axis of choice: which subset of atomic KPs to inject, and when. We introduce AdaKP, an online selector that re-chooses each problem's KP subset over the course of RL training. At its core is an entropy proxy that scores a KP by the reduction in next-token entropy it induces - a single inexpensive forward pass, with a provable bound on its truncation bias - in place of expensive rollout-based estimation. Three lightweight mechanisms make this signal usable online: a momentum smoother that absorbs per-step noise, a retirement-and-revival manager that prunes weak KPs while preserving exploration, and an adaptive scheduler that front-loads re-evaluations into early training. AdaKP further contributes a pre-flight validation gate that certifies the proxy against a leave-one-out ground truth before any expensive run is launched, turning method-level risk into a falsifiable check. Realized as a fully additive fork of a standard DAPO+GRPO trainer with no optimizer changes, AdaKP improves over a strong static-selection baseline on all eight competition-mathematics benchmarks at negligible added cost, positioning online, validated KP-subset selection as a practical and as-yet under-explored axis for reasoning-oriented reinforcement learning.

AI.tldr: AdaKP enables online selection of atomic knowledge points (KPs) during RL-finetuning of LLMs for competition-level math, using an entropy-based proxy to score KPs, with mechanisms for stability and a pre-flight validation gate; it achieves improvements across eight benchmarks with negligible added cost.
AI.motivation: Tackle reward sparsity in reasoning-focused RL for LLMs by selecting the most informative subset of atomic KPs, rather than fixed offline selections or naive scaling, to improve problem-solving performance efficiently.
AI.method: Introduce an online KP selector (AdaKP) that scores a KP by the reduction in next-token entropy it induces, using a single forward pass with a bound on truncation bias. Implement momentum smoothing, retirement-and-revival pruning, and adaptive scheduling to stabilize online scoring. Add a pre-flight validation gate that certifies the proxy against leave-one-out ground truth. Integrate as a fully additive fork of a standard DAPO+GRPO trainer with no optimizer changes.
AI.result: AdaKP improves over a strong static-selection baseline on eight competition-mathematics benchmarks with negligible added cost.
AI.conclusion: Online, validated KP-subset selection is a practical and under-explored axis for reasoning-oriented reinforcement learning in LLMs.

title: Human-in-the-Loop Signature Bootstrapping for UAV Hyperspectral PFM-1 Mine Detection
summary: Hyperspectral imaging (HSI) is useful for material discrimination, but operational mine screening also depends on how many false alarms must be inspected before targets are found. This paper studies PFM-1 landmine detection in unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) visible and near-infrared (VNIR) HSI using spectral angle mapper (SAM), matched filter (MF), adaptive coherence estimator (ACE), and constrained energy minimization (CEM). We compare a ground-measured SVC signature, a fully informed in-scene core-pixel signature, and a simulated human-in-the-loop signature bootstrap. Besides receiver operating characteristic area under the curve and average precision, we report target-discovery curves and spatial candidate-review counts. Full-review bootstrapping reaches the fully informed in-scene signature case after all seven target regions are verified, but the required inspection effort varies strongly: ACE confirms all regions in two rounds and nine candidate inspections, whereas the SAM variants need thousands of candidate reviews for their final target locations. Code is available at https://github.com/SagarLekhak/IEEE_WHISPERS_2026_UAV_HSI_PFM1.

AI.tldr: Evaluates UAV VNIR-HSI PFM-1 landmine detection using SAM, MF, ACE, CEM; compares ground-measured SVC, fully informed in-scene core-pixel, and simulated human-in-the-loop bootstrap signatures; ACE achieves efficient target confirmation, SAM requires extensive candidate reviews; full-review bootstrap can match fully informed in-scene with enough verification; code available on GitHub.
AI.motivation: Operational mine screening must balance high detection performance with manageable inspection effort; understanding how detector choice and signature strategy affect workload is essential for practical UAV-HSI mine detection.
AI.method: Apply four detectors (SAM, MF, ACE, CEM) to UAV VNIR-HSI data for PFM-1. Compare three signature scenarios: ground-measured SVC, fully informed in-scene core-pixel, and simulated human-in-the-loop bootstrap. Evaluate ROC AUC, average precision, target-discovery curves, and spatial candidate-review counts. Report results and provide code.
AI.result: Full-review bootstrapping reaches the fully informed in-scene case after seven target regions are verified. ACE confirms all regions in two rounds and nine candidate inspections, whereas SAM variants require thousands of candidate reviews for final target locations.
AI.conclusion: ACE offers the most efficient detection with far fewer inspections; in-scene-informed signatures can approach fully informed performance but with variable effort; detector-signature choices significantly affect operator workload and overall system effectiveness; code is provided at the cited repository.

title: Bridging Compute- and Data-Optimal Pretraining
summary: Classical compute-optimal scaling laws assume an unbounded supply of fresh pretraining data, yet pretraining is increasingly entering a regime in which compute grows faster than the availability of high-quality data. We propose Compute-Data (CD) scaling laws, a unified framework that bridges compute-optimal scaling, where data scales freely with compute, and data-optimal scaling, where the corpus is fixed while compute can grow without bound. CD scaling extends classical scaling laws by introducing a token-effectiveness function, $η$, which quantifies the value of a derived token-produced, for example, through multi-epoch repetition or paraphrasing-relative to a fresh token, ranging from a perfect substitute to having no value. We fit $η$ for two data-expansion strategies, multi-epoch repetition and paraphrasing, across model sizes from 14M to 600M parameters using the Dolma-3 corpus. We find that token effectiveness is far from constant: it depends jointly on model size, the tokens-per-parameter ratio, and the amount of derived data, and it saturates as the corpus is expanded. The functional form of $η$ implies diminishing returns when substituting compute for data as either model size or data availability increases. It also partitions training into three operational regimes---compute-bound, data-bound, and model-bound---and shows that classical compute-optimal allocation is suboptimal across most practically relevant settings.

AI.tldr: Proposes Compute-Data (CD) scaling laws with a token-effectiveness function η to model the value of derived tokens relative to fresh tokens, bridging compute-optimal and data-optimal limits and revealing regime transitions and diminishing returns when substituting compute for data.
AI.motivation: Classical scaling laws assume unbounded fresh data, but real-world pretraining faces data scarcity as compute grows. A unified framework that accounts for the value of derived data is needed to guide resource allocation across data expansion, model size, and compute.
AI.method: Introduce a token-effectiveness function η that quantifies the value of a derived token produced via data-expansion strategies (e.g., multi-epoch repetition, paraphrasing). Fit η for two strategies across model sizes from 14M to 600M parameters on the Dolma-3 corpus. Analyze η's dependence on model size, tokens-per-parameter, and amount of derived data; derive the functional form of η and its saturation behavior.
AI.result: η is not constant; it depends jointly on model size, tokens-per-parameter, and amount of derived data, and it saturates as the corpus expands. The functional form implies diminishing returns when substituting compute for data as either model size or data availability increases. CD scaling partitions training into three regimes—compute-bound, data-bound, and model-bound—and shows that classical compute-optimal allocation is suboptimal across many practical settings.
AI.conclusion: CD scaling provides a unified framework that bridges compute-optimal and data-optimal scaling, accounts for data-value saturation, and guides more efficient resource allocation under data constraints in pretraining.

title: DC-WAM: Dynamic-Centric Visual Supervision and Reasoning for World-Action Models
summary: World-Action Models (WAMs) augment robot policies with future visual prediction, but it remains unclear what the visual modality should learn for control. While photorealistic future prediction provides dense supervision, it also incurs substantial computation and can allocate capacity to texture, illumination, and background variations that are only weakly related to action selection. Recent efficient WAM variants suggest that the main benefit of the video branch may not lie in the rendered future itself, but in the control-relevant visual representations induced during training. In this work, we revisit future video prediction from a dynamic-centric perspective and ask whether an existing RGB-based WAM can be redirected from appearance-dominated reconstruction toward interaction-induced visual dynamics without introducing additional modality-specific predictions or online inputs at deployment. We propose DC-WAM, a dynamic-centric WAM framework that redistributes supervision and computation in the RGB video branch. At the supervision level, DC-WAM combines temporal-difference flow matching with trajectory-guided weighting, emphasizing dense temporal changes and localized regions where the gripper, manipulated objects, and contact areas move. At the reasoning level, DynaRoute predicts token-wise dynamic relevance and converts it into an attention bias, guiding the model toward control-relevant future tokens. Experiments in simulation and on real-world manipulation tasks show that DC-WAM consistently improves policy performance, especially under out-of-distribution perturbations in lighting, object appearance, and background texture.

AI.tldr: DC-WAM reframes RGB-based World-Action Models to emphasize interaction-driven visual dynamics, using temporal-difference flow matching with trajectory-guided weighting for supervision and a DynaRoute attention bias for reasoning, yielding more robust, control-relevant predictions without extra modalities.
AI.motivation: Photorealistic video prediction in WAMs is computation-heavy and can allocate capacity to appearance (texture, lighting) rather than action-relevant dynamics. A dynamic-centric RGB approach aims to extract control-relevant dynamics without modality-specific predictions or online inputs, improving robustness to appearance changes.
AI.method: Two-level approach: (1) Supervision: temporal-difference flow matching with trajectory-guided weighting to emphasize dense temporal changes in regions around the gripper, manipulated objects, and contact areas. (2) Reasoning: DynaRoute predicts token-wise dynamic relevance and converts it into an attention bias to steer future-token focus toward control-relevant dynamics.
AI.result: Empirical results in simulation and real-world manipulation show DC-WAM consistently improves policy performance, especially under out-of-distribution perturbations in lighting, object appearance, and background texture.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic-centric RGB WAM without additional modality predictions or online inputs can improve control performance by reallocating supervision toward dynamics and using dynamic relevance to bias future-token reasoning, enabling more robust visuomotor control.

title: MusiChat: Vibe Composing for Music Creation
summary: Recent advances in AI music generation have enabled users to create complete musical pieces from natural-language prompts. However, most existing systems follow a prompt-and-regenerate paradigm, making iterative refinement difficult because users must repeatedly recreate compositions instead of directly evolving existing musical ideas. We present MusiChat, a conversational vibe composing system that enables collaborative human-AI music creation through natural-language interaction and iterative refinement. At the core of MusiChat is a hierarchical controllable music generation framework that separates lyric-aligned musical structure generation from expressive surface realization, allowing flexible stylistic transformations and structure-preserving edits. The system integrates a large language model with a hybrid symbolic music engine through a memory-augmented architecture that maintains the active composition state and user history across interactions. A hybrid intent-routing mechanism further enables efficient interpretation of both precise musical edits and open-ended creative requests. Rather than regenerating compositions from scratch, MusiChat incrementally transforms an evolving musical artifact while preserving relevant musical structure and user intent. We evaluate MusiChat through objective analysis and human studies, achieving 95.31% and 100% accuracy for single- and multi-turn interactions, respectively, and obtaining like-to-dislike ratios of 2:1 for melody naturalness and 3:1 for musical quality. Our results demonstrate that MusiChat supports coherent multi-turn music authoring and interactive human-AI co-creation through a conversational interface.

AI.tldr: MusiChat introduces a conversational, hierarchical, memory-augmented system for incremental music authoring that preserves structure while applying surface-level edits, addressing the prompt-regeneration bottleneck.
AI.motivation: To overcome the iterative recreation requirement in prompt-based AI music systems by enabling iterative, structure-preserving edits through natural-language conversations.
AI.method: A hierarchical controllable music generation framework that separates lyric-aligned structure generation from expressive surface realization; memory-augmented architecture to track composition state and user history; hybrid intent-routing to handle precise edits and open-ended requests; integration of LLM with a hybrid symbolic music engine to incrementally transform evolving musical artifacts.
AI.result: Objective analysis and human studies report 95.31% accuracy for single-turn and 100% accuracy for multi-turn interactions; like-to-dislike ratios: 2:1 for melody naturalness, 3:1 for musical quality.
AI.conclusion: MusiChat enables coherent multi-turn music authoring and interactive human-AI co-creation via a conversational interface, demonstrating effective collaborative editing without regenerating from scratch.

title: Sense it with your eyes: Sensation Generation and Understanding for Advertisements
summary: Sensory advertising evokes human senses through visual cues, enabling audiences to mentally simulate experiences and increasing persuasive impact. Despite the recent increase in using AI in generating and understanding creative and persuasive content, how advertisements visually evoke sensations remains largely unexplored. In this work, we introduce the first study of understanding, evaluating, and generating sensory ads. We introduce the Sensory Ad dataset, and define sensation classification tasks (SenseClass) to benchmark LLMs and MLLMs. We further propose SenseScore, an automated evaluation metric for sensation evocation achieving strong agreement with human judgments. Finally, we introduce the Sensory Ad Generation (SenseGen) task and propose SAGA, a multi-agent framework that improves message image alignment, sensory evocation, and persuasion. Our work establishes a foundation for sensory-aware visual persuasion.

AI.tldr: First study of sensory advertising using AI; introduces the Sensory Ad dataset, SenseClass classification tasks, SenseScore evaluation metric, and SenseGen generation task with the SAGA multi-agent framework to enhance message-image alignment, sensory evocation, and persuasion.
AI.motivation: Addresses a gap in understanding and evaluating how visual ads evoke sensory experiences in the age of AI-generated and AI-understood creative content; aims to standardize benchmarks and evaluation for sensory evocation in advertising.
AI.method: 1) Build Sensory Ad dataset; 2) define SenseClass sensation classification tasks for LLMs and MLLMs; 3) propose SenseScore as automated evaluation aligned with human judgments; 4) define SenseGen generation task; 5) propose SAGA, a multi-agent framework to optimize message-image alignment, sensory evocation, and persuasion.
AI.result: SenseScore demonstrates strong agreement with human judgments; SenseGen within the SAGA framework improves alignment, sensory evocation, and persuasive impact compared with baselines (as claimed in the abstract).
AI.conclusion: Lays a foundation for sensory-aware visual persuasion by providing datasets, benchmarks, and generation frameworks for evocative advertising.

title: HeAD-CP: Heterophily-Aware Diffused Conformal Prediction Sets for Graph Neural Networks
summary: Conformal prediction (CP) provides distribution-free uncertainty quantification, and its extension to graphs is an active research direction. Diffused Adaptive Prediction Sets (DAPS) is a widely used graph-aware diffusion baseline, propagating Adaptive Prediction Sets (APS) non-conformity scores along edges with a uniform coefficient $λ$. We identify a fundamental shortcoming of this design: the uniform low-pass diffusion presupposes graph homophily and proves detrimental on heterophilic graphs, enlarging the mean prediction-set size by up to 10.6% relative to plain APS. To mitigate this, we propose HeAD-CP, a family of node-wise diffusion variants whose coefficients are determined by a label-free local-homophily estimate derived from the GNN softmax. Three variants, namely signed-$γ$, edge-compatibility, and a DAPS-baseline-with-correction, are most effective at extreme heterophily, intermediate heterophily, and moderate-to-high homophily, respectively, and all preserve the marginal coverage guarantee. On ten benchmarks, the HeAD-CP family stays at or below plain APS on every dataset, while DAPS exceeds APS on six. The post-hoc oracle over the family improves over DAPS on 8/10 datasets at $p<0.01$ (paired Wilcoxon), with the largest gains on heterophilic graphs (10.3% on Texas); on the two homophilic datasets where DAPS still wins (CiteSeer, PubMed), it retains a marginal advantage of at most 0.002, statistically insignificant on CiteSeer ($p=0.23$). Designing a calibrated label-free selector that approaches this oracle is the main outstanding empirical question.

AI.tldr: Adaptive, node-wise diffusion (HeAD-CP) tailors diffusion coefficients to local homophily, improving conformal prediction on graphs by outperforming uniform DAPS on heterophilic graphs and matching plain APS on benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Conformal prediction on graphs suffers from DAPS' uniform diffusion which assumes homophily; there is a need for adaptive, label-free diffusion that preserves calibration across varying graph homophily.
AI.method: Introduce HeAD-CP, a family of node-wise diffusion variants with diffusion coefficients determined by a label-free local-homophily estimate derived from the GNN softmax. Three variants are highlighted: signed-γ, edge-compatibility, and a DAPS-baseline-with-correction.
AI.result: HeAD-CP remains at or below plain APS on all ten benchmarks, while DAPS exceeds APS on six. A post-hoc oracle over the HeAD-CP family beats DAPS on 8/10 datasets (p<0.01, paired Wilcoxon), with the largest gain on heterophilic graphs (Texas: 10.3%). On two homophilic datasets (CiteSeer, PubMed), HeAD-CP holds only negligible gains (≤0.002; CiteSeer p=0.23).
AI.conclusion: Node-wise, label-free diffusion (HeAD-CP) effectively stabilizes conformal prediction across graph heterophily levels; the main open empirical question is designing a calibrated label-free selector that approaches the oracle.

title: Physics-Aware End-to-End Deep Reinforcement Learning for Quadcopter Control with Actuator Dynamics
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures, 2 tables. Presented at the Aeronautical and Astronautical Society of the Republic of China (AASRC) Conference, Tamsui, Taiwan, November 15, 2025, Paper No. 1075. Received an Honorable Mention for the Best Paper Award
summary: Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), particularly quadcopters, present unique challenges for autonomous control due to their underactuated dynamics: only four available control inputs must govern six degrees of freedom. This paper investigates a physics-aware, end-to-end deep reinforcement learning (DRL) approach that acts directly on low-level body inputs, total thrust and body torques $(T, τ_x, τ_y, τ_z)$, and closes the loop through a high-fidelity Simulink environment. Our simulator integrates a 12-state rigid-body model (MATLAB Level-2 S-Function) with (i) an Action2RPM allocation based on the Moore-Penrose pseudo-inverse of a coefficient matrix derived from thrust and drag terms, and (ii) first-order actuator dynamics for each motor (time constant $T_m = 0.076$ s), including rotor gyroscopic coupling. A shaped reward balances goal-reaching and stability using an exponential position well, attitude penalties, and quadratic velocity costs. Four DRL algorithms, DDPG, TD3, PPO, and SAC, are evaluated in two stages: (S1) thrust-only hover and (S2) hover with pitch torque and a translated goal. Results show that SAC and TD3 achieve superior stability and exploration efficiency, while PPO is less sample-efficient. The study highlights the significance of modeling actuator lags and aerodynamic moments for stable low-level control and provides a reproducible benchmark for quadcopter DRL.

AI.tldr: Physics-aware, end-to-end DRL for quadcopters using low-level inputs in a high-fidelity Simulink model; SAC and TD3 outperform DDPG and PPO in two hover tasks; actuator dynamics and aerodynamic moments are key for stability and provide a reproducible benchmark.
AI.motivation: Underactuated quadcopters (6-DoF with 4 inputs) pose challenging control problems. A physics-informed DRL approach operating on low-level thrust and torques aims to improve stability and sample efficiency, bridging simulation and potential real-world deployment.
AI.method: A 12-state rigid-body model in a MATLAB Level-2 S-Function-based Simulink environment. Action2RPM allocation via Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse of a thrust/drag-derived coefficient matrix. First-order motor dynamics (Tm = 0.076 s) with rotor gyroscopic coupling. Actuator lag and aerodynamic moments modeled. Reward shaped with exponential position well, attitude penalties, and quadratic velocity costs. Evaluated four DRL algorithms (DDPG, TD3, PPO, SAC) in two tasks: (S1) thrust-only hover; (S2) hover with pitch torque and translated goal.
AI.result: TD3 and SAC show superior stability and exploration efficiency; PPO is less sample-efficient. Incorporating actuator lags and aerodynamic moments improves low-level control stability. The work provides a reproducible quadcopter DRL benchmark.
AI.conclusion: Physics-aware, low-level DRL control for quadcopters is viable; accurate actuator dynamics and aerodynamic effects are crucial for stability. The study offers a benchmark for future research and potential transfer to real hardware, with caveats about sim-to-real gaps.

title: Understanding Semantic IDs: From Item Representation to Item Selection in Generative Recommendation
summary: Semantic IDs (SIDs) are now a central component of generative recommendation. Current SID-based systems assign three roles to the same token sequence. Shared prefixes are intended to organize related items, the complete SID identifies an individual item, and each generated token narrows the items that can still be returned. We systematically investigate SIDs from item encoding and SID construction to autoregressive generation and final recommendation. We examine how SID construction changes item representations and how those changes affect generation. Across three Amazon domains and eight SID constructions, SID neighborhoods recover only 32.2% of the encoder's ten nearest neighbors on average. Alternative item descriptions still retrieve the corresponding item first in 99.57% of controlled cases, yet change 38.4% of exact SIDs. These results show that SIDs retain broad organization but lose much of the encoder's fine local structure, while their exact tokens are not determined by item meaning alone. This loss becomes consequential during generation. After the final semantic token, TIGER retains only 29.9% of held-out targets that were plausible recommendations before SID filtering. Motivated by these findings, we propose Item-Supported Decoding (ISD), a lightweight inference-time method that allows a user-specific item ranking to support corresponding SID prefixes before beam search discards them. The same ranking then orders the generated items. ISD requires no additional parameters or retraining of the SID constructor or decoder. We empirically show that ISD improves NDCG@10 over the corresponding SID backbone in every evaluated setting, with relative gains of up to 31.2%. Our results show that SIDs provide useful coarse item organization, but their fine boundaries should not alone determine which items remain available during generation.

AI.tldr: SIDs provide coarse organization for items in generative recommendations but distort fine local structure; introducing Item-Supported Decoding (ISD) improves ranking metrics (NDCG@10) with no retraining, by incorporating user-specific item ranking into the decoding process.
AI.motivation: To understand how different SID constructions affect item representations and generation, and whether SIDs' token-level semantics align with encoder-near neighborhoods and final recommendations.
AI.method: Systematic analysis across three Amazon domains and eight SID constructions; evaluate SID neighborhood preservation, impact of alternative item descriptions on SID tokens, generation-level retention; propose ISD; empirical evaluation on NDCG@10 gains.
AI.result: SID neighborhoods recover ~32.2% of encoder's 10-nearest neighbors on average; alternative descriptions affect exact SIDs but preserve item retrieval at top; TIGER retains 29.9% of held-out plausible targets after SID filtering; ISD yields up to 31.2% relative NDCG@10 improvements without extra training.
AI.conclusion: SIDs offer coarse item organization but not reliable fine-grained control during generation; lightweight inference-time ISD effectively aligns generated results with user ranking, improving recommendation quality.

title: Beyond Background Bias: Saliency-Driven Prototype Alignment for Dataset Distillation
summary: Dataset distillation aims to synthesize compact datasets that can approximate the performance of full-data training while significantly reducing computational and storage costs. However, diffusion-based distillation methods often struggle to preserve structural coherence and generalization, especially in visually complex domains. This issue often stems from latent prototypes that are weakly aligned with class-discriminative regions and contaminated by irrelevant background, thereby degrading generation quality and generalization. To address this limitation, we propose a saliency-driven distillation framework that constructs class-discriminative latent prototypes to enhance representativeness and generalization. The framework proceeds in two stages: (1) ensemble Grad-CAM saliency is used to construct prototypes emphasizing high-confidence regions, and (2) hard prototype refinement is then applied to construct challenging yet class-consistent prototypes, thereby enhancing discriminability and diversity. Importantly, the diffusion backbones (e.g., LDM and DiT) remain frozen; only lightweight classifiers used for saliency extraction are trained. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate consistent performance improvements over strong baselines. Code will be released.

AI.tldr: Saliency-driven dataset distillation for diffusion models using ensemble Grad-CAM and hard prototype refinement to create discriminative, background-free latent prototypes, with frozen diffusion backbones and lightweight saliency classifiers, yielding consistent improvements.
AI.motivation: Diffusion-based distillation often yields weakly aligned prototypes contaminated by background, harming structure and generalization in complex visuals.
AI.method: Two-stage: (1) ensemble Grad-CAM to build high-confidence, class-discriminative prototypes; (2) hard prototype refinement to enforce class consistency and diversity. Diffusion backbones remain frozen; train lightweight classifiers for saliency extraction.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show consistent improvements over strong baselines across multiple benchmarks; code will be released.
AI.conclusion: Saliency-driven prototype construction enhances representativeness and generalization in diffusion-based dataset distillation while keeping model backbones frozen and training lightweight saliency modules.

title: When Does Deep Representation Learning Help Single-Cell Clustering? A Sensitivity-Aware Diagnostic Benchmark for Biomedical AI Pipelines
summary: Single-cell ribonucleic acid sequencing (scRNA-seq) is a foundational technology for precision-medicine workflows that contribute to United Nations Sustainable Development Goal 3 on Good Health and Well-being, and unsupervised clustering is the analytical step that turns raw expression matrices into interpretable cell populations. Practitioners therefore face a recurring engineering decision: is an additional deep representation stage worth its compute and tuning cost, or do classical principal component analysis (PCA) pipelines already suffice? We address this question with a diagnostic benchmark of nine clustering pipelines on ten real datasets (90-5,685 cells, 19,046-41,480 genes, 4-11 cell types), augmented by a partial scVI V2 specialized comparison on seven datasets. The protocol integrates Optuna hyperparameter search, repeated-run robustness, Friedman/Wilcoxon-Holm/TOST testing, and Sobol total-order sensitivity analysis. The contrastive autoencoder achieved the highest mean Adjusted Rand Index (0.7872), but Holm-corrected tests did not establish dominance over the strongest baselines. Per-dataset analysis reveals three reproducible regimes: probabilistic variational autoencoder (VAE) variants help on the smallest datasets, deep autoencoders win on mid-scale data with multi-batch or many-type structure, and classical PCA pipelines remain competitive when linear projection already captures the dominant variation. Sobol indices identify learning rate ($S_T=0.70$) and latent dimensionality ($S_T=0.56$) as the dominant variance contributors, indicating where limited tuning budgets should be allocated. The contribution is therefore a dataset-aware and compute-conscious decision framework for biomedical AI pipelines supporting sustainable healthcare analytics, rather than a universal superiority claim.

AI.tldr: A dataset-aware, compute-conscious benchmark compares nine clustering pipelines (plus partial scVI V2) on ten scRNA-seq datasets; deep representation learning can help in some regimes, but PCA remains competitive in many cases; learning rate and latent dimensionality dominate tuning variance.
AI.motivation: To determine whether adding deep representation stages yields meaningful gains in unsupervised clustering of scRNA-seq data, considering compute and tuning costs, and to provide a sustainable decision framework for biomedical AI pipelines.
AI.method: Benchmark of nine clustering pipelines on ten real scRNA-seq datasets (90–5,685 cells; 19,046–41,480 genes; 4–11 cell types), augmented by a partial scVI V2 comparison on seven datasets. Protocol includes Optuna hyperparameter search, repeated runs, Friedman/Wilcoxon-Holm/TOST tests, and Sobol total-order sensitivity analysis.
AI.result: The contrastive autoencoder achieved the highest mean ARI (0.7872); Holm-corrected tests did not establish dominance over the strongest baselines. Per-dataset regimes: probabilistic VAE variants help on small datasets; deep autoencoders excel on mid-scale data with batch/multi-type structure; PCA pipelines remain competitive when linear projection captures most variation. Sobol indices identify learning rate (S_T=0.70) and latent dimensionality (S_T=0.56) as dominant drivers of variance, guiding where tuning budgets should be allocated.
AI.conclusion: The work delivers a dataset-aware, compute-conscious decision framework for selecting biomedical AI pipelines in scRNA-seq clustering, emphasizing practical guidance over universal superiority; resources should prioritize tuning of learning rate and latent dimensionality, with model choice contingent on dataset regime.

title: S2A2: Audio-Visual Imitation Learning for Manipulation Tasks Using Acoustic Spatial Information
summary: Acoustic information provides rich cues about object location, material properties, and changes caused by contact or motion. This paper introduces a new set of acoustic-aware manipulation tasks for imitation learning, in which robots must use auditory cues to determine manipulation targets. These tasks require sound source localization and identification for active exploration in robotic manipulation. Also, we propose a multimodal imitation learning framework, Spatial-Spectral Audio Action (S2A2), that integrates visual features with acoustic spatial and acoustic signal information for the acoustic-aware manipulation tasks. We implemented S2A2 models that integrates policies such as ACT, Diffusion Policy, VQ-BeT, and $π_0$, into our framework. Simulation experiments showed that the proposed method is the most effective for tasks requiring both position and timbre. Furthermore, real-robot experiments confirm the applicability of the proposed tasks and framework to real-world manipulation.

AI.tldr: Proposes acoustic-aware manipulation tasks and a multimodal imitation learning framework (S2A2) combining visual and acoustic information; shows effectiveness in simulation and real-robot experiments for position and timbre cues.
AI.motivation: Auditory cues provide information about object location, material properties, and dynamics not fully captured by vision; enabling acoustic-aware manipulation requires tasks and models that utilize sound for localization and identification.
AI.method: Define acoustic-aware manipulation tasks requiring sound source localization/identification for active exploration; develop Spatial-Spectral Audio Action (S2A2) integrating visual features with acoustic spatial and spectral information; implement S2A2 models incorporating policies such as ACT, Diffusion Policy, VQ-BeT, and π0; evaluate in simulation and on real robots.
AI.result: Simulation experiments show the proposed method is most effective for tasks requiring both position and timbre; real-robot experiments confirm applicability to real-world manipulation.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates that acoustic information can enhance manipulation through a multimodal imitation learning framework; S2A2 is a viable approach for acoustic-aware robotic manipulation.

title: Localized Anomaly Detection via Differentiable D-vine Copulas
comment: Workshop paper accepted for presentation at the CAESAR workshop within ECML-PKDD (September 2026, Naples)
summary: Vine copulas provide a flexible framework for modeling complex multivariate distributions through a hierarchical decomposition into bivariate pair-copulas. Fitting a D-vine requires selecting a copula family and parameter configuration for each pair-copula from a set of candidates encoding different dependence patterns. As the number of variables and candidate families increases, the number of possible configurations grows combinatorially. Existing fitting procedures address this challenge through sequential greedy decisions, committing to a single locally optimal family at each step and potentially discarding configurations that would yield a better global fit. To overcome this limitation, we propose a novel estimation framework that combines gradient-based maximum likelihood estimation, enabled by our fully differentiable implementation, with a beam-search strategy that maintains multiple competing D-vine configurations throughout the fitting process. This allows a broader exploration of the configuration space while remaining computationally tractable. Building on the fitted D-vine, we introduce a localized anomaly detection framework that exploits the hierarchical decomposition to produce both global anomaly scores and edge-level explanations. Statistical guarantees are provided through Mondrian conformal prediction, while the pair-copula structure enables the localization of anomalies to specific variable relationships. We evaluate the proposed framework on both benchmark and real-world datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness for interpretable anomaly detection with uncertainty quantification.

AI.tldr: A differentiable, beam-search-based estimation for D-vine copulas with Mondrian conformal prediction-based anomaly detection, enabling edge-level explanations and uncertainty quantification; validated on benchmarks and real data.
AI.motivation: D-vine fitting induces a combinatorial configuration space; greedy methods may miss globally optimal configurations. There is a need for scalable fitting plus interpretable anomaly detection with uncertainty quantification.
AI.method: Fully differentiable gradient-based maximum likelihood estimation for D-vines; beam-search to maintain multiple competing configurations during fitting; Mondrian conformal prediction for statistical guarantees; anomaly scoring at global and edge levels leveraging the pair-copula structure.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on benchmark and real-world datasets demonstrates effective, interpretable anomaly detection with uncertainty quantification and localization to specific variable relationships.
AI.conclusion: The framework broadens configuration exploration in vine copula modeling, enabling interpretable anomaly detection with uncertainty, aided by edge-level explanations grounded in the pair-copula structure.

title: Balanced Soft mixture-of-expert model for Glaucoma Detection
summary: Glaucoma is a group of eye diseases that damage the optic nerve, often caused by elevated intraocular pressure. It is a leading cause of irreversible vision loss and is typically developed slowly and painlessly, making it difficult to notice until significant damage has occurred. Therefore, early detection is crucial to prevent or slow the progression of vision loss. In recent years, deep learning based uni-modal models have improved the accuracy and efficiency of glaucoma detection, empowering doctors with tools for earlier diagnosis, better monitoring, and timely treatment. Building on this, multi-modal models have emerged, leveraging the strengths of different imaging modalities to learn richer and more robust representations, further enhancing glaucoma detection accuracy. However, multi-modal learning faces challenges such as imbalanced and under-optimized uni-modal representations due to joint learning objectives. To address this, we propose a balanced soft mixture-experts model with three experts and load balancing loss. The performance is measured by AUC, our proposed method surpasses the performance of all uni-modal baselines, conventional multi-modal models, and current stateof- the-art balanced multi-modal models. The proposed model can be generalized to other disease detections such as diabetic retinopathy.

AI.tldr: A balanced soft mixture-of-experts (MoE) with three experts and a load-balancing loss improves multi-modal glaucoma detection, outperforming uni-modal baselines, standard multi-modal models, and competing balanced multi-modal methods, with potential generalization to diabetic retinopathy.
AI.motivation: Glaucoma detection benefits from multi-modal imaging, but joint learning can lead to imbalanced or under-optimized uni-modal representations; a balanced MoE aims to leverage complementary information from modalities while stabilizing training.
AI.method: Propose a tri-expert soft MoE architecture with a load-balancing loss to distribute learning across experts; train on multi-modal retinal data to detect glaucoma, optimizing with AUC.
AI.result: The proposed method surpasses all uni-modal baselines, conventional multi-modal models, and current state-of-the-art balanced multi-modal models in AUC.
AI.conclusion: The approach enhances glaucoma detection performance and can generalize to other retinal diseases such as diabetic retinopathy, indicating broader applicability of balanced MoE in medical multi-modal learning.

title: AMRD: Adaptive Multi-Teacher Relational Distillation for Lightweight Speech Emotion Recognition
summary: On-device speech emotion recognition (SER) is critical for real-time applications, yet large self-supervised models that excel at SER are too costly for edge devices. Multi-teacher knowledge distillation can compress them into a lightweight student, but two challenges remain: teacher reliability varies across batches, and logit-level distillation ignores inter-sample relational structure. We propose Adaptive Multi-teacher Relational Distillation (AMRD) to address both. A one-class SVM on each teacher's logit similarity matrix assigns per-batch weights favoring more coherent teachers. A relational distillation loss aligns teacher and student similarity matrices, capturing structure that logit matching misses. On IEMOCAP and CREMA-D datasets across four student architectures, AMRD outperforms single-teacher distillation baselines in most settings, and ablations confirm both components yield complementary gains.

AI.tldr: Adaptive Multi-teacher Relational Distillation (AMRD) improves on single-teacher distillation for on-device speech emotion recognition by adaptive per-batch weighting of teachers and relational distillation that preserves inter-sample structure, leading to better performance on IEMOCAP and CREMA-D across lightweight student models.
AI.motivation: Two key challenges hinder multi-teacher distillation for SER on edge devices: (1) teacher reliability varies across data batches, causing poor guidance when treated equally, and (2) logit-level distillation loses inter-sample relational information that could be beneficial for emotion separation.
AI.method: AMRD uses a one-class SVM on each teacher's logit similarity matrix to assign per-batch weights, selecting more coherent teachers. It also introduces a relational distillation loss that aligns teacher and student similarity matrices, capturing inter-sample structure beyond individual logits.
AI.result: Across four lightweight student architectures, AMRD outperforms single-teacher distillation baselines in most settings on the IEMOCAP and CREMA-D datasets. Ablation studies show each component provides complementary gains.
AI.conclusion: AMRD effectively combines adaptive teacher weighting with relational distillation to exploit inter-sample relationships and improve on-device SER performance over prior single-teacher approaches.

title: $π\mathbf{R}^2$: Reactive Real-time Flow Policies
summary: Generalist manipulation policies increasingly take the form of action-chunking flow policies built on large pretrained backbones. Such chunks run open-loop, so the policy cannot react to sensory input arriving mid-execution, sacrificing \emph{reactivity}. Replanning more often would restore it, but the perception-to-action pipeline (a large backbone plus multiple denoising steps) is too slow: this \emph{latency} forbids frequent replanning and leaves committed actions stale, making such policies ill-suited for dynamic, closed-loop control. We present $π\mathbf{R}^2$, which makes these policies reactive and real-time while retaining large backbones, expressive multi-modal policies, and multi-action prediction. Built on the per-position noise schedule of diffusion forcing, $π\mathbf{R}^2$ contributes two ideas. First, it splits conditioning into a fast channel (proprioception, fresh every tick) and an asynchronously updated slow channel (vision-language features), so the policy reacts to proprioception within a chunk while tolerating stale vision. Second, a latency-adaptive flow schedule treats in-flight actions as inpainting conditioning and emits actions in one denoising step per call, letting one trained model adapt to varying hardware latency. Requiring minimal modification to existing architectures, $π\mathbf{R}^2$ can be finetuned from a pretrained policy: applied to GR00T-N1.7 on a real xArm6+XHand platform, it replans closed-loop roughly $4\times$ faster than the base policy (~$25$Hz on an A5000 GPU), acting on a fresh observation every $40$ms. Across simulation and real-world manipulation tasks, $π\mathbf{R}^2$ improves the success rate by up to $23\%$ in simulation and $30\%$ in the real world over the strongest baseline. Project page: https://pi-r2-flow.github.io/

AI.tldr: Realtime reactive diffusion-based manipulation policy (πR^2) enabling fast replanning with separated fast proprioception and slow vision channels and a latency-adaptive flow schedule; improves speed and success on XArm6+XHand.
AI.motivation: Address open-loop action-chunking policies and high latency that hinder reactive, closed-loop control in manipulation; retain large backbone and multi-modal capabilities while enabling real-time inference.
AI.method: Introduce per-position diffusion forcing with two conditioning channels (fast proprioception updated every tick; slow asynchronously updated vision-language features) and a latency-adaptive flow schedule that treats in-flight actions as inpainting conditioning and emits actions in one denoising step per call; minimal architectural changes and finetuning from pretrained policies; evaluated on GR00T-N1.7 and real xArm6+XHand.
AI.result: Replanning rate ~4x faster than base policy (~25 Hz on A5000), with fresh observations every 40 ms; up to 23% improvement in simulation and 30% in real-world tasks over strongest baseline; successful on multiple tasks; project page provided.
AI.conclusion: πR^2 offers real-time reactiveness without sacrificing backbone capabilities, enabling fast, adaptive control in manipulation; compatible with pretrained policies and ready for deployment; broad applicability to diffusion-based generalist policies.

title: Chart-Supported or Model-Supplied? Examining MLLM-Generated Claims for Accessible Visualization
comment: Submitted to the 3rd Workshop on Accessible Data Visualization, IEEE VIS 2026
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can connect visualization patterns to external causes, consequences, and domain knowledge, but the evidential basis of these interpretations is often unclear. We present an exploratory study of 102 visualizations from four sources, three MLLMs, and four input conditions that vary access to the image, source-specific accessible chart context, and withheld-context framing. Across 1,224 descriptions, we analyze model-attributed DIRECT, DERIVED, and SPECULATIVE labels and conduct an automated audit of numeric agreement. Accessible chart context shifted Gemini and GPT toward DIRECT claims and improved numeric agreement for some models. Adding the image to the full context did not yield a consistent numeric benefit, and the withheld-context prompt did not reliably increase cautious language. The prompt-defined Real-World Significance section remained predominantly SPECULATIVE. These results motivate accessible description systems that distinguish claims supported by supplied evidence from model-supplied interpretation

AI.tldr: Explores evidential quality of multimodal LLM descriptions of visualizations by classifying claims as DIRECT, DERIVED, or SPECULATIVE across 102 visualizations and 1,224 descriptions. Finds accessible chart context nudges models toward DIRECT claims and improves numeric agreement for some models; adding the image or withheld-context framing has mixed or limited effects; Real-World Significance remains largely speculative. Calls for accessible description systems that separate evidence-supported claims from interpretation.
AI.motivation: Assess how multimodal LLMs attribute evidence in visualization descriptions, quantify the grounds of their claims (DIRECT/DERIVED/SPECULATIVE), and audit numeric agreement across varying context conditions.
AI.method: Exploratory study with 102 visualizations from four sources; three MLLMs; four input conditions varying access to image, chart-context accessibility, and withheld-context framing. Generated 1,224 descriptions; labeled claims as DIRECT, DERIVED, SPECULATIVE; automated audit of numeric agreement.
AI.result: Accessible chart context shifted Gemini and GPT toward DIRECT claims and improved numeric agreement for some models. Adding the image to full context did not yield a consistent numeric benefit. Withheld-context framing did not reliably increase cautious language. Real-World Significance sections remained predominantly SPECULATIVE.
AI.conclusion: Results motivate accessible description systems that distinguish evidence-supported claims from model-supplied interpretation, enabling users to assess when the model’s claims are backed by provided evidence versus when they are interpretive in nature.

title: PanoLess: Environment Reconstruction from Partial Reflective Views
comment: ECCV 2026. Main paper with supplementary material
summary: Reflections from shiny objects and glass facades naturally extend the field of view of a camera, capturing the surrounding environment without the need to pan the camera or acquire a full panorama. We propose PanoLess, a Gaussian-splat-based framework that reconstructs the surrounding environment as a distant illumination map from images captured on only one side of a reflective surface. PanoLess leverages surface-aligned 2D Gaussian splats with deferred shading to recover accurate per-pixel normals and reflection cues, which are fused into a neural cubemap representation of the environment. In addition, PanoLess produces a visibility map that explicitly denotes which regions of the environment are supported by the partial reflective observations. Unlike existing inverse-rendering and reflection-aware Gaussian-splatting approaches, which typically require full 360-degree coverage and struggle under incomplete views, PanoLess enables consistent, physically grounded illumination estimation from partial-view input. We show that PanoLess achieves high-fidelity and geometrically consistent environment reconstruction, outperforming reflection-aware baselines on a new custom synthetic benchmark and publicly available datasets, and demonstrating generalization to real-world reflective captures.

AI.tldr: PanoLess reconstructs distant illumination and the surrounding environment from a single-side observation of reflective surfaces by using surface-aligned 2D Gaussian splats with deferred shading to build a neural cubemap and a visibility map, enabling partial-view, physically grounded illumination estimates that surpass baselines on synthetic and real data.
AI.motivation: To enable robust environment illumination estimation from partial, reflection-based observations, addressing the limitation of existing methods that need full 360-degree coverage and struggle with incomplete views.
AI.method: Utilizes surface-aligned 2D Gaussian splats and deferred shading to recover per-pixel normals and reflection cues, fusing them into a neural cubemap representation of the environment. Produces a visibility map indicating which regions are supported by the partial observations. Evaluated on a new synthetic benchmark and public datasets, with demonstrations on real-world captures.
AI.result: PanoLess achieves high-fidelity, geometrically consistent environment reconstructions and outperforms reflection-aware baselines on synthetic and public benchmarks, with good generalization to real-world reflective captures.
AI.conclusion: The approach enables consistent, physically grounded illumination estimation from partial-view input, while explicitly signaling the supported environmental regions through a visibility map and avoiding dependence on full 360-degree coverage.

title: Breaking the Periodicity Assumption: Robust Tensorial Multi-View Clustering via Graph-Spectral Low-Rank Learning
summary: Tensorial multi-view clustering (TMC) has achieved strong performance due to its ability to capture high-order correlations across multiple views. Most existing t-SVD-based TMC frameworks apply the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) along the sample mode to impose frequency-domain low-rank constraints. However, we reveal that this widely adopted design critically relies on an implicit ``periodicity assumption'' induced by the sample arrangement. When samples are ordered by class, neighboring indices tend to be semantically similar, creating artificial local continuity along the sample mode and a favorable spectral structure for FFT-based low-rank regularization. Once this ordering is removed by random permutation, existing t-SVD-based TMC methods suffer severe performance degradation. This strong sensitivity to class ordering conflicts with the permutation-invariant nature of clustering and indicates that part of the reported performance may be attributed to a privileged sample arrangement rather than genuine high-order structure modeling. In this paper, we systematically investigate this phenomenon and its underlying algebraic and spectral mechanisms. To address this fundamental flaw, we further propose a graph-spectral low-rank tensor learning framework based on the Graph Fourier Transform (GFT), which replaces the fixed Fourier basis along the sample mode with a data-driven graph spectral basis, thereby capturing the intrinsic manifold structure without relying on a particular sample ordering. Moreover, we develop an anchor-based variant to address large-scale datasets efficiently. Extensive experiments on various benchmarks validate our findings and demonstrate the competitive or superior performance of the proposed methods compared with state-of-the-art TMC approaches.

AI.tldr: FFT-based t-SVD TMC is sensitive to sample ordering due to a hidden periodicity bias; replacing the fixed FFT basis with a data-driven graph Fourier transform (GFT) yields a permutation-invariant, robust framework, with an anchor-based scalable variant, achieving competitive or superior results on benchmarks.
AI.motivation: To remove artificial locality and periodicity biases introduced by sample ordering in FFT-based t-SVD TMC and to provide a permutation-invariant, scalable tensor clustering framework.
AI.method: Replace the standard t-SVD FFT along the sample mode with a graph-spectral low-rank tensor learning framework using the Graph Fourier Transform based on a data-driven sample-graph; introduce an anchor-based variant for scalability on large datasets.
AI.result: Empirical results on diverse benchmarks show competitive or superior performance compared with state-of-the-art TMC methods, and reduced sensitivity to sample ordering.
AI.conclusion: A graph-spectral, data-driven basis along the sample mode sidesteps the periodicity assumption of FFT-based TMC, yielding a permutation-invariant, scalable, and effective tensor clustering framework.

title: INTACT: Isomorphic Intent-to-Action Learning for Search-Free World Models
summary: Forward latent world models predict how actions change a scene, but recover actions for a desired change only through expensive test-time search. We introduce INTACT (INtent-To-ACTion), an end-to-end JEPA that turns action-labeled, reward-free trajectories into a deployable intent-to-action interface. Each transition supplies physical intent $z_{t+1}-z_t$, while a future goal supplies deployment intent $\operatorname{sg}(z_g)-z_t$. The architecture is isomorphic between the local and goal motion-intent backbone-input graphs through an identical four-slot grammar and shared parameters, and between supported local and goal motion-intent families through action-law semantics induced by the same predictor rather than pointwise latent equality. INTACT also provides intact transfer from RGB evidence to action-effective latent intent coordinates and from intent families to their corresponding action-law families. Asymmetric endpoint gradients ground physical successors and fix future goals as anchors, joining representation learning and control without pointwise latent matching or globally linear dynamics. The resulting coordinates support a robust distributional action law: its conditional mean serves directly as a search-free policy, while sampling remains available for diversity or optional verification. On the four official LeWM tasks, one-epoch, zero-search models reach 85.78\%, 100.00\%, 97.67\%, and 97.89\% success. Optional local CEM centered on the Direct plan reaches 96.86\% macro success using 384 instead of 9,000 candidate sequences, reducing sampling by $23.44\times$ while improving pure CEM by 16.00 points. One shared four-task encoder reaches 89.39\% E5 Direct macro and improves every task over jointly trained LeWM, while predicted--expert action-family kNN tracks Direct success at $r=0.954$. Direct inference takes 2.9--5.5 ms.

AI.tldr: INTACT is an end-to-end intent-to-action framework for forward latent world models that converts action-labeled, reward-free trajectories into a deployable interface, enabling search-free policies via learned action-law semantics and robust transfer across local and goal motion intents with fast inference.
AI.motivation: To avoid expensive test-time search in forward latent world models by learning a unified intent representation that aligns local and goal motions and imposes action-law semantics, enabling direct, efficient control with robust transfer from RGB evidence.
AI.method: Introduce INTACT with a four-slot grammar and identical backbone-input graphs that are isomorphic across local and goal motion-intent branches. Use asymmetric endpoint gradients to ground successors and anchor goals. Learn action-law semantics via a predictor rather than enforcing pointwise latent equality.
