Provide transfer from RGB evidence to latent intents and between intent families and their action-law counterparts. Train a shared encoder across four tasks; use distributional action laws for a direct mean-policy and stochastic sampling for verification/diversity. Optional CEM refinement on a Direct plan reduces sampling. Evaluate on four LeWM tasks with strong performance and fast direct inference.
AI.result: On four LeWM tasks, one-epoch, zero-search models reach 85.78%, 100.00%, 97.67%, and 97.89% success. Local CEM centered on the Direct plan achieves 96.86% macro success using 384 candidates (23.44x fewer than 9,000) and improves pure CEM by 16.0 points. A shared four-task encoder attains 89.39% E5 Direct macro and improves all tasks vs. joint LeWM training; predicted-expert action-family kNN tracks Direct success at r=0.954. Direct inference latency is 2.9–5.5 ms.
AI.conclusion: INTACT provides a deployable, end-to-end interface that eliminates or reduces test-time search in forward latent world models by leveraging an intent-to-action framework with robust transfer, fast direct inference, and competitive performance on established benchmarks, while enabling sampling for diversity and verification.

title: SAFAARI: Schema-Aware Framework for Accelerated Advertiser Response Intelligence
summary: The evolution of customer support systems is rapidly advancing with agentic chatbots, yet these systems face significant limitations when accessing enterprise data without predefined API endpoints. This paper presents SAFAARI (Schema-Aware Framework for Accelerated Advertiser Response Intelligence), a multi-agent framework that addresses the critical bottleneck of schema linking in Natural Language to SQL (NL-to-SQL) systems through specialized content, metadata, and orchestration agents. We also introduce SEAL (Schema Evaluation and Accuracy in Language-to-SQL), a novel composite metric that holistically evaluates system performance while penalizing inconsistent results. Through systematic experimentation with five feature set configurations, SAFAARI achieves an 81.66% SEAL score (6.65% improvement over baseline), with notable gains in datapoint accuracy (5.51%) and schema-linking precision (4.69%). The framework's effectiveness is validated through human-in-the-loop evaluation with domain experts, which proves its adaptability across diverse support domains. By automating the labor-intensive process of schema linking and query generation, our framework demonstrates 8x reduction in development time while maintaining high accuracy. The solution streamlines API development and enhances self-service capabilities, particularly benefiting customer support enterprises with complex data ecosystems.

AI.tldr: SAFAARI is a multi-agent NL-to-SQL framework addressing schema linking bottlenecks for enterprise data, paired with SEAL, a composite evaluation metric. It shows improved SEAL score, datapoint accuracy, and schema-linking precision, plus an 8x reduction in development time, validated by domain experts across diverse support domains.
AI.motivation: Access to enterprise data by agentic chatbots is hampered by the absence of predefined API endpoints; schema linking is a critical bottleneck in NL-to-SQL systems; need automated, scalable methods and robust evaluation.
AI.method: Develop SAFAARI with specialized content, metadata, and orchestration agents to perform schema linking in NL-to-SQL; introduce SEAL as a holistic performance metric that penalizes inconsistent results; conduct systematic experiments with five feature-set configurations; perform human-in-the-loop evaluation with domain experts; compare against baseline.
AI.result: SAFAARI achieves 81.66% SEAL score, a 6.65% improvement over baseline; datapoint accuracy improves by 5.51%; schema-linking precision improves by 4.69%; 8× reduction in development time; framework validated across diverse support domains.
AI.conclusion: SAFAARI, coupled with SEAL, effectively automates schema linking and query generation, enabling streamlined API development and enhanced self-service for customer-support enterprises operating with complex data ecosystems.

title: Leak-Free Cross-Validated Stacking with Per-Architecture Calibration for Sand-Boil Segmentation in Earthen Levees
comment: 24 pages, 17 figures, 14 tables. Supported by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers under Contract No. W912HZ-23-2-0004
summary: Sand boils, points where water seeping beneath an earthen levee re-emerges at the surface, are early warnings of internal erosion, and deep segmentation networks are increasingly used to find them in inspection photographs. Annotated examples are scarce, and two common ways of working around that scarcity quietly inflate reported accuracy: tuning ensemble weights on the same images later used to score them, and training on synthetic images derived from the very photographs held out for testing. We present a sand-boil segmentation framework that closes both loopholes. Every synthetic image carries a pointer to its real parent, and a per-fold filter excludes any image whose parent is held out; five encoder-decoder backbones are trained under five-fold cross-validation, calibrated by one temperature scalar each, and combined by a per-pixel meta-learner fitted only on out-of-fold predictions. On the held-out test set the proposed Updated SandBoilNet reaches an intersection-over-union of 0.707 over three seeds, against 0.608 for the published original re-evaluated on the same split. Under the stacking protocol the calibrated stack reaches 0.681 against 0.694 for the strongest fold-averaged member, so it does not improve on the best single model; eight meta-learner families reproduce that outcome, which we trace to a mean pairwise error correlation of 0.894 among members. A synthetic pool filtered for label fidelity lifts the champion to 0.718 over three seeds against a 0.707 control. We also introduce a mask-conditioned synthesis route that makes the conditioning mask the label by construction, giving labelled training images at zero annotation cost.

AI.tldr: A leakage-safe sand-boil segmentation framework using parent-linked synthetic data, cross-validated backbones, calibration, and a per-pixel meta-learner; stacking underperforms due to high error correlation, while label-fidelity synthetic data and mask-conditioned synthesis reduce annotation costs.
AI.motivation: Tackling data scarcity and evaluation leakage in sand-boil segmentation to achieve robust generalization without inflating accuracy via using the same images for training and testing or synthetic data derived from test images.
AI.method: Five encoder-decoder backbones trained under five-fold cross-validation with per-fold filtering that excludes images whose synthetic parent is held-out; one temperature scalar per fold for calibration; per-pixel meta-learner for stacking, fitted only on out-of-fold predictions; a synthetic pool filtered for label fidelity; a mask-conditioned synthesis route that makes the conditioning mask the label.
AI.result: On held-out test, Updated SandBoilNet achieves IoU 0.707 (three seeds) vs 0.608 for the re-evaluated baseline; stacking yields 0.681 vs 0.694 for the best fold-averaged member; eight meta-learners replicate the lack of stacking gain due to mean pairwise error correlation of 0.894; a label-fidelity synthetic pool raises the champion to 0.718; mask-conditioned synthesis enables zero-annotation training data.
AI.conclusion: The approach successfully mitigates data leakage and yields robust improvements over a baseline; ensembling offers limited gains when model errors are highly correlated; leveraging label-fidelity synthetic data and mask-conditioned synthesis can further boost performance while reducing annotation costs.

title: Zhinv: Real-time hub-height wind field reconstruction using only local sparse observations
summary: The high proportion of wind power connected to the grid places higher demands on fine-grained knowledge of regional wind fields. Since the wind information directly obtainable in actual operations is mostly sparse, discrete, and irregularly distributed local observations, it is difficult to directly meet the needs of tasks such as wind power regulation, wind resource assessment, and low-altitude environmental perception of continuous regional wind fields. Therefore, we propose Zhinv, an end-to-end reconstruction framework that directly weaves sparse and irregular observations into a fine-grid wind field at hub-height. Experiments in Northeast China, Europe, and Southeast Asia demonstrate that Zhinv can accurately, robustly, and efficiently reconstruct fine-grid wind fields from sparse observations, reducing the error by about 66% compared with Kriging. With local wind-power observations as input, Zhinv enables wind power centers to bypass NWP and complex assimilation processes, supporting direct and real-time wind resource assessment from locally available data.

AI.tldr: An end-to-end framework (Zhinv) reconstructs fine-grid hub-height wind fields from sparse, irregular observations, outperforming Kriging by ~66% error reduction and enabling real-time wind-resource assessment without relying on NWP.
AI.motivation: High penetration of wind power increases the need for fine-grained regional wind fields. Observations are typically sparse, discrete, and irregularly distributed, hindering accurate field reconstruction and real-time assessment; existing interpolation and NWP-based methods are insufficient for operational needs.
AI.method: An end-to-end reconstruction framework (Zhinv) that directly weaves sparse irregular observations into a high-resolution wind field at hub-height. Demonstrated across multiple regions (Northeast China, Europe, Southeast Asia).
AI.result: Zhinv achieves accurate, robust, and efficient reconstruction of fine-grid wind fields from sparse data, reducing error by about 66% compared with Kriging; enables wind centers to bypass NWP/assimilation and perform real-time wind-resource assessment from local observations.
AI.conclusion: Zhinv provides a practical, scalable solution for real-time, fine-grained wind-field reconstruction from sparse data, with demonstrated cross-region effectiveness and potential to simplify wind-resource monitoring.

title: CogEEGAgent: Toward Autonomous Cognitive EEG Analysis with Grounded Execution and Selection-Aware Verification
comment: 16 pages, 5 figures, and 16 tables. The supplementary material is included in the same PDF
summary: Electroencephalography (EEG) analysis in cognitive studies requires specialized expertise and involves many defensible choices over contrasts, channels, time windows, and statistical tests. LLM agents can translate varied natural-language questions into analysis choices, offering a flexible interface for automation. Yet fluent reports alone cannot establish that an agent selected the requested analysis or evaluated a confirmatory claim independently of adaptive search. We present CogEEGAgent, a cognitive-EEG analysis agent grounded in MNE-Python. Its EEG-specific scientific harness separates semantic from scientific authority. The LLM interprets intent and proposes registered analyses, while deterministic components validate typed contracts, control confirmation access, and authorize evidence-bound release. On a prespecified routing benchmark, CogEEGAgent maps language to registered analyses more accurately than a matched deterministic router, while matched preflight makes both systems abstain whenever required. In an externally model-authored, outcome-blind campaign, the complete system releases supported analyses with participant-disjoint confirmation and blocks prespecified capability hazards and lifecycle-reuse requests. Policy stress testing shows that held-out confirmation curbs false positives from uncorrected adaptive search. Together, these studies establish bounded autonomy and an auditable automation framework for cognitive-EEG workflows. More broadly, they show how scientific agents can combine flexible language understanding with fail-closed control over inference and release.

AI.tldr: A language-enabled, auditable EEG-analysis agent (CogEEGAgent) pairs LLM interpretation with deterministic safeguards to map natural-language queries to registered analyses, achieving accurate routing with bounded autonomy and safe release of results.
AI.motivation: To enable flexible, NL-driven cognitive-EEG analyses while ensuring verifiability, reproducibility, and safety through auditable, fail-safe automation.
AI.method: Integrate an LLM for intent recognition and proposed registered analyses with deterministic validators that enforce contracts, control confirmation access, and authorize evidence-bound release; compare routing accuracy against a matched deterministic router; include an externally model-authored, outcome-blind campaign and policy stress tests to assess safety guarantees.
AI.result: CogEEGAgent more accurately maps language to registered analyses than a matched deterministic router; deterministic preflight and abstentions prevent unsafe actions; the complete system releases analyses with participant-disjoint confirmation and blocks specified hazards; policy stress tests show held-out confirmation reduces false positives from adaptive search.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates bounded autonomy and an auditable automation framework for cognitive-EEG workflows, showing how flexible NL understanding can be coupled with fail-closed control over inference and release, with implications for broader scientific automation.

title: Hyperspectral Intrinsic Decomposition: Joint Recovery of Reflectance and Photometric Components for Non-Lambertian Scenes
summary: Hyperspectral intrinsic decomposition (HID) aims to disentangle material-related spectral properties and photometric effects in hyperspectral images (HSIs), which is essential for understanding real-world imaging processes and benefits a variety of downstream applications. Most existing HID studies have been developed under Lambertian or near-Lambertian assumptions. The few prior non-Lambertian efforts rely on simplified specular assumptions insufficient to handle diverse real-world specularity, and typically require auxiliary inputs or recover only a subset of the coupled reflectance and photometric components, hindering complete and blind decomposition. In this paper, we revisit the dichromatic reflection model (DRM) and develop a unified inversion paradigm that reformulates the recovery of four coupled reflectance and photometric components as the estimation of two spectral--spatial target variables. Building on this reformulation, we propose a dual-scale decomposition scheme to handle non-Lambertian effects with distinct spatial characteristics. At the global scale, photometrically invariant descriptors serve as edge priors for high-fidelity intrinsic boundary preservation; at the local scale, specularity-guided attention directs refinement with emphasis on specularity-dominated regions, including those affected by clipping distortion. To facilitate future research, we establish CITE, the first public real-world HID dataset for non-Lambertian objects, and develop a Physically-faithful Intrinsic Set Generator (PISG) for controllable data synthesis. Extensive ablation studies and experiments on the CITE and additional HSIs demonstrate the effectiveness of our method and its robustness across diverse scenes.

AI.tldr: Unified non-Lambertian hyperspectral intrinsic decomposition (HID) via a DRM-based inversion and dual-scale scheme, introducing two spectral–spatial targets, global edge priors, and specularity-guided attention, plus public dataset (CITE) and data generator (PISG).
AI.motivation: Current HID largely assumes Lambertian or near-Lambertian surfaces; non-Lambertian methods are limited by oversimplified specular models, need auxiliary inputs, or recover only partial components, hindering complete blind decomposition. A comprehensive, physically grounded approach for real-world non-Lambertian scenes is needed.
AI.method: Reformulate four coupled reflectance and photometric components as estimation of two spectral–spatial targets within the dark-channel-like DRM framework. Propose a dual-scale decomposition: global scale uses photometrically invariant descriptors as edge priors to preserve intrinsic boundaries; local scale uses specularity-guided attention to refine specularity-dominated regions and handle clipping. Introduce CITE, a public real-world HID dataset for non-Lambertian objects, and PISG, a Physically-faithful Intrinsic Set Generator for controllable synthetic data.
AI.result: Extensive ablation studies and experiments on CITE and additional HSIs demonstrate the method’s effectiveness and robustness across diverse scenes, validating the proposed unified inversion and dual-scale strategy.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a physically grounded, blind HID framework for non-Lambertian HSIs, enabling complete decomposition of reflectance and photometric components, supported by public data resources for future research.

title: Retraction-Free Optimization over the Stiefel Manifold for the LoRA Fine-Tuning
summary: Optimization over the Stiefel manifold plays a significant role in various machine learning tasks. Existing methods either use the retraction operators, requiring costly orthonormalization for large-scale matrices, or employ landing methods that rely on careful step size selection and penalty parameter tuning. To address these challenges, we propose a retraction-free and penalty parameter-free algorithm that directly lands on the manifold. By leveraging the strongly-convex-like property of the quadratic penalty function and the proximal smoothness of the Stiefel manifold, we establish global convergence guarantees with the best-known iteration complexities under both constant and diminishing step sizes. Then, we reformulate the low-rank adaptation (LoRA) fine-tuning problem for large language models as a manifold optimization problem, introducing Manifold-LoRA for geometry-accelerated adaptation. This approach employs the proposed landing technique and a carefully designed step size strategy to accelerate the training process. Numerical experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate the efficiency and strong downstream performance of the proposed method.

AI.tldr: Retraction-free, penalty-free landing on the Stiefel manifold with global convergence guarantees; introduces Manifold-LoRA for geometry-accelerated LoRA fine-tuning; empirical results show efficiency and strong downstream performance.
AI.motivation: Overcoming computational cost of retractions (orthonormalization) and instability of landing methods due to step-size/penalty tuning; extend efficient manifold optimization to large-scale learning tasks, including LLM fine-tuning.
AI.method: Develop a direct-landing algorithm on the Stiefel manifold using a quadratic penalty with strongly-convex-like properties and proximal smoothness to ensure convergence; prove global convergence with optimal iteration complexities under constant and diminishing step sizes. Reformulate LoRA fine-tuning as a manifold optimization problem and apply the landing technique with a carefully designed step-size strategy (Manifold-LoRA).
AI.result: Theoretical results establish global convergence with best-known iteration complexities for both step-size regimes. Practically, Manifold-LoRA accelerates training and yields strong downstream performance on benchmark datasets.
AI.conclusion: A retraction-free, parameter-free optimization framework on the Stiefel manifold is achieved, coupled with a geometry-aware LoRA fine-tuning method that demonstrates efficiency and robust performance in practice.

title: Psychological Influences of Conversational AI: Research and Design Directions for Reducing Harm and Promoting Well-Being
summary: As conversational AI systems become increasingly integrated into daily life, their potential effects on user well-being require ongoing attention. While consumer-facing generalist models can provide benefits, including improved access to information, learning, productivity, self-reflection, and companionship, they also introduce risks, such as emotional entanglement, unhealthy dependence, and the amplification of psychological vulnerabilities. Drawing on prior research and empirical observations of AI chatbot behavior, we propose a set of aspirational directions for guiding the behavior of general-purpose AI systems in ways that may reduce potential psychological harms and support user well-being. We acknowledge the difficulty of systematically assessing the long-term impacts of AI chatbot use and frame these directions as hypotheses for studying how AI behavior may influence users across general interactions, role-playing scenarios, and contexts that could be characterized as providing psychological support. While some proposed directions are supported by existing research and expert insights, others identify open questions and areas requiring deeper study. We hope that this formulation and these hypotheses encourage further discussion, empirical investigation, and exploration of interactive design approaches aimed at better accommodating users' psychological needs and promoting their well-being.

AI.tldr: Proposes aspirational, hypothesis-driven directions to guide general‑purpose AI chatbots to support user well-being and mitigate psychological harms, acknowledging measurement challenges and calling for empirical investigation across interactions and role‑play contexts.
AI.motivation: As conversational AI becomes ubiquitous, balancing benefits (information access, learning, productivity, companionship) with risks (emotional entanglement, dependency, vulnerability amplification) and safeguarding user well‑being.
AI.method: Synthesis of prior research and empirical observations; frames directions as hypotheses; discusses interactions, role‑play, and contexts of psychological support; distinguishes supported vs open questions; suggests design approaches and empirical study.
AI.result: A set of aspirational directions framed as hypotheses intended to guide AI behavior toward reducing harm and supporting well‑being; not all directions are fully proven; some are supported by evidence, others require further study.
AI.conclusion: Encourages further discussion, empirical investigation, and design exploration to better accommodate users' psychological needs and well‑being; acknowledges long‑term impact assessment challenges.

title: Gaussian Volumetric Representation for Efficient Shear-Warp Visualization
summary: Medical image visualization requires volumetric rendering algorithms that preserve anatomical fidelity while maintaining high rendering speeds. To address the high computational cost of large volumetric datasets, we propose a Gaussian-based volumetric representation for efficient visualization of dense medical volumes without compromising structural and radiometric details. We optimize the proposed representation using Monte Carlo volumetric estimation, which enables training on a highly sparse subset of voxels while maintaining consistency with the dense volumetric objective. In addition, we introduce a curriculum learning strategy that progressively incorporates structured slice-based sampling during training. Sparse voxel samples provide an early global coverage of the volume, while slice samples capture spatially correlated regions that aid geometric structure and texture continuity. This combination enables the Gaussian representation to learn anatomical details of various structures and corresponding textures from sparse supervision while significantly reducing the computational cost associated with dense voxel processing. The learned representation supports slice-based rendering methods such as shear-warp volume rendering, enabling efficient visualization of multimodal medical datasets including MRI and Cryosection volumes while preserving anatomical structures. Using sparse supervision, our method achieves up to 43.86 FPS rendering with a compression ratio of 11.31:1.

AI.tldr: Gaussian-based volumetric representation enables fast, high-fidelity medical visualization by learning a dense volume with sparse supervision using Monte Carlo estimation and curriculum learning, achieving up to 43.86 FPS and 11.31:1 compression, compatible with slice-based rendering (e.g., shear-warp) on multimodal data.
AI.motivation: Address the high computational cost of rendering large medical volumes while preserving anatomical and radiometric fidelity; enable real-time or near-real-time visualization by learning compact representations from sparse supervision.
AI.method: Propose a Gaussian-based volumetric representation optimized via Monte Carlo volumetric estimation. Train on a highly sparse voxel subset with a curriculum learning strategy that combines structured slice-based sampling. Sparse voxels provide global coverage; slice samples capture spatially correlated regions to maintain geometric and textural continuity. The learned representation supports slice-based rendering methods (e.g., shear-warp).
AI.result: Achieves accelerated rendering with up to 43.86 FPS and a compression ratio of 11.31:1 on multimodal volumes such as MRI and cryosection data, while preserving anatomical structures and textures.
AI.conclusion: The approach delivers fast, memory-efficient visualization of dense medical volumes with preserved anatomical fidelity and radiometric details, enabling efficient, real-time-like exploration of multimodal datasets using slice-based rendering.

title: Guiding Posterior Exploration with Optimizer-Derived Geometry
comment: Accepted for presentation at the OPTIMAL Workshop at AISTATS 2026
summary: Sampling-based methods offer a principled approach to uncertainty quantification in Bayesian neural networks. Their practical use, however, is often challenged by the computational cost of exploring high-dimensional and multimodal posterior distributions. To overcome these difficulties, Bayesian Deep Ensembles, i.e., warmstarting the sampling from several optimized solutions, have proven to be an effective strategy. In this paper, we demonstrate that curvature estimates computed during the warmstart as a byproduct in adaptive optimizers such as AdamW can inform the sampling phase at negligible additional cost. Specifically, our proposed preconditioned sampling strategy based on optimizer-derived geometries can substantially reduce or even eliminate the need for a lengthy sampling burn-in phase and leads to greater numerical stability. This approach consistently maintains or improves predictive performance and uncertainty quantification without any additional computational costs. We confirm the consistency of our findings across various datasets and network architectures.

AI.tldr: Optimizer-derived curvature preconditions enable efficient Bayesian sampling, reducing burn-in and stabilizing uncertainty without extra cost.
AI.motivation: Uncertainty quantification in Bayesian neural networks via sampling is costly in high-dimensional, multimodal posteriors; warmstarted Bayesian Deep Ensembles help but require burn-in; leverage AdamW curvature to accelerate and stabilize sampling.
AI.method: Derive curvature estimates during warmstart from adaptive optimizer (AdamW) and use them to precondition the sampling process; implement a preconditioned sampling strategy based on optimizer geometries; evaluate across datasets and architectures.
AI.result: Burn-in can be substantially reduced or eliminated; improved numerical stability; predictive performance and uncertainty quantification maintained or improved; results consistent across datasets and networks; no additional computational cost.
AI.conclusion: Optimizer-derived geometries are effective priors for Bayesian sampling, enabling more scalable and reliable Bayesian deep ensembles.

title: HOME: Robust Hough-space Matching Method for Structured and Textureless Videos
summary: Visual front-ends for robotic localization typically rely on point-based features such as Oriented FAST and Rotated BRIEF (ORB), which frequently fail in structured environments dominated by strong linear structures or textureless surfaces. While line-based Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) systems mitigate this by utilizing line segments, conventional line extraction and description algorithms are computationally prohibitive for real-time edge robotics. To address this fundamental bottleneck, we propose HOME (Hough-space One-dimensional Matching of Extrema), an ultra-lightweight, training-free feature matching framework. HOME transforms images into Hough space, mapping global linear structures to stable local extrema, which serve as keypoints, thereby reformulating complex line matching into highly efficient one-dimensional point matching. The proposed 1D radial descriptor mathematically guarantees rotational and translational invariance without the overhead of explicit orientation estimation. As a proof of concept to validate the matching accuracy and efficiency of HOME, this paper focuses on homography estimation. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that HOME achieves robust registration in challenging scenarios where point-based methods fail, operating at a much faster speed than existing line-based methods. Extending this robust matching engine to full 3D pose estimation remains a highly promising future direction.

AI.tldr: HOME: a training-free, ultra-lightweight line-based feature matching framework that maps global linear structures into stable local extrema in Hough space, turning line matching into 1D extrema matching with a 1D radial descriptor that is rotational and translational invariant; demonstrated as a homography-estimation proof-of-concept; claims robust, fast, outperforming existing line-based methods; future work includes extending to full 3D pose estimation.
AI.motivation: Point-based features (e.g., ORB) underperform in structured, textureless, or line-dominated environments. Line-based SLAM offers robustness but traditional line extraction/description is computationally expensive for real-time robotics. A lightweight, training-free approach to reliable line-based matching is needed.
AI.method: Transform images into Hough space to reveal stable local extrema corresponding to global linear structures; use these extrema as keypoints. Reformulate line matching as 1D point matching on a radial descriptor that provides rotation and translation invariance without explicit orientation estimation.
AI.result: Extensive evaluations show robust image registration in challenging scenarios where point-based methods fail, with significantly faster performance than existing line-based methods in the context of homography estimation.
AI.conclusion: HOME provides an ultra-lightweight, training-free line-based matching paradigm by leveraging Hough-space extrema and a 1D radial descriptor, enabling robust and fast registration; extension to full 3D pose estimation is a promising future direction.

title: Similar Models Learn Differently: Final-Window Pretraining Shapes Post-Training Beyond SFT
summary: Developers judge a model checkpoint by how it behaves. After supervised fine-tuning (SFT), two checkpoints that perform about the same across relevant benchmarks are treated as interchangeable, equally ready for the next alignment stage, typically preference optimization. We ask whether this judgment misses a pretraining imprint: a difference that no post-SFT benchmark reveals, yet that decides how each checkpoint responds to further training. To find out, we run a controlled experiment on the final window of pretraining, the last data trained on before instruction tuning. Six branches fork from one partially pretrained checkpoint and differ only in this window: 500 million tokens, 0.1% to 1% of the tokens that precede it. Each branch trains its window on a single data source: generic web text, filtered web text, normative discourse, safety text, mathematical text, or synthetic educational text. SFT and post-training are then identical. After SFT the branches behave near-identically, within about one point on instruction following, refusal, and capability, yet the same post-training carries them to very different endpoints, under both a direct preference optimization update and a reinforcement learning update with a verifiable reward. We measure this deviation through refusal of harmful requests: when post-training begins the safety text branch refuses no more than the web text branch, yet by the end it has lost far less of its refusal. The other four branches gain little or no protection, so the effect is selective to what the window contained. The protection requires the safety text to arrive last rather than earlier in pretraining, and it reproduces on a second model family. What a model is pretrained on last shapes how it reacts to alignment. Therefore, a checkpoint should not be evaluated by its post-SFT behavior alone, and what it was trained on last should be reported with it.

AI.tldr: Pretraining last data imprints alignment outcomes: a tiny last-window data window (0.1%-1% of tokens) from different data sources changes post-alignment behavior, especially safety/refusal, despite near-identical post-SFT behavior. This imprint means evaluation should report what data was last used in pretraining, not just post-SFT performance.
AI.motivation: Investigate whether post-SFT benchmarks fully capture a model's readiness for alignment by uncovering latent pretraining imprints that influence response to subsequent training.
AI.method: Create six branches from one partially pretrained checkpoint differing only in the last pretraining window (0.1%-1% of tokens) trained on distinct data sources (generic web text, filtered web text, normative discourse, safety text, mathematical text, synthetic educational text). After identical SFT and post-training, assess instruction following, refusal, and capability under direct preference optimization and RL with verifiable reward, focusing on refusal of harmful requests.
AI.result: Post-SFT behavior converges across branches, but post-training diverges significantly; the 'safety text last' branch preserves higher refusal rates and is protected from degradation during alignment; other branches show little protection. The effect is selective to the window content and requires safety text to be last; reproduces on a second model family.
AI.conclusion: A model's alignment response is shaped by the content of its last pretraining data window. Therefore, evaluating checkpoints solely by post-SFT behavior is insufficient; researchers should report the content of the last pretraining data window.

title: Explainable AI for Chronic Kidney Disease Prediction Using Simulated Federated Learning
summary: Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD), characterized by the gradual loss of kidney function, remains a significant public health challenge. Early detection is crucial for preventing severe complications and enhancing patient outcomes. In this study, Federated Learning (FL) with a VotingClassifier was used to predict CKD using a clinical dataset, where Random Forest, AdaBoost, and XGBoost were utilized to compare and identify the best-fitting model for the global server. Additionally, GridSearchCV was applied to optimize the models' performance on the client's side. To enhance model transparency and trustworthiness, explainable AI (XAI) techniques were incorporated to interpret the prediction mechanisms. The global model's average accuracy was 99%, highlighting the potential of interpretable FL models in supporting early CKD diagnosis and advancing data-driven healthcare solutions.

AI.tldr: Federated Learning with a VotingClassifier ensemble (RF, AdaBoost, XGBoost) applied to CKD prediction; GridSearchCV used for client-side tuning; XAI for interpretability; reported global model accuracy of 99%.
AI.motivation: Address privacy-preserving, data-efficient CKD prediction across distributed clinical datasets while ensuring model transparency and trust.
AI.method: Federated Learning framework using a VotingClassifier to aggregate three base models (Random Forest, AdaBoost, XGBoost); the global server selects the best-fitting model; GridSearchCV performs hyperparameter tuning on each client; XAI methods are employed to interpret predictions.
AI.result: Global model achieved an average accuracy of 99%, suggesting high predictive performance and potential for interpretable FL in CKD diagnosis.
AI.conclusion: Interpretable FL models show promise for early CKD detection; to establish generalizability and deployment viability, further validation across heterogeneous datasets and exploration of privacy-preserving and calibration aspects are needed.

title: Pictura: Perspective-View Self-Play at Scale for Driving
summary: Self-play in simulation produces robust driving policies at scale. Demonstrations of such behavior have been made using privileged vectorized observations such as exact poses and velocities, even for occluded agents. This assumes that perception is solved and introduces a representation gap with the partial observation of a deployed agent driving from the perspective view of egocentric cameras. A common fix, distilling the privileged policy into a camera-input student, leaves the student imitating decisions its own view cannot justify. Instead, we establish perspective-view self-play as a practical training regime. We introduce Pictura, a GPU-accelerated multi-agent driving simulator that renders each agent's egocentric view at every step, mitigating the representation gap at its source. Pictura sustains up to 500K agent-steps/s (2M images/s) on a single H100. Using Pictura, we train Alberti by self-play with plain PPO. It is the first large-scale driving self-play policy trained directly from perspective images, without privileged observations. Training spans 50B agent steps for ~35M km of driving. It approaches the driving performance of its privileged vectorized counterpart, and transfers zero-shot to Waymo Open Motion Dataset layouts re-rendered in Pictura, where it outperforms privileged vectorized agents. Project page: https://valeoai.github.io/Pictura/

AI.tldr: Introduces Pictura, a GPU-accelerated, perspective-view driving simulator enabling self-play training directly from egocentric images; with 50B agent steps (~35M km), it closes the gap to privileged policies and achieves zero-shot transfer to re-rendered Waymo layouts, outperforming vectorized agents.
AI.motivation: Address the representation gap between privileged, vectorized observations and real-world driving from egocentric camera inputs. Traditional distillation from privileged policies into camera-input students can misalign decisions with the student’s own view; a training regime that uses perspective views end-to-end is needed.
AI.method: Introduce Pictura to render each agent’s egocentric view at every timestep, achieving high-throughput simulation (up to 500K agent-steps/s, ~2M images/s on a single H100). Train Alberti with plain PPO via large-scale self-play (50B agent steps, ~35M km). Zero-shot transfer evaluations on Waymo Open Motion Dataset layouts re-rendered in Pictura.
AI.result: Alberti’s performance approaches that of its privileged vectorized counterpart. It transfers zero-shot to Waymo Open Motion layouts re-rendered in Pictura and outperforms privileged vectorized agents on those layouts.
AI.conclusion: Perspective-view self-play in a GPU-accelerated simulator closes the representation gap and enables scalable, image-based driving policy training that transfers across datasets without privileged observations.

title: Addressable Recall Compaction for Long Context-Window Control in AI Agents
summary: Long-horizon LLM agents accumulate reasoning traces, actions, and tool observations that can eventually exceed a model's fixed context window. Existing compaction methods address this limitation by discarding, summarizing, or retrieving earlier information, but they may remove task-critical details or fail to recover them reliably. We propose ARC (Addressable Recall Compaction), a context-management framework that separates archival storage from active-context presentation. ARC stores tool observations in an append-only, ID-addressable log and replaces older observations with compact citations when compaction is required. The agent can subsequently use these identifiers to request stored content without re-executing the corresponding tools or depending solely on similarity-based retrieval. We evaluate ARC using Qwen3-8B with a 16k context window and Qwen3-32B with a 32k context window. On the Needle-in-a-Haystack evaluation, ARC achieves an average exact-answer accuracy of 99.40%, compared with 88.12% for the best-performing baseline in our evaluation. ARC also reduces estimated serving time and HBM traffic under our hardware-cost model. On the LongBench-v2 Hard subset, ARC obtains an average accuracy of 29.97%, compared with 28.25% for the best-performing baseline. These results indicate that explicit, address-based recall can improve information retention and serving efficiency relative to the evaluated context-management baselines under the tested settings.

AI.tldr: ARC provides addressable archival recall to manage long-horizon context, outperforming baselines on Needle-in-a-Haystack and LongBench-v2 Hard.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon LLM agents accumulate reasoning traces, actions, and tool observations that can exhaust fixed context windows. Traditional compaction risks losing task-critical details or failing to reliably recover them. ARC separates archival storage from active context to preserve information and enable precise recall.
AI.method: ARC stores tool observations in an append-only, ID-addressable log (archival storage) and replaces older observations with compact citations in the active context. The agent can use these identifiers to fetch stored content on demand, avoiding re-execution of tools and avoiding reliance on similarity-based retrieval.
AI.result: On Needle-in-a-Haystack evaluation, ARC achieves average exact-answer accuracy of 99.40% vs 88.12% for the best-performing baseline. ARC also reduces serving time and HBM traffic under a hardware-cost model. On LongBench-v2 Hard, ARC achieves 29.97% average accuracy vs 28.25% for the best baseline.
AI.conclusion: Explicit, address-based recall improves information retention and serving efficiency relative to evaluated context-management baselines under the tested settings.

title: Noise-Free One-Step LoRA for Task-Driven Image Restoration with Diffusion Priors
summary: Degraded images not only reduce visual quality but also impair downstream high-level vision tasks. Task-driven image restoration (TDIR) addresses this issue by jointly optimizing restoration quality and task performance. Recent works show that pretrained diffusion priors benefit TDIR, yet diffusion-based restoration is inherently stochastic, as the sampling process depends on a random noise term, which can undermine task consistency. In this paper, we show that a deterministic, noise-free one-step forward pass with pretrained diffusion priors can substantially improve TDIR, but the benefit critically depends on the adaptation module: LoRA yields consistent gains, whereas ControlNet-style conditioning does not. This enables one-step forwarding that surpasses conventional multi-step diffusion TDIR baselines. Furthermore, we introduce a task-preserving GAN training strategy that improves perceptual quality without sacrificing task performance. Extensive experiments on classification, segmentation, and detection demonstrate consistent gains over prior TDIR methods, and we further validate generalization on real-world degraded images and OCR.

AI.tldr: One-step deterministic forward pass with pretrained diffusion priors improves task-driven image restoration; LoRA adaptation yields consistent gains, while ControlNet-style conditioning does not. A task-preserving GAN training strategy further improves perceptual quality without hurting task performance. Gains are demonstrated across classification, segmentation, detection, and real-world/degraded images including OCR.
AI.motivation: TDIR is hampered by the stochastic nature of diffusion-based restoration, which can reduce task consistency and performance. A deterministic, data-efficient approach using diffusion priors aims to stabilize task-driven restoration.
AI.method: Employ a deterministic, noise-free one-step forward pass with pretrained diffusion priors. Evaluate adaptation modules: LoRA vs ControlNet-style conditioning. Introduce a task-preserving GAN training strategy to improve perceptual quality while maintaining task performance.
AI.result: The one-step forward method with LoRA adaptation surpasses multi-step diffusion TDIR baselines. ControlNet-style conditioning does not yield consistent task gains. The GAN-based training improves perceptual quality without sacrificing task accuracy. Experiments on classification, segmentation, detection show consistent gains; generalization confirmed on real-world degraded images and OCR.
AI.conclusion: Deterministic, one-step diffusion priors with appropriate adaptation (LoRA) offer effective, stable gains for TDIR. The added task-preserving GAN training further enhances perceptual quality, with strong cross-task and real-world generalization.

title: Raven: High-Recall Sequence Modeling with Sparse Memory Routing
summary: Long-context recall in linear-time sequence models highlights a tradeoff in how they write to memory. State-based linear models, such as state-space models (SSMs) and linear Transformers, write densely, updating the entire state for each newly arrived token, which leads to interference and makes specific past tokens hard to recover. Sliding-window attention (SWA) exhibits the opposite behavior: it writes sparsely by storing explicit token representations, but only within a fixed window, so recall drops once the relevant token is evicted. Interpolating between these models, we introduce Raven, a linear-time sequence model that maintains a fixed set of memory slots and, at each step, decays and updates only a selected subset via learned, input-dependent routing. This lets Raven mitigate SWA's position-based overwriting and hard eviction while reducing interference from dense state updates in SSMs, thereby preserving long-range content much more effectively. Across recall-intensive benchmarks, Raven is competitive with or outperforms prior linear-time baselines, achieving strong long-context recall where both SWA and SSMs sharply degrade. It remains effective when extrapolating to context lengths as large as 16x its training length, with similar gains in hybrid architectures.

AI.tldr: Raven is a linear-time sequence model that uses a fixed memory slot set with input-dependent routing to improve long-context recall over state-based models and sliding-window attention.
AI.motivation: To overcome the fundamental trade-off in long-context linear models: dense writes cause interference and degradation of specific past tokens (state-space models), whereas sparse, fixed-window memory (sliding-window attention) suffers from eviction and loss of recall beyond the window.
AI.method: Raven maintains a fixed set of memory slots and, at each step, decays and updates only a selected subset through learned, input-dependent routing. This selectively updates memory to interpolate between state-space models and sliding-window attention, reducing both interference and hard eviction. The approach preserves long-range content and extends to hybrid architectures.
AI.result: On recall-intensive benchmarks, Raven matches or surpasses prior linear-time baselines, showing strong long-context recall where SWA and SSMs degrade. It generalizes well to context lengths up to 16x its training length, with similar gains in hybrid models.
AI.conclusion: Raven mitigates the overwriting tendencies of SWA and the dense interference of SSMs, yielding improved long-range recall in linear-time sequence models and enabling effective extrapolation to very long contexts.

title: How Often Should a Recommender Call an LLM? Value-Weighted Routing, Monitoring, and Seasonal Robustness
summary: Routing decisions between a cheap heuristic and an expensive large language model (LLM) are typically framed as a difficulty problem: send the hard cases to the expensive path. We argue this framing is incomplete because difficulty and business value are distinct axes - a difficult cheap item and a difficult costly item do not have the same cost of error. We present Value Router, a fully synthetic simulation of a retail merchandising pipeline that routes items using only estimated difficulty and estimated value, never ground truth. The study has three stages. First, a value-weighted threshold router is compared with a difficulty-only and a random baseline on a synthetic catalog with an inverse correlation between category volume and value. Value-weighting matches the difficulty-only baseline's recall of true high-value items (60%) while achieving substantially higher precision (98.3% vs. 94.3%). Second, a decision logger and monitor expose a failure mode hidden by aggregate metrics showing that the aggregate result is driven almost entirely by between-category differences rather than per-item discrimination. Third, a simulated Black Friday demand surge (2.5 volume with a shift toward higher-value categories) compares a static router, a seasonally tuned router, and two slow-path budget policies. All results are from a controlled synthetic simulation with experimenter-defined ground truth and illustrate design principles for cost-aware routing systems rather than validated real-world claims.

AI.tldr: Value Router introduces a synthetic, cost-aware routing framework that uses estimated difficulty and value to decide whether to send items to cheap heuristics or expensive LLMs; in synthetic experiments it improves precision while preserving recall, but conclusions are limited to synthetic settings.
AI.motivation: Difficulty alone is insufficient for routing decisions because business value and cost of error differ; need cost-aware routing that optimizes for value rather than difficulty alone.
AI.method: A fully synthetic retail pipeline is built; Stage 1 compares a value-weighted threshold router vs difficulty-only and random baselines on a catalog with inverse volume-value correlation; Stage 2 logs decisions to reveal per-item discrimination vs aggregate; Stage 3 simulates Black Friday demand surge and compares static, seasonally tuned, and two slow-path budget policies; experiments use ground-truth defined by the experimenter.
AI.result: Value-weighted router matches recall of high-value items (60%) but achieves higher precision (98.3% vs. 94.3%); a hidden failure mode shows aggregate metrics are dominated by cross-category differences rather than per-item discrimination; under demand surge, router performance varies with policy; results are purely synthetic with experimenter-defined ground truth and do not validate real-world claims.
AI.conclusion: The study illustrates design principles for cost-aware routing and cautions against overreliance on aggregate metrics; demonstrates potential for improving precision by incorporating business value into routing decisions, but claims are limited to synthetic simulations and require real-world validation.

title: RDVSv2: A Large-scale Benchmark for RGB-D Video Salient Object Detection
summary: We introduce RDVSv2, a large-scale benchmark for RGB-D video salient object detection (RGB-D VSOD) with dense frame-level annotations. Existing datasets in this emerging field are often limited in scale and annotation quality, while also relying on less geometry-consistent depth cues. To address these limitations, RDVSv2 is built from publicly accessible stereoscopic online videos and contains 249 video sequences with 29,077 annotated frames. It includes depth maps derived from stereoscopic videos, together with frame-wise salient object masks annotated with eye-tracking guidance. Compared with existing datasets, RDVSv2 is much larger in scale and covers more diverse and challenging scenarios. In addition, we establish a strong baseline for RGB-D VSOD based on Segment Anything Model 2 (SAM2). Specifically, we employ a parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) strategy to adapt the SAM2 encoder to jointly encode RGB, depth, and optical flow cues. Extensive experiments show that RDVSv2 is substantially more challenging for existing RGB-D VSOD methods. Meanwhile, the proposed baseline achieves state-of-the-art results on RDVSv2 and existing RGB-D VSOD benchmarks. We hope that RDVSv2 and the provided baseline will serve as useful resources for future research on RGB-D VSOD and related multi-modal video understanding tasks. Our dataset and code will be available at https://github.com/ltynick/RDVSv2.

AI.tldr: RDVSv2 is a large-scale RGB-D VSOD benchmark (249 videos, 29,077 frames) with stereo-derived depth and eye-tracking masks, plus a SAM2-based PEFT multi-modal baseline; shows RDVSv2 is more challenging for existing methods while achieving SOTA results on both RDVSv2 and prior benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing RGB-D VSOD datasets suffer from limited scale and annotation quality, and depth cues that lack geometry-consistency. A larger, better-annotated benchmark with reliable depth and multi-modal cues is needed to drive progress and robust baselines.
AI.method: Construct RDVSv2 from publicly accessible stereoscopic videos, producing 29,077 frames with depth maps derived from stereo geometry and frame-wise eye-tracking saliency masks. Establish a strong baseline by fine-tuning SAM2 with a parameter-efficient approach to jointly encode RGB, depth, and optical flow cues, enabling RGB-D VSOD performance improvements.
AI.result: RDVSv2 is notably larger and more challenging than existing datasets; the SAM2-based PEFT baseline achieves state-of-the-art results on RDVSv2 and on existing RGB-D VSOD benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: RDVSv2 and the accompanying baseline are valuable resources for future RGB-D VSOD and multi-modal video understanding research, with dataset and code released at the authors' GitHub.

title: Rethinking Likelihood distributions: Student's t Likelihood Boosts Bayesian Neural Network Performance
summary: In Bayesian neural networks (BNNs), variational inference is a widely adopted framework for modeling uncertainty in a distributional way, with the evidence lower bound (ELBO) serving as the standard objective function. Several distributions contribute to the ELBO loss, such as the prior, approximated posterior, and likelihood distribution. Typically, these distributions are all approximated by a Gaussian distribution, since it is easy to compute, allows for reparameterized gradients, and provides a closed-form loss for training. However, several works have highlighted that this assumption may not generally hold, posing the risk of model misspecification. Alternative distributions have been proposed for the prior specifically, while the effect of distribution choice on the likelihood distribution remains unexplored. In this work, our aim is to close this gap by investigating whether alternative assumptions for the likelihood distribution can outperform the commonly used Gaussian. We compare several likelihood distribution assumptions, such as skewed or heavy-tailed, across regression tasks on both artificial and real-world datasets using standard multilayer perceptrons (MLPs). Our findings demonstrate that Student's t yields better predictive performance than a Gaussian likelihood distribution, independent of the data distribution and MLP architecture (depth and width). In some cases, Student's t can also lead to shorter training times, while still being easy to implement.

AI.tldr: Student's t likelihood improves Bayesian neural net regression over Gaussian likelihood across datasets and MLP architectures; sometimes faster to train; robust performance to data distribution and model size.
AI.motivation: Gaussian likelihood is standard in VI for BNNs but can cause misspecification; likelihood choice has been understudied compared to priors, particularly for regression tasks; investigate whether non-Gaussian, heavy-tailed or skewed likelihoods yield better predictions.
AI.method: Empirical evaluation on regression tasks using standard MLPs (varying depth/width); compare Gaussian vs skewed/heavy-tailed likelihoods (notably Student's t) within the ELBO framework; test on artificial and real-world datasets; assess predictive performance and training time.
AI.result: Student's t likelihood yields better predictive performance than Gaussian across data distributions and architectures; in some cases it also shortens training time; easy to implement.
AI.conclusion: Non-Gaussian likelihoods, especially Student's t, can improve BNN regression performance and training efficiency, suggesting broader exploration of likelihood choices in VI for BNNs; future work could include other non-Gaussian likelihoods, learning degrees of freedom, and extensions to classification tasks.

title: Towards an Agent Operating System - Lessons from Classical and Cloud OS
summary: Every major wave of platform software follows the same arc: an initial period of experimentation with competing frameworks and ad-hoc implementations, followed by the articulation of a small set of stable abstractions with well-defined semantics, and finally consolidation around those abstractions into a platform that applications can portably target. POSIX did this for classical operating systems; Kubernetes did it for the cloud. Agentic AI systems - autonomous, LLM-driven agents that plan, use tools, maintain memory, and collaborate - are currently in the experimentation phase of the third such wave. dozens of frameworks and protocols have emerged, but no community consensus exists on what the core abstractions are or what guarantees they carry. Without that consensus, agentic applications cannot be written portably, platforms cannot compose reliably, and the field cannot advance beyond prototype deployments. We argue that the path forward is to follow the prior-wave methodology: derive new agentic abstractions by extending classical OS and cloud OS primitives to stochastic, natural-language-mediated execution, specify their semantics precisely, and consolidate around them - just as POSIX and Kubernetes consolidated their respective waves.

AI.tldr: Agentic AI systems are still in the experimentation phase of the third wave of platform software. The authors propose deriving stable abstractions by extending classical OS and cloud primitives to stochastic, NL-mediated execution, formally specifying semantics, and consolidating around these abstractions to enable portable, reliable agentic applications.
AI.motivation: To overcome fragmentation among agentic AI frameworks and enable portable, composable, and reliable platforms by establishing a shared, formally defined set of core abstractions.
AI.method: Extend classical OS/cloud primitives to support stochastic, natural-language-mediated execution; specify precise semantics; advocate consolidation around a common abstraction layer.
AI.result: A roadmap to standardize agentic abstractions, drawing parallels with POSIX/Kubernetes, to improve portability, interoperability, and platform reliability.
AI.conclusion: Adopt the prior-wave methodology: derive new agentic abstractions from established OS/cloud primitives, formalize them, and converge on a unified set of core abstractions to advance the field.

title: Towards Reliable Stain Transfer: An Iterative Data-Model Co-Optimization Framework Based on Multimodal Expert-Guided Assessment
comment: 10 pages, accepted by ACMMM2026 Main Track
summary: Histopathological examination primarily relies on hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) and immunohistochemistry (IHC) staining. Although IHC provides critical molecular information, it is costly and requires specialized expertise. Stain transfer provides an efficient alternative by computationally generating IHC from H&E images, but remains challenged by unified and interpretable modeling for heterogeneous biomarkers under pixel-unaligned supervision. We propose DMCoStain, a novel Data-Model Co-optimization framework for Stain transfer. It iteratively co-refines training data and model capability, improving staining accuracy and interpretability in both pathological and structural consistency. To refine training data in a clinically meaningful manner, it incorporates the Multimodal Expert-Guided Finer Selection (MEGFS) strategy, built upon a pioneering IHC-positive-expression (IPE) vision-language model (VLM) that emulates pathologist reasoning. To support MEGFS, we construct ImmunoInstruction, the first large-scale IPE instruction-following dataset with 150K VQA samples. Extensive experiments on multiple tissues and biomarkers demonstrate that DMCoStain achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) accuracy. This paradigm offers strong practical value, and MEGFS also functions as a specialized evaluation tool for future model development. Dataset, code, and more details are in https://github.com/SikangSHU/DMCoStain.

AI.tldr: DMCoStain introduces Data-Model Co-optimization for stain transfer to generate IHC from H&E, using MEGFS guided data refinement based on an IPE vision-language model and a large ImmunoInstruction dataset, achieving state-of-the-art staining accuracy across tissues and biomarkers.
AI.motivation: IHC provides essential molecular information but is expensive and requires specialized expertise. Stain transfer aims to efficiently generate IHC from H&E but faces challenges in unified, interpretable modeling under pixel-unaligned supervision; need data-driven, clinically meaningful refinement and robust evaluation.
AI.method: Iterative data-model co-optimization (DMCoStain). MEGFS selects training data guided by an IHC-positive-expression (IPE) vision-language model that mimics pathologist reasoning. ImmunoInstruction (150k VQA samples) underpins MEGFS. The approach refines training data and model capability to improve staining accuracy and interpretability while maintaining pathological and structural consistency.
AI.result: Demonstrates state-of-the-art (SOTA) accuracy for stain transfer across multiple tissues and biomarkers. Presents a practical framework with MEGFS functioning as a specialized evaluation tool for future model development; dataset and code are provided.
AI.conclusion: DMCoStain advances stain transfer through data-model co-optimization and a clinically aligned data refinement strategy, yielding improved accuracy and interpretability. The work also supplies the ImmunoInstruction dataset and code, promoting further research and clinical translation.

title: Learned, Relied Upon, or Necessary? Separating Checkpoint Dependence from Task-Level Value in Sheaf GNNs
summary: Learned restriction maps in sheaf graph neural networks are often treated as proof that the model has discovered useful edge geometry. That conclusion does not follow from parameter movement or from a post-hoc ablation: both can show how one checkpoint is organized while leaving open whether learned transport still helps after the rest of the model adapts. We separate these claims with two estimands. Checkpoint reliance intervenes on the maps of a fixed predictor; protocol-relative replacement retrains matched families that remove map capacity, edge variation, or persistent edge assignment. A task-null theorem shows why the claims can diverge: labels identify only the transported classifier directions, leaving $d^2-d$ invisible degrees of freedom in every full $d\times d$ map. An exact frame model then gives the boundary at which reliance becomes unreplaced task value. Label-only training realizes the predicted separation, while audits of public NSD, DNSD, and Directed Sheaf Neural Network (DSNN) implementations recover both replaceable and unreplaced transport regimes on real graphs. All five DNSD benchmarks exhibit fixed-checkpoint reliance. After retraining, assignment-breaking or shared-map controls recover Full performance on four; Roman-Empire retains a $.0675$ advantage over continually resampled assignment and a $.0391$ advantage over a parameter-matched shared map across ten official splits. Thus, a learned map can govern a fitted computation without constituting indispensable edge geometry. Claims of learned transport should pair checkpoint interventions with matched retraining.

AI.tldr: Learned transport in restriction maps of DNSD/DSNN graphs can be confounded by training artifacts; two estimands (checkpoint reliance and retraining-based replacement) reveal that maps may be replaceable or not, challenging the interpretation that learned maps encode indispensable edge geometry. A task-null theorem explains divergence, and an exact frame model bounds reliance. Label-only training supports separation; real-graph audits show both regimes, with fixed-checkpoint reliance across five benchmarks. Retraining with assignment-breaking or shared-map controls recovers full performance on most datasets, suggesting transport does not imply essential edge geometry; thus claims should pair checkpoint interventions with matched retraining.
AI.motivation: To rigorously test whether learned restriction maps in sheaf-based GNNs reveal true edge-geometry or are artifacts of particular training checkpoints and data processing; provide a framework to separate reliance on learned maps from actual transport value.
AI.method: Define two estimands: checkpoint reliance ( intervene on maps of a fixed predictor ) and protocol-relative replacement retraining (retrain matched families removing map capacity, edge variation, or persistent edge assignment). Introduce a task-null theorem showing labels identify only transported classifier directions, leaving d^2-d invisible degrees of freedom in any d×d map. Propose an exact frame model to bound when reliance remains task value. Use label-only training to realize predicted separation. Audit five DNSD benchmarks (NSD, DNSD, DSNN) on real graphs for transport regimes. Conduct retraining with assignment-breaking or shared-map controls to test recoverability. Compare performance across ten official splits (Roman-Empire and others).
AI.result: Key findings: (1) In all five DNSD benchmarks, learned maps exhibit fixed-checkpoint reliance. (2) After retraining with assignment-breaking or shared-map controls, four of five datasets recover full performance, implying transport is replaceable in those cases. (3) In the Roman-Empire dataset, a small persistent advantage remains for the original, compared to both continual resampling and a parameter-matched shared map, across ten splits (0.0675 and 0.0391 margins). (4) Label-only training demonstrates the predicted separation between transport and task value. (5) Public NSD/DNSD/DSNN implementations show both replaceable and unreplaced transport regimes on real graphs.
AI.conclusion: A learned map can influence fitted computation without constituting indispensable edge geometry. Evaluations claiming learned transport should pair checkpoint interventions with matched retraining to distinguish genuine edge geometry from artifact-driven performance.

title: PLATO: Pointer Learner for Agent and Task Openness
summary: Open agent systems (OASYS) are increasingly prevalent in real-world domains where the sets of agents and tasks change unpredictably over time. Such openness, including agent openness (AO) and task openness (TO), poses a fundamental challenge to multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), which typically assumes fixed state and action spaces. Existing methods address openness only partially: padding and masking approaches introduce artificial bounds, while recent graph-based or hypergraph methods handle one dimension of openness but still depend on restrictive assumptions. In this paper, we introduce Pointer Learner for Agent and Task Openness (PLATO), a pointer-network-based actor combined with a centralized graph neural network (GNN) critic, trained with multi-agent proximal policy optimization under a centralized training and decentralized execution paradigm. Our pointer-based actor outputs distributions directly over the current task set. This directly supports changing action spaces without masking or retraining. Our GNN critic encodes agent-task interactions as a graph that changes shape with task and agent composition. Together, these components consider AO and TO without the boundedness of existing approaches. We formalize PLATO in a Task-and-Agent-Open Markov Game (TaAgO-MG), extending prior task-open formulations, and prove it is well-defined over the resulting unbounded state and action spaces. We evaluate PLATO with the Methods for Open Agent Systems Evaluation Initiative (MOASEI) wildfire suppression domain, an environment designed for open multi-agent system evaluation, and we demonstrate strong performance and more consistent zero-shot generalization than state-of-the-art baselines in OASYS.

AI.tldr: PLATO unbounds action/state spaces in open agent/task environments by using a pointer-network actor over the current task set and a centralized GNN critic, trained with multi-agent PPO under centralized training and decentralized execution, in TaAgO-MG, showing strong performance and improved zero-shot generalization in MOASEI.
AI.motivation: Open agent systems (OASYS) introduce agent openness (AO) and task openness (TO), breaking fixed state/action-space assumptions. Padding/masking and single-dimension openness are insufficient; a framework that handles dynamic action spaces and interactions without artificial bounds is needed.
AI.method: Develop a pointer-network-based actor that directly outputs distributions over the current task set; employ a centralized graph neural network (GNN) critic that encodes agent-task interactions as a graph whose shape changes with composition; train via multi-agent proximal policy optimization (MAPPO) under centralized training and decentralized execution; formalize the setting as a Task-and-Agent-Open Markov Game (TaAgO-MG).
AI.result: Empirical evaluation in the MOASEI wildfire suppression domain shows PLATO achieves strong performance and more consistent zero-shot generalization than state-of-the-art baselines for open agent systems.
AI.conclusion: PLATO provides a principled, well-defined approach to open multi-agent learning with unbounded state/action spaces, avoiding artificial bounds and enhancing generalization; the TaAgO-MG formalization supports theoretical coherence.

title: ANFI: Rethinking Neighbor Feature Interaction in Person Re-ID
summary: In person re-identification, neighbor-based methods have achieved significant success by interacting with neighbor samples to obtain more robust representations. However, existing methods rely only on affinity relations, causing their success to depend heavily on the reliability of selected neighbors. We find that affinity-only interaction often fails in challenging scenarios due to the inevitable presence of noisy neighbors. To enable effective interactions under noisy neighborhoods, we revisit neighbor-based methods under distinct reliability conditions and propose a novel Adaptive Neighbor Feature Interaction (ANFI) method. The core idea of ANFI is to account for negative effects from noisy neighbors, allowing samples to remain distinguishable from false positive neighbors. Unlike existing methods, ANFI models not only affinity relations but also discrepancy relations, and employs sample-wise adaptive weighting for these two types of relations. Given that capturing negative effects from noisy neighbors differs significantly from traditional relation learning, we derive discrepancy relations from a new neighborhood similarity, which provides more information than pairwise similarity. In addition, we propose Noisy Relation Supervision (NRS) to train ANFI, gradually injecting robustness to noisy relations into the model. Extensive experiments conducted under standard, cross-modal, and cross-domain settings, including comparisons with neighbor-based methods and re-ranking methods, demonstrate the superiority of our method across various neighbor distributions.

AI.tldr: ANFI is a neighbor-based re-ID method that accounts for noisy neighbors by modeling both affinity and discrepancy relations with adaptive weighting and Noisy Relation Supervision to improve robustness across standard, cross-modal, and cross-domain settings.
AI.motivation: Affinity-only neighbor interactions fail under noisy neighborhoods; negative effects from noisy neighbors degrade discriminability.
AI.method: Proposes Adaptive Neighbor Feature Interaction (ANFI) that uses two relation types (affinity and discrepancy) with sample-wise adaptive weights; derives discrepancy relations from a novel neighborhood similarity; introduces Noisy Relation Supervision (NRS) to gradually inject robustness during training.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show ANFI outperforms existing neighbor-based and re-ranking methods under standard, cross-modal, and cross-domain settings across varying neighbor distributions.
AI.conclusion: ANFI effectively mitigates noise in neighbor interactions and improves re-ID performance by leveraging complementary relationship information and progressive robustness training.

title: TWICE: Two-Clock, Two-Window Learning for Long-Horizon Conversion Prediction in Online Advertising
summary:
Long-horizon conversion prediction under delayed feedback creates a two-clock, two-window learning problem in online advertising. A short base observation window releases recent clicks on the click clock before their outcomes mature, whereas conversions continue to arrive on the conversion clock throughout a longer target conversion window. The click clock provides timely but partially observed status supervision. The conversion clock reveals long-tail delays, but the delay composition within an arrival-time slice is weighted by historical click cohorts with different traffic volumes and target-window conversion rates.
  We present TWICE, a framework that factorizes long-horizon post-click conversion rate (CVR) into a target-window conversion probability and a grouped elapsed-delay cumulative distribution function (CDF). The two clocks provide complementary supervision. Click-clock records train the target-window CVR head through a current-status likelihood over the base observation window. Newly arrived conversions train the delay model on the conversion clock. To account for the cohort mixture, TWICE uses fixed click-time predicted CVR (pCVR) mass as cohort exposure in an arrival-conditioned likelihood. This accounts for differences in cohort traffic and conversion propensity. The resulting aggregate records are self-contained. A single learned CDF produces monotone predictions for all requested horizons up to the target conversion window. Serving requires neither historical lookup nor convolution. Experiments on a public benchmark and an industrial advertising dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of TWICE. In an online A/B test in Kwai's advertising system, TWICE increased expected revenue, revenue, and conversions by 2.486%, 1.858%, and 2.061%, respectively. It was subsequently deployed to full traffic.

AI.tldr: TWICE tackles delayed feedback in long-horizon post-click CVR by factorizing CVR into a target-window probability and an elapsed-delay CDF, using two supervisory signals (click clock and conversion clock) to produce monotone horizon predictions. It accounts for cohort mix with fixed pCVR exposure, yielding a self-contained, serving-friendly model that supports all horizons up to the target window.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon post-click conversions suffer from delayed outcomes and heterogeneous traffic, causing partial supervision and horizon-specific prediction challenges. A framework that jointly leverages early click outcomes and late conversion arrivals can improve calibration, timeliness, and serving efficiency.
AI.method: Introduce two clocks: a click clock for the base observation window to train a target-window CVR head via current-status likelihood, and a conversion clock for arrivals within a longer target window to train an elapsed-delay CDF. To handle cohort mixture, TWICE uses fixed click-time pCVR mass as arrival-conditioned exposure. The framework yields self-contained aggregate records and a single learned CDF that gives monotone predictions for all horizons up to the target window; serving avoids historical lookups or convolutions.
AI.result: Experiments on a public benchmark and an industrial dataset show effectiveness. In an online A/B test in Kwai's advertising system, TWICE increased expected revenue by 2.486%, revenue by 1.858%, and conversions by 2.061%, and it was deployed to full traffic.
AI.conclusion: TWICE provides a principled two-clock factorization for long-horizon CVR under delayed feedback, addressing cohort heterogeneity and serving efficiency. It achieves monotone horizon predictions and demonstrated real-world impact in advertising system deployment.

title: Matryoshka Agent: Unfolding Sub-Agents for Long-Horizon Machine Learning Engineering
summary: Machine learning engineering (MLE) tasks require long-horizon decision making over iterative solution debugging and refinement, under expensive and feedback-driven environment interactions. Developing and training a monolithic agent for such tasks is fundamentally challenging, as it must simultaneously manage extremely long and noisy contexts, explore vast solution spaces, and remain effective under limited model capacity and computational budgets. To address these challenges, we propose Matryoshka Agent, a unified hierarchical agent framework for complex long-horizon tasks. Matryoshka Agent decomposes agentic problem solving into a coordinated hierarchy of decision making and execution: a high-level Orchestrator maintains compact, long-horizon exploration states and issues strategic instructions, while lower-level Sub-Agents execute concrete solution attempts through direct environment interaction, mediated by standardized Tool interface. This design decouples strategic exploration from costly execution, substantially reducing the burden of long-context reasoning and enabling efficient iterative refinement. We further develop an efficient training paradigm for Matryoshka Agent. Experimental results on a broad range of MLE tasks with diverse model types and scales demonstrate that Matryoshka Agent is an effective and scalable paradigm for long-horizon MLE tasks and complex agentic problem solving. Notably, Matryoshka Agent enables Qwen3-4B-Instruct to reach Orchestrator performance comparable to o4-mini. Applying Matryoshka Agent to Qwen3-30B-Coder results in at most 36.7% relative performance gain.

AI.tldr: A hierarchical Matryoshka Agent decouples strategic planning from execution to tackle long-horizon MLE tasks, achieving scalable improvements across model scales; Orchestrator handles long-horizon exploration while Sub-Agents perform concrete actions via a Tool interface, with an efficient training paradigm.
AI.motivation: MLE tasks demand long-horizon decision making with noisy, lengthy contexts, expensive environment interactions, and limited compute.
