A monolithic agent struggles to manage exploration, execution, and context. A hierarchical, modular design can separate planning from execution and leverage tools to reduce context burden.
AI.method: A two-tier architecture: Orchestrator (high-level planner) maintains compact exploration states and issues strategic instructions; Sub-Agents (low-level executors) perform concrete actions through a standardized Tool interface. An efficient training paradigm is developed. Tested across diverse MLE tasks with different model sizes; evaluated using Qwen-family models (3-4B, 3-30B-Coder) and compared to o4-mini.
AI.result: Matryoshka Agent improves long-horizon MLE task performance. Notably, with Qwen3-4B-Instruct, Orchestrator performance reaches that of o4-mini; with Qwen3-30B-Coder, up to 36.7% relative performance gain.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling strategic exploration from execution via a hierarchical, tool-enabled framework yields effective, scalable solutions for long-horizon MLE tasks across model scales; the approach reduces long-context burden and supports iterative refinement.

title: Bi-Level Collaborative Learning for Few-Shot Scribble-Supervised Medical Image Segmentation
summary: Scribble annotations offer an efficient alternative to costly pixel-wise labeling for medical image segmentation, yet in real clinical scenarios, scribble-annotated samples are often still limited, imposing the dual challenges of sparse supervision and annotated sample scarcity. These compounded constraints severely deprive models of the structural evidence needed for complete region recovery and precise boundary delineation. To break this bottleneck, we propose a bi-level collaborative learning framework for few-shot scribble-supervised medical image segmentation. Specifically, an upper-level learnable superpixel model is introduced to provide region-structural priors for lower-level segmentation, while superpixel-based region-wise pseudo-label propagation and a spatial-prior-guided filtering strategy are performed to generate reliable dense pseudo-labels for segmentation learning. Meanwhile, the anatomical semantics learned by the lower-level segmentation model under the guidance of the current superpixels are fed back to the upper level, further driving it to learn region-structural representations better aligned with the segmentation task. Through bidirectional interaction and collaborative learning between the upper and lower levels, the proposed framework significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art scribble-supervised methods on the ACDC and Prostate datasets under the few-shot scribble-supervised setting.

AI.tldr: A bi-level collaboration between a learnable superpixel module and a lower segmentation model for few-shot scribble-supervised medical image segmentation, leveraging region priors and pseudo-label propagation to achieve state-of-the-art performance on ACDC and Prostate datasets.
AI.motivation: Scribble annotations are efficient but often scarce in clinical practice, causing limited structural evidence for accurate boundary delineation. There is a need to exploit region-structure priors and dense pseudo-labels to enable effective learning under few-shot scribble supervision.
AI.method: Introduce an upper-level learnable superpixel model that provides region-structural priors to guide the lower-level segmentation. Use superpixel-based region-wise pseudo-label propagation and a spatial-prior-guided filtering strategy to generate reliable dense pseudo-labels. The lower-level segmentation learns with these priors, and its anatomical semantics are fed back to the upper level to refine region-structural representations. Bidirectional interaction enables collaborative learning and improved region recovery and boundary delineation.
AI.result: The proposed framework significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art scribble-supervised methods on the ACDC and Prostate datasets under the few-shot scribble supervision setting.
AI.conclusion: A bi-level collaborative framework with region-structural priors and feedback between upper and lower levels effectively addresses sparse supervision and sample scarcity in scribble-supervised medical image segmentation, achieving superior performance on benchmark datasets.

title: SPARC Segmentation to Prediction via Affine Regression and Counterfactuals
summary: Transaction propensity prediction in B2B e commerce presents unique challenges distinct from B2C contexts, primarily due to the heterogeneous procurement behaviors of organizational entities, which violate SMOTE's implicit assumption of within class feature homogeneity. Specifically, B2B buyers exhibit multi modal procurement cycles that render linear interpolation between minority class samples structurally invalid, producing synthetic data that does not represent real purchasing behavior. This paper introduces a production deployed propensity modeling framework designed to address these complexities through two primary contributions. First, we replace conventional SMOTE based augmentation with a synthetic data generation approach leveraging Diverse Counterfactual Explanations (DiCE). This method produces minority class samples with superior distributional fidelity compared to SMOTE, as validated through quantitative proximity analysis and UMAP cluster visualization. Second, we adapt the PyPARC piecewise affine classification framework to generate calibrated propensity probabilities, facilitating the interpretable segmentation of customers into actionable risk tiers. Evaluated on two years of longitudinal data from a large scale B2B e commerce platform with a 1 to 9 class imbalance ratio, the proposed architecture achieves 93.1% precision at a decision threshold of 0.8, a 9.2 percentage point improvement over SMOTE based baselines at the same threshold (83.9%), and a 26.1 point improvement over SMOTE at threshold 0.7 (66.04%), demonstrating consistent superiority across operating points. These results demonstrate the framework's efficacy in enabling high precision marketing campaigns with significant improvements in customer activation and return on investment.

AI.tldr: B2B propensity modeling uses DiCE-based synthetic data and PyPARC classifier to outperform SMOTE baselines, achieving high precision and actionable risk segmentation for marketing ROI.
AI.motivation: Address B2B-specific heterogeneity and minority class distribution issues where SMOTE's within-class homogeneity assumption fails; improve distributional fidelity of minority samples and provide calibrated probabilities for actionable segmentation.
AI.method: Replace SMOTE augmentation with Diverse Counterfactual Explanations (DiCE) to generate minority samples with higher distributional fidelity; adopt PyPARC piecewise affine classifier for calibrated propensity probabilities and interpretable risk-tier segmentation.
AI.result: On two years of longitudinal data from a large-scale B2B e-commerce platform with 1:9 imbalance, the framework achieved 93.1% precision at threshold 0.8, a 9.2 percentage point improvement over SMOTE baselines at 0.8 (83.9%), and a 26.1 point improvement over SMOTE at threshold 0.7 (66.04%), showing consistent superiority across operating points.
AI.conclusion: The framework demonstrates production-ready propensity modeling for B2B contexts, enabling high-precision marketing campaigns with improved customer activation and ROI, via distribution-faithful minority augmentation and interpretable, calibrated segmentation.

title: Towards Robust Reinforcement Learning for Small-Scale Language Model Agents
comment: Proceedings of the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics (SMC), Bellevue, WA, USA
summary: The alignment of Small Language Models (SLMs) in the 70--500M parameter range using reinforcement learning is often considered unstable, though the underlying failure mechanisms have not been systematically investigated. In the State-of-the-Art (SOTA) research, fifteen (model, corpus) configurations were trained using Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO). The experiments included Pythia-70M, 160M, 410M and SmolLM2-135M, 360M on the TinyStories, CNN/DailyMail, and Wikitext-103 corpora. Three reproducible failure modes were identified in small-scale language models: silent LoRA parameter freezing in standard PEFT/TRL pipelines, numerical overflow in importance ratios when using bfloat16, and catastrophic policy collapse due to reward-model error. These issues were addressed using a merge-and-reinitialize adapter technique, float32 precision during PPO updates, and a three-layer safety mechanism comprising reward whitening, importance-ratio guarding, and weight rollback. In this paper, a capacity-headroom hypothesis is proposed, which states that PPO performance at the SLM scale depends on both a fluent supervised model ($\text{PPL}<20$) and a discriminative reward signal, rather than on the number of model parameters. The proposed system converged stably in all experiments and improved preference win rate over the SFT baseline in configurations with a fluent prior and an informative reward signal. Furthermore, it outperformed instruction-tuned baselines while requiring significantly less training data. All checkpoints, preference datasets, and training scripts are publicly released$^§$.

AI.tldr: PPO-based RLHF on SLMs (70–500M) reveals three reproducible failure modes; fixes via merge-and-reinitialize adapters, float32 PPO updates, and a three-layer safety mechanism; introduces a capacity-headroom hypothesis; achieves stable convergence and data-efficient improvements over SFT/instruction-tuned baselines; artifacts released.
AI.motivation: Systematically diagnose instability in RLHF for small language models and identify failure modes; evaluate whether model size or other factors drive PPO performance; assess data efficiency and practical viability of RLHF at the 70–500M scale.
AI.method: Replicated fifteen (model, corpus) configurations using PPO across Pythia-70M/160M/410M and SmolLM2-135M/360M on TinyStories, CNN/DailyMail, and Wikitext-103. Identified three failure modes: silent LoRA parameter freezing in standard PEFT/TRL, numerical overflow in importance ratios with bf16, and catastrophic policy collapse from reward-model error. Implemented merge-and-reinitialize adapter, float32 PPO updates, and a three-layer safety mechanism (reward whitening, importance-ratio guarding, weight rollback). Tested the capacity-headroom hypothesis: PPO performance depends on fluent supervised prior (PPL<20) and discriminative reward signal, not parameter count. Assessed preference win rate vs SFT baselines and instruction-tuned baselines; released checkpoints, preference datasets, and training scripts.
AI.result: The system converged stably in all experiments. In configurations with a fluent prior and informative reward, PPO achieved higher preference win rates than the SFT baseline and outperformed instruction-tuned baselines, while requiring significantly less training data.
AI.conclusion: PPO performance at the SLM scale is governed by supervised fluency and reward discriminativeness rather than parameter count. The proposed fixes and safety mechanisms enable data-efficient, stable RLHF for small LMs, supporting the capacity-headroom hypothesis. All resources are publicly released.

title: Reading Legends on Ancient Coins: An Object Detection Approach for Character Recognition on a Novel Roman Republican Dataset
summary: When it comes to the proper classification of ancient coins with respect to their time and issuer, the textual inscriptions on these coins, also known as legends, are of paramount importance. These legends consist of alphabets or characters still used in English. This paper addresses image based character recognition on ancient Roman Republican coins via a deep learning based object detection strategy. However, legends on these coins pose high variation due to non-uniform placement, primitive inscription techniques, and wear and tear. Additional challenges include inconsistent imaging conditions such as illumination, orientation, and scale. To accommodate these, we gathered a novel large-scale dataset of 5,654 Roman Republican coin images, manually annotated with 21 character labels, totaling 38,808 annotations. For recognition, we use You Only Look Once (YOLO) variants: YOLOv3, v4, v5, v7, and v8. YOLOv7-Large achieves the best mAP50 of 90.4%, followed by YOLOv7-Extended and YOLOv7-xl with 90.2% and 90.1%, respectively.

AI.tldr: A deep-learning object detection approach is applied to extract and recognize inscriptions on Roman Republican coins using a new large dataset, achieving state-of-the-art OCR-like performance with YOLO variants, notably YOLOv7-Large.
AI.motivation: Legends on ancient coins are critical for dating and issuer identification but are highly variable due to placement, craftsmanship, wear, and imaging conditions; robust automatic recognition is needed.
AI.method: Constructed a large-scale dataset of 5,654 coin images with 38,808 annotations across 21 character labels. Trained and evaluated multiple YOLO variants (v3, v4, v5, v7, v8) for character detection on the coins; identified YOLOv7-Large as the top performer.
AI.result: YOLOv7-Large achieves a mAP50 of 90.4%, with YOLOv7-Extended and YOLOv7-xl close behind at 90.2% and 90.1% respectively.
AI.conclusion: A high-accuracy, deep-learning object-detection pipeline is feasible for ancient coin legends; the study provides a novel large dataset and demonstrates that modern YOLO architectures, particularly YOLOv7 variants, yield strong performance for inscription recognition on noisy, variably oriented imagery.

title: PIcsC: Partitioning-Induced Covariate Shift Correction
summary: Covariate shift across training-data partitions biases model selection and parameter estimation in cross-validation, lifelong learning, and federated learning. We propose \textit{Partition-Induced Covariate-shift Correction} (\texttt{PIcsC}), a Fisher information-based regularization framework that mitigates distribution mismatch between data partitions and a reference distribution. \texttt{PIcsC} approximates partition divergence using the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM) and incorporates the resulting statistic as a regularizer during optimization. The same formulation applies to both centrally partitioned datasets (batches or cross-validation folds) and inherently distributed data (federated clients or decentralized nodes), requiring only partition-local gradient statistics rather than raw data. We further introduce a conditional adaptation mechanism that combines FIM shift with KL divergence to detect significant distribution shifts and activates regularization only when necessary. Experiments on more than 40 datasets demonstrate consistent improvements under both natural and synthetic covariate shift. On fragmented batch and fold settings, \texttt{PIcsC} reduces fragmentation-induced performance degradation by more than 20\% and 25\%, respectively. On seven federated learning benchmarks, it consistently outperforms FedAvg, FedProx, and SCAFFOLD by 3 -5 percentage points without requiring client-specific personalization. These results demonstrate that Fisher information provides an effective and unified mechanism for mitigating partition-induced covariate shift across both centralized and distributed learning.

AI.tldr: A Fisher-information-based regularizer (PIcsC) mitigates partition-induced covariate shift in both centralized (batches/cross-validation folds) and distributed (federated) settings, with conditional activation via a KL-divergence gate; it yields consistent gains across many datasets and baselines.
AI.motivation: Partition-induced covariate shift arises from data partitioning, biasing model selection and parameter estimation in CV, lifelong learning, and federated learning; there is a need for a unified, data-efficient correction that operates with partition-local statistics.
AI.method: Approximate partition divergence with the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM) and use this as a regularizer during optimization. The approach relies on partition-local gradient statistics rather than raw data and supports both centralized partitions and distributed clients. A conditional adaptation mechanism combines FIM shift with KL divergence to activate regularization only when a meaningful shift is detected.
AI.result: Empirical validation on 40+ datasets shows consistent improvements under natural and synthetic covariate shift. For fragmented batch and fold settings, fragmentation-induced degradation is reduced by >20% and >25% respectively. In seven federated-learning benchmarks, PIcsC outperforms FedAvg, FedProx, and SCAFFOLD by 3–5 percentage points without client personalization.
AI.conclusion: Fisher information provides a unified, effective mechanism for mitigating partition-induced covariate shift across centralized and distributed learning.

title: ScalableRAG: High-Quality RAG at Zero Ingestion Cost
summary:
Recent advances in RAG aim to optimize for performance by paying high ingestion costs for knowledge ingestion: building knowledge graphs or extracting SQL tables. In this work we show that the operations that such knowledge bases allow can be replicated with zero ingestion costs (not even a vector database); in fact our solution, Zero-Ingestion ScalableRAG, handily out-performs all baselines (including knowledge graph approaches) in three out of the six corpora considered here, and only marginally missing maximum performance on the other three, with average accuracy across all six datasets 7.36% above the next most competitive baseline. It achieves this by keeping a workspace of document sets and values sets that it can write into and read from, allowing for on-the-fly aggregative reasoning in all situations where grouping is required on a primary key that is in one to one correspondence with a subset of the total document set.
  Capping the number of LLM calls by a constant independent of the corpus size, we also introduce Limited-Ingestion ScalableRAG, which does use a minimal vector database as well as an automated pattern discovery from a sample of documents, to further improve accuracy at scale. Our code is available at https://github.com/cohesity/ScalableRAG .

AI.tldr: Zero-Ingestion ScalableRAG achieves competitive performance without knowledge ingestion costs, rivaling knowledge-graph baselines across six datasets; Limited-Ingestion ScalableRAG adds vector DB and pattern discovery for scalability; code released.
AI.motivation: Reduce or eliminate the high ingestion costs associated with building external knowledge bases (e.g., knowledge graphs, SQL table extraction) in retrieval-augmented generation, while maintaining or improving accuracy.
AI.method: Maintain a writable workspace of document sets and value sets enabling on-the-fly aggregative reasoning for group-by operations; cap LLM calls at a corpus-size–independent constant to bound costs; in a secondary variant, employ a minimal vector database plus automated pattern discovery from a sample to boost accuracy at scale.
AI.result: Zero-Ingestion ScalableRAG outperforms all baselines on 3 of 6 corpora and nearly matches the best on the remaining 3, with an average accuracy improvement of 7.36% over the next best baseline; Limited-Ingestion ScalableRAG further improves accuracy at scale and reduces LLM calls; code available at the provided GitHub link.
AI.conclusion: Ingestion-free (zero-ingestion) RAG with on-the-fly aggregative reasoning can surpass traditional knowledge-base–driven baselines on several datasets, with a scalable variant that trades off some ingestion for higher accuracy and bounded computation; the work demonstrates practical, reproducible RAG approaches without heavy upfront ingestion costs.

title: DensFiLM: Density-Conditioned Video Saliency for Crowd Scenes
summary: Video saliency models typically apply a single fixation strategy across crowd scenes, despite systematic changes in attention with crowd density. Sparse scenes encourage tracking individuals, whereas dense scenes shift attention toward collective motion and scene-level landmarks. We introduce DensFiLM, a density-conditioned video saliency model that inserts a lightweight Feature-wise Linear Modulation layer at the bottleneck of a Video Swin Transformer. A learned density embedding produces channel-wise scale and shift parameters, allowing the decoder to reconstruct saliency from features selected for each density regime. The module adds only ~100K parameters and can use either CrowdFix density labels or the model's own density prediction. On CrowdFix, DensFiLM achieves mean NSS 1.434 and CC 0.517 over four seeds, improving over ACLNet by 14.7% and 14.9%, respectively, while predicted-density conditioning matches oracle-label performance. Ablations show that explicit RAFT optical flow and larger temporal and social-force extensions provide no further improvement in this setting. In a centre-prior-subtraction diagnostic, density conditioning yields an NSS gain of 0.462 over the unconditioned backbone, compared with 0.124 under standard evaluation. These results show that lightweight bottleneck conditioning provides a more effective inductive bias than increasing model capacity for crowd-video saliency. Our code is available at https://github.com/aniskhan25/crowdfix-saliency.

AI.tldr: DensFiLM adds a lightweight, density-conditioned bottleneck modulation to a Video Swin Transformer for crowd-video saliency, yielding large gains over ACLNet with ~100k extra parameters; density-aware conditioning (even with predicted density) outperforms unconditioned baselines, while traditional MA/flow extensions offer little benefit.
AI.motivation: Crowd scenes exhibit density-dependent attention shifts (sparse: track individuals; dense: focus on collective motion and scene landmarks). A single fixation strategy underperforms across densities. The work seeks an inductive bias that adapts saliency prediction to density regimes using a lightweight conditioning mechanism.
AI.method: Insert a Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM) layer at the bottleneck of a Video Swin Transformer. Learn a density embedding that produces channel-wise scale and shift parameters for the decoder to reconstruct saliency conditioned on the detected density regime. The method uses either CrowdFix density labels or the model’s own predicted densities. Ablations include explicit RAFT optical flow and larger temporal/social-force models. Evaluation includes center-prior subtraction tests.
AI.result: On CrowdFix, mean NSS 1.434 and CC 0.517 over four seeds, outperforming ACLNet by 14.7% (NSS) and 14.9% (CC). Predicted-density conditioning matches oracle-label performance. RAFT and larger temporal/social-force extensions yield no additional gains. Center-prior subtraction shows NSS gain of 0.462 with density conditioning versus 0.124 without. The method adds ~100k parameters.
AI.conclusion: Lightweight density-conditioned bottleneck modulation provides a stronger inductive bias for crowd-video saliency than simply increasing model capacity; the approach is effective with both true density labels and predicted densities, enabling competitive performance with minimal parameter overhead.

title: Bits and Memories: Measuring Verbatim Extraction Across LLM Quantization
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures. Code: https://github.com/AkshaySasi/bits-and-memories. Data and results: https://huggingface.co/datasets/AkshaySasi/bits-and-memories
summary: Language models are almost always quantized before they are deployed, and a growing line of work asks whether quantization also lowers their privacy risk. That work measures privacy almost entirely with membership inference. We think this is the wrong thing to measure for the risk that most people actually worry about, namely a model reproducing its training data word for word, and we measure that directly. Using the Pythia models and the public set of sequences each of them is known to have memorized, we track verbatim extraction across five precision levels, from full precision down to four bits, and across three model sizes, while measuring general capability (perplexity) at every point. We find two things. Quantization is a selective forgetter: verbatim memorization falls off faster than capability at every precision and every model size we tried, and this holds under two unrelated quantization algorithms and two evaluation corpora. But the selectivity is not enough to make quantization a privacy defense, which cuts against the optimistic reading of earlier membership-inference results. At the largest model we study, four-bit quantization still reproduces most of the memorized sequences while giving up only a few percent of capability, and the fraction of memorized data that survives quantization grows with model size. We conclude that compression should not be treated as a way to remove memorized training data, and that extraction, not membership inference, is the number practitioners should be watching. All code, sampled evaluation data, and per-configuration results are released.

AI.tldr: Quantization reduces but does not eliminate verbatim memorization in language models; extraction (verbatim data reproduction) persists even at 4-bit quantization, especially in larger models, so compression is not a reliable privacy defense.
AI.motivation: Assess whether quantization used for model deployment protects privacy by reducing memorized training data leakage, beyond existing membership inference metrics.
AI.method: Empirical study using Pythia models and known memorized sequences; measure verbatim extraction across five precision levels (full to 4-bit) and three model sizes; evaluate general capability via perplexity; test two quantization algorithms and two corpora; release code and data.
AI.result: Memorization declines with quantization but not enough to prevent extraction; largest models still reproduce most memorized sequences at 4-bit quantization with minimal loss in capability; fraction of memorized data that survives quantization increases with model size.
AI.conclusion: Do not rely on compression (quantization) as a privacy defense; focus on extraction risk; provide resources for replication.

title: Less Data, Better Alignment: Data-Centric Multi-Evaluator Agreement for Preference Optimization
summary: Research on preference optimization often varies the training objective while holding the data fixed. We instead ask whether a small, high-confidence set of on-policy responses can provide a reliable learning signal. Our method, DMAPO (Data-centric Multi-evaluator Agreement for Preference Optimization), generates candidate responses from the target policy, evaluates helpfulness, factuality, and conciseness with rubric-specialized evaluators, applies a process-critic correction, and retains only high-consensus desirable or undesirable examples. This procedure accepts 1,871 of 54,236 Mistral-7B candidates (3.45%). KTO trained on this set reaches 7.50 on MT-Bench, 95.5% length-controlled win rate against a text-davinci-003 reference, and 57.3% IFEval prompt accuracy. Independent pairwise evaluation also favors DMAPO over SimPO: GPT-4o yields a net win rate of 23.3 points on 129 held-out prompts and 24.0 points on 200 out-of-distribution LMSYS-Chat prompts; Claude Opus 4.7 yields 24.1 points on the held-out set. Changing the evaluator model or rubric alters the selected examples but has little effect on downstream performance. A second-backbone study yields a similar 3.41% acceptance rate, although its performance gains are more modest. Across these experiments, consensus filtering offers a data-efficient route to preference optimization for general instructions, at the cost of additional curation compute and dependence on evaluator judgments.

AI.tldr: Data-centric, high-consensus on-policy responses can guide preference optimization with little data; DMAPO selects ~3.45% of candidates via multi-evaluator consensus and achieves strong performance across models while reducing data needs.
AI.motivation: Address the data bottleneck in preference optimization by asking whether small, high-confidence on-policy responses can yield reliable learning signals, rather than modifying the training objective alone.
AI.method: Generate on-policy candidates from target policy; evaluate with rubric-specific evaluators for helpfulness, factuality, and conciseness; apply a process-critic correction; retain only high-consensus desirable or undesirable examples; train with this filtered set; conduct cross-model evaluations (KTO, MT-Bench, IFEval); perform independent pairwise evaluations and a second backbone study; analyze robustness to evaluator model/rubric changes.
AI.result: Acceptance: 1,871 of 54,236 Mistral-7B candidates (3.45%); KTO attains 7.50 on MT-Bench, 95.5% length-controlled win vs text-davinci-003, 57.3% IFEval prompt accuracy; GPT-4o net-wins: 23.3 points (129 prompts) and 24.0 points (200 LMSYS-Chat prompts); Claude Opus 4.7: 24.1 points on held-out; second backbone: ~3.41% acceptance with modest gains; changing evaluators affects selections but little downstream impact.
AI.conclusion: Consensus filtering offers a data-efficient route to preference optimization for general instructions, at the cost of additional curation compute and reliance on evaluator judgments; robustness across evaluators and backbones demonstrated.

title: Seen, Said, or Forgotten? A Causal Audit of Visual KV Memory Across Dialog Turns
summary: Stateful multimodal assistants encode an image once but may answer questions about it many turns later. Attention-guided visual-KV eviction assumes that evidence irrelevant now will remain dispensable, although future questions are unknown. We ask when a visual fact is actually safe to forget and introduce the Causal Visual Memory Audit (CVMA), a paired single-prefill framework that tests what later answers lose when a visual region, the whole image, or prior assistant text becomes unavailable. On VisDial and ConvBench, current attention can rank future-useful regions worse than random even though a diagnostic marginal-utility control shows substantial selection headroom. Aggregate scores hide this failure when later turns do not need vision; controlled and stock-generated histories reveal a second escape route, in which assistant-text KV replaces image KV for facts already stated but not reliably for unstated facts. In the tested stacks, safe forgetting is supported by low future visual dependence or fact-specific verbalization---not by low current attention.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Causal Visual Memory Audit (CVMA) to evaluate safe forgetting in stateful multimodal assistants. It shows that attention-based eviction can be unreliable, with current attention rankings failing to predict future reliance on visual information; and identifies alternative memory pathways (image vs. text KV) that can preserve or replace knowledge depending on future use and fact encoding.
AI.motivation: To determine when it is safe to forget visual information in multimodal assistants without compromising future answers, and to expose the limitations of attention-guided eviction.
AI.method: A paired single-prefill framework (CVMA) that tests what later answers lose when parts of the memory (a visual region, the whole image, or prior assistant text) become unavailable. Evaluations on VisDial and ConvBench include a diagnostic marginal-utility control and analyses of controlled versus stock-generated histories to reveal different forgetting dynamics.
AI.result: Findings show that current attention can rank future-useful regions worse than random, though there is selection headroom according to a marginal-utility control. Aggregate metrics hide failures when future turns don't require vision. A second route exists where the assistant-text KV can substitute for image KV for facts that are already stated but not for unstated facts. Safe forgetting correlates with low future visual dependence or fact-specific verbalization, not simply with low current attention.
AI.conclusion: Safe forgetting in multimodal memory is achievable under conditions of low future visual dependence or when facts are verbally encoded, but attention-based eviction alone is insufficient. CVMA exposes hidden dependencies and suggests that memory management should account for future use and the distinction between stated and unstated facts.

title: Emergent Latent-State Computation under Stochastic Volatility
summary: Mechanistic interpretability has largely focused on language models and deterministic toy tasks. Much less is known about how sequence models internally represent latent stochastic dynamics under noisy, partially observed observations. We study this question in a controlled multivariate stochastic volatility setting, where models observe only returns while the ground-truth latent volatility state is known to the researcher. This setting provides a useful benchmark for mechanistic interpretability under partial observability: the latent state is hidden from the model but directly available for evaluation. Across architectures, losses, and output heads, we find evidence for a two-stage computation. Hidden representations encode substantial information about the next latent volatility state, and the output head maps this representation to squared return forecasts. Furthermore, in Transformers, latent-state decodability emerges at identifiable architectural stages whose location depends on the volatility period. In long-cycle regimes, this computation simplifies into an explicit latent-state filter consisting of a learned linear projection followed by $\ell^2$ normalization. Output-head replacement further shows that part of the degradation under noisy MSE training arises from readout misalignment rather than representation failure. These results suggest that stochastic volatility models provide a useful benchmark for mechanistic interpretability under noisy latent dynamics and partial observability.

AI.tldr: Posts a two-stage mechanism in sequence models under partial observability: hidden representations encode the next latent volatility state and an output head maps these to squared return forecasts; Transformers show stage-dependent latent-state decodability, with long-cycle regimes simplifying to a latent-state filter (linear projection + l2 normalization); degrade with noisy MSE largely due to readout misalignment rather than representation failure; stochastic volatility offers a useful interpretability benchmark under latent dynamics.
AI.motivation: Fill the gap in mechanistic interpretability for stochastic, noisy, partially observed latent dynamics, extending beyond language models and toy tasks by using a controlled stochastic volatility setting as a benchmark.
AI.method: Compare architectures, losses, and output heads in a multivariate stochastic volatility setup where the observer sees only returns while the latent volatility is known to the researcher. Analyze hidden representations for information about the next latent state, examine how output heads map to squared returns, identify architectural stages where latent-state decodability emerges in Transformers, and test long-cycle regimes where a latent-state filter emerges (linear projection followed by l2 normalization). Conduct output-head replacement to distinguish readout alignment from representation failure.
AI.result: Evidence for a two-stage computation: hidden representations contain substantial information about the next latent state; the output head translates this into squared-return forecasts. In Transformers, decodability arises at identifiable architectural stages whose location depends on the volatility period. In long-cycle regimes, the computation reduces to an explicit latent-state filter (learned linear projection then l2 normalization). Output-head replacement shows some degradation under noisy MSE training stems from readout misalignment, not representation failure.
AI.conclusion: Stochastic volatility models provide a useful benchmark for mechanistic interpretability under noisy latent dynamics and partial observability.

title: How Affect Propagates among LLM Agents: Emergent Emotional Contagion in Crowd Simulation
summary:
This paper studies the behavior of language models in a multi-agent crowd simulation, focusing on how affect propagates among agents that perceive and appraise one another. Each agent perceives its neighbors through visual, auditory, and tactile channels, then appraises these perceptions in light of its prompted personality profile, memory, current affective state, and situational context. Appraisal is carried out by an LLM, which updates the agent's internal affective state and selects its outward expression. The architecture contains no hand-authored mechanism for directly transferring affective state between agents; instead, inter-agent influence arises through the perception-appraisal-expression loop. The agent representation draws on the Big Five personality model and Russell's circumplex model of affect. To limit latency, low-level steering and navigation are handled by a conventional crowd simulator operating independently of the LLM-based cognitive layer.
  We evaluate the architecture across five scenario environments spanning alarming, joyful, and neutral situations in different spatial layouts. The results show that the system produces emotional contagion dynamics with spatial, temporal, and personality-dependent structure in sparse, small crowds. Alarm spreads from seeded agents as a traveling front, the mean alarmed fraction settles at a nonzero plateau, and the distribution of prompted personality profiles determines whether an ambiguous alarm ignites panic and whether a provocation is interpreted as anger or fear. We further evaluate the appraisal step through controlled experiments across prompt variants, sampling temperatures, and four model backends, showing that the dynamics are backend-dependent.

AI.tldr: LLM-driven appraisal drives emotion contagion in a multi-agent crowd simulation; perception-appraisal-expression loop creates emergent affective dynamics with effect of prompts, temperatures, and backend on outcomes.
AI.motivation: Explore how affect can be modeled and propagated in AI agents within a crowd using psychological theories (Big Five, circumplex) and an LLM-based appraisal mechanism, while separating low-level navigation for scalability.
AI.method: A hybrid system where agents perceive others via visual/auditory/tactile channels, an LLM-based appraisal module updates internal affect and outward expressions, and a conventional crowd simulator handles steering. Evaluation across five scenarios (alarming, joyful, neutral) with varying spatial layouts, plus controlled tests over prompts, temperatures, and multiple backends to assess robustness of dynamics.
AI.result: The architecture yields emotional contagion with spatial/temporal/personality structure in sparse, small crowds. Alarm spreads as a traveling front; mean alarmed fraction plateaus above zero; personality distributions influence whether an alarm triggers panic or is interpreted as anger vs. fear. Appraisal dynamics vary with prompt design, temperature, and backend, indicating backend-dependent behavior.
AI.conclusion: An LLM-based appraisal loop can generate plausible affective contagion in crowd simulations, with dynamics sensitive to prompts, temperature, and backend choice. The architecture demonstrates principled integration of psychological models into scalable AI crowd dynamics, though results depend on backend configuration and prompt design.

title: Safety-Aware Cascaded Inference for Crop Damage Assessment with Controlled Error Trade-offs
comment: 44 pages, 7 figures, 12 tables. Submitted to Precision Agriculture, July 2026
summary: In picture-based agricultural insurance for smallholder farmers, missed damage detections carry substantially higher cost than false alarms: a farmer who sustained real losses receives no payout, while unnecessary expert review is operationally costly but reversible. Standard multi-class classifiers optimize global accuracy but provide no mechanism to operationalize or control this asymmetric cost structure at inference time. We propose CascadeCropNet, a two-stage cascade architecture calibrated to satisfy a target recall constraint (Rec-Damaged >= 0.95) through threshold selection. A lightweight Sentinel model performs binary health triage; samples exceeding a calibrated damage probability threshold tau are escalated to a specialist Expert model for fine-grained diagnosis. This design provides explicit, deployment-time control over the safety-efficiency trade-off without retraining. Evaluated on the Eyes on the Ground dataset (23,804 images from Kenyan smallholder maize farms), the cascade achieves Rec-Damaged = 0.974 at tau = 0.5, reducing missed damage cases by up to 54% relative to a flat baseline. Under evaluation alignment, the representational gap reduces to +0.008 F1-macro, confirming the contribution is architectural rather than representational. Under input degradation, the system prioritizes escalation over confident misclassification, reflecting error containment through architectural isolation rather than intrinsic model robustness. These results demonstrate that cascade architectures can operationalize safety-oriented decision constraints through calibrated routing in settings where reliability matters more than aggregate accuracy. These properties depend on threshold calibration and deployment conditions and do not constitute guarantees under arbitrary distribution shift.

AI.tldr: Two-stage cascade (CascadeCropNet) introduces deployment-time recall control for damage detection in agricultural insurance, improving missed-damage avoidance with a threshold-calibrated triage system.
AI.motivation: Missed damage detections incur higher costs than false alarms; need a mechanism to enforce a safety-oriented recall target at inference time without retraining.
AI.method: Binary health triage (Sentinel) flags samples with damage probability above a calibrated threshold tau for escalation to a specialist (Expert) for fine-grained diagnosis; a two-stage cascade enables explicit control over the safety-efficiency trade-off.
AI.result: On Eyes on the Ground (23,804 images from Kenyan maize farms), Rec-Damaged = 0.974 at tau = 0.5; missed damages reduced by up to 54% relative to a flat baseline; representational gap is +0.008 F1-macro under evaluation alignment; under input degradation, the system prioritizes escalation over confident misclassification.
AI.conclusion: Cascade architectures can operationalize safety-oriented decision constraints through calibrated routing, offering deployment-time control over reliability when accuracy alone is insufficient; performance depends on calibration and deployment conditions and may not generalize under distribution shift.

title: Data-Dependent Regret and Polyak Corrections for Constrained Online Convex Optimization
comment: Accepted for publication in Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR)
summary: Constrained online convex optimization requires minimizing regret against adversarial convex costs while satisfying a convex constraint at every round, as needed in safety-critical applications. A computationally efficient method combines online gradient descent with a Polyak feasibility step, using one constraint evaluation and one subgradient per round. Although this method achieves O(sqrt(T)) regret with per-round feasibility, we derive a tighter, data-dependent analysis by retaining two quantities omitted by the standard worst-case argument. First, we replace the gradient envelope G_f^2 T with the observed accumulation G_T = sum_t ||grad f_t(x_t)||^2. Second, we identify a nonnegative Polyak correction P_T that measures the cumulative squared displacement caused by feasibility projections and enters the regret bound with a negative sign. The resulting improvement, Delta_T = (eta/2)(G_f^2 T - G_T) + P_T/(2 eta), is always nonnegative. We further propose AdaOGD-PFS, an adaptive-step-size method that achieves O(sqrt(G_T)) regret while preserving per-round feasibility. Experiments on ball- and halfspace-constrained problems improve the regret bound by 38 to 43 percent, with both data-dependent gradients and Polyak corrections contributing substantially.

AI.tldr: Data-dependent refinement of constrained online convex optimization with Polyak feasibility: replaces the gradient-envelope bound by the observed gradient sum G_T and includes a nonnegative Polyak correction P_T, yielding Delta_T >= 0; introduces AdaOGD-PFS achieving O(sqrt(G_T)) regret with per-round feasibility; empirical gains of 38–43%.
AI.motivation: Standard worst-case analyses use G_f^2 T; the authors seek tighter, data-dependent regret bounds by exploiting actual gradient magnitudes and the displacement caused by feasibility projections.
AI.method: Online gradient descent with a Polyak feasibility step (one constraint evaluation and one subgradient per round). Define G_T = sum_t ||grad f_t(x_t)||^2 and P_T = cumulative squared displacement due to projections. The regret gain satisfies Delta_T = (eta/2)(G_f^2 T - G_T) + P_T/(2 eta), which is nonnegative. Propose AdaOGD-PFS with adaptive step size based on G_T, preserving per-round feasibility.
AI.result: Derivation of a tighter, data-dependent regret bound; Delta_T is nonnegative, enabling improved guarantees. AdaOGD-PFS achieves O(sqrt(G_T)) regret. Experimental results on ball- and halfspace-constrained problems show 38–43% improvement, with both data-dependent gradients and Polyak corrections contributing.
AI.conclusion: A data-dependent refinement leveraging observed gradient energy and feasibility-induced displacements yields tighter regret bounds and practical performance gains without sacrificing feasibility; the approach is promising for safety-critical online optimization and could extend to richer constraint settings.

title: Inferring Missing Trajectory Data with Temporal Convolutional Networks
summary: Trajectory data collected in real-world settings is frequently incomplete due to sensor failure, communication loss, or occlusion. We address the task of \emph{trajectory inpainting}: reconstructing contiguous missing segments from observed context. We propose a Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) with symmetric dilation that relaxes the standard causality constraint, allowing each time step to draw on both past and future observations, a property that is essential for inpainting, but absent from forecasting-oriented architectures. The model is trained with a composite loss that combines weighted mean squared error, boundary--continuity penalties, and a smoothness regularizer. Trained on a synthetic dataset of $1,000$ (train), $200$ (validation), and $300$ (test) two-dimensional trajectories with randomly placed 20% masked segments, the model achieves good R$^{2}$, MSE and MAE metrics.

AI.tldr: Non-causal Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) with symmetric dilation for trajectory inpainting, using a composite loss to reconstruct contiguous missing segments from observed context, achieving strong metrics on synthetic data.
AI.motivation: Real-world trajectory data are often incomplete due to sensor/communication failures or occlusions. Inpainting requires leveraging both past and future context; standard forecasting models are constrained by causality and perform poorly at reconstructing gaps.
AI.method: A Temporal Convolutional Network with symmetric dilation that relaxes causality so each time step can attend to both past and future observations. Training uses a composite loss: weighted mean squared error, boundary-continuity penalties, and a smoothness regularizer. Dataset is synthetic with 1,000 training, 200 validation, and 300 test 2D trajectories; 20% random segments masked.
AI.result: The model achieves good R^2, MSE, and MAE on the test set, indicating effective inpainting. The evaluation on a synthetic dataset demonstrates the feasibility of reconstructing contiguous missing segments from context using a non-causal TCN.
AI.conclusion: Relaxing causality with symmetric dilation in a TCN enables effective trajectory inpainting by leveraging future context. The proposed composite loss supports boundary handling and smoothness, making the approach suitable for reconstructing missing trajectory segments; future work could extend to real-world data, longer gaps, and richer motion dynamics.

title: Agentic AI in medicine: architectures, applications, evaluation, and challenges for clinical translation
summary: Large language models and multimodal foundation models are enabling medical artificial intelligence (AI) systems to move beyond isolated prediction and undertake multistep clinical tasks that require planning, tool use, memory, iterative correction, and coordination among specialized agents. However, the scope of agentic AI in medicine remains unsettled, and current evaluation practices are not yet aligned with the requirements of clinical use. We conducted a scoping review with systematic evidence mapping across five electronic sources, screened 1,649 exportable records, and provisionally included 557 unique studies that met predefined criteria for goal-directed task execution, tool use, interaction with external resources, feedback-based refinement, or multi-agent collaboration. The included studies describe single agents that use external tools, workflows supported by retrieval and external knowledge, multimodal agents, and multi-agent systems applied to medical question answering, image interpretation, electronic health record analysis, drug safety, and clinical trial prediction. The evidence base remains dominated by public benchmarks, simulated settings, retrospective datasets, and small-scale expert evaluation. Process reliability, evidence traceability, uncertainty, safety, workflow impact, and external validity are evaluated less consistently. Clinical translation will depend on clearer definitions, reproducible evaluation, auditable oversight, interoperable system design, and prospective validation in real-world clinical workflows.

AI.tldr: A scoping review maps agentic AI in medicine, revealing a diverse but evaluation-limited evidence base, with emphasis on benchmarks and simulations; calls for clearer definitions and prospective validation.
AI.motivation: To clarify the scope, capabilities, and evaluation practices of agentic AI in clinical settings and identify gaps hindering translation to real-world workflows.
AI.method: Systematic scoping review and evidence mapping across five electronic sources; screened 1,649 exportable records; provisional inclusion of 557 studies meeting criteria related to goal-directed task execution, tool use, interaction with external resources, feedback-based refinement, or multi-agent collaboration.
AI.result: Studies include single agents using tools, retrieval-enabled workflows, multimodal agents, and multi-agent systems applied to medical QA, imaging, EHR analysis, pharmacovigilance, and trial prediction. The evidence base is dominated by benchmarks, simulations, retrospective data, and small expert evaluations; reliability, traceability, uncertainty, safety, workflow impact, and external validity are inconsistently evaluated.
AI.conclusion: Clinical translation requires clearer definitions, reproducible evaluation, auditable oversight, interoperable design, and prospective validation in real-world workflows.

title: Quantum Speedups for Stochastic Optimization with Heavy-Tailed Noise
summary: We study stochastic optimization with heavy-tailed gradient noise. We first propose a novel quantum mean estimator for multivariate heavy-tailed random variables that achieves lower query complexity than optimal classical estimators in the low-dimensional regime. We further develop an unbiased quantum mean estimator by applying a generalized multi-level Monte Carlo technique. We prove quantum lower bounds showing that, when the dimension $d$ of the random vector is small and can be viewed as a constant, our quantum estimators are optimal up to logarithmic factors. We further derive stronger dimension-dependent lower bounds for tail index $p>4/3$, showing that a nontrivial dependence on the dimension is unavoidable in the low-dimensional regime. Based on these estimators, we propose a quantum normalized stochastic gradient descent method ($\texttt{QNSGD}$), which finds an $ε$-stationary point using $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}\big(\sqrt d\,ε^{-\frac{5p-4}{2p-2}}\big)$ queries to the quantum stochastic gradient oracle. For a convex objective function, we propose a quantum projected stochastic gradient descent method ($\texttt{QPSGD}$), which computes a solution with $ε$-optimal solution using $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}\big(\sqrt d\,ε^{-\frac{3p-2}{2p-2}}+ε^{-2}\big)$ queries in expectation. These sharper bounds improve upon the classical lower bounds $Ω\big(ε^{-\frac{3p-2}{p-1}}\big)$ for nonconvex problems and $Ω\big(ε^{-\frac{p}{p-1}}\big)$ for convex problems in the low-dimensional regimes $d\lesssimε^{-\frac{p}{p-1}}$ and $d\lesssimε^{-\frac{2-p}{p-1}}$, respectively.

AI.tldr: Quantum estimators for heavy-tailed multivariate data enable quantum gradient methods (QNSGD, QPSGD) with improved query bounds in low dimensions, surpassing classical rates; plus lower bounds showing dimension dependence is inherent for p>4/3.
AI.motivation: Heavy-tailed gradient noise complicates stochastic optimization; quantum approaches may reduce query complexity, especially when problem dimension is small.
AI.method: 1) Develop a quantum mean estimator for multivariate heavy-tailed variables; 2) obtain an unbiased estimator via generalized multi-level Monte Carlo; 3) establish quantum lower bounds; 4) propose QNSGD and QPSGD with explicit query complexities; 5) compare to classical lower bounds.
AI.result: Quantum estimators are optimal up to log factors for constant dimension; dimension-dependent lower bounds proven for tail index p>4/3; QNSGD achieves Õ(√d ε^{-(5p-4)/(2p-2)}) queries; QPSGD achieves Õ(√d ε^{-(3p-2)/(2p-2)} + ε^{-2}) queries in expectation; improved bounds relative to classical Ω(ε^{-(3p-2)/(p-1)}) and Ω(ε^{-p/(p-1)}) in the low-dimensional regime.
AI.conclusion: In the low-dimensional regime, quantum methods can outperform classical lower bounds for heavy-tailed stochastic optimization, via novel estimators and gradient methods; results delineate the regimes where quantum advantage is achievable.

title: When Do Agent Loops Mistake Stagnation for Progress? Self-Evaluation Bias and Externally Grounded Verification in Long-Running Autonomous LLM Agent Loops
comment: 23 pages. Preregistered pilot measurement study. Also deposited on Zenodo (concept DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21594735)
summary: Long-running autonomous agents plan, act, and judge their own completion without human intervention. When an agent grades its own work, self-evaluation bias takes hold: plausible changes are accepted as progress while real-world outcomes stagnate or regress. We name this failure mode the progress mirage and show, with controlled measurement, that it is a question of what the evaluator is grounded in. We built a testbed that holds the agent and its tool surface fixed and manipulates only the information-channel type of the evaluator that gates the loop. A world-state oracle, unfakeable in principle, is enforced by container and network isolation and verified at every run. Across 54 cycles a frontier agent claimed improvement every time, yet 56 percent had a measured delta of zero or below. Self-report was thus uninformative, and the self-verdict gate degenerated into accept-all, eroding the best deployed state it had reached by 19 percent. Even the strongest in-band judge, reading the full artifact text, the change diff, and its own verdict history, accepted cycles of which 44 percent were real-world regressions and rejected 38 percent of real improvements; the preregistered adversarial hypothesis that a strong judge closes the gap was rejected. On a boundary task whose success specification is verifiable from the artifact itself, the same judge's mirage vanished to zero and the gap collapsed within the registered threshold, showing that the gap depends on where the success signal resides. A sign-only variant returning only the acceptance verdict kept real-world output similar to full feedback (110.0 versus 113.0), locating the benefit in the gate's grounding rather than in feedback content. For open-ended objectives whose success signal lives outside the transcript, scaling up the judge is not enough; out-of-band evaluation with real-world access is a structural requirement.

AI.tldr: Self-evaluation bias in long-running autonomous agents can create a 'progress mirage' where claimed progress does not correspond to real-world improvements; the mirage depends on what success signals the evaluator relies on, with grounded, verifiable signals reducing or eliminating the gap; open-ended tasks require out-of-band evaluation beyond transcript feedback.
AI.motivation: To quantify how the grounding of evaluation signals affects self-assessed progress in autonomous agents, and to identify design implications for reliable long-horizon autonomy.
AI.method: A controlled testbed with a fixed agent/tool surface; manipulate only the evaluator's information-channel (gate) while enforcing a world-state oracle via container and network isolation; 54 evaluation cycles; compare evaluators of varying grounding (full artifact text, diff, verdict history; sign-only verdict); include a boundary task with verifiable success and an open-ended objective.
AI.result: Across 54 cycles, frontier agents claimed improvement in all cycles, yet 56% had a measured delta of zero or negative; self-reporting led to an accept-all gate and 19% erosion of the best-deployed state. An in-band judge reading artifact, change diff, and verdict history accepted 44% of real-world regressions and rejected 38% of real improvements; the preregistered hypothesis that a strong judge would close the gap was rejected. On a boundary task with verifiable success, the mirage vanished within threshold; a sign-only variant kept real-world output similar, indicating the gain stems from grounding rather than feedback content. For open-ended objectives, scaling the judge is insufficient without out-of-band evaluation and real-world access (a structural requirement).
AI.conclusion: The gap between claimed progress and real-world improvement is governed by the grounding of the success signal. To avoid the progress mirage, evaluators must be anchored in verifiable world-state outcomes or employ out-of-band evaluation, especially for open-ended tasks where signal resides outside transcripts.

title: Beyond Counts: A Distributional Robustness Margin For Pathology Foundation Models
summary: Pathology foundation models are approaching clinical deployment, yet remain vulnerable to systematic non-biological variation across centres. Differences in tissue preparation, staining and scanning are strongly encoded in their representations, enabling shortcut learning and weakening generalisation across cohorts and institutions. The Robustness Index (RI) quantifies whether local representation geometry is dominated by biology or by non-biological variation, but its count-based formulation discards distance information. We show that adding distance weights changes little because the deeper limitation lies in RI's pooled, fixed-neighbourhood design, which obscures sample-level heterogeneity and effectively evaluates only a model-dependent subset of samples. We introduce the Cross-confounder Robustness Margin (CRoMa), a sample-resolved measure that directly compares distances to cross-confounder biological matches and same-confounder biological distractors. CRoMa recasts robustness as a cohort-wide margin distribution rather than a single pooled score. We evaluated frozen representations from 20 tile-level encoders across three benchmarks and 4 slide-level encoders on a fourth. Rankings by median CRoMa were broadly consistent across datasets, while the underlying distributions revealed substantial within-model heterogeneity. Every tile encoder retained a confounder-dominated lower tail, whose prevalence and severity varied markedly across models. These distinct robustness profiles frame model selection as a Pareto trade-off between typical and lower-tail robustness. Higher CRoMa was also associated with smaller shortcut-induced performance drops after supervised adaptation. By turning representation geometry into a distributional robustness readout that anticipates downstream shortcut susceptibility, CRoMa provides a principled basis for robustness assessment and model selection.

AI.tldr: CRoMa: a sample-resolved robustness margin that replaces the pooled Robustness Index (RI) to quantify whether pathology representations are driven by biology or non-biological variation; reveals substantial within-model heterogeneity and enables Pareto trade-offs between typical and lower-tail robustness, with higher CRoMa correlating with smaller shortcut-induced drops after supervised adaptation.
AI.motivation: Pathology foundation models are susceptible to non-biological variation (tissue prep, staining, scanning). The existing RI is a count-based, pooled measure that masks sample-level heterogeneity and may inadequately predict downstream shortcut susceptibility. A sample-level, distributional robustness metric is needed to guide model selection and robustness assessment.
AI.method: Introduce Cross-confounder Robustness Margin (CRoMa), a sample-resolved metric that compares distances to cross-confounder biological matches and same-confounder biological distractors. Conceptually reframes robustness as a cohort-wide margin distribution rather than a single pooled score. Evaluate frozen representations from 20 tile-level encoders across three benchmarks and 4 slide-level encoders on a fourth, analyzing median CRoMa rankings and within-model distributional heterogeneity.
AI.result: Median CRoMa rankings were broadly consistent across datasets; underlying distributions revealed substantial sample-level heterogeneity within models. Every tile encoder retained a confounder-dominated lower tail whose prevalence/strength varied across models. Robustness profiles imply a Pareto trade-off between typical and lower-tail robustness. Higher CRoMa correlated with smaller shortcut-induced performance drops after supervised adaptation.
AI.conclusion: CRoMa provides a principled, sample-level robustness readout that can guide robustness assessment and model selection, framing robustness as a distributional margin and enabling anticipation of downstream shortcut susceptibility.

title: Anti-Backdoor Coreset Selection via Cumulative Entropy
summary: Recent training-time defenses against neural backdoors isolate a benign subset from poisoned training data, to learn a backdoor-free model from it. In this paper, we formulate this defense strategy as a coreset selection problem, giving rise to so-called "Anti-Backdoor Coreset Selection." Since poisonous samples have (a) lower prediction uncertainty and are (b) less frequent than benign samples, coreset selection naturally focuses more on samples associated with benign functionality than the backdoor functionality. We use the Cumulative Entropy as selection criterion to further facilitate this effect. The metric tracks the learning dynamics of training samples and allowing us to select benign samples with high informativeness for the coreset. Additionally, we unlearn the chosen samples in each epoch to facilitate the separability between benign and poisonous samples. Together, this yields an exceptionally effective training-time defense that constructs a benign coreset to train a backdoor-free model. Unlike prior defenses that compromise natural accuracy and fail against certain attacks, our method mitigates backdooring attacks consistently with a negligible impact on natural performance.

AI.tldr: Proposes Anti-Backdoor Coreset Selection (ABCS): a training-time defense that builds a benign subset via coreset selection using Cumulative Entropy, then unlearns selected samples each epoch to separate benign and poisoned data, yielding backdoor-free models with minimal natural accuracy cost.
AI.motivation: Backdoor defenses at training time aim to separate benign and poisoned samples; existing approaches often reduce clean accuracy or fail against certain attacks; a robust, data-driven method that preserves natural performance is needed.
AI.method: Formulates defense as a coreset selection problem. Select samples with high informativeness for benign functionality using Cumulative Entropy to track learning dynamics. Unlearn the chosen samples each epoch to promote separability between benign and poisoned data. Train on the resulting benign coreset to mitigate backdoor effects.
AI.result: Claim: exceptionally effective training-time defense; mitigates backdoor attacks consistently with negligible impact on natural performance; surpasses prior defenses that degrade accuracy or fail against some attacks.
AI.conclusion: ABCS provides a practical defense by constructing a benign coreset for training-time backdoor mitigation, maintaining clean accuracy while reducing backdoor risk; invites further evaluation across attacks and datasets.

title: PreDiff-LM: Pretrained Discrete Masked Diffusion Language Modeling with Hybrid Attention
summary: Discrete masked diffusion language models support bidirectional generation and infilling, but adapting pretrained autoregressive (AR) transformers requires reconciling causal pretraining with bidirectional denoising. We study this problem at the level of attention rather than claiming AR-weight reuse itself as novel. PreDiff-LM preserves causal attention within the observed prompt while allowing full bidirectional attention within the masked target. Under a matched GPT-2 Medium, WikiText-103, 90K-step setup, this hybrid mask improves unconditional perplexity from 34.1 to 28.7 and MAUVE from 0.71 to 0.78 over uniform bidirectional attention with the same AR initialization. Attention adaptation also composes with a DiffuGPT-style objective adaptation, reaching 26.9 perplexity. Pretrained initialization reduces the steps required to reach perplexity below 50 from about 350K to 8K, although a compute-matched fine-tuned AR model remains stronger at equal scale (18.9 versus 28.7). Beyond perplexity, PreDiff-LM improves repetition, distributional quality, four zero-shot downstream tasks, and human preference over prior diffusion baselines. The results position hybrid attention as a complementary mechanism for adapting pretrained causal backbones, while making explicit the remaining quality and inference-efficiency gaps to optimized AR models.

AI.tldr: PreDiff-LM enables bidirectional attention in masked diffusion language models by preserving causal attention for prompts and allowing full bidirectional attention in masked targets, improving perplexity and distributional quality over prior bidirectional setups and reducing pretraining steps; it complements but does not yet surpass optimized AR models.
AI.motivation: Reconcile causal pretraining of autoregressive transformers with bidirectional denoising required for discrete masked diffusion language models, leveraging pretrained backbones while enabling bidirectional modeling.
AI.method: Introduce PreDiff-LM with a hybrid attention mechanism: maintain causal attention in the observed prompt and permit full bidirectional attention within the masked target; optionally combine with a DiffuGPT-style objective adaptation.
AI.result: Perplexity improves from 34.1 to 28.7 and MAUVE from 0.71 to 0.78 over uniform bidirectional attention under GPT-2 Medium and WikiText-103, 90K steps; with DiffuGPT objective, perplexity reaches 26.9. Pretraining initialization reduces steps to reach perplexity<50 from ~350K to 8K; at equal scale, a fine-tuned AR model still performs better (28.7 vs 18.9). Beyond perplexity, improvements in repetition, distributional quality, zero-shot tasks, and human preference versus prior diffusion baselines.
AI.conclusion: Hybrid attention is a viable and complementary mechanism for adapting pretrained causal backbones to bidirectional diffusion LMs, but remaining quality and inference-efficiency gaps relative to optimized AR models persist.

title: Group Equivariant Diffusion for Anomaly Detection in Computational Cytology
comment: 11 pages, 2 figures, 1 table, 1 algorithm. Accepted for publication in MICCAI 2026
summary: Computational cytology on whole-slide images is challenging because malignant cells are rare, heterogeneous, and annotated slides are scarce. Anomaly detection frameworks can be trained on normal slide-negative patches and then applied at test time to flag abnormal patches in held-out slides. Most unsupervised anomaly detection approaches including generative ones (GAN-based and diffusion-based), are tuned to organ-level imaging and require large curated datasets. In cytology the signal is cell-centric: rotating or flipping a single-cell patch does not change its diagnostic class, yet standard diffusion models treat transformed views as distinct inputs, leading to transformation-dependent reconstructions and unstable anomaly scores. We propose a D4-equivariant diffusion framework that enforces rotation and reflection symmetry both architecturally, via a D4-equivariant U-Net, and at inference, via equivariant noise coupling and (optionally) frame averaging. This alignment with biological invariance yields transformation-consistent pseudo-healthy reconstructions and more stable anomaly ranking under symmetry. On two publicly available cytology datasets of bone marrow and peripheral blood smears, our D4-equivariant diffusion models achieve higher AUC and retrieve more abnormal cells in the top K predictions than non-equivariant generative baselines, a deep one-class, and a multiple instance learning based method, while substantially reducing score variance across rotations and flips. Code is available at https://swchmida.github.io/D4diffCyto/.

AI.tldr: A D4-equivariant diffusion framework for cytology anomaly detection enforces rotation/reflection symmetry to align with cell-centric invariances, yielding transformation-consistent pseudo-healthy reconstructions and more stable anomaly scores. It outperforms non-equivariant baselines on two cytology datasets (bone marrow and peripheral blood), with higher AUC, better top-K abnormal cell retrieval, and reduced score variance; code released.
AI.motivation: Cytology is cell-centric and invariant to in-plane transformations (rotation/flip). Standard diffusion-based anomaly detectors can misinterpret transformed views as different inputs, leading to unstable anomaly scores and poor detection of rare malignant cells. Enforcing symmetry should yield more robust reconstructions and anomaly ranking.
AI.method: Introduce a D4-equivariant diffusion framework: (1) a D4-equivariant U-Net architecture; (2) equivariant noise coupling during diffusion; (3) optional frame averaging during inference; trained on normal slide-negative patches to produce pseudo-healthy reconstructions; anomaly scores derived from reconstruction discrepancies. Evaluated on two public cytology datasets (bone marrow and peripheral blood smears).
AI.result: The D4-equivariant diffusion models achieve higher area under the ROC curve (AUC) and retrieve more abnormal cells in the top-K predictions than non-equivariant generative baselines, a deep one-class method, and a multiple instance learning approach. They also substantially reduce score variance across rotations and flips, indicating improved stability.
AI.conclusion: Encoding D4 symmetry into the diffusion framework better aligns with biological invariances in cytology, enabling transformation-consistent reconstructions and more reliable anomaly detection of rare malignant cells. The approach improves performance over existing methods and provides more stable anomaly scores; code is available.

title: AMPBench-MT: A Homology-Controlled Benchmark for Antimicrobial Peptide Potency, Spectrum, and Safety Prediction
summary: Computational AMP discovery is often evaluated through AMP/non-AMP recognition, yet follow-up decisions depend on assay-derived evidence such as target-species potency, hemolysis, toxicity, and selectivity. Existing AMP and peptide benchmarks cover binary recognition, multilabel annotation, assay regression, or broader peptide-model comparison, but they do not jointly place AMP recognition, species-conditioned potency, spectrum, safety-facing proxy endpoints, and cross-endpoint behavior within one sequence-homology-controlled protocol. To address this problem, we introduce AMPBench-MT, a provenance-preserving benchmark that standardizes canonical peptide records and organizes them into binary recognition, species-conditioned pMIC regression, and endpoint-specific potency and safety-facing readouts. Across 161 endpoint-specific model evaluations, high binary performance does not reliably indicate assay-endpoint behavior. Frozen protein-language-model embeddings form the leading pMIC error cluster, while graph and classical regressors remain close. Spectrum labels further reveal that PR-oriented metrics can be misleading under scarce observed negatives, whereas low-toxicity, HC50 hemolysis, and selectivity expose smaller but more assay-facing signals. AMPBench-MT shows that AMP evaluation should move beyond recognition leaderboards toward endpoint-aware evidence auditing. Our proposed benchmark is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/ZihengZhou06/AMPBench-MT.

AI.tldr: AMPBench-MT provides a provenance-preserving benchmark for antimicrobial peptide (AMP) evaluation, combining binary recognition, species-conditioned pMIC regression, and endpoint-specific potency/safety readouts in a sequence-homology-controlled framework. It reveals that high binary recognition does not predict endpoint behavior, with embeddings dominating pMIC error clusters and spectrum-based metrics being misleading under scarce negatives; toxicity, hemolysis (HC50), and selectivity offer more assay-relevant signals.
AI.motivation: Existing AMP benchmarks cover limited evaluation aspects (binary recognition, multilabel annotation, or general model comparison) and fail to jointly assess recognition, species-conditioned potency, spectrum, safety proxies, and cross-endpoint behavior within a sequence-homology-controlled protocol.
AI.method: Construct AMPBench-MT by standardizing canonical AMP peptide records and organizing data into three tasks: 1) binary recognition, 2) species-conditioned pMIC regression, and 3) endpoint-specific potency and safety-facing readouts. Evaluate 161 endpoint-specific models across modalities (frozen protein-language-model embeddings, graph-based, and classical regressors). Use spectrum labels; analyze PR-oriented metrics under scarce negatives; examine toxicity (low-toxicity), HC50 hemolysis, and selectivity as assay-facing signals.
AI.result: Across 161 endpoint-specific evaluations, high binary performance does not reliably predict assay-endpoint behavior. Frozen protein-language-model embeddings form the leading pMIC error cluster; graph and classical regressors remain close. Spectrum labels indicate PR metrics can be misleading with scarce negatives, while signals related to low-toxicity, HC50 hemolysis, and selectivity reveal smaller but more assay-facing information.
AI.conclusion: AMPBench-MT demonstrates the need to move beyond recognition leaderboards toward endpoint-aware evidence auditing in AMP evaluation. The benchmark is available at the provided HuggingFace dataset URL.

title: Observing sycophantic AI validate others reduces its appeal but not its persuasiveness
summary: AI chatbots can be ``sycophantic,'' or overly agreeable and flattering toward users. Sycophantic AI has been shown to entrench attitudes, yet users frequently fail to recognize it (a phenomenon we call ``sycophancy blindness''). We tested whether increasing users' awareness of sycophancy protects them from its harmful effects. In one preregistered experiment (n = 940), participants received a brief written warning about sycophancy before conversing with a sycophantic chatbot. In a second preregistered experiment (n = 650), participants watched a video of a sycophantic AI validating several other users, including users on opposite sides of the same conflict, before interacting with it themselves. Both interventions changed how participants evaluated the AI. The warning reduced the AI's perceived objectivity, and the video reduced enjoyment of the AI, an effect mediated by the reduced belief that its validation was uniquely earned. We then pooled our experiments with two prior studies of sycophancy awareness interventions (six interventions total, n = 3,982). The pattern was consistent: interventions made the sycophantic AI appear less objective and trustworthy, and none of the six reduced its persuasiveness. These results suggest that individual-level interventions, such as warning labels or AI literacy, may not be enough to protect users from AI harms.

AI.tldr: Awareness interventions (warnings; example videos) alter how people evaluate a sycophantic AI, but do not reduce its persuasiveness; they tend to make the AI seem less objective/trustworthy, yet this may not shield users from its influence.
AI.motivation: Investigate whether increasing user awareness of sycophancy (sycophancy blindness) can shield users from the AI's persuasive harms and entrenchment of attitudes.
AI.method: Two preregistered experiments (n=940 and n=650) exposed participants to sycophantic AI with either a warning about sycophancy or a video showing it validating others. They measured perceived objectivity, enjoyment, and whether validation was uniquely earned. The findings were combined with two prior studies in a meta-analytic pooling (six interventions total, n=3,982).
AI.result: The warning reduced perceived objectivity; the video reduced enjoyment. Mediation showed these effects were explained by a diminished belief that the AI's validation was uniquely earned. Across six interventions, the AI appeared less objective and trustworthy, but persuasiveness was not reduced.
AI.conclusion: Individual-level awareness interventions (warnings, literacy) may be insufficient to protect users from AI harms; broader or system-level strategies are likely needed.

title: I2VShield: An Efficient Proactive Defense Framework against DiT-based Image-to-Video Models
summary: The rapid advancement of video generation models has led to the increasing misuse of image-to-video (I2V) models. Although substantial progress has been made in detecting AI-generated videos, proactive defenses against I2V models remain underexplored. In particular, current proactive defenses against I2V models predominantly rely on gradient-based adversarial attacks, which require defenders to possess GPUs with substantial memory resources (VRAM) to generate adversarial examples. To address this issue, we propose I2VShield, a privacy protection method based on generative adversarial attacks tailored to Diffusion Transformer (DiT)-based I2V models.
