The proposed method primarily consists of two components: (1) a text-adaptive perturbation generation framework integrating adversarial learning to mitigate computational overhead while maintaining visual imperceptibility; and (2) an untargeted Multimodal Attention Disruption (MAD) attack that exploits the inherent vulnerabilities of DiT-based I2V models, maximizing the deviation of the internal attention features from their clean states. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach achieves highly competitive protection performance across various datasets and mainstream DiT-based I2V models, particularly in disrupting spatiotemporal coherence, while substantially reducing computational costs.

AI.tldr: I2VShield provides an efficient privacy-protecting defense against diffusion Transformer–based image-to-video models by combining a text-adaptive perturbation framework with an untargeted Multimodal Attention Disruption (MAD) attack to degrade spatiotemporal coherence while reducing computation.
AI.motivation: Current proactive defenses against I2V models rely on gradient-based adversarial attacks that demand high VRAM and significant compute, hindering practical deployment.
AI.method: Two-part approach: (1) text-adaptive perturbation generation with adversarial learning to lower computational overhead while keeping perturbations visually imperceptible; (2) MAD attack that targets DiT-based I2V models by disrupting multimodal attention, maximizing changes in internal attention features away from clean states.
AI.result: Empirical evaluations across multiple datasets and mainstream DiT-based I2V models show competitive protection performance, notably in breaking spatiotemporal coherence, with substantially reduced computational costs.
AI.conclusion: I2VShield demonstrates a practical, efficient defense strategy against I2V attacks using diffusion transformers, balancing effectiveness and efficiency.

title: Multi-Scale Structural Features for Continual, Comprehensible Visual Recognition in a Developmental Learning Framework
summary: Contemporary machine learning struggles to learn continually, reuse prior knowledge, and expose a comprehensible internal structure. A recently proposed developmental, gradient-free learning framework addresses these limitations by learning a discrete, topological model of its inputs through local variation and selection, yielding an inherent continual-learning guarantee: new observations refine existing structure without overwriting past knowledge, and without replay buffers or predefined task boundaries. Its extension to visual inputs demonstrated this principle on shape recognition, but relied on a feature representation of limited expressivity that capped recognition accuracy. We introduce a new visual feature representation that encodes shape structure across multiple scales, capturing edge and contour features together with their spatial relations, and integrate it with the network-refinement learning process; we further improve the learning dynamics and the read-out used to predict from the learned model. The study targets two-dimensional shape, with class-incremental MNIST as a controlled, interpretable benchmark in which continual-learning behavior can be measured directly. Our approach substantially increases accuracy over the prior representation, matching or exceeding replay- and regularisation-based baselines at comparable storage while storing no past data, and preserves the framework's defining behavior: earlier-learned classes are retained as new ones are introduced, with no destructive adaptation, and the learned representations remain human-interpretable. What separates the methods is retention: the baselines surrender most of a just-trained class within its own cycle and relearn it afterwards, which ours does not. The significance lies in the manner of learning. The system integrates information one sample at a time while provably preserving its responses to...

AI.tldr: A gradient-free, developmental learning framework builds a discrete topological model of inputs, enhanced with a multi-scale shape-feature representation; it learns incrementally with no past data, retains earlier classes, and achieves high accuracy on class-incremental MNIST with interpretable representations.
AI.motivation: To overcome continual-learning challenges such as catastrophic forgetting, lack of interpretable internal structure, and reliance on replay buffers or predefined task boundaries by learning a compact, topological input model.
AI.method: A discrete, topological model is learned via local variation and selection (gradient-free). The visual feature representation is expanded to encode shape structure across multiple scales (edges, contours, and spatial relations). This is integrated with a network-refinement learning process; learning is performed one sample at a time with no past-data storage and with improved read-out for predictions.
AI.result: Significant accuracy gains over the prior representation, matching or exceeding replay- and regularisation-based baselines at similar storage without storing past data. The approach preserves previously learned classes as new ones are introduced, with no destructive adaptation; representations remain human-interpretable.
AI.conclusion: The key contribution is retention: the system continuously integrates information while provably preserving its previously learned responses, yielding interpretable internal structure and robust continual learning without data replay.

title: Everyone is unique: Towards Behaviorally Heterogeneous Negotiation Dialogue Systems for Debt Collection
summary: Debt collection is a critical negotiation task in the financial industry, with strong practical relevance and exceptional academic value as a behaviorally rich, high-stakes testbed for human-centered dialogue systems. While large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in dialogue and negotiation, effectively evaluating their performance in this complex scenarios remains a major challenge: existing benchmarks uniformly assume users to be static, rational agents with fixed preferences, failing to capture the rich behavioral heterogeneity inherent in real-world debt collection. To bridge this gap, we propose DebtBench, the first public persona-enriched debt collection benchmark, that highlights behavioral heterogeneity in negotiation. Moreover, we develop DebtGPT, a debt collection agent trained to jointly optimize financial recovery and interaction experience. Our experimental results, using 16 state-of-the-art LLMs, find that most existing models struggle in this complex but realistic scenarios, whereas DebtGPT outperforms all open-source baselines and achieves performance on par with GPT-4o. The code and data are available at https://github.com/YYuHhhh/DebtNegotiation.

AI.tldr: Introduces DebtBench and DebtGPT to address behavioral heterogeneity in debt-collection negotiation; benchmarks LLMs and shows DebtGPT matches GPT-4o.
AI.motivation: Existing negotiation benchmarks assume static, rational users with fixed preferences, which fails to capture heterogeneous, real-world debt-collection behavior; a persona-enriched benchmark is needed to evaluate and train human-centered LLM negotiation agents.
AI.method: Create DebtBench with persona-enriched debt-collection scenarios to reveal behavioral heterogeneity; train DebtGPT to jointly optimize financial recovery and interaction experience; evaluate 16 state-of-the-art LLMs against baselines.
AI.result: Most existing models underperform in heterogeneous, realistic scenarios; DebtGPT outperforms all open-source baselines and achieves performance on par with GPT-4o.
AI.conclusion: First public persona-enriched debt-collection benchmark; demonstrates the value of modeling behavioral heterogeneity; DebtGPT offers a strong, human-centered negotiation agent; code and data are released.

title: ReLATE: Reliability-Guided Evidence Fusion for Robust UAV--Satellite cross-view Geo-Localization
summary: Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV)-satellite cross-view geo-localization matches UAV images against satellite imagery and has achieved impressive accuracy on clean (non-degraded) image benchmarks. In real-world flights, however, UAV observations are frequently affected by adverse weather, illumination changes, platform motion, sensor noise, and compression, while the robustness of existing methods under such degradations remains largely unexamined. In this paper, we present UAVSat-Deg, a large-scale robustness benchmark for degraded UAV-satellite geo-localization, comprising University-1652-Deg and SUES-200-Deg. UAVSat-Deg covers 27 corruption types, including 19 core and 8 compound corruptions, at three severity levels, supports bidirectional drone-to-satellite and satellite-to-drone retrieval as well as multi-height UAV acquisition, and contains more than 11.7 million pre-generated corrupted test images. Benchmarking representative methods under this protocol reveals substantial robustness gaps, particularly under severe and compound corruptions. To address this problem, we propose ReLATE, a Reliable Evidence Learning framework with Adaptive Token Evidence Regulation, which realizes reliability-adaptive feature fusion during descriptor construction. ReLATE estimates a structure-smoothed reliability field over visual tokens, aggregates trustworthy local evidence, and adaptively integrates it into query-derived representations; the regulated query representations are then combined with the CLS-token and GeM-pooled branches to form the final cross-view descriptor. Across both test sets and retrieval directions, ReLATE achieves the best average corrupted-test performance among the compared methods while maintaining competitive accuracy on clean images. The code and dataset will be available at https://github.com/JHC626/ReLATE.

AI.tldr: A robust UAV-satellite cross-view localization benchmark (UAVSat-Deg) with 27 corruptions and 11.7M images, plus ReLATE, a reliability-guided feature fusion framework that improves robustness to degraded inputs while preserving clean-image accuracy.
AI.motivation: Address the lack of robustness evaluation and methods under real-world degradations in UAV-satellite geo-localization; provide a large-scale corrupted benchmark and a reliability-aware descriptor method.
AI.method: Construct UAVSat-Deg (two datasets: University-1652-Deg and SUES-200-Deg) covering 27 corruption types (19 core, 8 compound) across three severities; enable bidirectional drone-to-satellite and satellite-to-drone retrieval; include multi-height UAV acquisitions; generate >11.7M corrupted test images. Propose ReLATE (Reliable Evidence Learning with Adaptive Token Evidence Regulation): compute a structure-smoothed reliability field over visual tokens, gather trustworthy local evidence, adaptively fuse into query representations; combine regulated query with CLS-token and GeM-pooled branches to form final cross-view descriptor.
AI.result: ReLATE achieves the best average performance on corrupted tests across directions and datasets, while preserving competitive accuracy on clean images; code and data to be released on GitHub.
AI.conclusion: Highlights robustness gaps in existing methods under severe/compound degradations; demonstrates effectiveness of reliability-adaptive token evidence fusion; sets a benchmark and a method path for robust cross-view localization under real-world conditions.

title: Mind the Missing Split: Resolving Feature Heterogeneity in Swarm Learning with Random Forests
summary: Swarm Learning is a decentralized collaborative learning mechanism that allows multiple organizations to train a shared model without central coordination or direct data sharing. In typical horizontal Swarm Learning, datasets across sites are usually assumed to share the same feature set. However, in real-world applications, sites often have partially overlapping features because measurements, protocols, and available covariates differ across sites. This feature heterogeneity creates a practical issue for machine learning algorithms such as Random Forests. Specifically, when decision trees are pooled into a global Random Forest, inference at a given site can become ill-defined if a traversal encounters a split on a feature that is not available locally, often forcing organizations to discard site-specific variables upfront. In this paper, we address feature heterogeneity in Swarm Learning with Random Forests under partially overlapping feature spaces. We propose several deterministic and probabilistic inference-time strategies that resolve such missing splits without restricting training to the intersection of features. We evaluate the methods on nine datasets and demonstrate that they outperform both the intersection baseline and locally trained models across a broad range of scenarios.

AI.tldr: Proposes inference-time strategies to handle feature heterogeneity in Swarm Learning with a pooled Random Forest, enabling use of partially overlapping features and outperforming intersection-based and locally trained baselines across nine datasets.
AI.motivation: Horizontal Swarm Learning assumes shared feature sets across sites, but real-world deployments have partially overlapping features. When aggregating trees into a global RF, inference can fail if a local site lacks a feature used by a split, forcing reliance on the intersection or local models. This work addresses that gap.
AI.method: Introduce deterministic and probabilistic inference-time strategies to resolve missing splits at inference without restricting training to the feature intersection. Evaluate these strategies on nine datasets, comparing against an intersection baseline and locally trained models.
AI.result: The proposed inference-time strategies outperform both the intersection baseline and locally trained models across a broad range of scenarios on nine datasets.
AI.conclusion: Feature-heterogeneity-aware inference-time strategies enable effective pooling of Random Forests in Swarm Learning with partially overlapping feature spaces, removing the need to train solely on feature intersections and improving performance.

title: CADENCE: A Cardiac Atom Dictionary for Interpretable Neural Concept Extraction from ECG Foundation Models
comment: 21 pages, 5 main figures, 15 appendix figures, 6 tables
summary: Foundation models for 12-lead electrocardiograms (ECGs) transfer well across clinical tasks, but the physiological knowledge encoded in their representations remains opaque. We present CADENCE, a framework that decomposes an ECG foundation model into a human-interpretable, queryable dictionary of physiological concepts. Using a BatchTopK sparse autoencoder, CADENCE factorizes Layer-6 embeddings from more than nine million ECG tokens into 8,192 sparse cardiac atoms. These atoms align better than individual dense embedding dimensions with clinical phenotypes and waveform morphology, recovering arrhythmias, conduction abnormalities, infarction and repolarization patterns, chamber and axis findings, and lead- and beat-phase-specific waveform primitives. At Layer 6, the best atoms achieve mean AUROCs of 0.88 for clinical phenotypes and 0.90 for morphology, versus 0.78 and 0.83 for the best dense dimensions. Sparse atom probes match or outperform dense probes for phenotype, morphology, and age prediction while attributing each prediction to a small set of interpretable atoms; phenotype AUROC improves from 0.93 to 0.95. Atom-space geometry recovers physiologically coherent relationships, and targeted atom ablation selectively changes frozen downstream outputs. An automated LLM pipeline generates and quantitatively validates atom descriptions by predicting held-out activations. On independent external ECG datasets, CADENCE recovers overlapping concepts and maintains consistent phenotype-prediction performance. CADENCE provides a scalable framework for discovering and auditing the physiological knowledge encoded by ECG foundation models.

AI.tldr: CADENCE decomposes ECG foundation-model embeddings into a sparse dictionary of 8,192 cardiac atoms, yielding interpretable physiological concepts that outperform dense embeddings in phenotype and morphology tasks and enable targeted ablation, auditing, and cross-dataset validation.
AI.motivation: ECG foundation models encode rich physiological knowledge but remain opaque. There is a need for an interpretable, queryable representation of cardiac physiology that can be used for auditing, attribution, and clinical trust.
AI.method: Apply a BatchTopK sparse autoencoder to factor Layer-6 embeddings from over 9 million ECG tokens into 8,192 sparse atoms. Assess alignment of atoms with clinical phenotypes and waveform morphology, compare sparse atoms to dense embeddings, perform atom-probes, targeted ablation, and automated LLM-based atom descriptions. Validate on external ECG datasets to test generalization.
AI.result: Layer-6 best atoms achieve mean AUROCs of 0.88 (phenotypes) and 0.90 (morphology), vs 0.78 and 0.83 for best dense dimensions. Sparse probes match or exceed dense probes for phenotype, morphology, and age prediction, with predictions attributed to few atoms. Phenotype AUROC improves from 0.93 to 0.95. Atom-space geometry reveals physiologically coherent relationships; targeted atom ablation alters downstream outputs. Automated LLM pipeline validates atom descriptions by predicting held-out activations. External datasets show overlapping concepts and stable phenotype-prediction performance.
AI.conclusion: CADENCE provides a scalable framework to discover, interpret, and audit the physiological knowledge encoded by ECG foundation models, enabling interpretable atom-level reasoning and robust cross-dataset generalization.

title: Argus-Unified: Towards A Compact and Economical Unified Model for Image Understanding and Generation
summary: Unifying visual understanding and generation in one model holds immense promise, but remains challenging and expensive due to heavy compute and data demands and conflicts between the visual features needed for these two capabilities. To address these challenges, we present Argus-Unified, a compact, effective and unified multimodal model built with low demand on computation and data. Instead of aligning modalities from scratch, Argus-Unified effectively leverages pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) that provide strong multimodal priors. Specifically, we introduce hybrid visual tokens that preserve continuous tokens for understanding while learning discrete tokens for generation from a frozen unified vision encoder. Our training pipeline includes two stages: the first stage learns a quantizer and image decoder on top of the frozen vision encoder, the second stage trains the LLM initialized from a pretrained VLM for the unified multimodal modeling. Using by far the least amount of data (15.6M) and the lowest cost (~$2,000), we demonstrate that unified multimodal models can be trained economically while achieving strong performance in both understanding and generation. Notably, our model attains state-of-the-art multimodal understanding on GQA, POPE, and VQAv2, and competitive generation quality compared to models with dedicated vision encoders (e.g., Janus, Janus-Pro), all at ~10x lower cost and with ~5x less data. We envision Argus-Unified as a useful baseline that lowers the development barrier for unified models.

AI.tldr: Argus-Unified is a compact, low-cost, unified multimodal model that leverages pretrained vision–language models with hybrid visual tokens, enabling strong multimodal understanding and competitive generation at high data and compute efficiency.
AI.motivation: Unifying visual understanding and generation is promising but typically expensive due to heavy data/computation needs and modality conflicts. The work seeks to reduce data and compute demands by leveraging strong priors from pretrained VLMs.
AI.method: Use hybrid visual tokens: continuous tokens for understanding and discrete tokens for generation, built atop a frozen unified vision encoder. Two-stage training: (1) learn a quantizer and image decoder on the frozen vision encoder; (2) fine-tune an LLM initialized from a pretrained VLM for unified multimodal modeling.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art multimodal understanding on GQA, POPE, and VQAv2, and competitive generation quality relative to models with dedicated vision encoders (e.g., Janus, Janus-Pro). Data usage: 15.6M, cost ~$2,000, ~10x cheaper and ~5x less data than comparators.
AI.conclusion: Argus-Unified offers a practical baseline for unified multimodal models, demonstrating that strong performance can be achieved with substantially reduced data and compute by leveraging pretrained VLM priors and hybrid tokens.

title: OrthKD: Extracting Generalized Clinical Knowledge from Heterogeneous Teachers for Lightweight Deployment
comment: Accepted to the IJCAI-ECAI 2026 Special Track on AI and Health. 8 pages, 3 figures
summary: Deploying diabetic retinopathy (DR) screening models in primary care requires edge-efficient systems that remain accurate, safe, and reliable under domain shift. Multi-teacher knowledge distillation (KD) is a natural compression strategy, but existing approaches largely assume that all teachers provide equally trustworthy supervision. In our setting, this assumption fails: a strong CNN teacher (EfficientNet-B3, 0.876 QWK) and a weaker Transformer teacher (Swin-Base, 0.830 QWK) are complementary, yet the Transformer's logits can still mislead the student. We therefore propose OrthKD, a selective-trust distillation framework that transfers full supervision from the strong CNN, uses feature-only distillation from the weak ViT, and enforces orthogonality between teacher-specific student projections to encourage complementary rather than redundant evidence. This design preserves local lesion precision, injects global structural context, and improves robustness to distribution shift. On 132,049 retinal images, a 5.4M-parameter MobileNetV3 student reaches 0.885 QWK on EyePACS and improves zero-shot Messidor-2 performance from 0.507 to 0.728 QWK, while also achieving strong referral AUC and calibration. These results show that selectively distilling heterogeneous teachers can enable practical DR screening on resource-constrained devices.

AI.tldr: OrthKD enables selective-teacher distillation for diabetic retinopathy screening by combining full supervision from a strong CNN with feature-level distillation from a weaker ViT, plus orthogonality constraints to foster complementary evidence; it delivers strong accuracy on EyePACS and zero-shot performance on Messidor-2 on a compact MobileNetV3 student, demonstrating robustness to distribution shift and suitability for edge devices.
AI.motivation: Deploy DR screening models on edge devices requires compact, accurate models that remain robust under domain shift. Traditional multi-teacher KD often treats all teachers as equally trustworthy, which can mislead the student when weaker teachers provide poor logits. The work seeks to exploit complementary information from heterogeneous teachers through selective trust and orthogonality constraints.
AI.method: Use a strong CNN (EfficientNet-B3) to provide full supervision (logits) to the student; use a weaker ViT (Swin-Base) to provide only feature-level distillation signals to the student; enforce orthogonality between teacher-specific student projections to encourage complementary rather than redundant evidence; evaluate on EyePACS and Messidor-2 with a MobileNetV3 student (~5.4M parameters).
AI.result: 5.4M-parameter MobileNetV3 student achieves 0.885 QWK on EyePACS and improves zero-shot Messidor-2 QWK from 0.507 to 0.728; also shows strong referral AUC and calibration, indicating robust performance under domain shift.
AI.conclusion: Selective distillation from heterogeneous teachers, with full supervision from a strong CNN and feature distillation from a weak ViT plus orthogonality constraints, yields accurate, calibrated DR screening on resource-constrained devices and improves robustness to distribution shift.

title: The User Asks, Platforms Compete: How Agentic Recommendation Markets Take Shape
summary: Online recommendation has traditionally taken place after a user enters a platform, which determines the candidate pool and the ranking shown to the user. LLM-based user agents enable a different recommendation process: a user specifies a need before choosing a platform, leaving platforms to compete for the user's attention, which we refer to as an agentic recommendation market. In our controlled LLM-based experiments across three product domains, we find this new setting of recommendation creates a tension between access and attention. Compared with traditional platform-centric recommendation, user-centric recommendation greatly expands the opportunity for relevant items to enter comparison; yet broader participation does not translate directly into effective exposure. Competition directly triggers platforms' strategic play: selectively positive explanations occupy 73--78% of first-ranked positions. When the user agent relates platforms' actions to subsequent user feedback, this share falls to 36--41%, while the chance of a user purchasing the relevant item increases. A user agent is therefore more than a ranker over a larger pool of candidates: its querying, ranking, and feedback mechanism governing who can compete, how scarce attention is allocated, and how earlier outcomes shape the evaluation of platforms directly affect user utility. Designing agentic recommendation therefore requires treating access, attention, and accountability as a joint mechanism design problem.

AI.tldr: LLM-based user agents enable agentic recommendation markets where users specify needs before choosing platforms, shifting competition to gain attention and access; results show access expands candidate pools but does not guarantee exposure quality, with strategic platform explanations dominating early rankings; user feedback and outcomes influence evaluation, implying joint design of access, attention, and accountability.
AI.motivation: To explore the shift from platform-centric to user-centric recommendations enabled by LLM-based agents, and to understand how competition for user attention affects exposure, user experience, and outcomes, informing the design of future agentic recommendation systems.
AI.method: Controlled LLM-based experiments across three product domains measuring: (1) the distribution of first-ranked explanations, (2) how platforms' actions relate to subsequent user feedback, and (3) the effect on users' likelihood of purchasing relevant items.
AI.result: Competition prompts platforms to use positive explanations in 73–78% of first-ranked positions. When the user agent ties platforms’ actions to subsequent feedback, this share falls to 36–41%, while the probability of purchasing the relevant item increases. Overall, broader candidate pools from agentic recommendations raise access but do not automatically improve exposure quality; the agentic mechanism—querying, ranking, and feedback—shapes who competes, attention allocation, and evaluation of platforms, affecting user utility.
AI.conclusion: Agentic recommendation requires joint mechanism design of access, attention, and accountability; system design must account for how querying, ranking, and feedback control competition and user outcomes.

title: Visual prompt engineering for video models
summary: In the age of foundation models, a model is only as good as its prompt. For this reason, prompt engineering has become an essential technique for improving language model performance. Since video models are currently becoming foundation models for visual tasks (e.g., visual reasoning), we here ask whether they similarly benefit from visual prompt engineering: automatically modifying the task image to improve model performance. For example, for a visual physics reasoning task ("Where does the ball land, after passing a set of obstacles?"), an abstract sketch-like scene can be turned into a photorealistic version with a simple call to an image editing model. We find that visual prompt engineering, or VIPE for short, improves video reasoning performance across tasks. In fact, for video models, visual prompt engineering can be even more effective than classic text-based prompt engineering or test-time scaling. Ultimately, just as text-based prompt engineering systematically improves language model performance, visual prompt engineering can serve as a simple, compute-efficient approach to elicit better visual reasoning performance from video models. Example videos on our project page at https://visual-prompt-engineering.github.io/.

AI.tldr: Visual prompt engineering (VIPE) automatically edits input videos/images to boost video reasoning performance, often outperforming text prompts and test-time scaling, offering a compute-efficient alternative to elicit stronger visual reasoning from video foundation models.
AI.motivation: Video foundation models exist but may underperform due to suboptimal input representations. Visual prompts seek to reshape the task input (e.g., sketch-to-photorealistic edits) to better align with model capabilities and improve reasoning tasks.
AI.method: Automatically modify the task image/video frames using an image editing model to produce a better prompt on the visual input (VIPE). Examples include converting abstract sketches into photorealistic scenes. Systematically evaluate VIPE across video reasoning tasks and compare against text-based prompting and test-time scaling.
AI.result: VIPE improves video reasoning performance across tasks, and in the video-model setting, visual prompt engineering can be more effective than traditional text prompts or test-time scaling.
AI.conclusion: Visual prompt engineering provides a simple, compute-efficient approach to boost visual reasoning in video models, paralleling the benefits of prompt engineering in language models; a practical tool for enhancing visual reasoning without extensive model retraining.

title: Physics-Informed Broad Learning System: An Efficient Backpropagation-Free Framework for Solving Partial Differential Equations
summary: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have emerged as a powerful paradigm for solving partial differential equations (PDEs) by embedding governing physical laws into deep neural networks. However, their reliance on computationally expensive gradient-based optimization and deep architectures often results in slow training, high computational cost, and limited scalability. In this work, we propose a novel physics-informed broad learning system (PI-BLS), the first physics-informed learning framework based on broad RdNNs. The proposed formulation embeds the governing differential operator and the associated initial and boundary constraints directly into a linear output-layer optimization problem, thereby replacing nonlinear gradient-based training with a deterministic least-squares solution obtained via the pseudoinverse. Consequently, the entire learning process is reduced to a single linear optimization stage while preserving the underlying physical constraints. As a result, PI-BLS offers an efficient learning paradigm for a physics-informed learning framework for solving PDEs that eliminates iterative backpropagation while preserving the underlying physical constraints. Experimental results on representative forward PDE benchmarks demonstrate that PI-BLS achieves competitive and often superior performance with reduced training time and model parameters compared with conventional PINNs.

AI.tldr: PI-BLS is a physics-informed learning framework based on broad RdNNs that replaces backprop with a linear least-squares solution, embedding PDE operators and boundary/initial conditions into a linear output layer. It aims to solve PDEs more efficiently than PINNs while maintaining physical constraints, achieving competitive or superior accuracy with fewer parameters and reduced training time.
AI.motivation: To overcome the computational inefficiency and slow training of PINNs due to gradient-based optimization and deep architectures, while preserving physics-informed constraints.
AI.method: Use broad RdNNs with random hidden representations; embed the PDE operator and IC/BC constraints into a linear output-layer optimization problem; solve for output weights via pseudoinverse (deterministic least squares), eliminating iterative backpropagation; training reduces to a single linear stage.
AI.result: Experimental forward PDE benchmarks show PI-BLS achieving competitive and often superior accuracy with reduced training time and fewer model parameters compared to conventional PINNs.
AI.conclusion: PI-BLS offers an efficient physics-informed solver by converting the learning process into a single linear optimization while preserving physical constraints; promising for scalable PDE solving, though its performance on nonlinear/inverse problems and robustness to random features warrants further study.

title: Many-body Tipping Dynamics of ChatGPT-like AIs
summary: Why do ChatGPT-like AIs, despite major architectural and training differences, unexpectedly tip to undesirable content (e.g. harmful, misleading, repetitive) even under deterministic greedy decoding? We show that a broad class of such tippings is caused by the many-body interactions between tokens (spins) as they cross the finite-layer system. Tipping emerges as a dynamical first passage process between competing output basins. Attention disorder controls the transport toward, away from, or along the basins' boundary. A few-basin reduction yields a closed finite-layer threshold, whose coarse-grained predictions show good agreement across ChatGPT-like families. These results suggest that a broad class of AI failures represents 'foreseeable engineering risk' rather than inherently unpredictable behavior, with important implications for legal and societal assessments of AI harm.

AI.tldr: A theory explaining why ChatGPT-like models tip to undesirable content under greedy decoding, caused by many-body token interactions across finite model layers, modeled as a dynamical first-passage problem between competing output basins. Attention disorder modulates transport toward/away from/boundary basins. A few-basin reduction yields a finite-layer threshold with coarse predictions that align across model families. This implies tipping is an engineering risk rather than intrinsic unpredictability, with implications for liability and policy.
AI.motivation: To understand the universal, architecture-agnostic reasons for undesirable output tipping in large language models and to assess whether such failures are foreseeable engineering risks rather than fundamental limits, enabling better risk assessment and mitigation.
AI.method: Model the generation process as a many-body spin system with tokens as spins crossing a finite-layer transformer. Analyze tipping as a dynamical first-passage process between output basins. Examine the role of attention disorder on transport across basins. Reduce the system to a few-basin finite-layer threshold and perform coarse-grained analysis, comparing predictions across different ChatGPT-like families.
AI.result: The study finds that tipping arises from basin-to-basin dynamics in the token-state space, with tipping rates governed by a first-passage process. Attention disorder directs transport toward or away from basin boundaries. A reduced few-basin model yields a finite-layer threshold whose coarse-grained predictions closely match observations across ChatGPT-like models.
AI.conclusion: Many AI failures can be viewed as foreseeable engineering risks rather than inherently unpredictable; this perspective informs legal and societal evaluation of AI harms and motivates targeted design strategies to mitigate tipping phenomena.

title: Less is More: Modality-Decoupling for General AIGC Audio-Video Detection
comment: First place in the General AIGC Audio-Video Detection Challenge at the IJCAI-ECAI 2026 DDL 2.0 Workshop
summary: Generative AI has rapidly expanded audio-visual forgery beyond human-centric deepfakes into general scenes. Existing AIGC detection methods assume audio-visual content correspondence, identifying forgeries by spotting cross-modal inconsistencies. However, we empirically find that this assumption does not consistently hold in general scenarios. We argue that, for general audio-visual AIGC detection, decision-level fusion is a more robust alternative to feature-level fusion. Therefore, we propose DAV-Det, a decoupled audio-visual AIGC detection system that independently models forensic evidence from each modality. The visual detector leverages multi-granularity representations at global, patch, and segment levels to capture spatial forgery cues, while the audio detector exploits both temporal and spectral irregularities via a gated temporal-spectral dual-branch architecture to model acoustic artifacts. Our method ranks 1st in the General AIGC Audio-Video Detection Challenge of the IJCAI-ECAI 2026 DDL 2.0 Workshop, with a final score of 0.8460. Code is available at https://github.com/tuffy-studio/DAV-Det.

AI.tldr: A decoupled audio-visual AIGC detector (DAV-Det) uses independent forensic cues from visual and audio streams with decision-level fusion; visual uses multi-granularity cues; audio uses gated temporal-spectral branch; achieves 1st place in a challenge with score 0.8460; code released.
AI.motivation: Question the assumption of audio-visual content correspondence in general AIGC detection and seek a robust approach via modality-wise analysis.
AI.method: Proposed DAV-Det with decoupled detectors. Visual detector uses global, patch, and segment-level representations to capture spatial forgery cues; audio detector uses temporal and spectral irregularities via a gated temporal-spectral dual-branch architecture.
AI.result: Rank 1 in the General AIGC Audio-Video Detection Challenge (IJCAI-ECAI 2026 DDL 2.0 Workshop) with a final score of 0.8460; code available at GitHub.
AI.conclusion: Decoupled, decision-level fusion improves robustness for general audio-visual AIGC detection; the approach is reproducible with released code.

title: Contrastive Representation Learning of Longitudinal Disease Trajectories on Temporal Graphs
summary: Understanding disease trajectories from longitudinal clinical data remains challenging due to complex temporal dynamics and heterogeneous patient cohorts. Here, we present a contrastive representation learning framework that models multivariate disease trajectories as temporal graphs and learns representations using contrastive graph neural networks. Nodes represent patient observations over time, while edges capture temporal continuity and structural similarity between trajectories. Structure-aware random walks guide contrastive learning to generate embeddings that preserve temporal context and trajectory topology. The resulting representations enable robust clustering of patients with similar disease progression patterns and reveal latent structure in longitudinal data.

AI.tldr: Temporal graph-based contrastive learning for longitudinal disease trajectories enabling clustering.
AI.motivation: Longitudinal clinical data exhibit complex temporal dynamics and cohort heterogeneity. Capturing both temporal continuity and trajectory topology is essential for robust patient clustering and insight discovery.
AI.method: Model multivariate disease trajectories as temporal graphs; nodes are temporal observations; edges encode temporal continuity and structural similarity. Use structure-aware random walks to guide contrastive learning with graph neural networks to learn embeddings that preserve temporal context and topology.
AI.result: Learned embeddings enable robust clustering of patients with similar disease progression and reveal latent structure within longitudinal data.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides temporally-aware, topology-preserving representations for longitudinal health data, improving clustering and interpretability of disease trajectories.

title: ContractHIL-HLS: Contract-Aligned Multi-Agent Workflow with Hardware-in-the-Loop Feedback for HLS Design
summary: This paper presents ContractHIL-HLS, a contract-aligned multi-agent workflow for practical high-level synthesis (HLS) engineering. The workflow makes three contributions. First, it introduces a structured contract as the semantic-alignment and task-execution artifact that translates natural language requirements into explicit interfaces, constraints, validation checks, and rollback rules. Second, it incorporates hardware information into the feedback loop by feeding HLS, Vivado, PYNQ runtime, power, and failure evidence back into generation, thereby extending LLM-assisted HLS from kernel code toward system- and board-level closure. Third, it decomposes agents by semantic lowering and execution tasks rather than by conversational roles: a Contract Agent lowers natural language into the contract, an HTML Agent renders the contract as persistent structured HTML, and a Hardware-in-the-Loop Agent implements and revises the design with measured evidence. We evaluate ContractHIL-HLS in two parts. On 94 locally executable HLS-Eval tasks, the structured contract provides the largest small design gain, improving the estimated single-sample testbench pass rate from 64.0% to 70.2%; the full flow reaches 70.4% pass@1 and 76.6% pass@5. Because HLS-Eval does not exercise board-level design, we also validate ContractHIL-HLS on a board tested ML-KEM/ML-DSA post-quantum cryptography (PQC) secure-message accelerator, where the retained dual-bitstream organization reduces six-message average text runtime from 207.3 ms to 52.4 ms with positive routed WNS on both images while preserving decrypted-message verification. We open-source our work at BJUT-CS316-LAB/ContractHIL-HLS (https://github.com/BJUT-CS316-LAB/ContractHIL-HLS).

AI.tldr: ContractHIL-HLS introduces a contract-aligned, multi-agent workflow for high-level synthesis (HLS) that integrates hardware feedback and decomposes tasks by semantic roles; results show improvements in testbench pass rates and significant runtime reductions on a board-level PQC accelerator; open-source.
AI.motivation: Translate natural-language requirements into explicit, verifiable interfaces for HLS, and close the loop by integrating hardware feedback to extend LLM-assisted HLS from kernel code to system- and board-level design.
AI.method: Propose a structured contract as alignment artifact; decompose agents: Contract Agent lowers NL into contract; HTML Agent renders it into persistent HTML; Hardware-in-the-Loop Agent uses measured evidence to implement and revise design; feedback loop includes HLS tools (HLS, Vivado), PYNQ runtime, power, and failure data.
AI.result: On 94 HLS-Eval tasks: pass rate improved from 64.0% to 70.2% single-sample; full flow: 70.4% pass@1 and 76.6% pass@5. On board-level ML-KEM/ML-DSA PQC accelerator: dual-bitstream reduces six-message average text runtime from 207.3 ms to 52.4 ms with positive routed WNS on both images and preserved decryption verification. Open-source at https://github.com/BJUT-CS316-LAB/ContractHIL-HLS.
AI.conclusion: Structured contract plus hardware-in-the-loop enables better contract adherence and performance, extending LLM-assisted HLS to system- and board-level closure; demonstrated on both task-level and board-level evaluations and released as open-source.

title: Few-Shot Open-Vocabulary Remote Sensing Segmentation via Textual Inversion
summary: Open-vocabulary segmentation labels arbitrary categories from a text query without per-class training, yet on remote sensing imagery it underperforms on categories it handles reliably elsewhere. We find that much of this gap traces to the text query rather than to the segmentation model. Because these models are not specialized for overhead imagery, the class name that serves as the query is often a weak address into the vision-language embedding space. We show that a better name repairs part of the gap, while the remaining failures call for an address that the tested natural-language rephrasings do not provide. We recover that address from a few examples through textual inversion on a frozen model, keeping inference text only. On a representative benchmark this raises the mean intersection over union on the affected categories from 3.9 to 39.4, and across eight remote sensing datasets it improves over few-shot methods that instead inject visual prompts at inference.

AI.tldr: Open-vocabulary segmentation in remote sensing can be dramatically improved by domain-adapting the query text via textual inversion on a frozen model, addressing the text-space mismatch without retraining the segmentation model.
AI.motivation: Open-vocabulary segmentation relies on text queries that may poorly map to remote-sensing imagery in embedding space; misaligned class names limit performance despite strong segmentation models. A lightweight, inference-only adaptation of the text prompt could bridge this gap.
AI.method: Analyze the text-query gap in remote sensing; replace weak class names with a better address. Use textual inversion on a frozen vision-language model to extract a domain-specific textual token (address) from a few exemplars, keeping inference text unchanged. Evaluate against few-shot visual prompts across multiple remote-sensing datasets on a representative benchmark.
AI.result: Mean IoU on affected categories rises from 3.9 to 39.4 with textual inversion; across eight remote-sensing datasets, results surpass few-shot methods that inject visual prompts at inference time.
AI.conclusion: Domain-specific textual inversion on a frozen model substantially improves open-vocabulary segmentation in remote sensing by refining the query address, achieving large gains without retraining; future work could explore scaling to more categories or combining with other prompts.

title: MemSFT: Mitigating Alignment Tax with an External Parametric Memory
summary: Adapting Large Language Models (LLMs) to specialized domains often incurs an alignment tax, as fine-tuning on domain-specific tasks can cause catastrophic forgetting and substantially degrade performance on general tasks. We propose MemSFT, which mitigates the alignment tax by decoupling domain specialization from backbone parameter updates through a plug-and-play parametric memory. The memory is trained to imitate the behavior of a non-parametric retriever operating over domain data, thereby memorizing knowledge and patterns that would otherwise be accessed through retrieval. Once trained on a specific domain, the memory can be reused across LLMs of different sizes. During generation, a learned router dynamically fuses the output distributions of the memory and backbone at each decoding step, allowing domain expertise to be invoked selectively. Across biology, geoscience, and law, evaluations with models ranging from Qwen3-8B to Qwen3-235B-A22B show that MemSFT consistently improves domain performance with negligible degradation in general performance, whereas full SFT suffers severe forgetting on general tasks. Overall, our results demonstrate a practical path to decoupling general model capabilities from domain-specific knowledge at the parameter level, thereby equipping LLMs with new specialized capabilities without compromising their general capabilities.

AI.tldr: MemSFT decouples domain specialization from backbone updates using a plug-and-play parametric memory trained to imitate a domain non-parametric retriever. A learned router fuses memory and backbone outputs at each step, enabling selective invocation of domain expertise. It improves domain performance with negligible general-task degradation and is reusable across LLM sizes.
AI.motivation: Fine-tuning on domain data often causes catastrophic forgetting of general capabilities (alignment tax). There is a need to acquire domain knowledge without degrading broad performance.
AI.method: Train a parametric memory to imitate a non-parametric retriever over domain data. Integrate with LLMs via a learned router that dynamically fuses memory and backbone distributions at each decoding step. The memory is plug-and-play and transferable across models; memory captures domain patterns that would be retrieved non-parametrically.
AI.result: Across biology, geoscience, and law, with models from Qwen3-8B to Qwen3-235B-A22B, MemSFT improves domain performance while incurring negligible degradation on general tasks, whereas full fine-tuning (SFT) causes significant forgetting on general tasks.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling domain knowledge at the parameter level via a trainable memory and router provides a practical path to equip LLMs with domain expertise without sacrificing general capabilities; the approach enables domain specialization to be reused across model sizes.

title: Instruction-Tuned Language Models Cannot Sample from Distributions They Can Describe
summary: Silicon sampling uses language models as proxies for human survey respondents, treating each model call as an independent draw from the persona's response distribution. We show this draw does not exist: instruction-tuned models do not sample from distributions, they collapse to a single output. The same persona on the same question returns the same answer on more than half of items in a public-opinion benchmark. The collapse is sharp: the model's internal probabilities concentrate on a single option, and the failure is substantially amplified by instruction tuning: across three model families with materially different post-training pipelines, every instruction-tuned model fails on every task we test, while base models fail far less often. Strikingly, the same model that cannot sample from a distribution can describe it accurately in a single call. We call this gap the KNOWS/DOES split, and trace it to a degenerate sampling primitive visible in the logits and induced by alignment training. Exploiting this split, asking the model to describe the response distribution in one call more than halves the error against human survey data compared to persona aggregation. For applications that require per-persona outputs, we propose Prompt-Perturbed Argyle (PPA), which reduces the same error by 21% at no added cost.

AI.tldr: Instruction-tuned LMs do not sample from response distributions; outputs collapse to a single option per persona-question, undermining the assumption that model calls are independent samples. A KNOWS/DOES split arises: models 'know' the distribution but 'do' produce a single output. Describing the distribution in one call improves alignment with human data; Prompt-Perturbed Argyle (PPA) reduces error by ~21% without additional cost.
AI.motivation: Evaluate whether language models' outputs can be treated as samples from a respondent distribution, assess the impact of instruction tuning on sampling, and explore mitigation strategies for persona-based surveys.
AI.method: Empirical evaluation across three model families with different post-training pipelines on a public-opinion benchmark. Analyze per-question outputs from persona-consistent prompts, examine internal logits/probability concentration, compare base vs instruction-tuned models, and test describing the distribution in one call and PPA as mitigation.
AI.result: Instruction-tuned models fail to sample; outputs collapse to a single option per item; >50% of items yield the same answer for the same persona-question. Internal probabilities concentrate on a single option; alignment amplification worsens the collapse. Base models are less prone. A model can describe the distribution accurately in one call. PPA reduces error by 21% without added cost.
AI.conclusion: The sampling primitive is degenerate due to alignment-induced collapse, challenging the use of sampling as a proxy for human survey responses. Describing the distribution in a single call and using PPA offer practical mitigations, but fundamental sampling limitations persist; further work is needed to develop robust persona-based evaluation methods.

title: ReDesign: Recovering Editable Design Structures from Images via Agentic Decomposition
summary: Recovering an editable design file from a raster image is a common and costly bottleneck in modern design workflows, yet remains challenging since editability depends on recovering multi-modal attributes, such as typography, vector geometry, colors, grouping, and layer ordering. We present ReDesign, an agentic framework that grows an editable layer hierarchy by selecting and composing specialized tools across modalities. To keep this long decision process reliable despite imperfect tool outputs, we introduce graceful verification at each expansion, which provides local accept, prune, or retry feedback that prevents error accumulation and avoids large scale reruns. To evaluate editability at scale, we introduce the Figma Edit Replay Benchmark, consisting of 909 raw Figma files and 14,796 controlled edit instructions that replay edits on reconstructed outputs. Across this benchmark and standard reconstruction metrics, ReDesign achieves strong visual fidelity while delivering the highest editability across layout, color, and text edits, outperforming layered decomposition baselines and serial tool use pipelines.

AI.tldr: ReDesign is an agentic framework that reconstructs editable design files from raster images by composing specialized tools across modalities, with graceful verification to prevent error accumulation, evaluated on the Figma Edit Replay Benchmark showing superior editability and fidelity.
AI.motivation: Recovering editable design files from raster images is costly and challenging because editability requires restoring multi-modal attributes (typography, vector geometry, colors, grouping, layer order). A reliable end-to-end pipeline must support downstream edits.
AI.method: ReDesign grows an editable layer hierarchy by selecting and composing specialized tools across modalities. It uses graceful verification at each expansion, providing local accept, prune, or retry feedback to avoid error accumulation and large reruns. Evaluation is performed on the Figma Edit Replay Benchmark (909 raw Figma files and 14,796 controlled edit instructions) and standard reconstruction metrics, comparing against layered decomposition baselines and serial tool pipelines.
AI.result: ReDesign achieves strong visual fidelity and the highest editability for layout, color, and text edits across benchmarks, outperforming baselines.
AI.conclusion: An agentic framework with graceful verification can reliably recover editable designs from raster images, enabling scalable editability assessments and leading to improved reconstruction quality compared with traditional decomposition or serial tool approaches.

title: Using Data-Derived Priors to Guide CNN Architecture Design for NIR Chemometrics
comment: 25 pages, 4 figures, submitted to peer-review journal
summary: Convolutional neural networks (CNN) for near-infrared (NIR) chemometrics are often designed using generic architectural rules, although spectral datasets differ in sampling, smoothness, redundancy, and sample size. We tested whether these properties can provide empirical priors for CNN design. Across 25 NIR regression tasks, we computed descriptors of dataset size, spectral length and spacing, entropy, intrinsic rank, autocorrelation, and wavelet-scale structure. Two interpretable 1D-CNN scaffolds (a minimal single-convolution model and an extended shallow model with optional branching, dilation, etc) were optimized using five-fold cross-validated Bayesian hyperparameter optimization (HPO). Relationships extracted from near-optimal trials were converted into warm-start heuristics and evaluated directly and through leave-one-dataset-out (LODO) validation. The clearest relationships involved convolutional receptive fields. In the minimal CNN, the preferred kernel fraction decreased with spectral entropy and intrinsic rank, increased with the wavelet energy-support fraction, and the learning rate tended to decrease with training-set size. Direct and LODO heuristics were competitive with HPO, with median test-RMSE ratios of 0.953 and 1.017, respectively. The extended CNN showed similar but less transferable structure across branch usage, dilation, dropout, filter counts, and receptive-field choices. Ten stochastic refits showed seed sensitivity comparable to that of HPO-selected configurations. In a separate experiment, joint preprocessing and CNN HPO outperformed standardized-spectra HPO in 19 of 25 tasks, although gains were dataset-dependent. These results show that spectral descriptors can provide practical CNN design priors, guiding shallow NIR models toward plausible hyperparameter regions before target-specific tuning

AI.tldr: Spectral descriptors from NIR datasets can serve as practical priors to guide the design of shallow 1D-CNNs for regression tasks, enabling near-HPO performance with simpler search strategies.
AI.motivation: NIR spectral datasets vary in sampling, smoothness, redundancy, and size; generic CNN design rules may not transfer well. The study seeks data-driven priors to inform CNN architecture and hyperparameter choices.
AI.method: Compute descriptors (size, spectral length/spacing, entropy, intrinsic rank, autocorrelation, wavelet-scale structure) for 25 NIR regression tasks. Evaluate two interpretable 1D-CNN scaffolds (minimal and extended shallow) using five-fold cross-validated Bayesian hyperparameter optimization. Derive warm-start heuristics from near-optimal trials and test via direct optimization and leave-one-dataset-out (LODO). Additional experiment combines preprocessing with CNN HPO and compares to standardized-spectra HPO.
AI.result: Convolutional receptive fields emerge as the clearest design signal. In the minimal CNN, preferred kernel fraction decreases with spectral entropy and intrinsic rank, increases with wavelet energy-support fraction, and learning rate declines with larger training sets. Direct and LODO heuristics perform close to HPO (median test-RMSE ratios ~0.95–1.02). The extended CNN shows similar but less transferable patterns across branches, dilation, dropout, and other choices; seed variability resembles that of HPO. Joint preprocessing+CNN HPO outperforms standardized-spectra HPO in 19/25 tasks, with gains depending on dataset. Overall, spectral descriptors can steer shallow NIR CNN design toward plausible regions before target-specific tuning.
AI.conclusion: Spectral descriptors provide practical, transferable priors that guide shallow NIR CNN design, reducing tuning effort while maintaining performance across diverse datasets.

title: Physics-Grounded Fluid Video Generation with a Simulation Dataset and Dual-Stream Optical-Flow Supervision
summary: Video diffusion models generate visually compelling content but routinely violate elementary physics when the subject involves fluids: liquid columns break apart in mid-air, container water levels fail to rise as liquid is poured in, and splashes disperse without regard to momentum or gravity. We attribute this gap to the fact that large-scale video-text corpora contain almost no explicit motion supervision, so models learn to imitate fluid appearance rather than dynamics. We address this with two contributions. First, we build a physics-simulation fluid dataset combining 1,638 MPM-simulated pouring/sloshing videos with 2,320 keyword-filtered real pouring videos mined from stock footage, plus two held-out test sets: a 1,515-video real-video benchmark and an 18-prompt text-to-first-frame generalization benchmark. Second, we introduce a dual-stream image-to-video architecture built on a pretrained diffusion-transformer video generator. It augments the standard RGB decoder with a lightweight Optical-Flow Decoder branch trained with explicit end-point-error and smoothness losses, fused into the RGB stream via zero-initialized convolutions so the pretrained backbone starts undisturbed. Only the two decoders are updated; the encoder, temporal transformer, and text encoder remain frozen. Across two model scales (1.3B and 14B) and two test sets, our method improves VideoPhy-2 Physical-Commonsense and Video-Quality scores over the frozen backbone by up to 8.75 and 4.65 points, outperforms a leading open competitor, and is preferred by human raters in a blind study. A direct optical-flow read-out evaluation further shows an end-point error as low as 0.54 pixels in-distribution, confirming the model has internalized a coherent motion prior rather than merely improving surface appearance.

AI.tldr: Adds explicit motion supervision to video diffusion for fluids via a dual-stream RGB+optical-flow architecture built on a frozen diffusion-transformer backbone, trained on a physics-based pouring dataset, achieving improved physical consistency and video quality while preserving backbone weights.
AI.motivation: Video diffusion models learned from large video-text corpora lack explicit motion supervision, causing fluids to behave unrealistically; need to inject a motion prior to capture dynamic fluid physics.
AI.method: A dual-stream architecture augments a pretrained diffusion-transformer video generator with a lightweight Optical-Flow Decoder trained with end-point-error and smoothness losses. The two decoders are fused into the RGB stream via zero-initialized convolutions. Only the decoders are updated; encoder, temporal transformer, and text encoder remain frozen. Training uses a physics-simulation fluid dataset (1,638 MPM-simulated videos + 2,320 real pouring videos) and two held-out test sets (real-video benchmark and text-to-first-frame benchmark). Evaluations cover two model scales (1.3B and 14B).
AI.result: Physical-composition and quality metrics (VideoPhy-2 Physical-Commonsense and Video-Quality) improved by up to 8.75 and 4.65 points over the frozen backbone. The method outperforms a leading open competitor and is preferred by human raters in blind tests. Optical-flow read-out reports end-point error as low as 0.54 pixels in-distribution, indicating a coherent motion prior rather than mere appearance enhancement.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating an explicit motion stream into a frozen diffusion backbone with targeted optical-flow supervision yields coherent fluid dynamics in video generation and robust physical-consistency improvements, supported by a physics-based training dataset and strong cross-dataset, human-evaluated gains.

title: The LAIA Dataset: Labelled Attention for Intelligent Automobiles
comment: 11 pages, 12 figures, 3 tables. Dataset and supplementary information available from the project website
summary: The development of autonomous vehicles (AVs) usually relies heavily on data-driven artificial intelligence (AI) models that require large volumes of sensor data with ground-truth annotations. While modular architectures are widely used, end-to-end driving paradigms offer a promising alternative by directly mapping sensor inputs to control actions. However, their adoption is limited by challenges in interpretability and explainability. To address this, we present LAIA (Labelled Attention for Intelligent Automobiles), a novel synthetic dataset designed to enrich end-to-end driving research with human attention data. Collected using the CARLA simulator in closed-loop environments, LAIA comprises over 15 hours of driving from 44 participants across carefully crafted scenarios designed to evoke natural responses. Each sequence includes RGB images under six weather conditions, semantic and instance segmentation, depth, optical flow, CAN bus signals, and synchronized eye-tracking data. LAIA enables applications including training attention-aware end-to-end AI drivers, predicting driver behavior, developing methods to detect anomalous driver-attention patterns, and improving model explainability. In this work, we use LAIA to compare human attention with the perceptual attention emerging in our end-to-end driving models, thereby providing insight into their behavior.

AI.tldr: LAIA provides a synthetic, attention-rich driving dataset for end-to-end AV research, linking human eye-tracking with multi-modal sensor data to study and improve interpretability and attention-aware driving models.
AI.motivation: End-to-end driving models face interpretability challenges; incorporating human attention data (eye-tracking) and rich sensors can improve explainability, predict driver behavior, and detect anomalous attention patterns.
AI.method: Collected via CARLA in closed-loop driving with 44 participants across 15+ hours, under six weather conditions, providing RGB, semantic/instance segmentation, depth, optical flow, CAN bus data, and synchronized eye-tracking; designed to evoke natural responses and enable attention-focused analyses.
AI.result: LAIA enables training attention-aware end-to-end drivers, behavior prediction, anomaly detection in attention, and improved model explainability; the current study uses LAIA to compare human attention with emergent perceptual attention in end-to-end models, shedding light on their alignment and differences.
AI.conclusion: LAIA offers a rich, multi-modal, human-attention–annotated dataset to advance interpretability in end-to-end autonomous driving research and to develop methods that align model attention with human attention.

title: Contextual Deconvolution for Variance-Stable Demand Sensing: Kernel-Modulated Operators in Promotional Retail
summary: Machine learning demand forecasts optimize statistical accuracy yet leave excess operational volatility that inflates safety stock and amplifies the Bullwhip effect. We introduce \textbf{Contextual Deconvolution} (CD), a two-stage estimator that reframes demand sensing as a convex decomposition: a kernel-modulated banded operator separates transient promotion-driven shocks from a smooth structural baseline, and hierarchical partial pooling enables catalog-scale deployment without per-SKU training. The operator is data-derived, not imposed---it reduces to the identity wherever the promotional response is impulsive (most of M5, all of Favorita) and contributes only where genuine multi-day carryover exists, so the gains rest on the structural decomposition itself. Evaluating strictly out-of-sample on 30,490 M5 SKUs and 2,845 Favorita items, with calendar-aware baselines given CD's identical future calendar, we anchor the contribution on a full inventory-cost accounting: CD lowers safety stock, holding cost, and order variance but under-provisions event spikes, reducing total cost only when holding costs exceed $\sim$20\% of stockout costs (95\% CI $[17\%,25\%]$); otherwise it is an operational-stability and inventory-capital layer, not an expected-cost minimizer. Its accuracy contribution is reliability rather than central tendency: across eleven baselines, CD attains the lowest cross-sectional dispersion of per-SKU error and mis-forecasts by more than 200\% on 0.8\% of SKUs versus 9.9--20.6\% for every baseline, ranking first on both in all four M5 draws. Because the Variance Ratio and std-based safety stock are minimized by any sufficiently smooth forecast, we treat them as diagnostics, not objectives. A supporting analysis shows the learned demand operators are non-normal, yet CD's compact parametric kernel matches their operational performance interpretably.

AI.tldr: Two-stage Contextual Deconvolution (CD) for demand sensing that separates transient promotion shocks from a smooth baseline using a data-derived kernel operator and hierarchical partial pooling for catalog-scale deployment without per-SKU training. CD aims to reduce operational volatility (safety stock, holding cost, order variance) while preserving reliability; gains are realized under certain cost structures rather than universal cost minimization.
AI.motivation: Statistical accuracy in ML demand forecasts often increases operational volatility (Bullwhip) due to promotions and carryover effects. A robust, scalable method is needed to disentangle transient shocks from structural demand so as to stabilize inventories and costs without sacrificing accuracy, especially in large catalogs.
AI.method: A two-stage estimator: (1) kernel-modulated banded operator (data-derived) decomposes demand into transient (promotion-driven) and smooth baseline components; (2) hierarchical partial pooling enables catalog-scale deployment without per-SKU training. The operator reduces to identity when the promotion response is impulsive and only contributes where multi-day carryover exists. Evaluation uses strictly out-of-sample forecasts with calendar-aware baselines on 30,490 M5 SKUs and 2,845 Favorita items.
AI.result: CD lowers safety stock, holding cost, and order variance but may under-provision event spikes. Total cost reduction occurs when holding costs exceed ~20% of stockout costs (CI 17–25%). CD mainly improves reliability (reduced cross-sectional dispersion) rather than central tendency. Across eleven baselines, CD achieves the lowest dispersion and ranks first on four M5 draws; improvements are dramatic for a small minority of SKUs (0.8%) vs baselines (9.9–20.6%). The learned operators are non-normal, yet their compact kernel matches operational performance interpretably.
AI.conclusion: CD provides a scalable, interpretable mechanism to stabilize demand sensing by separating structural baseline demand from promotional carryover. Performance is framed as reliability and inventory capital efficiency rather than universal cost minimization; variance reductions appear as diagnostics. The learned operators’ non-normality is accommodated by a compact, interpretable kernel.

title: From Cellular Responses to Pharmacological Domains: Multimodal Zero-Shot Drug Representation Learning
summary: Multimodal drug discovery enables drug representation learning beyond chemical structure by incorporating cellular responses such as gene expression and cell morphology. However, direct fusion and instance-level contrastive alignment may mix mechanism-related signals with modality-specific noise and incorrectly separate structurally dissimilar but biologically related compounds. This limitation can obscure transferable mechanism patterns required for predicting the properties of unseen compounds. We introduce PMRD, a pharmacological response domain-guided framework for multimodal zero-shot drug property prediction. PMRD separates mechanism-consistent factors from modality-specific information and constructs a consensus response domain across three modalities. Mechanism candidate augmentation identifies locally stable factors, while retrieval-geometry attribution dynamically reweights the alignment and augmentation objectives according to whether their updates preserve inter-drug discriminability.This feedback suppresses training signals that conflict with mechanism-discriminative retrieval. PMRD further combines complementary representations through reliability-aware multiview retrieval. Experiments on public datasets show improved zero-shot property prediction and more biologically coherent drug neighborhoods. Hard-negative analysis further indicates fewer conflicts between structurally dissimilar but response-related compounds. These results support PMRD as an effective framework for mechanism-aware multimodal drug representation learning.\footnote{The code will be released upon publication.}

AI.tldr: PMRD is a pharmacology-response domain-guided framework for multimodal zero-shot drug property prediction that disentangles mechanism-related signals from modality noise and uses a consensus response domain with mechanism-guided augmentation and retrieval to improve predictions for unseen compounds.
AI.motivation: Multimodal drug representations that fuse molecular structure with cellular readouts often conflate mechanism-related signals with modality-specific noise, hindering transfer to unseen compounds and obscuring transferable mechanism patterns.
AI.method: PMRD disentangles mechanism-consistent factors from modality-specific information, builds a consensus response domain across three modalities, uses mechanism candidate augmentation to identify locally stable factors, applies retrieval-geometry attribution to adaptively reweight alignment and augmentation objectives to preserve inter-drug discriminability, and employs reliability-aware multiview retrieval to combine complementary representations while suppressing conflicting training signals.
AI.result: On public datasets, PMRD improves zero-shot property prediction and yields biologically coherent drug neighborhoods; hard-negative analysis indicates fewer conflicts between structurally dissimilar but response-related compounds.
AI.conclusion: PMRD is an effective framework for mechanism-aware multimodal drug representation learning with improved zero-shot prediction, and code release is anticipated.

title: Forensic Reproducibility Audit of a Radiology Vision-Language Model Benchmark: From Intended Protocol to Released Artifact
comment: 25 pages, 5 figures, 7 tables. Retrospective artifact audit; no new model calls or annotations. Corrective audit and archival reconstruction: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21629849
summary: Medical-imaging AI benchmarks combine datasets, DICOM rendering, prompts, provider APIs, automated labels, statistical code, manuscripts, and repository releases. Agreement across these artifacts is usually assumed rather than tested. We performed a retrospective forensic reproducibility audit of a preserved chest-radiograph vision-language model (VLM) pilot; no model was called again and no image or report was newly annotated. We traced prompt bindings, DICOM metadata, output completeness, label extraction, matched analyses, and release propagation. Of 300 planned model-prompt calls, 297 yielded nonempty reports. Sixty Claude calls labeled A/B were executed with the same C prompt. The 30 studies represented 28 patients. Four MONOCHROME1 images were rendered without required polarity inversion, dataset split membership was not retained, and the unvalidated extractor truncated five reports to 4000 characters. Reconstructing one common cohort of 369 complete case-finding blocks changed Cochran's Q from 154.73 to 182.29. Of 45 McNemar comparisons, 27 had unadjusted p < 0.05 and 20 remained below 0.05 after Holm adjustment. These values describe only the archived automated-label matrix; they do not recover the intended prompt comparison or establish clinical performance. We withdraw the original performance, ranking, prompt-effect, and clinical claims and specify machine-verifiable controls for cohort, DICOM rendering, prompt and model identity, call status, annotation provenance, keyed analysis, and derived artifacts.

AI.tldr: A retrospective forensic reproducibility audit of a chest-radiograph vision-language model reveals substantial provenance and data-handling gaps in medical-imaging AI benchmarks, leading to withdrawal of performance claims.
AI.motivation: To test agreement and reproducibility across artifacts (datasets, DICOM rendering, prompts, provider APIs, automated labels, statistical code, manuscripts, and repository releases) in a medical-imaging AI benchmark.
AI.method: Retrospective audit tracing prompt bindings, DICOM metadata, output completeness, label extraction, matched analyses, and release propagation; reanalysis of 300 planned model-prompt calls; evaluation of 45 McNemar tests; reconstruction of a common cohort; analysis with Cochran's Q and Holm adjustment.
AI.result: High rate of nonempty reports (297/300); issues: MONOCHROME1 polarity inversion missing; dataset split membership not retained; unvalidated extractor truncated five reports to 4000 characters; reconstruction altered Cochran's Q from 154.73 to 182.29; 27 of 45 McNemar comparisons had unadjusted p<0.05, 20 remained <0.05 after Holm correction; findings pertain to archived automated-label matrix and do not verify intended prompt comparison or clinical performance.
AI.conclusion: Withdraw original performance, ranking, prompt-effect, and clinical claims; propose machine-verifiable controls for cohort, DICOM rendering, prompt/model identity, call status, annotation provenance, keyed analyses, and derived artifacts to enable reproducible benchmarking.

title: A Physics-Informed Neural Operator for Thermal Ranking of Low-Cost Wall Materials in Hot-Dry Climates
comment: 41 pages, 13 figures. Code and data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21311299
summary: Identifying cost-effective indigenous building materials that minimise heat penetration through walls is critical for indoor thermal comfort in low-income rural housing in hot-dry climates, where summer temperatures routinely exceed 45 C. We present a two-stage computational framework for thermal ranking of five low-cost indigenous wall materials: mud brick, clay-straw adobe, lime-stabilised bamboo panel, fired clay brick, and lime-mud composite. First, a validated Crank-Nicolson finite difference method (FDM) solves the one-dimensional transient heat equation with Robin boundary conditions under diurnal solar and outdoor air-temperature forcing, generating 1500 periodic-day solutions across a nine-dimensional parameter space by Latin Hypercube sampling. Second, a Physics-Informed Neural Operator (PINO) with a Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) backbone learns the parameter-to-solution operator mu -> T(x,t), enforcing both data fidelity and PDE consistency. The trained PINO attains a relative L2 field error of 5.14e-4 and a 0.201 K mean absolute error on the peak inner surface temperature, preserving the FDM material ranking exactly; PINO trained on 150 FDM samples matches a data-only FNO trained on twice as many, so the physics loss is most valuable when data are scarce. The periodic-day formulation also yields the ISO 13786 time lag and decrement factor, reproduced to within 0.99 h and 0.010. At nominal hot-dry summer conditions, clay-straw adobe achieves the best cost-performance index among widely available materials. A climate sweep, confirmed by FDM spot checks, reveals a regime boundary: under sub-ambient outdoor conditions the ranking inverts to conductive fired clay brick, delineating heat-exclusion and heat-rejection regimes. The framework supports evidence-based material selection for post-flood reconstruction in hot-dry regions.

AI.tldr: Two-stage hybrid modeling (FDM + PINO/FNO) ranks five indigenous wall materials for hot-dry climates, showing clay-straw adobe often best for cost-performance; reveals regime boundary where ranking reverses under cooler outdoor conditions; supports evidence-based selection and post-flood reconstruction.
AI.motivation: To identify cost-effective, low-heat-penetration wall materials for rural hot-dry housing, improving indoor thermal comfort and resilience.
AI.method: 1) Solve 1D transient heat equation with Crank–Nicolson FDM and Robin boundary conditions under diurnal forcing; 1500 samples via Latin Hypercube across 9D parameter space. 2) Train a Physics-Informed Neural Operator (PINO) with a Fourier Neural Operator backbone to learn the parameter-to-solution map T(x,t) with physics-informed loss and data fidelity.
AI.result: PINO achieves relative L2 field error 5.14e-4 and mean absolute error 0.201 K on peak inner surface temperature, preserving the FDM-derived material ranking. A PINO trained on 150 FDM samples matches a data-only FNO trained on twice as many samples; physics loss is most valuable when data are scarce.
