However, collecting training data for all possible combined movements is time-consuming and requires re-training of the model for any new combination. We propose two novel recognition approaches, Compositional Prototype Interpolation (CPI) and Synthetic Adaptation for Prototypes (SAP), that enable zero-shot learning of combined, novel and unseen movements in Prototype Networks after training only with basic movements. Our methods rest on a linear interpolation assumption in the embedding space, which we study by inspecting the geometry of combined motions in signal and embedding space. In experiments on the NearLab and NinaPro DB3 data sets as well as our newly recorded BasCom dataset, our proposed SAP outperforms prior zero-shot learning methods with accuracy improvements on combined movements of more than 20%. This advantage is maintained in online inference experiments in a user study.

AI.tldr: Proposes CPI and SAP for zero-shot learning of unseen combined sEMG movements in prosthesis control; relies on linear embedding-space interpolation; SAP achieves >20% accuracy gains over prior zeroshot methods across multiple datasets (NearLab, NinaPro DB3, BasCom) and in online user study.
AI.motivation: Training data for all possible combined movements is impractical; need scalable, zero-shot approaches that can compose basic movements into novel, unseen combinations for robust prosthesis control.
AI.method: Two approaches: Compositional Prototype Interpolation (CPI) and Synthetic Adaptation for Prototypes (SAP). They exploit a linear interpolation assumption in the embedding space to compose prototypes for new combined movements from basic movement prototypes. SAP includes synthetic adaptation of prototypes. Evaluations conducted on NearLab and NinaPro DB3 datasets and a newly recorded BasCom dataset, with online user-study validation.
AI.result: SAP outperforms prior zero-shot learning methods in recognizing combined movements, with accuracy improvements >20% for unseen combinations; gains persist in online/inference user studies.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates feasibility of zero-shot compositional recognition for sEMG-based prosthesis control; reduces calibration data requirements and enables scalable handling of combined movements. Further work needed on robustness, generalization to more complex combinations, and detailed ablation studies.

title: A Control System, a Dataset, and a Recipe for Making Frozen LLM Agents Learn a Domain
comment: 8 pages, 1 figure, 3 tables. Code and dataset: https://github.com/dpaul0501/context-optimization-rl
summary: Production LLM agents are increasingly assembled from a frozen model wrapped in a harness: a prompt template, a tool set, a memory/retrieval layer, a planning strategy, and a verification policy. Two 2026 systems, Meta-Harness (Lee et al., 2026) and HyperAgents (Meta AI, 2026), show that this harness can itself be optimized or even self-rewritten by an agentic proposer -- at the cost of either an expensive code-search loop or unconstrained self-modifying code, neither of which is auditable or usable with a fully black-box model API. We take a narrower, more constrained position: treat the harness as a small, fixed, human-legible action space and learn a policy over it online with classic sample-efficient reinforcement learning (an $ε$-greedy contextual bandit and REINFORCE), scored against a multi-objective reward (task success, verifier score, policy compliance, cost, latency, and an unsupported-claim penalty). We instantiate this control system with DSPy (Khattab et al., 2024) as both the context assembler and the source of the strongest non-adaptive baseline (a DSPy BootstrapFewShot static prompt), and evaluate it across three verifiable task domains -- tool-use workflows, code generation (HumanEval), and multi-hop retrieval QA (HotpotQA) -- and two model providers (a local Ollama model and AWS Bedrock). We release the harness-control-system code, the cross-domain verifiable task suite, the full trajectory/reward-decomposition logs from training, and a provider-agnostic deployment recipe for applying this to a new organization's domain and verification setup.

AI.tldr: A constrained harness optimization for Production LLM agents: treat the harness as a small, fixed, human-legible action space and learn a policy online with ε-greedy contextual bandit and REINFORCE, guided by a multi-objective reward (task success, verifier score, policy compliance, cost, latency, and an unsupported-claim penalty). Evaluated with DSPy as context assembler and BootstrapFewShot as a non-adaptive baseline across tool-use, code generation (HumanEval), and multi-hop retrieval (HotpotQA) on Ollama and AWS Bedrock; code and evaluation artifacts are released for reproducibility and deployment in new domains.
AI.motivation: To address the vulnerability of production LLM agents to self-modifying or opaque harnesses, by constraining the harness to a small, human-interpretable action space and optimizing it with sample-efficient online RL to achieve verifiable, auditable, and domain-transferable behavior.
AI.method: Define a fixed, human-legible harness action space. Use online reinforcement learning with an ε-greedy contextual bandit and REINFORCE to learn a policy over harness actions, optimized by a multi-objective reward including task success, verifier score, policy compliance, cost, latency, and an unsupported-claim penalty. Use DSPy as the context assembler and as the strongest non-adaptive baseline (DSPy BootstrapFewShot). Evaluate across three domains (tool-use workflows, HumanEval code generation, HotpotQA multi-hop retrieval QA) and two providers (Ollama and AWS Bedrock). Release code, complete trajectory/reward logs, and a deployment recipe for domain transfer.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation across three verifiable task domains and two model providers demonstrates feasibility of the constrained harness-learning approach. The work provides reproducible artifacts: harness-control-system code, a cross-domain verifiable task suite, full trajectory/reward decomposition logs, and a provider-agnostic deployment recipe.
AI.conclusion: A practical path toward auditable, domain-transferable Production LLM agents by constraining the harness and optimizing it online; the work supplies end-to-end artifacts to replicate and apply the approach to new domains and verification setups.

title: FLASH: Efficient Impact Fall Detection with Unified Hypergraph State-Space Model
comment: 6 pages, 2 figures. Accepted at IEEE International Conference on Image Processing (ICIP 2026), to appear September 2026
summary: Falls represent a critical public health challenge, and accurate detection of the impact moment when an individual hits the ground is crucial for timely intervention. Existing skeleton-based methods rely on graph neural networks modeling only pairwise joint connections, failing to capture multi-joint coordination characteristic of fall impacts, while transformer-based temporal models suffer from quadratic complexity limiting real-time deployment. We propose FLASH, a novel framework integrating single-matrix hypergraph representations with Mamba's selective state-space models through adaptive feedback mechanisms for efficient impact detection. Our approach constructs biomechanically-grounded hyperedges to model functional joint coordination while leveraging Mamba's linear-time complexity to capture temporal dynamics. Experiments on UP-Fall and UMAFall datasets demonstrate that FLASH achieves state-of-the-art accuracy with real-time inference capability and strong zero-shot cross-dataset generalization, while significantly reducing computational cost compared to dual-representation and transformer-based methods. The model provides interpretable feedback through learned attention patterns aligned with biomechanical principles. Code is available at https://github.com/Tresor-Koffi/FLASH-Impact-Fall-Detection.

AI.tldr: FLASH combines biomechanically-grounded hypergraphs with Mamba's linear-time selective state-space models to detect ground-impact moments in falls, achieving real-time performance, strong cross-dataset generalization, and lower computation than dual-representation or transformer baselines.
AI.motivation: Accurately identifying the exact moment of ground impact is crucial for timely fall intervention. Skeleton-based methods that use only pairwise joint graphs miss multi-joint coordination during impact, while transformer-based temporal models incur quadratic complexity, hindering real-time deployment. There is a need for a model that captures multi-joint coordination efficiently and supports real-time inference with good generalization.
AI.method: Constructs biomechanically-grounded hyperedges to form a single-matrix hypergraph capturing multi-joint coordination during falls. Integrates Mamba's selective state-space models with adaptive feedback mechanisms to model temporal dynamics in linear time. Emphasizes interpretability through learned attention patterns aligned with biomechanics and achieves real-time inference.
AI.result: On UP-Fall and UMAFall datasets, FLASH achieves state-of-the-art accuracy with real-time inference, strong zero-shot cross-dataset generalization, and substantially reduced computation compared with dual-representation and transformer-based methods. The approach yields interpretable feedback via attention patterns that align with biomechanical principles. Code is publicly available.
AI.conclusion: FLASH effectively unifies biomechanically-grounded hypergraph representations with linear-time temporal modeling to deliver accurate, efficient, and interpretable fall-impact detection with strong cross-dataset generalization and real-time applicability.

title: DRIFT: Direct-Recursive Intervention-Conditioned Forecasting of ICU Physiological Trajectories
comment: 34 pages, 1 figure; extended technical appendices included
summary: Many time-series forecasts depend not only on prior observations but also on actions specified during the forecast period. In intensive care units (ICUs), future vital signs and laboratory values are influenced by treatments such as vasopressors. However, models that predict the full future sequence all at once make little use of these treatments, whereas autoregressive models can accumulate errors. We introduce DRIFT, a hybrid framework in which a direct model produces the primary forecast and a recursive, action-conditioned model contributes constrained corrections. We evaluate DRIFT on 6,046 admissions from MIMIC-IV and 8,345 admissions from eICU-CRD. Averaged across the 8-, 24-, and 48-hour forecast endpoints, DRIFT reduces mean absolute error for mean arterial pressure (MAP) by 0.673% relative to an action-conditioned Temporal Fusion Transformer (TFT-action) on MIMIC-IV and achieves the lowest corresponding error among the compared models on eICU-CRD. Although the overall accuracy improvement is modest, a MIMIC-IV audit restricted to windows in which the supplied treatment sequence was altered showed that DRIFT achieved lower observed-target MAP error than TFT-action at 8 and 24 hours. Treatment-sequence alteration increased DRIFT's MAP error by 0.21-0.26 mmHg more than it increased TFT-action's error, with prediction changes occurring primarily after the supplied paths diverged. In a separate robustness experiment, the MAP advantage persisted under three shared checkpoint-selection rules emphasizing overall endpoint error, MAP error, or both equally.

AI.tldr: DRIFT is a hybrid time-series forecasting framework for ICU data that combines a direct forecast with a constrained recursive, action-conditioned correction to leverage treatment sequences; shows modest but robust improvements in mean arterial pressure (MAP) forecasting over an action-conditioned TFT across MIMIC-IV and eICU-CRD.
AI.motivation: Many ICU forecasts depend on treatments during the forecast horizon; existing full-sequence models underuse actions and autoregressive models accrue errors. DRIFT aims to incorporate action sequences to improve multi-step MAP predictions.
AI.method: DRIFT couples a direct model that outputs the primary forecast with a recursive, action-conditioned model that provides constrained corrections. Evaluated on 6,046 MIMIC-IV and 8,345 eICU-CRD admissions, across 8-, 24-, and 48-hour horizons, against TFT-action, with a MIMIC-IV audit on altered treatment sequences and robustness checks using three checkpoint-selection rules.
AI.result: MAP MAE reduced by 0.673% (relative) vs TFT-action on MIMIC-IV; DRIFT had the lowest corresponding MAP error among comparisons on eICU-CRD. In a MIMIC-IV audit with altered treatment sequences, DRIFT showed lower observed-target MAP error than TFT-action at 8 and 24 hours. When sequences were altered, DRIFT’s MAP error increased by 0.21–0.26 mmHg more than TFT-action’s, indicating sensitivity to path divergence after divergence. The MAP advantage persisted under three checkpoint-selection rules emphasizing endpoint error, MAP error, or both equally.
AI.conclusion: DRIFT delivers modest but consistent improvements in MAP forecasting in action-conditioned ICU settings and demonstrates robustness across different checkpoint strategies; gains are somewhat sensitive to actual treatment-path changes, suggesting further refinements could enhance integration of treatment dynamics in multi-step ICU forecasts.

title: Salient Knowledge Pathways: Sparse Cross-Modal Routing for Efficient Knowledge-Intensive Multimodal Question Answering
comment: Accepted at the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026) Workshop on Efficient Multimodal Question Answering (EMM-QA), Seoul, South Korea. Copyright 2026 by the author(s). (Archival)
summary: Knowledge-intensive multimodal question answering (KI-MMQA) sits at the intersection of three expensive primitives: long visual token sequences, dense retrieval over large external corpora, and full cross-modal fusion. Existing systems pay all three costs uniformly per query, even though only a small fraction of visual content and retrieved knowledge is actually relevant to any given question. We introduce SKIP (Salient Knowledge-Injected Pathways), a unified inference architecture that routes computation along sparse pathways jointly conditioned on the question, the image, and a difficulty estimate. SKIP combines question-guided visual token pruning, region-conditional sparse retrieval, bipartite sparse cross-attention, and speculative knowledge verification with an adaptive budget controller that allocates compute proportional to predicted question difficulty. We derive an information-bottleneck bound showing that the optimal visual sparsity rate scales as $O(1/\sqrt{N})$ under realistic question-image mutual-information assumptions, with retained accuracy guarantees. Across five KI-MMQA benchmarks (OK-VQA, A-OKVQA, InfoSeek, Encyclopedic-VQA, and ViQuAE), SKIP matches or exceeds the accuracy of strong dense baselines while using $3.4$--$6.8\times$ fewer FLOPs and $2.7\times$ less end-to-end latency. Code available at: https://pmlrbd.github.io/skip/

AI.tldr: SKIP is a sparse, question-guided inference architecture for knowledge-intensive multimodal QA that routes computation through salient pathways to prune visuals, sparsify retrieval, and verify knowledge, achieving strong accuracy with large compute savings.
AI.motivation: KI-MMQA tasks incur high costs from long visual token sequences, dense external retrieval, and full cross-modal fusion. Only a small fraction of visual content and retrieved knowledge is typically relevant to a given question, motivating sparse, conditional computation.
AI.method: SKIP combines: (1) question-guided visual token pruning; (2) region-conditional sparse retrieval; (3) bipartite sparse cross-attention for cross-modal fusion; (4) speculative knowledge verification; and (5) an adaptive budget controller that scales compute with predicted question difficulty. An information-bottleneck bound shows the optimal visual sparsity rate scales as O(1/√N) under plausible MI assumptions, with retained accuracy guarantees.
AI.result: Empirically evaluated on five KI-MMQA benchmarks (OK-VQA, A-OKVQA, InfoSeek, Encyclopedic-VQA, ViQuAE). SKIP matches or exceeds strong dense baselines in accuracy while reducing FLOPs by 3.4×–6.8× and lowering end-to-end latency by ~2.7×.
AI.conclusion: SKIP demonstrates that sparse, jointly conditioned pathways can achieve competitive or superior KI-MMQA performance with substantial compute efficiency, supported by a theoretical sparsity bound and multiple benchmark gains. Code is available at the project page.

title: Fine-Grained Food Image Understanding via Target-Aware Data Alignment
summary: Fine-grained food visual--semantic understanding requires models to capture subtle distinctions across ingredients, cooking methods, doneness, color, texture, and plate composition. Although CLIP-style vision-language models provide a natural framework for this task, their effectiveness is limited when training relies on heterogeneous web-collected image--text pairs. Such data often exhibit a web-to-target domain gap and cross-modal misalignment, where images differ from the target distribution and captions are noisy, multilingual, or weakly grounded in visual content. We propose a data-centric multimodal alignment method for fine-grained food description and recognition. Our method first performs target-aware data selection to identify visually relevant training subsets, then applies VLM-based caption refinement to generate visually grounded, target-style descriptions. Using these curated image--caption pairs, we train complementary CLIP-style retrieval experts and further combine their decisions through a hierarchical VLM-assisted multi-expert decision-level fusion strategy that invokes the VLM only when experts disagree. Experiments show that our data refinement strategy significantly improves retrieval performance over naive web supervision, with VLM-based caption refinement alone yielding an average performance gain of approximately 19%. Our full method also achieves more than twice the retrieval score of pure VLM-based retrieval while remaining substantially more efficient.

AI.tldr: Data-centric alignment for fine-grained food understanding using target-aware data selection, VLM-based caption refinement, and hierarchical multi-expert fusion to boost CLIP-style retrieval over web supervision.
AI.motivation: CLIP-like vision-language models struggle with domain shift and noisy captions in web-sourced image-text pairs, particularly for fine-grained food attributes where subtle cues are critical.
AI.method: 1) Target-aware data selection to filter visually relevant training samples. 2) VLM-based caption refinement to generate visually grounded, target-style captions. 3) Train complementary CLIP-style retrieval experts on curated data. 4) Hierarchical fusion: invoke the VLM only when experts disagree to combine decisions.
AI.result: Data refinement yields significant retrieval gains over naive web supervision; VLM-based caption refinement alone yields ~19% average gain; the full method achieves >2x retrieval score vs pure VLM-based retrieval and is more efficient.
AI.conclusion: A data-centric, multi-stage alignment pipeline can substantially improve fine-grained food retrieval by reducing misalignment and leveraging complementary models, with notable efficiency benefits.

title: A2TTA: Anchored-and-Agile Test-Time Adaptation for Evolving Traffic Sensor Networks
summary: Traffic forecasting is important for efficient traffic management and route planning in smart cities. Existing traffic forecasting studies typically assume fixed sensor graphs, overlooking the continuous evolution of real-world traffic networks, e.g., ongoing road network construction and evolving human mobility patterns. These dynamic changes can substantially degrade conventional forecasting models, motivating test-time adaptation (TTA) to efficiently adapt pretrained models during deployment. However, applying TTA to evolving traffic sensor networks remains challenging in two aspects. First, topology expansion introduces new sensors and connections, continuously reshaping the sensor graph. Second, tem- poral shifts vary in time scale and stability, requiring differentiated adaptation to long-term and short-term shifts. In this study, we address these challenges by proposing A2TTA, an Anchored-and-Agile Test-Time Adaptation framework for evolving traffic sensor networks, which transforms topology-induced forecasting errors into an expandable output calibration problem and separates tem- poral adaptation into persistent global correction and agile context-specific specialization. By jointly addressing topology evolution and multi-scale temporal shifts, A2TTA enables efficient and robust adaptation to continuously evolving traffic environments. Extensive experiments on ten real-world traffic networks demonstrate that A2TTA consistently improves forecasting performance across different backbones, datasets, and prediction horizons. Our code is available in https://github.com/lixus7/A2TTA.

AI.tldr: A2TTA introduces Anchored-and-Agile Test-Time Adaptation for evolving traffic sensor networks, combining topology-aware output calibration with multi-scale temporal adaptation to robustly adjust pretrained models during deployment as the sensor graph grows and weather/mobility patterns shift.
AI.motivation: Real-world traffic networks continually evolve: new sensors and connections expand the topology, and temporal shifts occur at multiple time scales. Fixed-graph forecasting models degrade under such changes, necessitating effective test-time adaptation.
AI.method: A2TTA decouples topology-induced errors into an expandable output calibration problem and splits temporal adaptation into persistent global correction plus agile context-specific specialization, enabling joint handling of topology evolution and multi-scale temporal shifts.
AI.result: Empirical validation on ten real-world traffic networks shows consistent forecasting improvements across different backbones, datasets, and horizons; code provided at https://github.com/lixus7/A2TTA.
AI.conclusion: A2TTA offers efficient and robust test-time adaptation for evolving traffic environments by integrating topology-aware calibration with multi-scale temporal adaptation, applicable across diverse backbone models and settings.

title: The Disruptive Impact of Large Language Models on Capture the Flag Competitions and the Path Toward Fair Play
summary: Capture the Flag (CTF) competitions are among cybersecurity's most effective training grounds, developing practical skill across cryptography, web exploitation, and binary exploitation. Large language models (LLMs) can now solve a growing share of challenges with minimal human input, raising urgent questions about fairness, the validity of rankings, and whether participation still delivers the learning that justifies the effort. This paper reports a mixed-methods study of LLM impact on modern CTFs, combining a synthesis of published benchmarks, including a recent government evaluation, case studies of live competition across three challenge categories, structured observation of the public channels where the community debates AI use, and semi-structured interviews with experienced players and organisers. We map the current human-machine capability boundary by category, showing that easy and intermediate challenges in cryptography, web, and binary exploitation are now reliably automated while narrower sub-categories continue to resist. We find that community disagreement about whether AI should be permitted is downstream of an undeclared prior question: what a competition is for. Against this backdrop we contribute a four-component safeguard framework, combining tiered competition divisions, LLM-resistant challenge design, telemetry used investigatively, and a draft community code of conduct, together with a decision tool that ties the combination of safeguards to a competition's declared purpose. The argument reaches beyond CTFs to any setting in cybersecurity where a demonstrated result is taken as evidence of an underlying ability.

AI.tldr: LLMs now reliably automate easy/intermediate CTF challenges across crypto, web, and binary domains, prompting governance concerns about fairness, rankings, and learning; the paper proposes a four-component safeguard framework and decision tool to preserve purpose in CTFs and similar cybersecurity contexts.
AI.motivation: To understand how large language models affect modern CTFs—affecting fairness, validity of rankings, and educational value—and to clarify what a competition should measure in the presence of AI capabilities.
AI.method: Mixed-methods study combining: (1) synthesis of published benchmarks including a government evaluation; (2) case studies of live competitions across three challenge categories; (3) structured observation of public channels where the community debates AI use; (4) semi-structured interviews with experienced players and organizers.
AI.result: Mapping of human–machine capability by category shows easy and intermediate cryptography, web, and binary challenges are reliably automated; narrower sub-categories resist. Community disagreement about AI-permitted use reflects a deeper question of the competition’s purpose. A four-component safeguard framework is proposed: tiered divisions, LLM-resistant challenge design, telemetry for investigative use, and a draft community code of conduct, plus a decision tool linking safeguards to declared purpose.
AI.conclusion: The framework and decision tool extend beyond CTFs to broader cybersecurity settings where observable results are used as evidence of underlying ability, highlighting governance needs to align AI use with learning objectives and competition goals.

title: Explicit Layer Modeling for Video Object Insertion and Layer Decomposition
summary: Most video editing systems still lack explicit layered video representations, limiting their ability to perform realistic compositing, object reuse, and consistent manipulation. This limitation is especially pronounced in video object insertion and video layer decomposition, where existing methods rely on implicit inference or per-scene optimization due to the absence of explicit foreground-layer supervision. We introduce TriLayer, a large-scale triplet video dataset containing aligned composite, background, and foreground videos, where the foreground layers include both object appearance and associated visual effects. This explicit supervision enables models to learn layered video representations directly rather than inferring them implicitly. Building on this dataset, we propose DBL-Diffusion, a dual-branch diffusion framework that jointly models RGB composites and RGBA foreground layers through shared denoising and cross-branch interaction. We instantiate the framework in two tasks: DBL-Insert for layered object insertion, which generates explicit RGBA layers for realistic compositing and flexible post-editing, and DBL-Decompose for video layer decomposition, which recovers foreground and background layers using triplet supervision. Experiments demonstrate that explicit layer modeling substantially improves both insertion fidelity and decomposition quality.

AI.tldr: TriLayer introduces a large-scale triplet video dataset with aligned composite, background, and foreground videos (foreground includes appearance and visual effects) and presents DBL-Diffusion, a dual-branch diffusion model that jointly models RGB composites and RGBA foreground layers for two tasks: DBL-Insert (layered object insertion) and DBL-Decompose (layer decomposition). Explicit layer supervision improves insertion fidelity and decomposition accuracy.
AI.motivation: Existing video editing systems lack explicit layered representations, hindering realistic compositing, object reuse, and consistent manipulation. Foreground-layer supervision is scarce, causing reliance on implicit inference or per-scene optimization.
AI.method: Provide TriLayer dataset with explicit foreground/background/combined triplets; develop DBL-Diffusion, a dual-branch diffusion framework with shared denoising and cross-branch interaction to model RGB composites and RGBA foreground layers. Define two tasks: DBL-Insert (generate RGBA layers for compositing and editing) and DBL-Decompose (recover foreground/background layers with triplet supervision).
AI.result: Experiments show that explicit layer modeling via the TriLayer dataset and DBL-Diffusion framework improves insertion fidelity and decomposition quality compared to baseline methods.
AI.conclusion: Explicit layered video representations, learned through triplet supervision and dual-branch diffusion, enhance capability for layered editing tasks such as insertion and decomposition, enabling more realistic compositing and flexible post-editing.

title: A Machine-Learning-Based Gas Lift Optimization Workflow for Unconventional Fields
summary: In this paper, we present an automated data-driven workflow using Machine Learning (ML) for gas lift optimization in unconventional fields. This workflow integrates a ML model that accurately forecasts the Gas Lift Performance Curve, and a Bayesian Optimization Framework to solve for the optimal gas injection rates under the constraints of facility capacity. The ML model leverages the historical production time series data without requiring downhole gauges or multi-rate well tests. We piloted this workflow on 30 wells across 5 well pads in Bakken and obtained >5% production uplift on average. With the success of the pilot, we have now fully-deployed this workflow in Bakken across 200+ gas lift and plunger-assisted gas lift (PAGL) wells. Moreover, the ML-based gas lift optimization workflow presented in this paper is an effective and economic solution for other assets where downhole data or multi-rate testing are not available/feasible due to cost or facility constraints.

AI.tldr: An ML-driven, data-driven gas lift optimization workflow using ML forecast of Gas Lift Performance Curve plus Bayesian Optimization to optimize gas injection under facility constraints; validated on 30 wells (5 pads) in Bakken; scaled to 200+ wells; reports >5% uplift on average.
AI.motivation: Enable economically efficient gas lift optimization without downhole gauges or multi-rate tests, reducing cost and enabling scalable deployment across assets with limited instrumentation.
AI.method: Train ML model on historical production time series to forecast the Gas Lift Performance Curve; use a Bayesian Optimization framework to choose injection rates that maximize production under facility capacity constraints; pilot on 30 wells across 5 pads in Bakken; then deployed across 200+ gas lift / PAGL wells; applicable to assets lacking downhole data or multi-rate testing.
AI.result: Pilot yielded average production uplift >5%; full deployment across 200+ wells; presented as an effective and economical solution for assets without downhole data or multi-rate testing.
AI.conclusion: ML-based gas lift optimization workflow is scalable, economical, and adaptable to assets with limited data, with potential for widespread adoption in unconventional fields.

title: Toward an Organizational Science of Multi-Agent LLM Systems: Decoupling Who, How, and Which Algorithm
summary: Multi-agent frameworks built on large language models (LLMs) routinely entangle three logically distinct concerns: who is on the team (organization), how members align (coordination), and which algorithm fuses their work (collaboration protocol). IMACS (Intelligent Multi-Agent Collaboration System) separates the three into orthogonal, independently swappable layers. Classic organizational theory (Belbin roles, Mintzberg coordination, RACI accountability) becomes executable, validated configuration, and the framework places six published collaboration algorithms behind a common interface while exposing roles, coordination, and accountability as independently configurable factors. We use this separation to conduct controlled comparisons in which organizational assignments vary while the collaboration protocol is held fixed. It also turns protocol choice into a variable that can be learned: Adaptive Org Routing, a contextual-bandit meta-protocol, selects a protocol per task under an explicit quality-cost tradeoff, outperforms every fixed protocol in a controlled study, and trains online on real benchmark and LLM-judge rewards. The ablations expose a mechanism. Accountability placement changes outcomes exactly when the protocol routes the deliverable through the accountable agent, and the winning placement flips across model families, so organizational design cannot be hard-coded; it must be revalidated, or learned, for each model binding.

AI.tldr: IMACS decouples organization, coordination, and collaboration protocol into orthogonal layers, enabling controlled comparisons and learnable protocol selection; design must be revalidated per model binding.
AI.motivation: To address entanglement of organizational structure, coordination, and collaboration protocols in multi-agent LLM frameworks and to enable systematic comparisons and learnable protocol choice.
AI.method: Separate Belbin-style roles (organization), Mintzberg-style coordination, and RACI-style accountability into configurable layers; provide six collaboration algorithms behind a common interface; implement Adaptive Org Routing, a contextual-bandit meta-protocol that selects a protocol per task under a quality-cost tradeoff; evaluate via ablations on benchmark tasks and LLM judge rewards.
AI.result: Adaptive Org Routing outperforms all fixed protocols in controlled experiments; accountability placement affects outcomes only when the protocol routes through the accountable agent, with winner placement varying across model families; organizational design cannot be hard-coded and must be learned or revalidated per model binding.
AI.conclusion: Orthogonal layering enables controlled comparisons and learnable protocol selection; to generalize across models, organizational design must be revalidated or learned for each model binding.

title: Freq-RemoteVAR: Next-Frequency Autoregressive Modeling for Remote Sensing Change Detection
summary: Remote sensing change detection aims to identify land-cover changes from bi-temporal images. Most existing methods follow a one-shot dense prediction paradigm, directly regressing a change mask from fused features. However, such approaches overlook the intrinsic frequency characteristics of change patterns. We propose Freq-RemoteVAR, a frequency autoregressive framework that reformulates change detection as a structured generation problem in the frequency domain. Instead of predicting the change mask in a single step, we introduce a next-frequency prediction paradigm, where change information is progressively generated from coarse to fine. We design a frequency-aware mask tokenization strategy that decomposes change supervision into multi-frequency token targets via Fourier transformation and quantization. We develop a Frequency VAR Transformer, which performs causal autoregressive modeling over frequency tokens. The model starts from learned mask queries and progressively predicts frequency-level tokens conditioned on previously generated tokens and bi-temporal image features, effectively capturing long-range dependencies across frequency scales. We introduce Scale-Aligned RoPE Cross Attention (SRCA) module, which aligns frequency-domain mask queries with spatial-domain bi-temporal features under a unified coordinate system, enhancing spatial-frequency consistency during generation. We propose a Change-quality Control module that adaptively modulates the generation process through dynamic normalization, attention biasing, and spatial offset adjustment, thereby suppressing pseudo-change responses and improving robustness. Extensive experiments on CDD, GZ-CD, and LEVIR-CD demonstrate that Freq-RemoteVAR consistently outperforms existing methods, particularly in challenging scenarios with complex appearance variations and noisy disturbances.

AI.tldr: Transforms change detection into a frequency-domain autoregressive generation process, progressively predicting frequency tokens from coarse to fine with cross-attention and quality control.
AI.motivation: Standard one-shot dense prediction fails to leverage the intrinsic frequency characteristics of change patterns and is sensitive to appearance variations and noise.
AI.method: 1) Frequency-aware mask tokenization via Fourier transform and quantization; 2) Frequency VAR Transformer for causal autoregressive modeling over frequency tokens, starting from learned mask queries; 3) Scale-Aligned RoPE Cross Attention (SRCA) to align frequency-domain queries with spatial-temporal features; 4) Change-quality Control module with dynamic normalization, attention biasing, and spatial offset adjustment; 5) Next-frequency prediction paradigm; 6) Bi-temporal image features guiding generation.
AI.result: Empirical results on CDD, GZ-CD, and LEVIR-CD show consistent improvements over existing methods, especially in scenarios with complex appearance variations and noisy disturbances.
AI.conclusion: The framework validates that frequency-domain structured generation is effective for change detection, enabling long-range dependencies across frequency scales and enhanced robustness.

title: Minimizing Targeted Activations: Input-Only Suppression of Evaluation-Awareness Latents in Large Language Models
summary: Activation steering controls model behavior by editing internal activations at inference time. We study its input-side dual: optimizing a fluent prompt so that a chosen internal latent is driven toward zero, with no inference-time model access. Our target is an "evaluation-awareness" latent-linearly readable and steerable in recent work-whose control would threaten the validity of safety evaluations if models behave differently when they detect being tested. Adapting Fluent Dreaming / EPO with a negated feature term (GCG-style token optimization plus a self-cross-entropy fluency regularizer, swept over a fluency weight), we suppress the latent under five target constructions-a CAA direction, a subspace norm, an SAE feature, a single MLP neuron, and a behavioral logit-on Llama-3.2-3B and Llama-3.1-8B. The latent is robustly suppressible ($z\approx-7$), and a causally-validated Llama Scope SAE feature can be fully and selectively turned off. But our controls tell a cautionary story about the CAA direction: a placebo random direction is suppressed just as hard and shifts behavior just as far, and when we hold a real eval passage in context and optimize only a prefix, suppressing the eval-direction fails to reduce-and slightly increases-the model's behavioral eval judgment. Activation-readability, in short, is not behavioral controllability. We further find that a single MLP neuron is eval-correlated but not causal at both scales, and that scanning the real Pile yields a natural-text baseline competitive with the optimizer for the internal direction. A positive control validates our erasure detector, bounding an erasure-vs-rotation question earlier left open.

AI.tldr: Activation prompt optimization can suppress an evaluation-aware internal latent, but readability of the latent does not imply behavioral control. Placebo directions confound suppression, and causal influence is not established for the targeted components. Activation-readability is insufficient for controllability; an erasure detector is helpful, but results highlight limits of current approaches.
AI.motivation: Evaluate whether an internally readable, evaluation-aware latent direction can be suppressed at inference time through input-side optimization, without direct access to model internals, and whether such suppression yields reliable behavioral control during safety evaluations.
AI.method: Adapt Fluent Dreaming / EPO with a negated feature term; use GCG-style token optimization plus a self-cross-entropy fluency regularizer, sweeping the fluency weight. Target five constructs (CAA direction, a subspace norm, SAE feature, a single MLP neuron, and a behavioral logit) on Llama-3.2-3B and Llama-3.1-8B. Measure latent suppressibility (z≈−7), test selectivity of Llama Scope SAE feature, and perform positive control with an erasure detector. Compare against placebo random directions, and examine prefix-only suppression and natural-text baselines (the real Pile). Assess causality vs correlation for MLP neuron and analyze evaluation judgments.
AI.result: Latent suppression is robust for several target constructs, including the SAE feature, with z ≈ −7 and selective deactivation observed. However, a placebo random direction is suppressed just as strongly and shifts behavior similarly, undermining interpretability. Suppressing the eval-direction in a context where an evaluation passage is present (prefix-only optimization) does not reduce—and may slightly increase—the model’s behavioral evaluation judgment. A single MLP neuron shows eval-correlation but no causal role at either scale. Scanning the real Pile yields a natural-text baseline competitive with the optimizer. An erasure detector provides a positive control and bounds the erasure-vs-rotation question for the study.
AI.conclusion: Activation-readability does not guarantee behavioral controllability. Latent erasure via input-side optimization faces challenges such as directional ambiguity (placebo vs genuine directions) and context dependence. The findings urge caution in interpreting readable latents as reliable control levers and highlight the need for stronger causal validation and broader evaluation contexts.

title: TRWH: A Text-Driven Random Walk Heterogeneous GNN for Semantic-Aware Sparse Recommendation
summary: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and Large Language Models (LLMs) have each advanced recommendation systems by modeling structural and semantic signals, respectively. However, integrating their complementary strengths remains challenging, particularly in sparse settings where maintaining semantic precision is critical. We propose TRWH (Text-driven Random Walk Heterogeneous Graph Neural Network), a novel framework that fuses LLM-generated textual profiles with heterogeneous graph structures through strategic random walk augmentation. TRWH consists of three core components: (1) Embedding Creation, which produces user and item representations using both Word2Vec and LLM-based profiling; (2) a Heterogeneous Graph Neural Network (HeteroGNN) that propagates information across multi-relational edges; and (3) Random Walk-based Path Construction, which enriches sparse graphs with second-order user-user and item-item links. Experiments on the Amazon-2023 Fashion (2M users, 825K items) and Beauty (631K users, 112K items) datasets demonstrate that TRWH achieves substantial performance gains over state-of-the-art methods, including 80.0% RMSE and 52.6% MAE reductions on Fashion, and 25.7% and 10.8% improvements on Beauty. Notably, while random walks improve performance with traditional embeddings, they can dilute the nuanced representations learned by LLMs, underscoring the importance of adaptive integration strategies.

AI.tldr: TRWH fuses LLM-derived text profiles with heterogeneous graph reasoning via random-walk augmentation to improve recommender systems in sparse settings; achieves large gains on large fashion and beauty datasets; highlights need to adapt random-walk integration to preserve semantic precision.
AI.motivation: Combine the strengths of GNNs (graph structure) and LLMs (semantic textual profiles) to tackle sparsity and semantic alignment; address dilution risk from random-walk augmentation.
AI.method: Three components: Embedding Creation using Word2Vec and LLM-based profiling; Heterogeneous Graph Neural Network (HeteroGNN) on multi-relational edges; Random Walk-based Path Construction adding second-order user-user and item-item links to enrich sparse graphs.
AI.result: On Fashion: ~80% RMSE reduction and ~53% MAE reduction; on Beauty: ~25.7% RMSE improvement and ~10.8% MAE improvement; outperform state-of-the-art baselines.
AI.conclusion: TRWH demonstrates that text-driven profiles plus structured hetero-graphs with carefully integrated random walks yield strong performance, but adaptive integration is crucial to preserve semantic quality; random walks alone can degrade LLM-derived representations.

title: SepPrune:A Separator-based Pruning Framework for Efficient Multimodal Large Language Models
summary: Recent multimodal large language models (MLLMs), such as Qwen2.5-VL and InternVL3, generate large numbers of vision tokens for high-resolution inputs, leading to substantial computational cost. Existing vision token pruning methods either depend on cross-modal attention and cannot prune before the prefill stage, or rely on diversity estimation with high computational overhead. We observe that attention scores from both vision and text tokens peak at modality separator tokens, suggesting that these separators bridge the two modalities. Based on this observation, we propose SepPrune, an efficient, training-free, plug-and-play pruning method that uses the separator token as a unified query to rank and select informative vision tokens. SepPrune reuses the LLM's built-in projection parameters and requires no architectural changes. Experiments on Qwen2.5-VL-7B show that SepPrune achieves state-of-the-art performance, retaining 96.3% of the original accuracy while removing 80.2% of vision tokens.

AI.tldr: SepPrune is a training-free, plug-and-play vision token pruning method for multimodal LLMs that uses the modality separator token as a unified query to rank and trim vision tokens, achieving high token reduction with minimal accuracy loss.
AI.motivation: High computational cost from processing many vision tokens in multimodal LLMs and limitations of existing pruning methods (reliance on cross-modal attention or expensive diversity estimation); need pruning before prefill stage.
AI.method: Leverage the attention peak at the modality separator tokens to create a unified query from the separator, ranking vision tokens by informativeness. Reuse the LLM's existing projection parameters, require no architectural changes, and prune vision tokens before prefill.
AI.result: On Qwen2.5-VL-7B, SepPrune retains 96.3% of original accuracy while removing 80.2% of vision tokens, achieving state-of-the-art performance with substantial token reduction.
AI.conclusion: SepPrune provides a fast, training-free, plug-and-play solution for vision token pruning in high-resolution multimodal LLMs, delivering large token reductions with minimal accuracy loss without modifying model architecture.

title: Reinforcement Learning for Code Optimization
summary: RL for code correctness is now established: have the model generate a program, run it against hidden test cases, and reward solutions that pass. Extending this to code optimization seems straightforward: just add execution time to the reward. But in practice, once timing drives the reward, small problems in measurement noise, reward sparsity, or GRPO instability overwhelm the signal and make RL fail: generated solutions are barely faster, and more of them can fail. We make execution time learnable through three stages: (1) how code is tested, by building DMC-Optim with large optimization tests and a calibrated sandbox; (2) how speed is turned into reward, by composing correctness and speed in the RL environment and using an offline simulator to predict the most promising configurations; and (3) how the model learns from that reward, by adapting GRPO and evaluation to the sparser, noisier timed-execution setting. On DMC-Optim, the strongest optimization-aware configurations improve strict top-50% pass@1 from 18.0% to 31.3% on Qwen 2.5 7B and from 30.7% to 50.4% on CWM 32B. These gains further increase at stricter percentiles such as top-30%, with 125% relative improvement for CWM 32B, while preserving pure-correctness scores. When the timing sandbox is degraded, robust optimization RL reaches 100% to 200% improvement over standard RLVR, depending on the evaluation criterion. On LCB, CWM 32B wins up to 83% of median-sample speed comparisons against standard RLVR. Relative to the fastest correct human submissions per problem, it reaches about half the human rate of complexity-class improvements (14% vs. 28%).

AI.tldr: Extends RL for code correctness to code optimization by incorporating execution time into the reward, using a three-stage pipeline (enhanced test harness with DMC-Optim sandbox, reward shaping with speed via offline simulation, and learning adaptations to sparse/noisy timing).
AI.motivation: Address measurement noise, reward sparsity, and RL instability when timing signals are used; enable learnable speed signals for program optimization.
AI.method: Three-stage approach: (1) testing environment via DMC-Optim with large optimization tests and calibrated sandbox; (2) reward shaping by combining correctness and speed and using an offline simulator to predict promising configurations; (3) adapting GRPO and evaluation to sparse, noisier timed-execution.
AI.result: Significant improvements: on DMC-Optim, strongest optimization-aware configs raise strict top-50% pass@1 from 18.0% to 31.3% (Qwen 2.5 7B) and from 30.7% to 50.4% (CWM 32B); top-30% shows 125% relative improvement for CWM 32B; robustness under degraded timing sandbox yields 100-200% improvement over standard RLVR; on LCB, CWM 32B dominates median-sample speed by up to 83%; relative to fastest correct human submissions per problem, 14% versus 28% human rate of complexity-class improvements.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates that timed-execution signals can be learned and leveraged for code optimization without sacrificing correctness; a three-stage framework yields robust gains across benchmarks and evaluation regimes, suggesting practical potential for speed-aware program synthesis.

title: Food Image Segmentation with LLM-Derived Ingredient Labels and Multimodal Fusion
summary: Food image segmentation plays a vital role in health-related applications such as nutrition tracking and personalized health monitoring. However, existing models often underperform on visually similar ingredients and rare food categories. To address this issue, we propose two plug-and-play multimodal modules that enhance the segmentation performance by leveraging ingredient labels inferred from food images using large language models (LLMs). The first module, called LIM-F (Language Injection Module for Features), is designed to pair with any image encoder that produces multi-layer outputs (e.g., Swin Transformer), while the second module, LIM-Q (Language Injection Module for Queries), targets Mask2Former-style Transformer-based decoders. Both modules enable training without the need for pre-aligning images with text by directly injecting semantic ingredient information into the visual analysis pipeline. On the FoodSeg103 benchmark, the proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance. Specifically, integrating LIM-Q into the Mask2Former decoder with a Swin-L image encoder yields a mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) of 55.0. LIM-F also demonstrates strong generalization and competitive performance, reaching an mIoU of 54.4 under the same model (Swin-L+Mask2Former). Furthermore, its applicability extends beyond Transformer-based decoders, as evidenced by an improvement from 47.7 to 49.8 mIoU when integrated into a CNN-based architecture. Notably, the improved segmentation accuracy is achieved with only a moderate (at most 3.8 GB) increase in the GPU memory consumption during training. Thus, the proposed approach offers a practical and scalable solution for fine-grained food understanding.

AI.tldr: Two plug-and-play multimodal modules (LIM-F and LIM-Q) inject ingredient-label semantics from LLMs into segmentation pipelines to improve fine-grained food segmentation, achieving state-of-the-art on FoodSeg103 with modest compute overhead.
AI.motivation: Address underperformance on visually similar ingredients and rare foods by incorporating semantic ingredient information into image segmentation without requiring image-text alignment.
AI.method: LIM-F injects language-derived features into multi-layer image encoders (e.g., Swin); LIM-Q injects into Mask2Former-style decoders; both avoid pre-alignment of images and text. They are plug-and-play and tested across Transformer-based and CNN-based architectures.
AI.result: On FoodSeg103, LIM-Q with Swin-L + Mask2Former yields mIoU 55.0; LIM-F achieves mIoU 54.4 with the same backbone; CNN-based integration improves from 47.7 to 49.8 mIoU. Training memory overhead is modest (up to 3.8 GB).
AI.conclusion: The approach offers a practical, scalable solution for fine-grained food understanding with cross-architecture generalization and improved segmentation accuracy at limited training costs.

title: Generator-Aligned Representation Interfaces for Diagnostic Soft Equivariance
summary: Exact-equivariant architectures typically encode prescribed group actions in specialized operators, which can complicate their reuse with generic backbones and across data modalities. We introduce the Generator-Aligned Representation Interface (GARI), a representation-level design principle that exposes selected transformation generators to a generic sequence backbone through aligned canonical and generator-induced views. We formalize the resulting behavior using a probe-specific soft-equivariance residual defined over declared data and transformation distributions. This framework distinguishes representation consistency from task robustness and exact equivariance, and localizes residual mismatch to interface construction, shared stream processing, and terminal fusion. We instantiate the interface as GARI-Net, which constructs generator-indexed streams, converts them into a common interaction frame, processes them with shared parameters, repairs ordering-induced context mismatch, enables cross-stream information exchange, and aggregates them using inter-stream discrepancy. Direct Equivariance Error (DEE) provides a frozen-checkpoint diagnostic of the prescribed representation relation under known token or voxel actions. Experiments on genomic sequences, images, and three-dimensional point clouds examine sequence reversal, planar rotations and reflections, and controlled axial transfer. Across these settings, the same interface principle supports task-relevant transformation consistency and generalization to declared held-out probes without requiring group-specific redesign of the sequence backbone. GARI therefore provides a portable diagnostic complement to hard-equivariant architectures: it makes generator structure accessible, learnable, and measurable, while finite-probe evidence remains distinct from certification of exact equivariance over a continuous group.

AI.tldr: GARI exposes generator transformations at the representation level to a generic backbone, enabling soft-equivariance probing and cross-stream processing; it serves as a portable diagnostic complement to exact equivariant architectures across modalities.
AI.motivation: Exact equivariant architectures require bespoke operators per group, limiting reuse across backbones and data modalities. A representation-level interface can enable transformation-consistent behavior and measurable diagnostics without redesign.
AI.method: Introduce the Generator-Aligned Representation Interface (GARI) and instantiate it as GARI-Net, which creates generator-indexed streams, maps them to a common interaction frame, processes with shared parameters, repairs ordering mismatches, enables cross-stream information exchange, and aggregates via inter-stream discrepancy. It formalizes a probe-specific soft-equivariance residual and defines Direct Equivariance Error (DEE) as a diagnostic.
AI.result: Demonstrates transformation-consistent behavior and generalization to declared held-out probes in genomic sequences, images, and 3D point clouds, across sequence reversal, planar rotations/reflections, and axial transfer, without group-specific backbone redesign.
AI.conclusion: GARI provides a portable, learnable, and measurable diagnostic complement to hard-equivariant architectures. It reveals generator structure, remains finite-probe evidence rather than a full certification of continuous-group equivariance, and supports cross-modality, backbones, and transformation types.

title: Finding Optimal Cost-Bounded Plan Reductions: Refined Model
comment: Extended version of a paper accepted at ICAPS 2026 (doi: 10.1609/icaps.v36i1.42849). Includes a new model and expanded experimental results
summary: In some real applications a plan may later become unfeasible due to newly imposed budget constraints, yet, at the same time, using only the original actions of the plan and their order is mandatory. In this paper, we study the problem of extracting, from a precomputed plan, a valid subplan that maximizes utility while respecting a cost bound. Each goal is given a utility value and the plan is reduced by removing actions that support low-utility goals, while preserving both executability and the original action order. We show the decision variant is NP-complete and propose two exact methods to solve it: one via oversubscription planning (OSP) and another via Integer Linear Programming (ILP). This paper extends our previous work published at ICAPS 2026 (Del Toro, Fuentetaja, and García-Olaya 2026b). While the core framework remains as introduced there, we further introduce a refined ILP formulation that significantly decreases the model size and improves computational efficiency.

AI.tldr: From a precomputed plan, extract a valid subplan that preserves action order, maximizes utility under a cost bound; the decision problem is NP-complete. The authors present two exact solution methods: oversubscription planning (OSP) and an Integer Linear Programming (ILP) approach; they also propose a refined ILP formulation that reduces model size and improves efficiency. This extends their ICAPS 2026 work.
AI.motivation: In real applications, budget constraints may render a plan infeasible after it is computed, but the original plan order must be preserved. The goal is to prune low-utility actions while maintaining executability and order, maximizing utility within a cost bound.
AI.method: Formalize the subplan extraction problem from a precomputed plan. Propose two exact solution methods: (1) oversubscription planning (OSP) to obtain feasible subplans within the budget, and (2) a refined Integer Linear Programming (ILP) formulation that enforces ordering and feasibility. The refined ILP aims to reduce model size.
AI.result: The decision variant of the problem is NP-complete. The authors provide two exact methods (OSP and ILP) and introduce a refined ILP formulation that significantly decreases model size and improves computational efficiency.
AI.conclusion: The work enables valid subplan extraction under budget constraints while preserving plan order, with improved performance from the refined ILP. It builds on and extends the authors’ ICAPS 2026 work, contributing to planning under budget pressures.

title: Beyond Static Costs: Learning-Dynamics Aware Loss Functions for Long-Tailed Classification
summary: Deep learning models in computer vision face significant challenges when trained on long-tailed datasets, where a few majority classes dominate while many minority classes are severely underrepresented. Such imbalances frequently arise in real-world scenarios such as rare species recognition, manufacturing fault detection, and medical image understanding, leading to biased models that underperform on tail classes. Existing reweighting methods typically rely on static class frequencies to penalize the model, ignoring the dynamic nature of how effectively a network actually learns a class over time. We address this by introducing a novel Learning-Dynamics Aware Loss (LDAL) function that shifts the focus from static sample counts to dynamic learning progress. LDAL framework adjusts class weights continuously by leveraging: (i) the strength of learned feature representations (semantic scale), (ii) the intrinsic learning difficulty of each class, measured via the Shannon entropy of its predictions, and (iii) an inter-epoch regularizer term that tracks prediction shifts between consecutive epochs to stabilize training and avoid local minima. LDAL is purely a objective function which incurs negligible computational overhead while adapting to the feature learning of the model. Experimental results on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that our approach significantly surpasses state-of-the-art reweighting loss functions, providing an optimal trade-off between accuracy and generalizability. The source code is available at https://github.com/sdm2026/ldal

AI.tldr: Introduces LDAL loss that dynamically reweights classes in long-tailed CV by combining semantic scale, entropy-based difficulty, and inter-epoch prediction shifts to reflect learning progress, achieving state-of-the-art results with low overhead.
AI.motivation: Long-tailed class distributions cause bias in CV models; static frequency-based reweighting ignores how well a model is learning each class over time. A dynamic, learning-progress-aware loss can better allocate learning capacity to minority classes.
AI.method: LDAL computes per-class weights from three components: (i) semantic scale (strength of learned feature representations for a class), (ii) intrinsic learning difficulty via Shannon entropy of the class predictions, and (iii) an inter-epoch regularizer that tracks prediction shifts between consecutive epochs. The LDAL loss is an end-to-end objective with negligible computational overhead that adapts the weight of each class during training.
AI.result: Experiments on multiple benchmark datasets show that LDAL surpasses state-of-the-art reweighting losses, achieving a favorable accuracy/generalization trade-off and demonstrating robustness across tasks.
AI.conclusion: LDAL effectively leverages learning dynamics to address long-tail learning with minimal overhead, offering improved performance over static reweighting methods. Source code is publicly available.

title: Empirical Evaluation of Out-Of-Distribution Performance of Tabular Foundation Models
summary: Tabular Foundation Models (TFMs) have emerged as novel approaches for tabular predictive tasks, demonstrating competitive predictive performance to ensemble tree-based models. Most TFMs are trained and evaluated on independent and identically distributed data, but this assumption changes in real-world scenarios due to distribution shifts, which compromise the robustness of models. Limited research has been conducted of TFMs under distribution shifts. We present an empirical evaluation of Out-Of-Distribution (OOD) performance of nine TFMs, spanning diverse pre-training strategies and architectures: TabPFNv2, TabPFNv2.5, TabPFNv2.6, TabPFNv3, TabICL, TabICLv2, Mitra, LimiX and TabFM. Three real-world datasets from the TableShift study were considered (HELOC, Voting, Childhood Lead), covering label, socioeconomic, and geographic shift types. Our results show that all evaluated TFMs degrade systematically under distribution shift regardless of pre-training strategy, with shift gaps ranging from 0.003 to 0.060 depending on shift type. The relationship between in-distribution and OOD predictive performance documented for classical tabular models extends into TFMs. We also identified a scalability gap, as high-performing models demand significant memory and computational resources beyond what standard deployment infrastructure can support. This study extends existing benchmarks for OOD in tabular data, providing evidence to support their adoption in high-stakes domains characterized by structural distribution shifts.

AI.tldr: TFMs for tabular data degrade under distribution shifts; nine models evaluated show small to moderate OOD gaps; all degrade; high resource demands; extends OOD benchmarks in tabular data; implications for high-stakes use.
AI.motivation: Assess robustness of Tabular Foundation Models under real-world distribution shifts; limited prior work on OOD evaluation for TFMs.
AI.method: Empirical study of nine TFMs (TabPFNv2, v2.5, v2.6, v3, TabICL, TabICLv2, Mitra, LimiX, TabFM) across three real-world TableShift datasets (HELOC, Voting, Childhood Lead) representing label, socioeconomic, and geographic shifts; compare ID vs OOD performance; assess scalability.
AI.result: All TFMs exhibit systematic degradation under distribution shifts with shift gaps ranging 0.003–0.060; the ID-OOD performance relationship observed in classical tabular models holds for TFMs; notable scalability gap: high-performing models require substantial memory and compute beyond standard deployment; results extend OOD benchmarks for tabular data.
AI.conclusion: TFMs are not robust to distribution shifts in tabular tasks; robustness- and resource-efficiency considerations are essential for deployment in high-stakes domains; need for improved OOD benchmarks and potentially model improvements or deployment strategies.

title: PatientAgentBench: A Benchmark Framework for Evaluating Patient-Facing Health AI Agents
summary: Health AI is evolving from answering questions to agentic systems that converse with patients, reason about health records, and act on their behalf. Primary care guards against diagnostic errors and unsafe care; agents assisting in this domain warrant evaluation against the same risks. Current benchmarks focus on medical knowledge, assessed through isolated question-answering or clinician-facing tasks. PatientAgentBench benchmarks patient-facing agentic healthcare; it evaluates a foundation model, wrapped in an agent with a sandbox of healthcare tools, conversing with a simulated patient. Each conversation is scored by an LLM-as-a-Jury across six dimensions via over a hundred conversation-agnostic, clinician-grounded criteria. To validate alignment, licensed clinicians annotated shared conversations, yielding 79-93% adjacent agreement between jury and expert raters, on par with or exceeding clinician inter-rater agreement. We benchmarked 10 models across four families on the same 1,200 scenarios and found clinical gaps. Triage quality is the most discriminating dimension: pass rates rise from 32% for the weakest models to 88% for the strongest, with agents often acting on administrative requests without clinical screening. Clinical safety and workflow accuracy follow the same pattern: the weakest models fail often, fabricating unexecuted actions, while frontier models fail on only 1-3% of cases, from unverified tool outputs and omitted crisis resources in an emergency. More capable models narrow these gaps but do not close them; the strongest scores only 4.25 of 5 overall. These failures surface only in sustained, tool-using conversations against realistic patient records, confirming that static benchmarks are insufficient as healthcare agentic systems gain autonomy. We release the framework as a reproducible, clinician-validated evaluation standard to help the field close this gap.

AI.tldr: Introduces PatientAgentBench, a clinician-validated benchmark for patient-facing health AI agents, revealing meaningful gaps in current models and arguing that static knowledge benchmarks are insufficient for evaluating autonomous, tool-using healthcare agents.
AI.motivation: As health AI shifts toward agentic systems that interact with patients and manipulate health records/tools, evaluation must go beyond knowledge QA to assess safety, workflow, and decision-making under realistic conversations, to prevent diagnostic/administrative harm.
AI.method: Wrap a foundation model in an agent with sandboxed healthcare tools; conduct 1,200 simulated patient conversations; score via LLM-as-a-Jury on six dimensions using 100+ clinician-grounded criteria; validate jury with licensed clinicians, achieving 79-93% adjacent agreement; benchmark 10 models from four families; analyze pass rates and error modes.
AI.result: Triage is the most discriminating dimension; pass rates 32% to 88% across models; agents often perform administrative requests without clinical screening; safety/workflow accuracy show similar pattern; weakest models fabricate unexecuted actions; frontier models err 1-3% due to unverified tool outputs or missing crisis resources; strongest overall score 4.25/5; differences emerge only in sustained tool-using conversations with realistic records; static benchmarks inadequate.
AI.conclusion: Provides a reproducible, clinician-validated evaluation standard; demonstrates that even capable models have substantial gaps; calls for adoption of framework and further development to ensure safe, clinically aligned autonomous health agents.

title: Adversarial Deepfake Generation and an Investigation of Purification-Based Adversarial Detection
comment: Accepted at CLEF 2026, ImageCLEF-Deepfake task. Published in CEUR-WS CLEF 2026 Working Notes
summary: This paper describes the participation of team "Go To Germany" in the ImageCLEF 2026 Deepfake Detection and Generation Task. For the image generation task, we employ FLUX.1-dev with PuLID for identity-preserving face synthesis, combined with a multi-model PGD adversarial attack targeting 12 detectors simultaneously (DiffJPEG-in-loop, MI/DI/EoT, adaptive weighting, two-stage warm-start). Our approach achieved 90% evasion against organizer detectors and 57.6% against participant detectors, with a final generation score of 0.4170. For the image detection task, we combine two complementary detectors - SigLIP+DINOv2 for AI-generated images and GenD-DINOv3 for face manipulations - in a max-probability ensemble, achieving 99.4% accuracy on baseline deepfakes but suffering from high false-positive rates on real images, resulting in a final detection score of 0.6986. Beyond the official submission, we conducted a self-initiated investigation of purification-based adversarial detection, comparing three families of detection signals across six detectors that share a CLIP ViT-L/14 backbone. We find that raw $|Δ\text{logit}|$ under median-3 purification, applied through the EFFORT detector, separates adversarial inputs from clean inputs with AUROC 0.81-0.98 across four adversarial source types - a finding that refutes the simple backbone-preservation hypothesis and exposes a sharp JPEG-quality cliff at Q70 where the signal collapses.

AI.tldr: Summary of Go To Germany's ImageCLEF 2026 submissions: (1) generation task uses FLUX.1-dev with PuLID for identity-preserving face synthesis and a PGD-based multi-detector evasion pipeline, achieving a 0.4170 final generation score with 90% evasion of organizer detectors and 57.6% against participant detectors. (2) detection task uses a max-probability ensemble of SigLIP+DINOv2 (AI-generated) and GenD-DINOv3 (face manipulations), attaining 99.4% accuracy on baseline deepfakes but with high false positives on real images, yielding a final detection score of 0.6986. An additional self-initiated study on purification-based adversarial detection shows AUROC of 0.81–0.98 across four adversarial sources using raw |Δlogit| under median-3 purification (EFFORT detector), revealing a sharp JPEG-quality cliff at Q70 and challenging backbone-preservation hypotheses.
AI.motivation: Assess robustness of deepfake generation and detection methods and investigate purification-based signals as a general, backdoor-free proxy for adversarial detection; explore limits of detector ensembles and the impact of image quality on signal fidelity.
AI.method: Generation: FLUX.1-dev with PuLID for identity-preserving face synthesis; PGD-based adversarial attack across 12 detectors (DiffJPEG-in-loop, MI/DI/EoT, adaptive weighting, two-stage warm-start). Detection: max-probability ensemble of SigLIP+DINOv2 and GenD-DINOv3. Purification-based detection: evaluation of three signal families across six detectors sharing a CLIP ViT-L/14 backbone; EFFORT detector using raw |Δlogit| under median-3 purification.
AI.result: Generation: 90% evasion against organizer detectors; 57.6% against participant detectors; final generation score 0.4170. Detection: 99.4% accuracy on baseline deepfakes; high false positives on real images; final detection score 0.6986. Purification-based detection: AUROC 0.81–0.98 across four adversarial source types; JPEG quality cliff at Q70; signal refutes backbone-preservation hypothesis.
AI.conclusion: The approach demonstrates strong evasion for organizer detectors but limited reliability in detection due to false positives; purification-based signals offer robust discrimination across adversarial sources and reveal JPEG-induced signal collapse, informing future defense strategies and challenging simplistic backbone-preservation assumptions.

title: Sharpness-Aware Minimization and Muon: Robustness under the Spectral Norm
summary: Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) aims to improve generalization by encouraging insensitivity to small, worst-case parameter perturbations. However, the notion of a "small" perturbation is inherently geometry-dependent: while existing SAM variants have explored a wide range of choices, a clear perspective on which geometries are most effective in practice remains elusive. Recent work on matrix-aware optimization, particularly the Muon optimizer, suggests that respecting the matrix structure of hidden-layer weights can lead to strong empirical performance. Motivated by this, we study matrix-aware geometry in both stages of SAM: we introduce a layerwise spectral inner perturbation for matrix-valued hidden-layer parameters and combine it with either AdamW/SGDW or Muon in the outer update. Across ImageNet-1K experiments on ViT-Small/16 and ResNet-50, we find that the combination of a spectral inner step with a Muon outer step performs consistently strongly, achieving the best validation accuracy on both models among the evaluated methods.

AI.tldr: Layerwise spectral, matrix-aware perturbations in SAM with Muon outer updates improve ImageNet generalization for ViT-S/16 and ResNet-50.
AI.motivation: Standard SAM uses geometry-agnostic perturbations; incorporating the matrix structure of hidden-layer weights (spectral geometry) may yield stronger generalization, especially for large models.
AI.method: Introduce a layerwise spectral inner perturbation for matrix-valued hidden-layer parameters and pair it with an outer update using AdamW/SGDW or Muon within the SAM framework.
AI.result: Spectral inner step combined with Muon outer step consistently achieves the best validation accuracy among evaluated methods on ViT-S/16 and ResNet-50 for ImageNet-1K.
AI.conclusion: Matrix-aware SAM with spectral inner perturbations and Muon outer updates provides strong, consistent generalization gains and highlights the importance of respecting layer weight structure in SAM design.

title: CoTinyVLA: Chain-of-Thought Distillation for a Sub-Billion-Parameter Vision-Language-Action Model
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models translate natural-language commands into robot action sequences, but leading systems on the LIBERO-Plus robustness benchmark use three- to seven-billion-parameter backbones whose memory demands can exceed embedded robotic budgets. We present CoTinyVLA, a 0.9B-parameter action model on a Qwen3.5-0.8B backbone that obtains that robustness by structuring supervision instead of enlarging the model. Three components target different axes of the problem: dual-view temporal input of 16 history frames per step with textual camera and time markers; hierarchical chain-of-thought (CoT) distillation from a 35B teacher into an episode-level Plan and a chunk-level Think span over task phase, gripper state and next subaction; and paraphrase augmentation expanding 40 base commands into 800 variants. On LIBERO-Plus, spanning 10,030 perturbed tasks across seven perturbation dimensions, CoTinyVLA reaches 90.8% on Spatial, 87.3% on Object, 86.6% on Goal and 80.7% on Long, leading the strongest 7B baseline on all four suites by 4.7, 2.8, 15.9 and 3.0 points, with every margin interval excluding zero. The gains concentrate on the hardest axes of the benchmark: across the eleven published baselines none exceeds 53.2% on Robot Initial States in any suite, whereas CoTinyVLA reaches 73.6% on Goal against 39.9% for the strongest baseline. Ablations show the three components to be separable by perturbation axis, and at a matched image budget how frames are divided between the two cameras and across time accounts for 8.6 points on its own. Closed-loop inference peaks at 2.25 GiB of allocated GPU memory, and paired interventions show the episode Plan to be load-bearing: replacing it with an empty or contradictory span costs 40 to 45 points of success. Structured supervision thus lets a 0.9B backbone exceed all of them. Code: https://github.com/BrainJellyPie/CoTinyVLA

AI.tldr: CoTinyVLA shows that a compact 0.9B action model, aided by structured supervision (dual-view temporal input, hierarchical CoT distillation, and paraphrase augmentation), can surpass larger backbones on LIBERO-Plus robustness benchmarks while keeping memory efficiency.
AI.motivation: Reduce reliance on extremely large backbones for Vision-Language-Action robotics by leveraging structured supervision to improve robustness and generalization under perturbations, with practical memory constraints.
AI.method: Three-part approach: (1) dual-view temporal input with 16 history frames per step and textual camera/time markers; (2) hierarchical chain-of-thought distillation from a 35B teacher into an episode-level Plan and a chunk-level Think span over task phase, gripper state, and next subaction; (3) paraphrase augmentation expanding 40 base commands into 800 variants. Models evaluated on LIBERO-Plus benchmark (10,030 perturbed tasks, 7 perturbation axes) using a 0.9B backbone on Qwen3.5-0.8B.
AI.result: CoTinyVLA achieves 90.8% Spatial, 87.3% Object, 86.6% Goal, 80.7% Long on LIBERO-Plus; outperforms strongest 7B baseline by 4.7/2.8/15.9/3.0 points respectively, with largest gains on hard axes (e.g., Robot Initial States: 73.6% vs 39.9%). Ablations show components are separable by perturbation axis; frame budgeting between two cameras and time contributes 8.6 points. Inference memory peaks at 2.25 GiB; the episode Plan is essential (replacing it drops 40–45 points).
AI.conclusion: Structured supervision enables a small 0.9B VLA model to surpass larger baselines on robustness benchmarks while maintaining practical memory budgets; the combination of dual-view inputs, hierarchical CoT distillation, and paraphrase augmentation is key.

title: Open-Ended CT Volume Segmentation with Weak Supervision from Language
summary: We introduce a method for training a text-conditioned segmentation model for CT scans, which combines voxel-level supervision with coarse but scalable slice-level supervision from reports. We extract, from a large database of scan-report pairs, descriptions of findings with indices of slices where those findings occur. We then finetune a general-purpose 2D image segmentation model, SAM3, with standard segmentation losses from strongly labeled data and with a slice-level classification loss from the extracted weak supervision.
