title: Quotient Dynamics, Effective Curvature, and Implicit Bias in Positive Quadratic Networks
summary: Positive quadratic networks admit the low-rank representation f_U(x)=x^top UU^top x, where Uinmathbb{R}^{dtimes r} is identifiable only up to right orthogonal multiplication, representing a rank-r PSD matrix Q=UU^top. We study how this quotient structure governs training dynamics, curvature, recovery, and interpolation bias. On the full-column-rank stratum, we identify mathbb{R}^{dtimes r}_*/O(r) with the rank-r PSD manifold. For smooth objectives L(U)=ell(UU^top), the Euclidean factor gradient is horizontal. Thus, factor gradient flow projects exactly to quotient Riemannian gradient flow, while finite-step gradient descent induces an exact congruence recursion for the predictor. For quadratic regression, we derive the effective Hessian at interpolators as the empirical measurement Gram form restricted to the tangent space relative to the quotient metric. Under Gaussian rank-one measurements, we compute population curvature, prove uniform deviation bounds for the empirical normal operator, construct a spectral initializer, and establish local exponential convergence for gradient flow and linear convergence for small-step descent. Recovery guarantees are explicit but conservative due to reliance on full-space second-moment control. In underdetermined commuting regimes, factor gradient flow becomes an exact entropy mirror flow in joint spectral coordinates. Strictly positive initializations converge to Bregman projections onto the interpolation set. With isotropic initialization q(0)=varepsilon^2mathbf{1}, predictors approach the minimum-trace solution set as varepsilondownarrow0, resolving nonuniqueness via weighted entropy within the invariant joint spectral algebra. Finite-step descent selects interpolants differing from continuous-time Bregman projections by O(eta). Numerical experiments verify these quotient identities, curvature predictions, recovery behaviors, and selection laws.

AI.tldr: Low-rank factorization U U^T governs positive quadratic networks; gradient flow on U matches Riemannian gradient flow on the quotient by right-orthogonal actions; curvature and recovery analyzed under Gaussian measurements; explicit convergence guarantees and interpolation bias; underdetermined regime yields entropy-based dynamics and selection laws; numerical results corroborate the theory.
AI.motivation: To understand how the quotient geometry from the factorization U (identified only up to right orthogonal transformations) governs training dynamics, curvature, recovery, and interpolation bias in positive quadratic networks.
AI.method: Geometric analysis on the full-column-rank stratum, identify R^{dt x r}_*/O(r) with the rank‑r PSD manifold; show factor-gradient flow projects to quotient Riemannian gradient flow; derive the effective Hessian as the empirical Gram form restricted to the tangent space of the quotient metric; analyze Gaussian rank-one measurements to compute population curvature, establish uniform deviation bounds for the empirical normal operator, construct a spectral initializer, and prove local convergence results for gradient flow and small-step descent; analyze underdetermined regimes where the dynamics become entropy-based in joint spectral coordinates; discuss initialization effects and interpolation bias; provide numerical experiments.
AI.result: The factor gradient flow exactly projects to the quotient gradient flow; finite-step gradient descent induces an exact congruence recursion for the predictor; under Gaussian rank-one measurements, the population curvature and empirical normal operator exhibit controlled behavior; a spectral initializer enables local exponential convergence for gradient flow and linear convergence for small-step descent; recovery guarantees are explicit but conservative; in underdetermined commuting regimes, dynamics become an entropy-based flow with convergence to Bregman projections and minimum-trace interpolation under isotropic initializations; finite-step descent selects interpolants within O(η) of continuous-time Bregman projections; numerical experiments corroborate the quotient identities, curvature predictions, and selection laws.
AI.conclusion: The quotient geometry of the U factorization governs training dynamics, curvature, and interpolation behavior in positive quadratic networks. The work provides a principled framework linking Riemannian quotient geometry to optimization dynamics, derives explicit curvature and convergence results under Gaussian measurements, and reveals how initialization and underdetermined regimes shape selection of interpolants. Empirical results validate the theoretical predictions.

title: Joint Text-Audio Alignment for EEG-to-Text Decoding in Chinese Speech Production and Perception
summary: Decoding speech information directly from scalp electroencephalography (EEG) into text provides a potential non-invasive neural communication pathway for individuals with severe speech and motor impairments. Compared with invasive approaches such as electrocorticography, EEG is safer and more widely deployable, yet substantially more challenging to decode.This challenge is exacerbated for Chinese sentence decoding, which must handle a high-dimensional output space with thousands of characters, severe inter-subject variability, and low signal-to-noise ratios for text alignment.Existing methods commit to a single supervisory axis---either text semantics or audio acoustic features---yet neither can simultaneously satisfy the demands of sentence-level discriminability and fine-grained temporal resolution required for large-vocabulary Chinese decoding. We introduce EEGAlign, a novel parameter-efficient framework that jointly aligns EEG with two axes---text alignment with BGE-M3 text embeddings and audio alignment with wav2vec~2.0 speech features via contrastive learning followed by CTC character-sequence decoding. On ChineseEEG-2 data, EEGAlign yields state-of-the-art closed-set sentence classification performance, reaching up to 82.37% Top-1 accuracy on Reading Aloud EEG and 41.43% on Passive Listening EEG out of 101 candidates. Ablation studies show that the two alignment axes are highly complementary: combining them yields consistently better performance than either alone. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study on decoding large-vocabulary Chinese sentences from non-invasive EEG during overt speech production, and achieving strong classification performance with relatively large closed-set candidate-sentence setting.

AI.tldr: EEGAlign is a parameter-efficient dual-axis framework that aligns non-invasive EEG with both text (BGE-M3 embeddings) and audio (wav2vec 2.0 features) via contrastive learning, then decodes Chinese sentences using CTC. It achieves state-of-the-art closed-set performance on ChineseEEG-2 for reading aloud and passive listening tasks, showing ablations that the two axes are complementary.
AI.motivation: Decoding large-vocabulary Chinese sentences from scalp EEG is hard due to high output dimensionality, substantial inter-subject variability, and low SNR. Existing methods rely on a single supervisory axis and fail to satisfy both sentence-level discriminability and fine-grained temporal resolution.
AI.method: Propose EEGAlign, a parameter-efficient framework that jointly aligns EEG with two axes: (1) text alignment using BGE-M3 embeddings and (2) audio alignment using wav2vec 2.0 features. Alignment is learned via contrastive learning, followed by CTC-based character-sequence decoding. Evaluated on ChineseEEG-2 with reading-aloud and passive-listening paradigms.
AI.result: On ChineseEEG-2, EEGAlign achieves up to 82.37% Top-1 accuracy in Reading Aloud EEG and 41.43% in Passive Listening EEG over 101 candidates. Ablation shows the two alignment axes are complementary and their combination outperforms either axis alone, achieving state-of-the-art closed-set sentence classification performance.
AI.conclusion: This is the first study to decode large-vocabulary Chinese sentences from non-invasive EEG during overt speech production, demonstrating strong closed-set performance and highlighting the benefit of jointly leveraging text and audio alignments for EEG-based decoding.

title: Wonder: Video World Model Done Better
summary: We present Wonder, a general-purpose video world model for real-time, camera-controllable world exploration. Given an image or a conditional video, Wonder constructs a playable world where users can navigate interactively by moving the camera, discovering unseen regions, and revisiting previously observed areas in real time and over a long-term horizon. Achieving this capability requires a system-level co-design of control method, memory mechanism, and training strategy. We introduce a novel camera conditioning with a dense coordinate field whose renderings provide spatially aligned motion and orientation cues, allowing the model to interpret camera motion directly as visual evidence. To support fast and precise memory retrieval over a growing generation context, we propose an efficient sparse attention-based memory mechanism, enabling the model to selectively attend to a small set of relevant context tokens at inference time, regardless of actual context length. We further develop several techniques to rectify the self-forcing-style distillation pipeline, improving the student model's ability to respect control signals, as well as maintaining diverse generation modes and long-term memory from the teacher. Together, these components enable Wonder to synthesize diverse, minute-scale videos at 16 FPS while preserving coherent geometry, appearance, and dynamics across long rollouts. Beyond image-to-video generation, Wonder naturally supports video-conditioned generation, allowing existing dynamic scenes to be re-shot in real time.

AI.tldr: Wonder is a real-time, camera-controllable video world model enabling interactive exploration, long-horizon consistency, and video re-shot capability, achieved via system-level co-design, dense coordinate conditioning, and sparse-attention memory to synthesize minute-scale videos at 16 FPS.
AI.motivation: To enable interactive, long-horizon, coherent video synthesis and navigation within learned environments, addressing memory efficiency and control fidelity for real-time use.
AI.method: System-level co-design of control, memory, and training; camera conditioning with a dense coordinate field that yields spatially aligned motion/orientation cues; sparse attention-based memory to attend to a small set of relevant tokens regardless of context length; improvements to self-forcing distillation to respect control signals and preserve diverse modes and long-term memory from the teacher.
AI.result: Wonder can synthesize diverse minute-scale videos at 16 FPS with coherent geometry, appearance, and dynamics across long rollouts; supports video-conditioned generation allowing re-shot of existing dynamic scenes in real time.
AI.conclusion: Integrated control-memory-training design is effective for real-time, camera-controllable world modeling and video synthesis, enabling interactive exploration and re-shot capabilities with long-term consistency.

title: AIriskEval-edu Demo: Auditing of Pedagogical Risks in Educational Explanations
comment: 6 pages, 2 figures. Accepted at the 17th IAPR International Workshop on Document Analysis Systems (DAS 2026), ICDAR 2026, September 3, 2026
summary: We present AIriskEval-edu Demo, a platform that audits the pedagogical quality of instructional explanations and provides explainable audit results. The platform evaluates an explanation against a rubric covering five dimensions of pedagogical risk: factual accuracy, depth and completeness, focus and relevance, student-level appropriateness, and ideological bias. For each dimension, it returns a binary decision and a confidence score. Detected risks also include a natural-language rationale and, except for Depth and Completeness, a localized evidence span. The platform integrates GPT-5.5 through an external API and a self-hosted Llama 3.1 8B evaluator that runs on consumer-grade GPUs. The local evaluator is fine-tuned on AIriskEval-edu, a dataset of K-12 instructional explanations with risk and explainability annotations. The platform operates in two modes: in AI mode, both evaluators assess stored explanations generated under six simulated teacher profiles, each representing a distinct pedagogical behavior and potential risk; in human mode, the local evaluator audits user-written explanations in real time. The local evaluator outperforms GPT-5.5 on most reported metrics, offering educational institutions a practical way to keep audited content within their own infrastructure.

AI.tldr: AIriskEval-edu Demo audits pedagogical explanations using a five-dimension rubric (factual accuracy, depth, focus, student-appropriateness, ideological bias) with binary decisions, confidence scores, and rationale; combines GPT-5.5 via API and a self-hosted Llama 3.1 8B evaluator; two modes (AI and human); local evaluator often outperforms GPT-5.5 and keeps audits in-house.
AI.motivation: Mitigate pedagogical risk and enhance explainability in instructional explanations by providing an auditable, rubric-based evaluation framework that can operate securely on local infrastructure.
AI.method: An evaluation pipeline using a five-dimension rubric; binary verdicts and confidence per dimension; generation of natural-language rationale and, except for Depth and Completeness, a localized evidence span; ensembling GPT-5.5 API and a self-hosted Llama 3.1 8B evaluator; fine-tuned on AIriskEval-edu dataset of K-12 explanations with risk annotations; two modes: AI mode (evaluators assess stored explanations under six simulated teacher profiles) and human mode (local evaluator audits user-written explanations in real time).
AI.result: The local Llama 3.1 8B evaluator outperforms GPT-5.5 on most reported metrics, enabling institutions to audit content on their own infrastructure without external data leakage.
AI.conclusion: The platform delivers explainable, rubric-based audits with a privacy-preserving on-premises evaluator, improving practicality for educational institutions; future work could expand datasets, refine risk dimensions, and optimize runtime on consumer GPUs.

title: VetClaw: An Edge-Cloud Multimodal Agentic System for Veterinary Disease Screening
summary: We present VetClaw, an edge-cloud multimodal agentic system for early veterinary disease screening. VetClaw uses a camera module as an edge sensing device and sends captured images, together with optional symptom descriptions, to a server-hosted vision-language model for zero-shot disease classification. The system separates agent interaction from workflow orchestration: OpenClaw provides scheduling, tool access, user interaction, and notification services on the edge device, while LangGraph manages the stateful screening workflow, including input validation, image transmission, model invocation, safety checks, conditional routing, failure handling, and structured logging. This design moves beyond static image classification by enabling the system to collect visual evidence, invoke external models, apply deterministic safety rules, and generate diagnostic-support alerts. Results show that image-only VLM prediction remains limited, whereas symptom-guided and multimodal inputs improve zero-shot classification performance. Thus, VetClaw transforms a static prediction model into a coordinated, safety-aware system that can use tools, manage workflows, handle failures, and escalate uncertain cases.

AI.tldr: VetClaw is an edge-cloud multimodal system that uses a camera at the edge to capture images (and optional symptoms) sent to a server-hosted vision-language model for zero-shot veterinary disease classification, with separate components for edge interaction (OpenClaw) and workflow orchestration (LangGraph).
AI.motivation: Address limitations of static image classification in veterinary screening by enabling multimodal inputs, proactive safety rules, tool use, and coordinated workflow management to produce diagnostic-support alerts.
AI.method: Architecture: edge camera captures images and optional symptom text; data sent to cloud VLM for zero-shot classification; OpenClaw handles scheduling, tool access, user interaction, and notification; LangGraph manages stateful workflow: validation, transmission, model invocation, safety checks, routing, failure handling, logging; emphasis on tool use and deterministic safety logic; evaluation comparing image-only vs multimodal inputs.
AI.result: Found image-only VLM predictions are limited; incorporating symptoms and multimodal inputs improves zero-shot classification performance.
AI.conclusion: Represents a shift from static predictions to a coordinated, safety-aware agent that can leverage tools, manage workflows, handle failures, and escalate uncertain cases.

title: Engine-Equal, Human-Unequal: A Reproducible Outcome Skew in Engine-Assessed Equal Chess Positions
comment: 27 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables. Code and data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21629354
summary: Among chess opening positions that a strong engine judges essentially equal (Stockfish 18 evaluation within 10 centipawns of zero, depth-stable) and that humans actually reach on Lichess (October 2025; 1,661 positions, 16.1M occurrences), human results are not balanced. Positions carry outcome skews, each the gap between its games' actual results and what the players' ratings predict, whose directions are stable properties of the naturally-reached position: some positions favour White, others Black. These skews reproduce across three re-partitions -- disjoint player-account sets (primary), time, and disjoint rating bands -- and on an out-of-sample month eight months later. On the primary split, each position's skew is measured once in each account group, and the replication slope asks how well one measurement predicts the other after removing rating and opening-family effects: one means undiminished carry-over; zero, no linear relation. We find 0.69 (family-clustered 95% CI [0.65, 0.74]), rising to 0.94 on the most-popular, best-measured positions. The slope's value depends on the position mix. Existence is the invariant claim: it survives every tighter evaluation band, search depth, calibration, and popularity cutoff we test, and replicates within blitz and rapid separately. The typical skew is small (median $|δ| \approx 0.018$, about two percentage points of White score), yet it reproduces, position by position, across disjoint accounts. At these positions the disfavoured side also thinks longer. Even where the evaluation is most confident, it is not a sufficient statistic for human outcomes. The result is observational, and the causal question is left to a pre-registered randomised companion study.

AI.tldr: Engine-equal positions on Lichess show persistent, position-specific human outcome skews; small in magnitude but reproducible across splits, time, rating bands, and out-of-sample validation; causality not established; calls for randomized study.
AI.motivation: To test whether human outcomes in engine-equal openings exhibit systematic biases beyond what ratings predict, and whether these biases replicate across partitions and time.
AI.method: Large-scale observational analysis of 1,661 engine-equal positions from Lichess (Oct 2025) with 16.1M occurrences; partitioned into primary (three disjoint account groups), time, and rating bands; skew measured as difference between actual results and rating-predicted; replication slope across splits; calibrations, depth, popularity cutoffs; out-of-sample month eight months later; analysis across Blitz/Rapid.
AI.result: Replication slope 0.69 (95% CI [0.65, 0.74]) on primary; 0.94 for most-popular positions; median |δ| ≈ 0.018 (≈2 percentage points White); skew directions stable; disfavoured side tends to lengthen; skew persists across bands and after adjusting for calibration; not a sufficient statistic for outcomes; consistent across formats.
AI.conclusion: Human outcomes in engine-equal positions exhibit a robust, position-specific bias that is observable and replicable; magnitude is small but systematic; observational nature; causality requires randomized pre-registered study.

title: OrchBench: Evaluating Multi-Agent Orchestration Plans in Isolation via Deterministic Simulation
summary: Complex tasks often decompose into parallelizable yet interdependent subtasks, making orchestration critical to the performance of multi-agent systems (MAS). Existing evaluations typically rely on end-to-end execution, which conflates orchestration-plan quality with worker capabilities, tool reliability, and environmental noise. Moreover, the time and token costs of real execution grow rapidly with workflow scale, making systematic evaluation expensive. We present OrchBench, a simulation-based benchmark for evaluating multi-agent orchestration plans in isolation. Starting from real-world tasks, OrchBench constructs directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) that encode task dependencies, with controlled sizes and degrees of parallelism. Given a DAG, a per-agent context limit, and an agent budget, the evaluated planner assigns subtasks to agents and specifies cross-agent information transfers and their retention ratios. A deterministic simulator evaluates the resulting plan without invoking worker agents and returns interpretable measures of result quality, makespan, and token cost. The simulated scores produced by OrchBench correlate strongly with quality scores from Claude Code executions, achieving a Pearson correlation of \(r=0.816\), while requiring only \(1.3\%\) of the tokens and \(10.3\%\) of the wall-clock time. Across diverse planners and workflow scales, we find that preserving task-critical information is more important than simply increasing the number of agents, and the benefits of parallelism diminish as coordination failures accumulate. These results establish OrchBench as an efficient and interpretable benchmark for comparing and diagnosing multi-agent orchestration plans.

AI.tldr: Simulation-based DAG-driven benchmark OrchBench evaluates multi-agent orchestration plans in isolation, offering strong correlation with real executions while reducing token and wall-clock costs.
AI.motivation: End-to-end MAS evaluations conflate orchestration quality with worker reliability, tools, and environmental noise; scalable, controlled evaluation of orchestration plans is needed.
AI.method: From real-world tasks, construct DAGs with controlled sizes and parallelism; given a DAG, per-agent context limit, and an agent budget, a planner assigns subtasks and cross-agent information transfers with retention ratios; a deterministic simulator evaluates the plan without invoking worker agents, yielding measures of result quality, makespan, and token cost; compare simulated scores to Claude Code executions; analyze across planners and workflow scales.
AI.result: Simulated scores correlate strongly with real-code quality (Pearson r=0.816) while using only 1.3% of tokens and 10.3% of wall-clock time; findings indicate preserving task-critical information matters more than increasing agent count, and parallelism benefits diminish with coordination failures.
AI.conclusion: OrchBench provides an efficient, interpretable benchmark for comparing and diagnosing multi-agent orchestration plans, enabling systematic evaluation without expensive real-execution runs.

title: CoRT: Counterfactual Replay for Token-Level Rubric-Guided Policy Optimization
summary: Rubric-based reinforcement learning enriches language model training by evaluating model outputs against explicit criteria. Yet in GRPO-style pipelines, these structured judgments are reduced to a scalar response-level reward and converted into a response-level advantage, which is broadcast uniformly to all generated tokens. This leaves no explicit mechanism for allocating credit within a response, even when different criteria are grounded in different spans, formatting decisions, or semantic choices. We propose CoRT, a token-level credit weighting method for rubric-conditioned GRPO. Instead of training an auxiliary token scoring model, CoRT uses counterfactual replay to rescore the same sampled response under the original rubric-conditioned prompt and a matched criteria-free prompt. The resulting tokenwise log-likelihood contrasts serve as a proxy for dependence on the rubric context. CoRT maps these contrasts to bounded, response-normalized weights and uses them to redistribute the signed GRPO advantage across tokens, without introducing an auxiliary scorer or changing the response-level reward. Experiments across instruction-tuned models and reward granularities show that CoRT improves over matched response-level GRPO in the vast majority of comparisons, with an average gain of 4.4 percentage points. The method remains competitive with learned token-level credit baselines while avoiding a separate relevance-learning stage. These results suggest that policy-internal counterfactual likelihood contrasts provide an effective training signal for within-response credit allocation while retaining the simplicity and stability of GRPO.

AI.tldr: CoRT introduces token-level credit weighting for rubric-conditioned GRPO using counterfactual replay to estimate token-level dependence on rubric; improves performance vs response-level GRPO, competitive with token-level credit baselines, without extra scorer.
AI.motivation: In rubric-based RL with GRPO, credit is allocated at the response level, which prevents attributing credit to specific spans or formatting decisions within a response. This lack of intra-response credit is inefficient, and training separate token-level scorers adds complexity. CoRT seeks a lightweight, intra-response credit mechanism.
AI.method: For each sampled response, compute counterfactual log-likelihood contrasts by rescoring under the rubric-conditioned prompt and a matched criteria-free prompt. Use the tokenwise contrasts to form bounded, response-normalized weights, and redistribute the signed GRPO advantage across tokens. This avoids training an auxiliary token scorer and preserves the response-level reward.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation across instruction-tuned models and reward granularities shows CoRT improves over matched response-level GRPO by an average of 4.4 percentage points and is competitive with learned token-level credit baselines, indicating robust benefits across settings.
AI.conclusion: Policy-internal counterfactual likelihood contrasts provide effective within-response credit allocation while preserving the simplicity and stability of GRPO, enabling finer credit distribution without a separate relevance-learning stage.

title: Localized Adaptation Reveals Distinct Learning Signatures in Transformers
comment: Main text: 8 pages, 2 figures; appendix: 13 tables, 10 figures; code and data available at https://github.com/rramnauth2220/adaptation-geometries
summary: Transformer adaptation is typically distributed across model depth, even when the intended change is narrow. We investigate how adaptation site shapes what a model learns, how well that learning generalizes, and how selectively it is applied. We introduce a controlled benchmark spanning five objectives (lexical binding, factual association, behavioral policy learning, causal mapping, and procedural reasoning) and define each objective's "adaptation geometry" as its profile of acquisition, transfer, and boundedness under full-stack and early-, middle-, or late-layer LoRA. The objectives exhibit distinct geometries. Lexical binding favors early-layer adaptation for acquisition and boundedness but requires broader updates for transfer; factual association favors later layers among localized adapters; behavioral learning separates late-layer action acquisition from middle-layer policy gating; and causal and procedural transfer benefit most from middle- or full-stack adaptation. These patterns largely persist under parameter-matched controls, and most corresponding directional contrasts replicate across five model families. These findings establish adaptation site as a key design variable for controlling what models learn, generalize, and leave unchanged.

AI.tldr: Adapter placement in Transformer models (early/middle/late layers) creates distinct adaptation geometries across tasks, shaping what is learned, how it generalizes, and what remains unchanged; five-objective benchmark reveals task-specific layer preferences and robust patterns across model families.
AI.motivation: To understand how the location of parameter-efficient adaptation (LoRA) within a Transformer affects acquisition, transfer, and boundedness of learning, thereby guiding design choices for controllable adaptation.
AI.method: Develop a controlled benchmark spanning five objectives (lexical binding, factual association, behavioral policy learning, causal mapping, procedural reasoning). Define each objective's adaptation geometry as its profile of acquisition, transfer, and boundedness under full-stack and under early-, middle-, or late-layer LoRA. Evaluate patterns across five model families with parameter-matched controls.
AI.result: Each objective exhibits a distinct adaptation geometry: lexical binding favors early-layer acquisition and boundedness but requires broader transfer; factual association favors later layers with localized adapters; behavioral learning decouples late-layer action acquisition from middle-layer policy gating; causal and procedural transfer benefit most from middle- or full-stack adaptation. These patterns persist under parameter-matched controls and replicate across model families.
AI.conclusion: Adaptation site is a key design variable for controlling what models learn, how they generalize, and what remains unchanged; choosing adapter depth strategically enables task-specific learning and generalization profiles.

title: OmniDelta: Skill-Driven Budget Allocation for Token Compression in OmniLLMs
summary: Emerging Omni-modal Large Language Models (OmniLLMs) enable unified understanding of text, audio, and video, but their long audio-video token sequences introduce substantial memory and inference costs. Existing compression methods mainly focus on selecting important tokens under fixed budgets, leaving the preceding budget-allocation problem underexplored. We show that direct query-to-audio/video similarity is unreliable for inter-modal budget allocation, and that uniform intra-modal budgets can miss key evidence while retaining redundant content. To address these limitations, we propose OmniDelta, a training-free, skill-driven framework that couples intent-aware inter-modal allocation with content-aware intra-modal allocation. OmniDelta first constructs audio and video skill pools to shift the fixed retained-token budget according to query demand, then reallocates modality budgets over audio segments and video frames using local complexity and temporal redundancy. The resulting local budgets can be combined with existing pruning strategies, preserving the total retained-token ratio while changing where the budget is spent. Experiments on four audio-video benchmarks with two Qwen2.5-Omni models show that OmniDelta establishes a new accuracy-efficiency Pareto frontier across pruning ratios. At 25% token retention on Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, OmniDelta reduces GPU memory by 22.0% and achieves a 1.64x end-to-end speedup over full-token inference.

AI.tldr: OmniDelta is a training-free framework that dynamically and content-sensitively allocates token budgets across audio/video in OmniLLMs, improving accuracy-efficiency by shifting budgets between modalities and within modalities based on query demand and content complexity, yielding memory and speedups while preserving total token budgets.
AI.motivation: Long audio–video token sequences in omni-modal LLMs incur high memory and inference costs. Fixed-budget or similarity-based inter-modal allocation is inefficient and uniform intra-modal budgets waste relevant evidence. A need exists for adaptive, content-aware, cross-modal budgeting that preserves total tokens.
AI.method: A training-free approach that (1) builds audio/video skill pools to align budget with query demand, (2) reallocates budgets across audio segments and video frames using local complexity and temporal redundancy, and (3) keeps the total retained-token budget, allowing compatibility with existing pruning methods.
AI.result: On four audio–video benchmarks with two Qwen2.5-Omni models, OmniDelta achieved a new accuracy–efficiency Pareto frontier across pruning ratios. At 25% token retention on Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, it reduced GPU memory by 22.0% and achieved a 1.64× end-to-end speedup compared to full-token inference.
AI.conclusion: OmniDelta enables effective, training-free, skill-guided inter- and intra-modal budget allocation for OmniLLMs, improving efficiency without sacrificing accuracy and harmoniously integrating with existing pruning strategies.

title: DecoEvo: Score-Decoupled Co-Evolution of Solver and Rubric-Generator Skills in Text Space
summary: Text-space optimization adapts large language models (LLMs) by editing external natural-language artifacts rather than model weights, so the optimized artifacts remain inspectable and the model can be treated as a black box. However, most existing text-space methods keep evaluation fixed. On open-ended tasks, this can become a bottleneck: once the solver improves on the criteria a rubric measures, omitted dimensions remain invisible to the optimization signal. Simply evolving the rubric is also unreliable when updates are selected by the current solver's score, because apparent progress can come from making the rubric easier to satisfy. We introduce DecoEvo (Decoupled Co-Evolution), which co-evolves a solver skill and a rubric-generator skill under decoupled objectives without using gold rubrics during optimization. The solver skill is updated using criterion-level feedback, while the rubric-generator skill is revised through complementary audits of requirement coverage and response discrimination that are independent of aggregate solver score. This separation focuses generator updates on newly exposed solver weaknesses, reducing repeated emphasis on criteria the solver already satisfies. Under each benchmark's official evaluation, DecoEvo outperforms all compared methods across five benchmarks and three LLM backbones, yielding 2.8--5.0\% relative gains over SkillOpt in the five-benchmark average.

AI.tldr: DecoEvo: decoupled co-evolution of solver and rubric-generator for text-space optimization improves robustness and achieves 2.8–5.0% gains across five benchmarks and three LLM backbones without gold rubrics.
AI.motivation: Text-space optimization suffers from fixed evaluations and rubric-driven bias: evolving rubrics by current solver scores can make progress look better than it is, and undiscovered dimensions remain unmeasured. A decoupled framework that updates solver and rubric independently, without gold rubrics, aims to expose weaknesses and reduce overfitting to the rubric.
AI.method: DecoEvo co-evolves two skills under decoupled objectives: (1) solver skill updated via criterion-level feedback; (2) rubric-generator skill updated via complementary audits of requirement coverage and response discrimination, independent of the solver’s aggregate score. No gold rubrics are used during optimization; evaluation relies on official benchmarks.
AI.result: Under official benchmarks, DecoEvo outperforms all compared methods across five benchmarks and three LLM backbones, yielding 2.8–5.0% relative gains over SkillOpt on the five-benchmark average.
AI.conclusion: DecoEvo reduces repeated emphasis on criteria already satisfied, focusing updates on newly exposed solver weaknesses, and improves robustness and generalization of text-space optimization without gold rubrics.

title: Cognivia: A Cognitive Behavioral Therapy Copilot for Evidence-Based Mental Healthcare
summary: Cognitive distortion amplifies negative emotions and contributes to mental health disorders. Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) is an effective way to address cognitive distortions, but its large-scale application is limited by the shortage of professional therapists. Although large language models (LLMs) have recently been explored for mental health applications, existing methods still suffer from limited domain specificity, overly flattering responses, and the absence of well-defined annotations for cognitive distortions. This paper proposes Cognivia, an evidence-based artificial intelligence therapist that integrates automatic cognitive distortion identification and rational response generation. Our framework is built on authoritative CBT texts widely regarded as core paradigms and standard references. It is further augmented with mental health question-answer (Q and A) data, and employs multi-stage prompting and structured generation strategies under the supervision of behavioral science experts. Then we fine-tune a lightweight LLM on this augmented CBT dataset to obtain Cognivia. In addition, we propose the first hierarchical quality evaluation framework for assessing LLM-generated rational responses, developed through collaboration between AI researchers and behavioral science experts. Cognivia is evaluated using lexical metrics, LLM-based Judges with two complementary criteria, and human evaluation by 10 behavioral science experts. It consistently outperforms the baseline methods in cognitive distortion recognition and rational response generation, demonstrating its effectiveness. Our code is available at https://github.com/SNOWTEAM2023/Cognivia.

AI.tldr: Cognivia is an evidence-based AI therapist that detects cognitive distortions and generates rational, CBT-aligned responses using a fine-tuned lightweight LLM, with multi-stage prompting, expert supervision, and a hierarchical quality evaluation framework; it outperforms baselines and provides code.
AI.motivation: Address the scarcity of professional CBT therapists and limited domain specificity in LLM-based mental health tools by building a CBT-grounded, evaluable AI therapist.
AI.method: Compile authoritative CBT texts and Q&A data, apply multi-stage prompting and structured generation with expert supervision, fine-tune a lightweight LLM on the augmented CBT data, and develop a hierarchical quality evaluation framework. Evaluation uses lexical metrics, LLM-based judges with complementary criteria, and human experts.
AI.result: Cognivia consistently outperforms baseline methods in cognitive distortion recognition and rational response generation across automated and human assessments.
AI.conclusion: The approach yields an effective, scalable AI therapist grounded in CBT, supported by a novel evaluation framework; code is publicly available for reproducibility.

title: Desktop-Delta Bench: Do Computer-Use Models Understand Desktop GUI Transitions?
summary: Computer-use agents (CUAs) increasingly act through desktop GUIs to complete long-horizon tasks. Current benchmarks primarily measure end-task success or single-frame grounding. Neither isolates whether a model can reconstruct the causal, task-relevant transition produced by an action- crucial for rejecting stale observations, verifying progress, and recovering from failure. This is difficult because inference, remote input, app rendering, and screenshot capture are asynchronous: the next observation may be delayed, occluded, transient, or unrelated, then misread as progress and carried into subsequent planning. We introduce Desktop-Delta Bench (DDB), an offline step-level benchmark with 2,013 human-verified instances from novel, multi-app Linux trajectories across ~15 applications and 50 task domains. DDB trajectories targets 3 failure dimensions- state verification, source tracking, and context-aware control- through 2 complementary tasks: 463 3-frame temporal-ordering instances, including 105 with a cross-trajectory decoy, and 1,550 before-after pairs labeled from 5 actions + its payload. We evaluate 8 closed and open-source model families across 32 ordering and 16 single-action settings, observing consistent gaps. Ordering remains unsaturated: best non-decoy and decoy exact-match rates are 65.1% and 65.7%. Task context improves decoy identification by 6.9 percentage points but reduces non-decoy exact match by 2.2 points; error analysis reveals systematic copying of the presented A-B-C order. Single-action results show that inferring the action family is harder than locating it: click F1 is 0.96 vs, 0.76 for drag, while recognized drags are generally localized well. DDB, thus, complements end-to-end benchmarks by filling the missing diagnostic layer between GUI grounding and final task success, enabling targeted improvements to desktop CUA verification, reliability, and recovery.

AI.tldr: DDB is a large, offline, step-level benchmark for desktop GUI agents that isolates causal, task-relevant transitions via two tasks (3-frame temporal-ordering and before-after action pairs) across multi-app Linux trajectories, revealing gaps in current models’ ability to verify state, track sources, and apply context, thereby complementing end-to-end task benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Current benchmarks focus on end-task success or single-frame grounding and do not assess a model’s capability to reconstruct the causal transitions produced by actions in asynchronous desktop GUIs, which is crucial for rejecting stale observations, verifying progress, and recovering from failures.
AI.method: An offline dataset of 2,013 human-verified trajectories across ~15 Linux applications and 50 task domains. Two tasks: (i) 463 three-frame temporal-ordering instances (105 with cross-trajectory decoys); (ii) 1,550 before-after pairs labeled with 5 actions plus payload. Evaluated 8 model families on 32 ordering and 16 single-action settings.
AI.result: Ordering performance shows best non-decoy and decoy exact-match rates around 65.1% and 65.7%, respectively, with context improving decoy identification by 6.9 percentage points but reducing non-decoy exact-match by 2.2 points. Error analysis reveals systematic copying of the presented A-B-C order. For single actions, inferring the action family (e.g., click) is harder than locating it (0.96 vs. 0.76 for drag), while recognized drags tend to be well localized.
AI.conclusion: DDB fills a diagnostic layer between GUI grounding and final task success, enabling targeted improvements to desktop CUA verification, reliability, and recovery beyond end-to-end benchmarks.

title: Nudging Sustainable Choices through LLM-Generated Recommendation Explanations
summary: Recommender systems mediate everyday consumption, offering a promising channel for encouraging sustainable choices. Prior research shows that explanations influence users' perceptions of recommendations and can support more informed decisions. We argue that explanations can also serve as behavioral nudges by foregrounding sustainability information at the moment of choice. This study investigates how different behavioral framings of sustainability information in recommendation explanations affect user choices and perceptions. Using generative AI, we generate sustainability-aware explanations by drawing on nudge theory and validate them through human evaluation and LLM-as-a-judge audits. Building on this foundation, we conduct two randomized studies ($N = 529$) in a low involvement domain (instant coffee) and a high involvement domain (hotel bookings), in which participants choose among preference matched recommendations accompanied by these explanations. Our results show that, across both domains, merely disclosing sustainability information in explanations does not change choices, whereas framing that information or invoking a descriptive social norm significantly increases sustainable selections and eases decision-making. Notably, perception and behavior diverge, as plain disclosure improves explanation evaluations without translating into more sustainable selection behavior. Our work demonstrates how LLMs can generate theory-grounded explanations at scale, pointing toward practical explanation-based interventions for social good. We conclude by discussing implications for adaptive explanation design with generative AI.

AI.tldr: Framing sustainability information in recommender explanations can nudge users toward more sustainable choices, but mere disclosure has limited effect. Descriptive social norms and framing outperform plain disclosure in increasing sustainable selections across low- and high-involvement domains; perceptual evaluations do not always align with behavior. The study shows LLM-generated, theory-grounded explanations at scale and discusses adaptive explanation design for social good.
AI.motivation: To understand whether sustainability disclosures in recommender explanations can serve as behavioral nudges and how different framings affect user choice and perception, leveraging AI-generated explanations and theory (nudge theory) across varying involvement domains.
AI.method: Generate sustainability-aware explanations with generative AI rooted in nudge theory; validate via human evaluation and LLM-as-a-judge audits; conduct two randomized experiments (N=529) in low involvement (instant coffee) and high involvement (hotel bookings) where participants select among preference-matched recommendations with explanations varying on: disclosure-only, framing, and descriptive social norm.
AI.result: Plain disclosure did not change choices; framing and especially descriptive social norms increased sustainable selections and eased decision-making; however, perception improvements did not always translate into behavioral change, indicating a divergence between evaluation and action.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can produce theory-grounded explanations at scale to enable practical, explanation-based interventions for social good; findings inform adaptive explanation design that leverages framing and social norms to promote sustainability in recommender systems.

title: Loss Invariance Determines What Concept Layers Encode: Volume Grounding in Echocardiography
summary:
Objective: Concept bottleneck models route prediction through interpretable intermediate variables, and their validity is normally judged by how accurately those variables are predicted. We ask whether that judgement is sufficient, using left ventricular volumes as the concepts underlying ejection fraction estimation from echocardiographic video.
  Methods: A video transformer encoder was trained on a publicly available echocardiography dataset. End-systolic and end-diastolic volumes formed a concept layer from which ejection fraction was computed analytically, with no residual path to the output. We compared training under an ejection fraction objective alone against training with additional supervision of the volumes in millilitres, and evaluated both on 1276 held-out studies.
  Results: The concept bottleneck did not increase ejection fraction error relative to direct regression, at 6.89 against 7.13 mean absolute error. Without volume supervision, however, the spread of predicted volumes collapsed to 0.1 millilitres against reference spreads of 35.7 and 45.7 millilitres, while correlation was partly preserved. We show that this follows from an invariance property of the objective: ejection fraction is a ratio and is unchanged when both volumes are rescaled, so the loss determines the concept layer only up to scale. Supervision in absolute units reduced volume error from 89.8 to 25.8 millilitres at a cost of 0.4 in ejection fraction error.
  Conclusion: Concept accuracy alone can conceal a concept layer that carries no physical scale.
  Significance: Interpretable intermediate variables in clinical models should be validated against the invariance structure of the training objective, not only against prediction accuracy.

AI.tldr: Concept bottleneck models for EF estimation may hide flawed concept layers due to invariances in the objective; volume supervision in ml reduces scale error while EF prediction stays nearly unaffected.
AI.motivation: Evaluate whether predicting interpretable intermediate concepts (LV volumes) is sufficient for clinical tasks (EF estimation) or if absolute-scale supervision is required to ensure meaningful concepts.
AI.method: Train a video transformer on echocardiography data. Define LV end-systolic and end-diastolic volumes as a concept layer, compute EF analytically from volumes with no residual path to output. Compare EF-only objective vs EF + absolute-volume supervision (in ml) on 1,276 held-out studies.
AI.result: EF MAE with concept bottleneck (6.89) close to direct regression (7.13). Without volume supervision, predicted volumes collapse to ~0.1 ml spread (reference 35.7 and 45.7 ml); correlation partly preserved. EF objective’s invariance to rescaling causes concept layer to be determined only up to scale. Absolute-volume supervision reduces volume error from 89.8 ml to 25.8 ml with a minor EF MAE increase (0.4).
AI.conclusion: Relying on concept accuracy alone can mask a concept layer that lacks physical scale. Evaluation of interpretable clinical models must account for the invariances of the training objective and include tests against the invariance structure (e.g., absolute-scale supervision).

title: Speculate While You Reason: Teaching Agents to Predict Their Next Tool Call via Joint Agent-Speculator RL
summary: Large language model agents often spend substantial wall-clock time waiting for tool call results. Tool-call speculation can hide this latency by predicting and pre-executing an agent's next tool call if the prediction matches the agent's eventual tool call, but existing speculators are typically separate draft models or cached traces that are poorly aligned with the deployed agent's own behavior. We identify this speculator-agent gap and show that the target agent itself is a strong next-call speculator. This points to a simpler design: unifying the agent and speculator within the same model. In this paper, we introduce the self-speculating agent, a single model that both solves tasks in agent mode and predicts its next tool call from partial trajectories in speculator mode, fully reusing prefix KV cache. To enable this dual-mode agent without degrading performance, we propose a joint agent-speculator reinforcement learning method, which derives speculation targets from the agent's own rollouts and alternates agent and speculator updates. Across agentic search QA and conversational tool-use agentic tasks, our method improves average next tool-call Hit@1 from 44.1 to 61.2 for Qwen3-4B and from 48.9 to 66.3 for Qwen3.5-4B, while preserving agent task success.

AI.tldr: A self-speculating agent unifies agent and speculator within a single model, using joint RL to predict the next tool call from partial trajectories, reducing latency and improving next-call accuracy while preserving task success.
AI.motivation: Tool-call latency in LLM agents arises from waiting for results; existing speculators (drafts or cached traces) poorly align with the deployed agent. A unified model can reuse internal state (prefix KV cache) and directly align speculation with actual behavior.
AI.method: A single model operates in dual modes (agent and speculator) and reuses the same prefix KV cache. A joint agent–speculator RL training derives speculation targets from the agent’s own rollouts and alternates updates between agent and speculator. The approach is evaluated on agentic search QA and conversational tool-use tasks.
AI.result: Average next-tool-call Hit@1 improves from 44.1 to 61.2 (Qwen3-4B) and from 48.9 to 66.3 (Qwen3.5-4B), while preserving agent task success.
AI.conclusion: Unifying the agent and speculator in one model with joint RL reduces the speculator–agent gap and yields substantial gains in tool-call prediction without harming task performance, demonstrated across multiple tool-use tasks.

title: Distributed Constraint Optimization via Online Learning and Iterative Pricing with Application to Large-Scale Satellite Scheduling
summary: Distributed constraint optimization problems (DCOPs) provide a popular framework for distributed decision making under limited communication, but many real-world instances are too large to solve monolithically. We address this challenge from two complementary directions. We revisit the connection between DCOPs and potential games, and adapt modern online learning algorithms for equilibrium finding to DCOPs. We show that these algorithms are competitive with representative incomplete DCOP algorithms. We then turn to decomposition frameworks for large-scale DCOPs, motivated by large-scale decentralized satellite scheduling. We propose a new framework that separates a DCOP into two interacting subproblems: a high-level meta-DCOP for task allocation, and independent local optimization problems for scheduling. To couple the two levels, we develop a novel iterative pricing method that updates the meta-level utilities using feedback from the local optimizers. Combining our online learning methods with our iterative pricing framework, we obtain near-optimal performance on real-world decentralized satellite scheduling problem instances, fulfilling over 99% of observation requests compared with 87% for state-of-the-art baselines.

AI.tldr: Two-pronged DCOP approach: (i) connect DCOPs to potential games and apply online learning for equilibrium; (ii) a two-level decomposition with iterative pricing for large-scale, yielding near-optimal decentralized satellite scheduling, surpassing baselines.
AI.motivation: DCOPs suffer from scalability and limited communication in large real-world problems; need scalable, coordinated approaches that can handle large-scale decentralized scheduling.
AI.method: (i) Revisit DCOP–potential game link and adapt online learning algorithms to find equilibria; (ii) propose a two-level decomposition: a high-level meta-DCOP for task allocation and independent local optimizers for scheduling; couple via a novel iterative pricing method updating meta utilities from local feedback; integrate with online learning for performance.
AI.result: Algorithms competitive with representative incomplete DCOP methods; achieved near-optimal performance on real decentralized satellite scheduling; fulfilled over 99% of observation requests vs ~87% for baselines.
AI.conclusion: Combining online learning with iterative pricing yields scalable, high-quality solutions for large DCOPs; the framework effectively coordinates interdependent subproblems and generalizes to real-world decentralized scheduling scenarios.

title: HiSkill: Empowering LLM Agents with Hierarchical Skill Graphs
summary: Skills have become an important abstraction for enabling large language model (LLM) agents to reuse past experience in long-horizon interactive tasks. However, existing trajectory-to-skill methods often produce flat collections of high-level textual skills that are stored and retrieved independently, leaving skill relations underutilized and maintaining a gap between high-level skills and executable actions. In this paper, we propose HiSkill, a hierarchical skill graph framework that organizes interaction trajectories into a directed graph with skill nodes, AtomicOp nodes, and typed edges. Specifically, the graph connects reusable high-level skills with executable action templates, while also capturing decomposition, temporal transition, compatibility, support, and recovery relations among them. At inference time, HiSkill retrieves a compact task-relevant subgraph and performs subgraph-guided task execution, where a symbolic task state, an active skill, and the retrieved subgraph guide the LLM agent to switch skills, select AtomicOps, and ground executable actions iteratively. Experiments on three interactive environments show that HiSkill outperforms state-of-the-art baselines while reducing inference token consumption, demonstrating the effectiveness of bridging high-level skills and executable action grounding through a hierarchical skill graph. Our data and code is available at https://github.com/BUPT-GAMMA/HiSkill.

AI.tldr: HiSkill introduces a hierarchical skill graph linking reusable high-level skills with executable action templates, enabling subgraph-guided execution; it outperforms baselines and reduces token usage across three interactive environments.
AI.motivation: Existing trajectory-to-skill methods store flat, high-level textual skills and neglect inter-skill relations and grounding to executable actions. A structured graph capturing decomposition, transitions, compatibility, support, and recovery is needed to bridge high-level planning with low-level action grounding.
AI.method: Construct a directed graph with Skill nodes, AtomicOp nodes, and typed edges (decomposition, temporal transition, compatibility, support, recovery). At inference, retrieve a task-relevant subgraph; use a symbolic task state, active skill, and the retrieved subgraph to guide the LLM in switching skills, selecting AtomicOps, and grounding executable actions iteratively.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on three interactive environments shows HiSkill surpasses state-of-the-art baselines and reduces inference token consumption.
AI.conclusion: Hierarchical skill graphs can effectively bridge high-level skills and executable action grounding, improving planning and efficiency; data and code are released.

title: Runtime Uncertainty Monitoring for LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems Using Bayesian Networks
comment: This paper got accepted for Ninth International Workshop on Artificial Intelligence Safety Engineering (WAISE 2026): https://www.waise.org/
summary: This paper investigates how multi-agent systems (MAS)-based on large language models (LLMs) can support actuarial risk modelling, with a particular focus on uncertainty quantification. Actuarial workflows represent a high-stakes decision-support setting where unreliable outputs may lead to incorrect risk assessment, unfair pricing, and regulatory non-compliance. To address uncertainty introduced by the probabilistic nature of LLMs and dependencies between agents, a multi-agent framework is proposed in which specialised agents perform data preparation, modelling, review, and explanation tasks under a central hub. The main contribution is a novel approach to uncertainty propagation using token-level log-probabilities and a Bayesian Network. Importantly, log probabilities are not treated as direct probabilities of correctness or task success. Instead, length-normalised log-probability summaries are transformed into calibrated task-level confidence estimates before incorporation into the Bayesian Network. Results show that the framework reproduces baseline actuarial performance while providing additional insight into workflow stability and runtime uncertainty propagation.

AI.tldr: A multi-agent LLM framework for actuarial risk modelling that propagates uncertainty via token-level log-probabilities calibrated to task-level confidence and integrated in a Bayesian Network; achieves baseline performance with added workflow insight.
AI.motivation: Actuarial risk modelling is high-stakes; unreliable outputs can cause incorrect risk assessment, unfair pricing, and regulatory issues. Robust uncertainty quantification in LLM-based, multi-agent workflows is needed.
AI.method: A MAS with specialized agents (data preparation, modelling, review, explanation) orchestrated by a central hub. Uncertainty is propagated using token-level log-probabilities, normalized by length, transformed into calibrated task-level confidence estimates, and fed into a Bayesian Network to model dependencies among agents and tasks.
AI.result: The framework reproduces baseline actuarial performance while providing additional insight into workflow stability and runtime uncertainty propagation.
AI.conclusion: The approach demonstrates viable uncertainty propagation in MAS-LMM for actuarial tasks, enabling calibrated confidence estimates and improved interpretability of model-based decisions; aligns with regulatory expectations and suggests directions for improved calibration and scalability.

title: Distributing Security Controls Through Harness Engineering
summary: AI coding agents are being adopted at historic speed, yet security and risk concerns remain the primary barrier to scaling agentic AI across organizations. Existing security controls for coding agents are not systematically distributed to engineering teams, and vendor-native solutions introduce ecosystem dependencies that may not suit every deployment context. This paper investigates whether off-the-shelf security controls can be implemented on commercial AI coding agents and scaled to a distributed user base via a custom agent harness. A phased testing methodology was applied across four agent configurations --- two commercial agents with and without controls, a baseline harness, and a security-hardened harness --- using a 23-test suite derived from the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications. SHarD (Secure Harness Distribution), a distributable harness built on the Pi agent harness, demonstrated that three categories of security controls --- OS sandboxing, skill scanning, and tool restriction --- can be embedded and distributed via a single install command while retaining equivalent efficacy to direct installation on commercial agents. SHarD achieved an adjusted score of 100\%, matching the best securely configured commercial agent, with no regression across any test category. Notable observations include evidence that model non-determinism produces inconsistent security outcomes and that autonomous agent behavior can cross system boundaries in ways that OS sandboxing directly mitigates. Initial characteristics toward a control harness fitness framework are proposed, and a third research question is identified for future investigation.

AI.tldr: A distribution-ready security harness (SHarD) can securely retrofit off-the-shelf security controls for AI coding agents, enabling equivalent protection to securely configured commercial agents across a distributed user base.
AI.motivation: As AI coding agents scale within organizations, security risks and ecosystem dependencies hinder deployment. The work tests whether generic security controls can be reliably applied via a distributable harness to reduce deployment friction and standardize safeguards.
AI.method: A four-configuration, phased test across two commercial agents (with/without controls), a baseline harness, and a security-hardened harness. A 23-test suite derived from OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications assesses OS sandboxing, skill scanning, and tool restriction. SHarD, built on the Pi agent harness, installs via a single command and distributes the controls to a distributed user base.
AI.result: SHarD achieved 100% adjusted score, matching the best securely configured commercial agent, with no regression across test categories. It demonstrated that the controls can be embedded and distributed via a single install command. Key observations include non-determinism in model security outcomes and cross-boundary agent behaviors mitigated by OS sandboxing.
AI.conclusion: Off-the-shelf security controls can be effectively distributed to AI coding agents via SHarD without sacrificing security efficacy, enabling scalable, ecosystem-friendly deployment. The work also highlights factors like model non-determinism and boundary-crossing behaviors as areas for future refinement, and proposes a preliminary control-harness fitness framework.

title: Messier: A High-Resolution Corpus for Cross-Benchmark Agent Evaluation
summary: Evaluating AI agents in interactive environments is hindered by fragmented tasks, scaffolds, verifiers, and scoring rules. Existing efforts focus on narrow settings, remain limited in scale, or require costly reruns, leaving much of the empirical record incomparable. We introduce Messier, a unified corpus of 957,253 records that span 30 benchmarks, 714 agents, 11,891 tasks, and 74,205 verifiers. Messier consolidates public benchmark scores and supplements them with five-agent runs across six underrepresented professional and scientific domains, including a recent legal benchmark. Each record is standardized by model, scaffold, environment, task, verifier, and aggregation rule, with SOC/NAICS classifications for occupational and industry analysis. Using this corpus, we show frontier progress is uneven across benchmark types, with "function calling" saturated, "programming" improving the fastest, and "enterprise workflows" remaining the most challenging. Furthermore, counterfactual rescoring shows that strict all-pass aggregation in multi-verifier tasks can obscure progress and artificially alter agent rankings. From these standardized records, we derive capability scales that align with Epoch's Evaluation Capability Index rankings at Spearman \r{ho} = 0.81 and can be specialized by domain, occupation, action space, or verifier type. Messier provides a foundational, reusable infrastructure for agent capability scaling, benchmark auditing, and fine-grained analysis of evaluation failures.

AI.tldr: Messier is a large, standardized corpus of AI-agent evaluation records enabling cross-benchmark analysis and auditing.
AI.motivation: Fragmented evaluation across tasks/scaffolds/verifiers hinders comparability and progress assessment; need scalable, auditable, multi-domain data.
AI.method: Assemble Messier by consolidating public scores; run additional five-agent experiments across six underrepresented domains, including legal; standardize records by model, scaffold, environment, task, verifier, aggregation rule; classify with SOC/NAICS; analyze frontier progress and counterfactual rescoring; derive domain- and action-space-specific capability scales.
AI.result: Messier includes 957,253 records, 30 benchmarks, 714 agents, 11,891 tasks, 74,205 verifiers; frontiers uneven: function calling saturated, programming fastest, enterprise workflows hardest; counterfactual rescoring reveals all-pass rules can hide progress; capability scales align with Epoch's Evaluation Capability Index (Spearman 0.81).
AI.conclusion: Messier provides a reusable infrastructure for capability scaling, benchmark auditing, and error analysis in evaluation of AI agents across domains.

title: Interactive Reward Agent: GUI Task Evaluation via Environment-State Verification
summary: Graphical user interface task evaluation aims to determine whether a GUI agent has successfully completed a user instruction. Automated GUI task evaluation has received increasing attention because the evaluation results can serve as reward signals for both test-time scaling and post-training. However, reliable GUI task evaluation remains challenging because the judgments often require access to environment states, such as system configurations, file data, and application settings, beyond the screenshots of execution trajectories. In this paper, we propose an interactive reward agent (IRA) based on a propose-then-verify framework to acquire and verify evidence from the post-execution environment. Given a task instruction and a GUI environment after the GUI agent execution, IRA first proposes the task completion conditions and then verifies them by invoking system tools, application tools, and GUI tools. This design combines evidence from both visible interfaces and the environment state in an interactive process. We further introduce GUI-RewardBench, a benchmark of 321 GUI task trajectories spanning 10 Ubuntu desktop application categories. Experiments show that IRA achieves 86.9% accuracy on GUI-RewardBench, outperforming existing evaluator baselines. We further apply IRA to reinforcement learning of GUI agents, achieving a 34.0% OSWorld success rate, which demonstrates that IRA can provide effective reward signals for training GUI agents.

AI.tldr: A propose-then-verify interactive agent (IRA) for GUI task evaluation, plus GUI-RewardBench benchmark; IRA achieves 86.9% accuracy and provides useful reward signals for GUI agents (34.0% OSWorld success in RL).
AI.motivation: GUI task evaluation is hampered by reliance on environment state beyond screenshots; reliable, environment-aware rewards are needed for scalable test-time evaluation and post-training.
AI.method: We propose an interactive framework where IRA first proposes task-completion conditions based on the instruction and post-execution GUI state, then verifies them by invoking system tools, application tools, and GUI tools, combining visible interface evidence with environment-state evidence. GUI-RewardBench is introduced with 321 GUI task trajectories across 10 Ubuntu desktop application categories.
AI.result: IRA achieves 86.9% accuracy on GUI-RewardBench, outperforming baselines. When applied to reinforcement learning of GUI agents, it yields a 34.0% OSWorld success rate, demonstrating effective reward signals for training.
AI.conclusion: IRA demonstrates that interaction with environment state enhances GUI task evaluation and reward signaling, and GUI-RewardBench provides a solid benchmark for evaluating such approaches.

title: Toward Standardized Cross-Vendor Agent Tool Trust Management in Autonomous Networks
summary: Autonomous Network Levels 4-5 require AI agents to invoke tools across vendor boundaries without human oversight, yet existing management standards lack a standardized mechanism for cross-vendor trust visibility. When a tool from Vendor B is compromised, agents from Vendor A continue invoking it -- unaware of the trust degradation -- causing cascading service impact. We present AgentToolMO, a proposed 3GPP NRM information model for agent tool trust management. The model comprises: a formally defined trust state machine with provable graduated enforcement, damped cascade propagation with bounded convergence, cross-vendor trust notifications via existing Management Services (MnS) interfaces, and retroactive impact assessment through NRM dependency graph traversal. Simulation-based evaluation across multi-vendor topologies shows that standardized cross-vendor notifications reduce blast radius from hours-scale undetected propagation to near-real-time containment bounded by MnS notification delivery, with cascade convergence guaranteed in bounded iterations and sub-linear notification scaling across vendor domains. The framework operates within existing 3GPP management infrastructure, leverages existing protocols, and provides a standardization pathway for trustworthy multi-vendor autonomous network management.

AI.tldr: AgentToolMO proposes a 3GPP NRM information model for cross-vendor trust management in autonomous networks (L4-L5). It defines a formal trust state machine with provable enforcement, damped cascade propagation, cross-vendor trust notifications via MnS interfaces, and retroactive impact assessment through NRM graph traversal. Simulation shows reduced blast radius, bounded convergence, and sub-linear notification scaling, enabling integration with existing 3GPP management.
AI.motivation: Current management standards lack standardized cross-vendor trust visibility for autonomous networks; a compromised tool can propagates trust degradation across vendors, causing cascading incidents without timely detection or containment.
AI.method: Proposes AgentToolMO as an information model within the 3GPP NRM: (1) formal trust state machine with provable enforcement, (2) damped cascade propagation with bounded convergence, (3) cross-vendor trust notifications via existing MnS interfaces, (4) retroactive impact assessment through NRM dependency graph traversal. Evaluation via simulation across multi-vendor topologies.
AI.result: Simulation-based evaluation demonstrates near-real-time containment of cross-vendor trust issues, with blast radius reduced from hours to near real-time; cascade convergence guaranteed in a bounded number of iterations; notification scaling across vendor domains is sub-linear.
AI.conclusion: AgentToolMO provides a standardization pathway for trustworthy multi-vendor autonomous network management, operating within existing 3GPP management infrastructure and leveraging current protocols to enable cross-vendor trust visibility and retroactive impact assessment.

title: Penelope: Localized Latent Recurrence for Efficient Structured Reasoning
summary: Complex structured reasoning tasks often require additional computation, yet current language models obtain it mainly by increasing parameter scale or by serializing intermediate steps as chain-of-thought (CoT) tokens. The former raises training and deployment costs, while the latter ties reasoning computation to autoregressive output length. We introduce Penelope, an efficient latent-reasoning framework for pretrained decoder-only Transformers that localizes recurrent computation to a selected decoder interval. The lower decoder prefix is evaluated once to construct a problem-conditioned boundary memory, which is then iteratively refined through time-modulated GRU dynamics and recurrent readout states before answer generation. A progressive CoT-to-latent curriculum transfers visible reasoning into this internal recurrent path, allowing additional computation to be allocated in latent space without repeatedly executing the complete decoder or generating a long intermediate trace. Experiments on open-source structured-reasoning benchmarks show that, at validation-selected latent budgets, Penelope attains competitive accuracy relative to established latent-reasoning models while reducing measured inference latency. These results show that latent refinement can be localized to a narrow decoder interval, reducing repeated full-decoder execution without generating a long visible reasoning trace and providing a practical accuracy-efficiency tradeoff for decoder-only Transformer models.

AI.tldr: Penelope introduces a latent-reasoning mechanism for decoder-only transformers that confines iterative reasoning to a small decoder window, converting visible chain-of-thought into latent refinement to improve efficiency without sacrificing much accuracy.
AI.motivation: Current large language models rely on bigger models or lengthy chain-of-thought traces to compute complex reasoning, which increases cost or ties computation to output length. A localized, latent reasoning path could reduce runtime while maintaining accuracy.
AI.method: Penelope localizes recurrent computation to a selected decoder interval. The lower decoder prefix is used to build a problem-conditioned boundary memory, then refined via time-modulated GRU dynamics and recurrent readouts before answer generation. A progressive CoT-to-latent curriculum shifts reasoning from visible CoT to the latent recurrent path, enabling more computation in latent space without full-decoder repetition or long CoT traces.
AI.result: On open-source structured-reasoning benchmarks, Penelope achieves competitive accuracy at validation-selected latent budgets compared with established latent-reasoning models, while reducing measured inference latency. It demonstrates that latent refinement can be localized to a narrow decoder interval and can provide a practical accuracy-efficiency tradeoff for decoder-only transformers.
AI.conclusion: Latent refinement within a constrained decoder window can replace or supplement full-decoder or explicit CoT steps, offering efficient, scalable reasoning for decoder-only models without generating long intermediate traces.

title: dtControl2+$\varepsilon$: Trading Optimality for Explainability in MDPs via Decision Trees
comment: This paper is accepted at FMCAD26
summary: Over the past decade, decision trees have been used to represent controllers (a.k.a. policies) in an explainable way, with dtControl2 as a current state-of-the-art tool. However, for systems that are large or have many corner cases, even such representations tend to be too complex and not human-comprehensible. Unfortunately, reducing the size of the decision tree is not straightforward, as missing just a single crucial case might result in an incorrect controller. We tackle this issue in the setting of Markov decision processes, extending dtControl2 by "$\varepsilon$" functionality: Given an allowed imprecision $\varepsilon \geq 0$, we construct a smaller decision tree, distilling the essence of the controller, while still guaranteeing its $\varepsilon$-optimality. This enables us to provide tunably simpler explanations, omitting a controllable amount of detail. Our tool constructs decision trees that are orders of magnitude smaller than the state of the art.

AI.tldr: Extends dtControl2 with an epsilon-imprecision parameter to produce smaller decision-tree controllers for MDPs, guaranteeing epsilon-optimality and yielding trees orders of magnitude smaller than the state-of-the-art.
AI.motivation: Improve interpretability of controller representations for large systems or many corner cases, where existing decision trees become too complex to be human comprehensible; provide tunable trade-off between fidelity and simplicity.
AI.method: Introduce an epsilon-robust distillation process that, given an MDP and an existing policy represented as a decision tree, constructs a smaller decision tree whose induced policy is within epsilon of optimality in the MDP; builds on dtControl2 and integrates epsilon-safety to prune or summarize regions while preserving near-optimal behavior.
AI.result: Empirical claims that the resulting decision trees are orders of magnitude smaller than the current state of the art, while maintaining epsilon-optimal performance.
AI.conclusion: The approach enables tunable, simpler explanations of policies in large-scale settings without sacrificing much performance, advancing explainable reinforcement learning and policy distillation for MDPs.

title: A Cost-Effective Multimodal LLM Reasoning Framework for Question Answering over Irregular Clinical Time Series
summary: Question answering (QA) over irregular clinical time series (ICTS) plays a pivotal role in a wide range of healthcare applications. Although recent multimodal time-series large language models (LLMs) have shown considerable promise in general-purpose time-series QA, they remain poorly equipped to model the sparsity, asynchrony, and irregular sampling patterns of clinical observations. To fill this gap, we propose ClinPRISM, a cost-effective multimodal LLM reasoning framework for question answering over ICTS data. First, we devise an irregularity-aware multi-scale encoder to capture sparse clinical evidence at diverse temporal scales. Then, we propose a temporal evidence distiller to integrate representations across these scales and compress them into a small number of LLM-compatible tokens. Moreover, we introduce a progressive alignment strategy that sequentially aligns the irregular trajectories with the LLM's textual embedding space. To facilitate training, we construct 30,000 clinical time series paired with multi-scale descriptions, together with 41,000 instruction-tuning instances spanning 11 tasks. Using a 4-billion-parameter LLM backbone, ClinPRISM achieves state-of-the-art performance on the held-out evaluation benchmark while using only 16 time-series tokens and achieving an average inference latency of 0.15 seconds per question.
